hypotheses.statement: Part of the "paradoxical" rise in ATF4 during the ISR is post-translational: ATF4 is a high-turnover cullin-RING-ligase (CRL) substrate whose ubiquitin-conjugation flux depends on ongoing translation, so a drop in global protein synthesis lowers its degradation rate and lets ATF4 protein accumulate beyond what any change in its own translation would produce.
hypotheses.mechanism: kim2011 identifies ATF4 as a CRL substrate carrying CRL-dependent diGly (ubiquitination) sites, and shows in SILAC-switching experiments that ubiquitin-conjugate labelling is dominated by newly synthesized protein and requires continued protein synthesis. singh2019 shows that a global block of host protein synthesis rapidly changes the steady-state level of high-turnover proteins such as MCL1, i.e. that levels of short-lived proteins are set by the balance of synthesis and degradation on a timescale of minutes. If eIF2α-Ser51 phosphorylation suppresses the bulk synthesis that feeds the ubiquitin-proteasome system, the degradative arm acting on ATF4 is throttled at the same time, so ATF4 protein can rise even for modest changes in ATF4 ribosome occupancy.
hypotheses.prediction: During ISR induction the fold increase in ATF4 protein should substantially exceed the fold increase in ATF4 nascent synthesis rate (ribosome density or puromycin/AHA pulse labelling on ATF4), and ATF4 protein half-life should lengthen; pre-inhibiting CRL-mediated degradation (neddylation inhibitor MLN4924) or the proteasome should occlude a large fraction of the ISR-induced ATF4 accumulation.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured cell line, induce the ISR (e.g. thapsigargin or a small-molecule eIF2α-kinase activator) and in parallel samples measure (i) ATF4 ribosome occupancy by polysome fractionation/ribosome profiling normalized to ATF4 mRNA, (ii) ATF4 nascent synthesis by short puromycin or AHA pulse followed by ATF4 immunoprecipitation, and (iii) ATF4 protein half-life by cycloheximide chase — each ± MLN4924 or proteasome inhibitor. If selective translation alone explains the paradox, the ribosome-occupancy and nascent-synthesis increases should match the protein increase and ATF4 half-life should be unchanged; if stabilization contributes, half-life will lengthen and MLN4924 pretreatment will collapse the difference between induced and uninduced ATF4 levels.

citations.title: ATF4 degradation relies on a phosphorylation-dependent interaction with the SCF(betaTrCP) ubiquitin ligase.
NEDD8-activating enzyme inhibitor, MLN4924 (Pevonedistat) induces NOXA-dependent apoptosis through up-regulation of ATF-4.
Protein Stability Buffers the Cost of Translation Attenuation following eIF2α Phosphorylation.
A stay of execution: ATF4 regulation and potential outcomes for the integrated stress response.

novelty.note: I searched for ATF4 stabilization during the ISR, ATF4 half-life/degradation by SCF-βTrCP and CRLs, MLN4924/proteasome effects on ATF4, and for the general principle that translation attenuation throttles ubiquitin-proteasome flux on short-lived proteins. The degradative arm is well published — ATF4 is a rapid-turnover, phospho-dependent SCF(βTrCP)/CRL substrate (Lassot 2001) and neddylation inhibition raises ATF4 protein (Liu 2017) — and Schneider et al. show that which proteins change level after eIF2α-P is governed by their turnover/stability, but they frame this for long-lived proteins being buffered, not for ATF4. No source I retrieved claims that ISR-driven suppression of bulk synthesis lowers ATF4's ubiquitin-conjugation flux and thereby lengthens ATF4 half-life, nor that ATF4 protein fold-induction exceeds its nascent-synthesis fold-increase; a recent ATF4 regulation review treats degradation and translational induction as separate, unlinked modules, so the specific connection and prediction remain unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: A component of the apparent translational up-regulation of ISR target mRNAs is transcript-level superinduction: global translational shutdown depletes short-lived negative regulators (labile repressors and mRNA-destabilizing factors), raising the abundance and stability of the very transcripts scored as "selectively translated".
hypotheses.mechanism: nakao1997 shows that blocking translation with cycloheximide does not prevent but superinduces a specific stress-responsive transcript (Smad7), i.e. that a labile, synthesis-dependent factor normally caps its accumulation. schneider2014 shows the same logic for interferon-stimulated genes: cycloheximide prolongs ISG transcription and shortens the refractory interval, because establishing the desensitized state requires new protein synthesis. Since eIF2α-Ser51 phosphorylation produces exactly the condition these experiments impose pharmacologically — a genuine drop in new protein synthesis — the transcripts of ISR targets should be stabilized or superinduced by the shutdown itself, inflating estimates of "increased translation" that are read out as protein or total ribosome footprints rather than as ribosomes per mRNA.
hypotheses.prediction: ISR induction should raise ATF4 (and other target) mRNA abundance and lengthen mRNA half-life, and the increase in ribosome footprints per unit ATF4 mRNA (translational efficiency) should be markedly smaller than the increase in ATF4 protein; cycloheximide alone, which gives no eIF2α phosphorylation-driven reinitiation advantage, should reproduce part of the transcript-level increase.
hypotheses.test: Treat cells with an ISR inducer, with cycloheximide, or with both, and measure in parallel: ATF4 mRNA level by RT-qPCR, ATF4 mRNA decay rate by actinomycin-D chase, and ribosome density per ATF4 mRNA by polysome-gradient RT-qPCR (footprints normalized to transcript). If the paradox is purely initiation-level reinitiation, translational efficiency will rise while mRNA level and half-life are unchanged and cycloheximide alone will not raise the transcript; if superinduction contributes, mRNA level/half-life rise under both treatments and the efficiency gain accounts for only part of the protein increase.

citations.title: Hypoxic inhibition of nonsense-mediated RNA decay regulates gene expression and the integrated stress response.
Environmental stresses suppress nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) and affect cells by stabilizing NMD-targeted gene expression.
Both transcriptional regulation and translational control of ATF4 are central to the integrated stress response.
Cycloheximide can distort measurements of mRNA levels and translation efficiency.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in plain words (translation-inhibition superinduction / labile repressor and decay-factor depletion stabilizing transcripts), the entities together (eIF2α-P, ATF4/CHOP mRNA abundance and half-life, cycloheximide), and the prediction (translational-efficiency vs protein discrepancy, mRNA-level contribution to apparent selective translation). The component mechanisms are published: eIF2α phosphorylation-dependent loss of a translation-coupled mRNA-destabilizing pathway (NMD) stabilizes ISR effector transcripts and thereby augments the stress response (Gardner 2008; Nomura-type stress/NMD study 2019), ATF4 induction is explicitly shown to be transcriptional as well as translational so that ATF4 mRNA abundance rises during ER stress (Dey/Wek 2010), and translation inhibitors are documented to distort both mRNA-level and translation-efficiency measurements (Santos 2019). I found nothing that states the integrated claim as framed — that this transcript-level superinduction inflates estimates of 'selective translation' of ISR targets, with the specific prediction that the footprints-per-mRNA gain is markedly smaller than the protein gain and that cycloheximide alone reproduces part of the ATF4 transcript increase — so this is partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: The selectivity attributed solely to eIF2B blockade is partly a competition effect requiring parallel suppression of cap-dependent initiation through stress-kinase-to-TSC2-to-mTORC1 signaling, which frees limiting initiation capacity for reinitiation-competent uORF mRNAs.
hypotheses.mechanism: laplante2012 establishes that mTORC1, via 4E-BP1 and S6K1, sets the overall rate of protein synthesis, and that full mTORC1 inhibition significantly reduces bulk translation in proliferating cells. cargnello2011 shows that a stress-activated kinase (MK2) phosphorylates TSC2 at Ser1210 to promote 14-3-3 binding and can thereby regulate mTOR-dependent protein synthesis under stress, giving the same stresses that activate the ISR a second, eIF2α-independent route to shut down cap-dependent initiation. If the bulk cap-dependent pool is suppressed in parallel, the relative share of scanning ribosomes captured by uORF-containing mRNAs rises without any intrinsic increase in their initiation rate, so the "paradox" is a redistribution rather than an activation.
hypotheses.prediction: An mTOR active-site inhibitor alone, which suppresses global synthesis without phosphorylating eIF2α Ser51, should produce a measurable increase in ATF4 reporter output relative to total translation; conversely, an ISR inducer applied in cells where mTORC1 output is clamped high (e.g. 4E-BP1-null or constitutive mTORC1 signaling) should give blunted ATF4 induction per unit eIF2α phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In cultured cells carrying a uORF-containing ATF4 5'UTR luciferase reporter alongside a uORF-less control reporter, compare four conditions — vehicle, ISR inducer, mTOR active-site inhibitor, and both — while measuring eIF2α-Ser51 phosphorylation by immunoblot and global synthesis by puromycin incorporation. If eIF2B blockade is sufficient, the mTOR inhibitor alone will lower global synthesis without shifting the uORF/control reporter ratio; if competition for limiting initiation capacity contributes, the mTOR inhibitor alone will raise that ratio at zero change in eIF2α phosphorylation, and the combination will be more than additive.

citations.title: mTORC1 Balances Cellular Amino Acid Supply with Demand for Protein Synthesis through Post-transcriptional Control of ATF4.
ATF-4 and hydrogen sulfide signalling mediate longevity in response to inhibition of translation or mTORC1.
Eukaryotic Initiation Factor 5B (eIF5B) Cooperates with eIF1A and eIF5 to Facilitate uORF2-Mediated Repression of ATF4 Translation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the plain-language mechanism (global cap-dependent suppression redistributing limiting initiation capacity to uORF mRNAs), the entities together (mTORC1/4E-BP + eIF2α-P + ATF4 uORF reinitiation + MK2-TSC2), and the prediction (mTOR active-site inhibitor alone changing an ATF4 reporter without eIF2α Ser51 phosphorylation; blunted ISR response when mTORC1 output is clamped). The demand/competition framework is already published: Park et al. (Cell Rep 2017) show mTORC1 controls ATF4 translation through its uORFs entirely independently of eIF2α phosphorylation and explicitly reason in terms of eIF4F-set demand altering availability of limiting ternary complex — but with the opposite sign, since Torin1 alone depletes ATF4 protein within 30 min rather than raising the uORF/control ratio; eIF5B depletion (Ross et al. 2018) and mTORC1/translation inhibition in C. elegans (Statzer et al. 2022) likewise derepress ATF4/ATF-4 with unchanged eIF2α phosphorylation, supporting the eIF2α-independent arm, and Andreev et al. argue resistance of uORF mRNAs is intrinsic rather than passive redistribution. Because the competition mechanism and the eIF2α-independent mTORC1 route are established in general, but no source states that ISR selectivity requires parallel stress-kinase→TSC2→mTORC1 suppression (and the mammalian mTOR-inhibitor prediction runs against Park et al.), this is partial.

hypotheses.statement: The discrepancy is set by the ratio of betaglycan (TβRIII) to TβRI/TβRII rather than by absolute receptor expression: betaglycan-scaffolded preformed TβRI–TβRII complexes dominate at endogenous receptor levels, but are diluted to a small minority when receptors are ectopically overexpressed.
hypotheses.mechanism: Betaglycan binds TβRI and TβRII independently and stabilizes their association, so a limited endogenous pool of betaglycan can hold a substantial fraction of receptors in preformed heteromeric patches when receptor numbers are low; structural work shows betaglycan holds ligand while leaving the TβRII site accessible and hands it off to the higher-affinity TβRI/TβRII complex, i.e. betaglycan acts as an assembly platform rather than a passive binder. If receptor molecules are raised (even modestly) above the betaglycan pool, the scaffolded fraction becomes a minor species and single-molecule counting reports mostly monomers with ligand-driven sequential assembly.
hypotheses.prediction: In matched cells, the fraction of basal (unliganded) TβRI–TβRII co-diffusing/copatching complexes should scale with betaglycan level and with the betaglycan:receptor ratio, not with receptor number per se; betaglycan-null cells should show almost pure monomers and strictly ligand-induced sequential assembly even at low receptor expression.
hypotheses.test: In a single cell line, knock out TGFBR3 and re-express betaglycan over a titrated range while holding tagged TβRI/TβRII at fixed near-endogenous levels (inducible promoter, calibrated by fluorescence intensity per cell); quantify basal heteromer fraction by two-colour single-molecule colocalization/photobleaching-step counting and by chemical crosslinking followed by co-IP, then plot heteromer fraction against betaglycan:receptor ratio versus against receptor density to see which variable the data follow.

citations.title: Monomeric type I and type III transforming growth factor-β receptors and their dimerization revealed by single-molecule imaging.
Structures of TGF-β with betaglycan and signaling receptors reveal mechanisms of complex assembly and signaling.

novelty.note: I searched for betaglycan as a scaffold of preformed unliganded TβRI–TβRII complexes, for expression-level/overexpression artifacts in single-molecule receptor counting, and for betaglycan:receptor stoichiometric ratio as the determinant of basal heteromer fraction. The closest published work is single-molecule imaging showing TβRI/TβRIII are monomeric at low expression and dimerize as expression rises (the opposite expression dependence to that proposed), and the recent betaglycan structural work, which explicitly favors ligand-initiated stepwise assembly and does not discuss betaglycan:receptor ratios or betaglycan-scaffolded basal heteromers. No source states this ratio-based reconciliation, and none directly tests and negates it.

hypotheses.statement: Preformed receptor complexes reflect a limiting pool of intracellular scaffolds (Par6 at tight junctions, p85 constitutively bound to TβRII) that pre-associate a subset of receptors; ectopic overexpression and non-polarized culture leave most receptors scaffold-free and therefore monomeric.
hypotheses.mechanism: Par6 constitutively occupies TβRI at tight junctions and TGF-β then brings in TβRII to the TβRI/Par6 complex, and the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 associates constitutively with TβRII (and with TβRI after ligand), so receptors bound by these adaptors are localized and partnered before ligand arrives. Such scaffolds are present at fixed cellular amounts and are concentrated at junctional/polarized membrane domains, so the pre-associated fraction is high when receptor numbers are near endogenous and in polarized sheets (conditions closer to copatching experiments) and negligible in overexpressing, subconfluent ectopic systems used for single-molecule imaging.
hypotheses.prediction: Basal receptor heteromers and reduced receptor mobility should be enriched at cell–cell junctions in polarized monolayers and should decrease upon Par6 or p85 knockdown, while receptors in subconfluent or scaffold-depleted cells behave as freely diffusing monomers until ligand is added.
hypotheses.test: Image the same tagged receptors at fixed near-endogenous expression in polarized confluent monolayers versus subconfluent cells, with and without siRNA knockdown of Par6 and of p85; measure the basal two-colour colocalization/dimer fraction and diffusion coefficients separately in junctional versus non-junctional membrane regions, and confirm by crosslinking co-IP that the basal TβRI–TβRII complex is lost on scaffold knockdown.

citations.title: TβRIII independently binds type I and type II TGF-β receptors to inhibit TGF-β signaling.
Regulation of TGF-β receptor hetero-oligomerization and signaling by endoglin.
Single-molecule imaging reveals transforming growth factor-beta-induced type II receptor dimerization.
Regulation of TGF-β receptor activity.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the reconciliation question (why single-molecule imaging finds monomeric TGF-β receptors while copatching/co-IP found ligand-independent heteromers), the entities together (Par6–TβRI tight-junction complex; p85 constitutively bound to TβRII; scaffold-limited pre-association), and the prediction (junction-enriched basal heteromers, reduced mobility, loss on Par6/p85 knockdown, confluence/polarity dependence). The general principle that intracellular scaffolds drive ligand-independent TGF-β receptor hetero-oligomerization is published — TβRIII's ligand-independent homo- and hetero-complexes require its cytoplasmic tail and GIPC/β-arrestin2 binding, and endoglin homodimers act as a scaffold for ligand-independent TβRII/ALK5/ALK1 assembly — but no source attributes basal TβRI–TβRII complexes to a limiting pool of Par6/p85, predicts junctional enrichment of basal heteromers in polarized monolayers, or tests scaffold knockdown; instead, the published reconciliation of the monomer/preformed discrepancy runs the other way, ascribing preformed dimers to overexpression-driven self-assembly and monomers to near-endogenous levels. Hence partial: mechanism-in-general published, this specific explanation and prediction not.

hypotheses.statement: Differential surface turnover of the two receptors — ERK/p38-driven TACE/ADAM17 shedding of TβRI but not TβRII — depletes surface TβRI in the growth-factor-rich, overexpressing culture conditions used for single-molecule imaging, producing an apparent 'TβRII dimerizes first, TβRI is recruited later' order.
hypotheses.mechanism: TACE/ADAM17 cleaves the TβRI ectodomain but not TβRII downstream of ERK or p38 signalling, so mitogenic culture conditions selectively lower functional surface TβRI while leaving TβRII ligand binding intact. Because TβRI reaches the cell surface as efficiently as TβRII when expressed alone, any imbalance in the surface TβRI:TβRII ratio is a post-delivery processing effect, not a trafficking defect; a shed-down TβRI pool would make unliganded TβRI–TβRII heteromers rare and make TβRI appear only as a late arrival.
hypotheses.prediction: Blocking ADAM17 (or MEK/p38) should raise the surface TβRI:TβRII ratio and increase the fraction of basal, ligand-independent TβRI–TβRII heteromers detected at the same total receptor expression, whereas stimulating ERK/p38 should push the system further toward the monomer/sequential-assembly picture.
hypotheses.test: At fixed inducible receptor expression, treat cells with a broad metalloprotease/ADAM17 inhibitor or ADAM17 knockout versus MEK plus p38 inhibitors versus mitogen stimulation; quantify surface TβRI and TβRII by surface biotinylation and by single-molecule density counting, and in the same conditions measure the basal two-colour colocalization fraction and the kinetics of TβRI recruitment after ligand addition, testing whether basal heteromer fraction tracks surface TβRI availability.

citations.title: TACE-mediated ectodomain shedding of the type I TGF-beta receptor downregulates TGF-beta signaling.
Single-molecule imaging reveals transforming growth factor-beta-induced type II receptor dimerization.
Monomeric type I and type III transforming growth factor-β receptors and their dimerization revealed by single-molecule imaging.

novelty.note: I searched for TACE/ADAM17-mediated TβRI ectodomain shedding downstream of ERK/p38, for the single-molecule imaging literature on TβRII dimerization and sequential TβRI recruitment, and for any work linking surface TβRI:TβRII ratio or shedding to apparent receptor assembly order. The shedding mechanism is fully published (Liu et al., Mol Cell 2009: PMA/ERK-driven TACE cleavage selectively lowers surface TβRI but not TβRII, and TACE silencing/inhibition raises surface TβRI), and the single-molecule papers establish the ligand-induced TβRII-dimerization-then-TβRI model, but no source connects the two — i.e. none proposes that differential surface turnover of TβRI creates the apparent sequential-assembly order, nor predicts that ADAM17/MEK/p38 blockade would increase basal TβRI–TβRII heteromer fraction. Hence partial: the component mechanism is anticipated, the explanatory link and prediction are not.

hypotheses.statement: JAK1's ~100-fold reduced mobility is not a property of JAK1 itself but reflects that essentially the whole cellular pool is stoichiometrically clamped onto receptor Box1/Box2 motifs through a large, high-affinity FERM-SH2 interface, so JAK1 diffuses as a membrane protein rather than a cytosolic one.
hypotheses.mechanism: The JAK1 FERM-SH2 module grips a receptor Box1/Box2 segment over an extended groove burying ~1650 Å2, with Box1 Leu266/Phe268 inserted into a FERM hydrophobic pocket formed by Val194, Phe247 and Phe251 plus Box2 salt-bridge and hydrogen-bond contacts (glassman2022:findings:004), and full-length JAK1 domains form one extended unit bound to the receptor intracellular domain (philips2022:findings:002). Independent cell data fit an obligate receptor-bound state: JAK1 is detectable in crude membrane preparations and Jak-deficient cells fail to present a ligand-binding IFN-α receptor (darnell1994:findings:020, darnell1994:findings:021), and simply occluding the IFNAR2 intracellular domain with catalytically dead USP18 is sufficient to prevent JAK1 binding and signalling (schneider2014:findings:002). If binding is that dominant and that occlusion-sensitive, the receptor, not the cytosol, sets JAK1's diffusion coefficient — exactly matching gp130 mobility and co-immobilization.
hypotheses.prediction: Disrupting the FERM pocket (Val194/Phe247/Phe251) or the receptor Box1 anchor residues, or competitively occluding the receptor intracellular domain with catalytically inactive USP18, should convert fluorescent JAK1 from gp130-like mobility to fast, near-cytoplasmic recovery and abolish co-immobilization by receptor cross-linking, without requiring any change in JAK1 catalytic activity.
hypotheses.test: In cells co-expressing GFP-JAK1 and a receptor-mCherry, run parallel FRAP/FCS on (i) wild-type GFP-JAK1, (ii) GFP-JAK1 with the FERM hydrophobic-pocket residues mutated, (iii) wild-type GFP-JAK1 with the receptor Box1 Leu/Phe pair mutated, and (iv) wild-type pairs co-transfected with catalytically dead USP18 versus the arginine mutant that cannot bind the receptor intracellular domain; measure diffusion coefficient and immobile fraction and repeat the antibody cross-linking co-immobilization assay. Receptor anchoring predicts a stepwise return toward free-cytoplasmic mobility and loss of co-immobilization in (ii)–(iv) only, whereas an intrinsic-JAK1 explanation (e.g. bulk cytoskeletal or condensate tethering) predicts low mobility in every condition.

citations.title: Long term association of the cytokine receptor gp130 and the Janus kinase Jak1 revealed by FRAP analysis.

Janus kinase (Jak) subcellular localization revisited: the exclusive membrane localization of endogenous Janus kinase 1 by cytokine receptor interaction uncovers the Jak.receptor complex to be equivalent to a receptor tyrosine kinase.
The Janus Kinase (JAK) FERM and SH2 Domains: Bringing Specificity to JAK-Receptor Interactions.

novelty.note: I searched for JAK1 FRAP/diffusion with gp130, for JAK constitutive Box1/Box2 association and whole-pool membrane localization, and for USP18 occlusion effects on JAK1 receptor binding and receptor mobility. Giese et al. (JBC 2003) report that Jak1-YFP and gp130-YFP have equal plasma-membrane mobilities, that Jak1 diffuses like a transmembrane protein, and that antibody-induced immobilization of gp130 co-immobilizes Jak1 with no exchange via the cytosol; Behrmann et al. (JBC 2004) show endogenous Jak1 is essentially exclusively membrane-associated, that this is due solely to cytokine-receptor binding (a receptor-binding-deficient FERM mutant, L80A/Y81A, redistributes to the cytoplasm with no intrinsic membrane affinity), and conclude the Jak·receptor complex behaves as a receptor tyrosine kinase. That is the same explanation and includes the key predicted FERM-mutant test, so the status is established; only the specific Val194/Phe247/Phe251 and USP18-occlusion variants of the mobility experiment appear untested.

hypotheses.statement: The immobilized JAK1 pool is created before and independently of ligand-induced JAK dimerization, so cytokine stimulation and dimer-interface mutations should not be what lowers JAK1 mobility.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the resting, autoinhibited arrangement the TK folds back onto FERM-SH2 and this closed monomer is sterically incompatible with JAK dimerization (glassman2022:findings:011), while the head-to-head PK-PK fulcrum with its phenylalanine cluster and the oncogenic V657F triad forms only in the active 2:2 assembly (glassman2022:findings:007, glassman2022:findings:003); crystallography of the isolated Jak1 pseudokinase shows the V658F-type rearrangement of the SH2-PK linker occurs even in a wild-type molecule, i.e. it is a local conformational switch rather than a constitutive oligomerization signal (toms2013:findings:002, toms2013:findings:003). Since receptor engagement of FERM-SH2 does not require the dimer, the receptor-bound monomer already explains gp130-like mobility, and dimerization should add at most a modest further decrease.
hypotheses.prediction: Fluorescent JAK1 mobility measured in unstimulated cells should already be gp130-like and should change only marginally upon cytokine addition or upon introducing the V657F/V658F pseudokinase mutation, whereas mutating the PK-PK fulcrum phenylalanines should leave the low basal mobility intact.
hypotheses.test: Perform FRAP on GFP-JAK1 in the same cells before and after cytokine stimulation, and in parallel on V657F JAK1 and on a fulcrum phenylalanine-cluster mutant (Phe574/Phe635 substitutions), reading out diffusion coefficient and immobile fraction alongside an anti-phosphoJAK1 immunoblot to confirm the activation state of each construct. If ligand-driven dimerization is what immobilizes JAK1, mobility should drop sharply on stimulation and in V657F and be rescued by the fulcrum mutant; if receptor anchoring of the monomer is responsible, all four conditions should give similarly low mobility despite divergent phosphorylation.

citations.title: Long term association of the cytokine receptor gp130 and the Janus kinase Jak1 revealed by FRAP analysis.
Mechanism of homodimeric cytokine receptor activation and dysregulation by oncogenic mutations.
Dimerization of the cytokine receptors gp130 and LIFR analysed in single cells.

novelty.note: I searched for FRAP/single-molecule measurements of JAK1 membrane mobility, for 'JAK1 mobility unstimulated vs cytokine-stimulated', and for the mechanism in words (receptor-anchored JAK monomer vs ligand-induced pseudokinase dimerization as the source of immobility), plus targeted searches on the phenylalanine fulcrum / V657F-V658F interface and mobility. The receptor-anchoring half is already published: Giese et al. measured Jak1-YFP by FRAP at the plasma membrane of unstimulated cells and found it diffuses like a transmembrane protein with mobility equal to gp130 and does not exchange between receptors, i.e. a stimulation-independent immobilized pool; complementary single-molecule work (Wilmes et al.) and the gp130/LIFR FRAP-dimerization study instead show that ligand and the oncogenic pseudokinase VF mutation drive receptor dimerization, and that dimerization slows/confines diffusion. I found no source that states the specific claim that the immobile JAK1 pool forms before and independently of JAK dimerization, nor any test of JAK1 mobility in V657F/V658F or PK-PK fulcrum phenylalanine mutants, so the prediction and the link to the dimer-structure findings remain unaddressed.

hypotheses.statement: CARD14 is a keratinocyte-resident, interchangeable CARD–BCL10–MALT1 (CBM) scaffold module that couples the IL-17R/Act1 complex to TRAF6, so a loss-of-function phenotype (impaired IL-17A signaling) and a gain-of-function phenotype (E138A-driven constitutive NF-κB and psoriasis-like inflammation) are two readouts of the same scaffold rather than contradictory roles.
hypotheses.mechanism: Other papers show that CARD-family proteins act as receptor-proximal adaptors whose only job is to nucleate BCL10–MALT1 and relay to NF-κB: CARD9–BCL10–MALT1 transduces the NF-κB arm downstream of Dectin-1/SYK in myeloid cells (mcsai2010:findings:019), and in T cells MALT1, BCL10, TRAF6 and TAK1 form a single required chain into the IκB kinase complex (schmidt2022:findings:005). If CARD14 is the paralogous CARD unit in keratinocytes, then deleting it removes an obligatory node in IL-17R→BCL10/MALT1→TRAF6→TAK1 signaling, while a mutation that makes the CARD self-associate constitutively assembles the same signalosome ligand-independently.
hypotheses.prediction: IL-17A-induced NF-κB, JNK1/2 and p38 activation in keratinocytes should be lost to a similar extent by BCL10 or MALT1 depletion (or MALT1 catalytic/scaffold disruption) as by CARD14 deletion, CARD14 mutants that cannot bind BCL10 should fail to rescue CARD14-deficient keratinocytes even if they still bind Act1/TRAF6, and the CARD of CARD9 or CARD10 substituted into CARD14 should restore IL-17A responsiveness.
hypotheses.test: In CARD14-knockout keratinocytes (or a keratinocyte line with CRISPR knockouts of CARD14, BCL10, MALT1 individually), stimulate with IL-17A (± TNF co-stimulation) and quantify phospho-IκBα/p65, phospho-JNK and phospho-p38 by immunoblot plus CXCL1/CCL20 mRNA; in parallel reconstitute the CARD14-knockout cells with WT CARD14, a BCL10-binding-deficient CARD point mutant, and a CARD9-CARD/CARD14 chimera, and co-immunoprecipitate Act1, TRAF6, BCL10 and MALT1 from each. Scaffold-module hypothesis: BCL10/MALT1 knockouts phenocopy CARD14 loss and only BCL10-binding-competent constructs rescue; the alternative (CARD14 acting solely as a direct Act1/TRAF6 co-factor) predicts rescue by the BCL10-binding mutant and little effect of BCL10/MALT1 loss.

citations.title: Gain-of-Function Mutation of Card14 Leads to Spontaneous Psoriasis-like Skin Inflammation through Enhanced Keratinocyte Response to IL-17A.
Keratinocyte-intrinsic BCL10/MALT1 activity initiates and amplifies psoriasiform skin inflammation.
Psoriasis mutations disrupt CARD14 autoinhibition promoting BCL10-MALT1-dependent NF-κB activation.
CARD14/CARMA2 Signaling and its Role in Inflammatory Skin Disorders.
BCL10 - Bridging CARDs to Immune Activation.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (CARD14 as a keratinocyte CARD-BCL10-MALT1 scaffold linking IL-17R/Act1-TRAF6 to NF-κB), for the entities together (CARD14 + BCL10 + MALT1 + IL-17A + keratinocytes, CARMA2/ACT1/TRAF6), and for the prediction (BCL10/MALT1 loss phenocopying CARD14 loss for IL-17A-induced NF-κB/MAPK and chemokines; CARD-CC paralogue interchangeability/chimeras). The unified account is already published: Wang et al. (Immunity 2018) show CARMA2/CARD14 associates with the ACT1–TRAF6 complex and is required for IL-17A-induced NF-κB and MAPK activation in keratinocytes (Card14-knockout mice have impaired keratinocyte IL-17A signalling) while the self-aggregating E138A/ΔQ136 alleles constitutively activate the same molecule to cause psoriasis-like disease; Howes et al. show the gain-of-function alleles act by relieving linker autoinhibition to give constitutive BCL10/MALT1-dependent NF-κB and MAPK activation; and Kurgyis et al. show keratinocyte-intrinsic BCL10/MALT1 deletion both abolishes CARD14-GOF skin disease and blunts keratinocyte responses to IL-17A, which is the core of the stated prediction. Only the accessory predictions (a BCL10-binding-deficient CARD14 failing to rescue IL-17A responses, and a CARD9/CARD10-CARD chimera restoring them) appear untested, so the explanation itself is established rather than partial; the general interchangeable-CARD-module framing is stated in the BCL10 review cited as nearest.

hypotheses.statement: CARD14 acts by promoting TRAF6 RING-dependent K63-polyubiquitin chain assembly and consequent TAK1 activation, which is why a single adaptor deficiency simultaneously cripples three otherwise separate outputs (NF-κB, JNK1/2, p38) after IL-17A.
hypotheses.mechanism: TRAF6's RING finger is required to catalyze K63-linked chains with Ubc13/Uev1A and to activate NF-κB (deng2000:findings:009), and TRAF6 auto-/intramolecular polyubiquitylation is the step that scaffolds TAK1 ubiquitylation and activation leading to JNK and p38 (derynck2019:findings:030, xu2009:findings:029); TAK1 loss abolishes canonical NF-κB output in at least some receptor pathways (hayden2008:findings:007). A CARD14-nucleated CBM that clusters Act1 and TRAF6 — an interaction the anomaly reports is enhanced by IL-17A — would raise local TRAF6 density and hence K63 chain output, so its loss converges on one node (TRAF6→TAK1) and takes all three branches down at once, and E138A-type constitutive clustering would drive the same node without ligand.
hypotheses.prediction: CARD14-deficient keratinocytes should show reduced IL-17A-induced TRAF6 K63-ubiquitination and reduced TAK1 activation upstream of the three kinase branches; conversely, CARD14 overexpression should increase TRAF6 K63-chain output, and this enhancement should be abolished by a RING-dead TRAF6 (C70A or C85A/H87A), with the JNK/p38 branches more strictly RING-dependent than NF-κB (hayden2008:findings:002).
hypotheses.test: Co-express CARD14 (WT or E138A) with Flag-TRAF6 WT versus RING mutants C70A and C85A/H87A in TRAF6-null or TRAF6-knockdown cells, then (i) immunopurify Flag-TRAF6 and run the in vitro E1/Ubc13/Uev1A K63 ubiquitination immunoblot ± CARD14, and (ii) measure κB-luciferase plus phospho-JNK/phospho-p38 and phospho-TAK1 after IL-17A. If CARD14 works through TRAF6 catalysis, CARD14 increases K63 chain formation on WT TRAF6 and gives no enhancement of any output with the RING mutants; if CARD14 instead signals through MALT1/BCL10 downstream or parallel to TRAF6 ubiquitin ligase activity, CARD14-driven activation will persist on the RING-dead background and be lost only upon BCL10/MALT1 depletion.

citations.title: CARD14 signalosome formation is associated with its endosomal relocation and mTORC1-induced keratinocyte proliferation.

novelty.note: I searched for CARD14–Act1–TRAF6 in IL-17A keratinocyte signaling, for CARD14/TRAF6 K63-ubiquitination and TAK1 activation, and for the CARD14E138A signalosome. A 2024 Biochemical Journal study directly shows that CARD14E138A drives assembly of K63-ubiquitin chains, that TRAF6 (with HOIP) is required for the resulting IKK2/NF-κB and MAP kinase output, and that CARD14E138A-induced TAB2/TAK1 phosphorylation is strongly TRAF6-dependent — anticipating the convergence-on-TRAF6→TAK1 mechanism. It does not test the specific prediction (loss-of-function CARD14 keratinocytes after IL-17A, TRAF6 RING-dead C70A/C85A-H87A rescue, or differential RING dependence of JNK/p38 versus NF-κB), so the specific prediction remains unaddressed.

hypotheses.statement: The low Vmax on soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 reflects that PTEN's catalytically preferred substrate is the D3-phosphate of the membrane-embedded inositol phospholipid PI(3,4,5)P3, so the soluble head group can occupy the active site (low Km) but lacks the lipid/membrane contacts needed for efficient turnover.
hypotheses.mechanism: Independent papers assign PTEN to a DSP subgroup defined by dephosphorylation of the D3-phosphate of inositol phospholipids (alonso2004:findings:009) and characterize PTEN specifically as a PIP3 phosphatase opposing PI3K (manning2017:findings:002), while the G129E allele separates lipid from protein phosphatase activity, showing the lipid-directed catalytic mode is a distinct, physiologically dominant function (balla2013:findings:045). If the lipid moiety and its presentation contribute to productive substrate positioning and catalysis, a soluble head-group analogue would bind but be turned over slowly, exactly the low-Vmax/low-Km pattern observed.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified PTEN should show a substantially higher kcat (and kcat/Km) on PI(3,4,5)P3 presented in micelles or vesicles than on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, and the G129E substitution should abolish activity on both PI(3,4,5)P3 and Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 while sparing activity toward p-nitrophenylphosphate.
hypotheses.test: Assay the same recombinant PTEN preparation side by side on (i) p-nitrophenylphosphate, (ii) Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, and (iii) diC8- or long-chain PI(3,4,5)P3 in defined micelles/lipid vesicles, using malachite-green phosphate release for all three so rates are directly comparable, and repeat the full panel with wild-type versus G129E PTEN; a lipid-specific kcat gain plus loss of both inositol-directed activities in G129E supports the hypothesis, whereas equal kcat on lipid and soluble substrate, or G129E retaining Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 activity, favours the alternative that Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 is simply a poor substrate for an intrinsically slow enzyme.

citations.title: Interfacial kinetic analysis of the tumour suppressor phosphatase, PTEN: evidence for activation by anionic phospholipids.

The lipid phosphatase activity of PTEN is critical for its tumor supressor function.

novelty.note: I searched for PTEN kinetic comparisons of Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 versus PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 (Km/Vmax), for interfacial/micelle-vesicle kinetics of PTEN, and for whether G129E loses activity on soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4. McConnachie et al. (Biochem J 2003) performed exactly the proposed experiment: using unilamellar vesicles and surface-dilution analysis they show PTEN behaves as an interfacial enzyme whose kcat for membrane-presented PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 is at least 200-fold greater than for the water-soluble substrate Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, with PtdIns(4,5)P2/anionic lipids stimulating lipid-directed activity while inhibiting activity on the soluble head group. The G129E arm is also already published: the Cowden allele retains protein phosphatase activity but is defective in dephosphorylating both inositol phospholipids and soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, so both the mechanism and its specific prediction are anticipated.

hypotheses.statement: A fraction of the purified recombinant PTEN is oxidatively modified at its critical active-site cysteine, deflating the apparent Vmax specifically for the inositol-phosphate reaction while leaving the high-Km p-nitrophenylphosphate reaction detectable.
hypotheses.mechanism: One paper reports that modification of a critical PTEN cysteine by reactive oxygen/nitrogen species causes loss of PTEN lipid phosphatase activity (fruman2017:findings:048), and another shows that lipid-directed and protein/aryl-phosphate-directed activities of PTEN are genetically separable (balla2013:findings:045). Together these imply that redox damage accumulated during expression and purification could inactivate the inositol-directed catalytic mode of part of the enzyme population, which lowers measured specific activity (Vmax per mg) without altering the Km of the remaining active molecules.
hypotheses.prediction: Pre-incubating or assaying the purified enzyme under strongly reducing conditions should raise Vmax/kcat on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 with little change in Km, and deliberate mild oxidation of the preparation should lower Vmax further while again leaving Km largely unchanged.
hypotheses.test: Measure Km and Vmax on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 for the same PTEN preparation after (a) no treatment, (b) pre-reduction with DTT or TCEP followed by removal of excess reductant, and (c) controlled mild oxidation with H2O2, in parallel with quantification of free active-site thiol by a maleimide-thiol labelling or DTNB assay and of active-site occupancy by titration with a covalent phosphatase active-site probe; a redox-dependent Vmax with constant Km and a matching change in free-thiol/active-fraction supports partial inactivation, while Vmax insensitive to redox state with fully titratable active sites indicates the low turnover is an intrinsic property of the enzyme–substrate pair.

citations.title: Reversible inactivation of the tumor suppressor PTEN by H2O2.
Catalysis by the tumor-suppressor enzymes PTEN and PTEN-L.
Expanding coincident signaling by PTEN through its inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate 3-phosphatase activity.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the redox mechanism in plain words (oxidation of PTEN's active-site cysteine causing loss of lipid phosphatase activity, reversibility by DTT/thioredoxin), the entities together (recombinant PTEN + Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 + Km/Vmax + reducing agent), and the prediction (partial oxidation of a purified preparation deflating apparent Vmax/kcat with unchanged Km, active-site titration of active fraction). The mechanism is firmly published: Lee et al. show purified PTEN is inactivated by H2O2 via a Cys124–Cys71 disulfide that is reducible, and Johnston & Raines explicitly state PTEN's catalytic cysteine is 'extremely sensitive to oxidation', use a strong reductant (DTBA) to keep it reduced, attribute their kcat/KM values being orders of magnitude above earlier reports partly to enzyme quality and the reducing environment, and note that activity on canonical aryl-phosphate substrates such as p-nitrophenylphosphate is too low to be useful. However, no retrieved source tests the specific prediction — a redox-dependent Vmax with an invariant Km on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, quantified free active-site thiol/active-site occupancy, or a substrate-selective (inositol-phosphate versus aryl-phosphate) consequence of partial oxidation of one preparation — so the specific connection remains unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: The fast, light-tracking "phospho-PKCβ" RPPA signal is not PKCβ-specific but reports a phosphosite/motif context shared among basophilic AGC kinases, so it actually reads out the Erk→p90RSK arm that is itself class II.
hypotheses.mechanism: Phosphoproteomic profiling of AML lines found PKC activity-correlated sites (PKCδ Thr505, PKCθ Thr538) co-varying with Akt Ser473 and p90RSK Ser380 as one coordinated block, and PKC substrate-group enrichment fell together with p70S6K, p90RSK, Akt and mTOR groups under AKT/mTOR-pathway inhibitors, indicating that PKC-attributed readouts are not separable from other AGC kinase activity (casado2013:findings:002, casado2013:findings:004). Sequence-logo analysis shows PKC and Akt share basophilic determinants (R/K at −2/−3 and R at −3/−5), so antibodies and motif-based attributions built on such contexts are prone to conflate AGC family members (hornbeck2015:findings:011). Because p90RSK is itself a fast light-tracking node in the opto-SOS dataset, an AGC-cross-reactive signal would appear as "PKCβ" tracking light-activated Ras.
hypotheses.prediction: Depleting PKCβ should leave most of the light-induced antibody signal intact, whereas inhibiting or depleting RSK (or MEK upstream of it) should collapse it, and the residual signal should co-immunoprecipitate with RSK-family rather than PKCβ protein.
hypotheses.test: In NIH 3T3 opto-SOS cells, run parallel siRNA/CRISPR knockdown of PKCβ and of RSK1/2, then light-stimulate and probe lysates with the same phospho-PKCβ antibody by immunoblot; additionally immunoprecipitate PKCβ from light-stimulated lysates and compare the antibody signal in the immunodepleted supernatant versus the immunoprecipitate. Loss of signal only with RSK depletion, and retention of signal in PKCβ-depleted or PKCβ-immunodepleted lysates, supports cross-reactivity; loss only with PKCβ depletion refutes it.

citations.title: Contribution of S6K1/MAPK signaling pathways in the response to oxidative stress: activation of RSK and MSK by hydrogen peroxide.
Phosphoprotein analysis using antibodies broadly reactive against phosphorylated motifs.
mTORC2 Is Involved in the Induction of RSK Phosphorylation by Serum or Nutrient Starvation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (i) the mechanism in plain words (phospho-antibody cross-reactivity among AGC/basophilic kinases, hydrophobic-motif and activation-loop site homology), (ii) the entities together (phospho-PKC/Ser660 or PKCβ antibody vs RSK/S6K, opto-SOS RPPA light-tracking nodes), and (iii) the prediction (RSK or MEK knockdown/inhibition collapsing a signal attributed to another AGC kinase). The exact generic mechanism is published and experimentally demonstrated — but for the S6K1 Thr389 antibody, not PKCβ: Sanchez-Gonzalez et al. showed the commercial anti-P-T389-S6K1 antibody actually detects RSK/MSK at the homologous hydrophobic-motif site, that the signal is U0126 (MEK/ERK)-sensitive, and that RSK/MSK siRNA (not S6K1) removes it — essentially the proposed test and outcome, one AGC kinase substituted. Motif/epitope conflation among basophilic AGC kinases is likewise general knowledge (broadly reactive phospho-motif antibodies across Akt/PKC/PKA substrates; conserved HM sites in PKC, RSK, Akt, S6K), but no source states that a phospho-PKCβ RPPA readout specifically reports the Erk→p90RSK arm or that this explains fast light-tracking in opto-SOS cells, so this is partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: Light-activated Ras phosphorylates PKCβ through the MEK/Erk module itself — via PKC's physical association with ERK in a scaffolded complex — rather than through the receptor-proximal PLCγ route, which is why PKCβ behaves as a class II fast node despite receptor-proximal nodes staying silent.
hypotheses.mechanism: Protein-chemistry and immunoprecipitation work shows PKC and ERK are bound within the same calponin-containing complex that translocates upon stimulation, and that disrupting the scaffold changes ERK activity, establishing a physical PKC–ERK module in which the two are co-regulated (brozovich2016:findings:027). Network-inference work in PC12 cells places PKC (PKCδ) inside the MAPK feedback topology, where PKC activation and sustained MAPK activation are interconvertible inputs to the same loop (lemmon2010:findings:024). The classical PKC input is receptor-proximal PLCγ downstream of active EGFR (lemmon2010:findings:021), a route unavailable when Ras is activated directly by light while EGFR/HER2 and Src remain unresponsive — so any fast PKCβ response must be driven from within the Ras→Raf→MEK→Erk cascade.
hypotheses.prediction: A MEK or ERK inhibitor applied before light should abolish the light-induced PKCβ phosphorylation while leaving PDGF-induced PKCβ phosphorylation (PLCγ-driven) largely intact, and PKCβ kinetics under light should lag Mek/Erk rather than precede them.
hypotheses.test: In opto-SOS cells, pretreat with a MEK inhibitor or an ERK inhibitor versus vehicle and compare phospho-PKCβ time courses after (a) light and (b) PDGF by immunoblot/RPPA; in a parallel arm, disrupt the PKC–ERK scaffold by knocking down calponin and repeat the light stimulation. MEK/ERK-inhibitor-sensitive, scaffold-knockdown-sensitive light responses with a PDGF response that survives MEK inhibition support Erk-module-driven PKCβ phosphorylation; a light response that persists under MEK/ERK inhibition instead points to a Ras-direct or parallel route.

citations.title: Optogenetic actuator - ERK biosensor circuits identify MAPK network nodes that shape ERK dynamics.
Regulation of PKC autophosphorylation by calponin in contractile vascular smooth muscle tissue.
The hydrophobic phosphorylation motif of conventional protein kinase C is regulated by autophosphorylation.

novelty.note: I searched for ERK/MEK-dependent phosphorylation of PKCβ, for PKC–ERK scaffolded complexes (calponin), and for opto-SOS/optogenetic Ras 'fast vs slow' node proteomics. Optogenetic Ras–ERK network papers map RAF/MEK/ERK/RSK2 feedbacks but never place PKC downstream of the Erk module; the calponin literature does show a calponin-scaffolded PKC complex, but it places PKC hydrophobic-site autophosphorylation upstream of ERK rather than driven by it, and cPKC hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation is reported to be intramolecular autophosphorylation. No source states or directly tests MEK/ERK-driven PKCβ phosphorylation under direct Ras activation, so the claim is unpublished but its directionality sits against the nearest work.

hypotheses.statement: The fast, threshold-crossing activation of a resident nuclear PKA holoenzyme is lost in cardiac myocytes because those cells carry PKA-activated phosphodiesterase feedback (mAKAP-anchored PDE4D3 phosphorylated at Ser13/Ser54, plus kinase-stimulated PDE3) that clamps local cAMP as soon as it rises, so the nuclear pool never sustains a supra-threshold cAMP level.
hypotheses.mechanism: pawson2003:findings:011 shows that PKA phosphorylation of PDE4D3 on the mAKAP scaffold triples phosphodiesterase Vmax and attenuates cAMP signalling, i.e. the very act of activating an anchored holoenzyme accelerates local cAMP destruction; manning2017:findings:042 shows an analogous kinase-driven increase in PDE3B hydrolytic activity that blocks PKA activation. If the myocyte nuclear/perinuclear compartment contains these feedback-amplified PDEs while the HEK-293 nuclear compartment relies on the constitutive AKAP8-assembled PDE4D3/5 threshold described in zaccolo2021:findings:046, the same AC-generated cAMP flux would cross threshold in HEK nuclei but be truncated in myocytes, leaving only the slower, diffusion-limited catalytic-subunit component visible.
hypotheses.prediction: Nuclear cAMP transients and nuclear PKA reporter responses should show a fast rising phase followed by rapid self-truncation in cells with phospho-competent anchored PDE4D3, and the fast resident-holoenzyme activation phase should reappear (larger amplitude, faster half-time) when that feedback phosphorylation is removed or the PDE is inhibited.
hypotheses.test: In a cell line, co-express a nuclear/perinuclear-targeted PKA activity reporter together with (a) wild-type PDE4D3 plus mAKAP, (b) the S13A/S54A phospho-dead PDE4D3 plus mAKAP, or (c) catalytically dead PDE4D3, and compare the amplitude and half-time of nuclear PKA activation after a fixed AC stimulus; parallel runs with PDE4- versus PDE3-selective inhibitors identify which PDE class enforces the clamp. If feedback PDE activity explains the discrepancy, only the phospho-dead/inhibited conditions restore the fast kinetics; if diffusion of catalytic subunit is the sole determinant, kinetics will be indistinguishable across all conditions.

citations.title: PDE4 and mAKAPβ are nodal organizers of β2-ARs nuclear PKA signalling in cardiac myocytes.
Control of cytoplasmic and nuclear protein kinase A by phosphodiesterases and phosphatases in cardiac myocytes.
mAKAP assembles a protein kinase A/PDE4 phosphodiesterase cAMP signaling module.
Regulation of nuclear PKA revealed by spatiotemporal manipulation of cyclic AMP.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (PKA-phosphorylated mAKAP-anchored PDE4D3 feedback clamping nuclear cAMP), the entities together (nuclear PKA holoenzyme / AKAP8-AKAP95 / PDE4D3-PDE4D5 / HEK-293 vs cardiac myocyte), and the prediction (PDE inhibition or S13A/S54A phospho-dead PDE4D3 restoring fast, larger nuclear PKA activation). The component pieces are published: PKA phosphorylation of mAKAP-bound PDE4D3 forms a negative-feedback loop that stimulates local cAMP hydrolysis (Dodge 2001); AKAP-localized PDEs set the activation threshold for a resident nuclear PKA holoenzyme in HEK-293 (Sample 2012); PDEs keep nuclear PKA slow in cardiac myocytes despite a fast nuclear cAMP rise, with PDE inhibition enhancing nuclear PKA responses (Haj Slimane 2014); and PDE4 with mAKAPβ 'insulates' a nuclear-envelope PKA pool so that β2-AR stimulation fails to activate nuclear PKA unless PDE4 is blocked, which the authors explicitly contrast with the HEK-293 resident nuclear PKA pool (Bedioune 2018). What I could not find is any source stating that feedback phosphorylation of PDE4D3 (Ser13/Ser54) is the reason the fast resident-holoenzyme phase is absent in myocytes, nor the phospho-dead-rescue prediction; Bedioune instead argues against a nuclear resident pool in myocytes rather than proposing it is clamped, so the specific reconciliation remains unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: The discrepancy reflects where the PKA pool is anchored rather than how cAMP diffuses: AKAP-dependent PKA nanodomains determine whether a reporter sees a resident nucleoplasmic holoenzyme at all, and the dominant cardiac scaffold (mAKAP with its PKA/PDE4D3 complex) places the relevant pool outside the compartment sampled in myocytes.
hypotheses.mechanism: gest2024:findings:186 shows PKA activity is confined to ~350 nm domains that overlap AKAP clusters and that direct AKAP-PKA interaction is required for those domains to exist, so the presence of a locally activatable holoenzyme is set by the AKAP complement of the cell. pawson2003:findings:011 documents that in cardiac cells PKA is held on mAKAP together with PDE4D3, a different scaffold from the AKAP8-assembled complex invoked for HEK-293 nuclei in zaccolo2021:findings:046. A reporter placed in the myocyte nucleoplasm would then report only cAMP/kinase activity arriving from outside its anchored nanodomain, which is exactly the slow, diffusion-like behaviour reported.
hypotheses.prediction: Disrupting AKAP-PKA anchoring should abolish the fast component of nuclear PKA activation in cells where it is present, and imposing a specific nuclear AKAP should create a fast component in cells that previously showed only slow, diffusion-like kinetics; the fast phase should co-localise with AKAP clusters rather than being spatially uniform.
hypotheses.test: In cultured cells expressing a nuclear-targeted PKA activity reporter, compare activation kinetics after a fixed AC stimulus under three conditions: expression of the anchoring-disruptor peptide Ht31 versus the inactive Ht31-P control, knockdown of the nuclear AKAP, and re-expression of an RII-binding-deficient AKAP mutant; in parallel, image the reporter by super-resolution alongside labelled AKAP to test whether the fast-responding pixels coincide with AKAP clusters. Loss of the fast phase specifically with functional anchoring disruption supports the nanodomain hypothesis; unchanged kinetics support a purely diffusion-determined readout.

citations.title: AKAP95 Organizes a Nuclear Microdomain to Control Local cAMP for Regulating Nuclear PKA.
PDE4 and mAKAPβ are nodal organizers of β2-ARs nuclear PKA signalling in cardiac myocytes.
PKA catalytic subunit compartmentation regulates contractile and hypertrophic responses to β-adrenergic signaling.
Control of cytoplasmic and nuclear protein kinase A by phosphodiesterases and phosphatases in cardiac myocytes.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (AKAP anchoring determining whether a resident, locally activatable nuclear PKA holoenzyme exists vs. slow catalytic-subunit diffusion), the entities together (AKAP8/AKAP95, mAKAPβ, PDE4D3, nuclear AKAR/FRET reporters, HEK293 vs. cardiac myocytes), and the prediction (Ht31/anchoring disruption or AKAP knockdown abolishing fast nuclear PKA activation). Both halves of the mechanism are already published separately — Clister et al. show AKAP95/AKAP8 anchors a nuclear PKA holoenzyme inside a PDE-bounded nuclear microdomain in HEK293 cells, and Bedioune et al. show that in cardiac myocytes the relevant PKA pool is mAKAPβ-tethered at the nuclear envelope and insulated by PDE4, with mAKAPβ knockdown strongly reducing nuclear PKA activation — but I found no source that uses the differing AKAP complement to explain the HEK293-vs-myocyte kinetic discrepancy, nor one that tests whether imposing a nuclear AKAP creates a fast phase where only diffusion-like kinetics existed. The nearest directly opposing test is Yang et al., who examined AKAP-based compartmentation for nuclear PKA in cardiac myocytes and concluded the nuclear kinetics are set by passive transport/diffusion rather than anchoring, so the specific connection remains unstated.

hypotheses.statement: The ~20-fold WT/L834R gap reflects loss of the dimer cross-activation and membrane-confinement context that normally activates wild-type EGFR, rather than a fixed intrinsic property of the wild-type kinase domain, because the isolated soluble 672–998 construct is assayed as a dilute monomer.
hypotheses.mechanism: lake2016:findings:000 states that wild-type EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation depends on cross activation within the receptor dimer, which can be impaired by T669 phosphorylation; kholodenko2006:findings:002 states that confining EGFR-bound proteins to a small membrane-proximal volume raises their apparent affinity by 10^2–10^3-fold relative to bulk solution. Together these imply that wild-type catalytic output in cells is supplied by dimer-dependent cross activation at high effective local concentration, conditions absent in a dilute purified-kinase assay, whereas an activating mutation would be expected to raise activity without requiring that context.
hypotheses.prediction: Raising the effective dimer concentration of the purified wild-type kinase domain (higher enzyme concentration, or two-dimensional tethering) should increase its kcat/KM substantially and shrink the gap to L834R, while L834R activity should be comparatively insensitive to the same manipulations.
hypotheses.test: Measure kcat/KM for WT and L834R kinase domain over a wide enzyme-concentration range in the same coupled assay, and in parallel tether the His-tagged domains to Ni-NTA-lipid liposomes (or crosslink via an inducible dimerization tag such as FKBP/rapamycin) to impose two-dimensional confinement; a concentration- or tethering-dependent rise in WT kcat/KM that is absent or much smaller for L834R supports context loss, whereas concentration-independent parallel curves support a fixed intrinsic autoinhibition.

citations.title: An allosteric mechanism for activation of the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor.
The role of kinase domain dimerization in EGFR activation.
Oncogenic mutations counteract intrinsic disorder in the EGFR kinase and promote receptor dimerization.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in plain words (dilute monomeric purified EGFR kinase domain vs. dimer/membrane-confinement context), the entities together (EGFR 672–998, L834R/L858R, Ni-NTA liposome tethering, local concentration), and the prediction (does raising effective dimer concentration shrink the WT/L834R gap). The explanation is the central claim of Zhang, Gureasko, Shen, Cole & Kuriyan (Cell 2006), which reports that the isolated EGFR kinase domain is intrinsically autoinhibited in dilute solution and is activated either by increasing its local concentration — done precisely by tethering the His-tagged domain to Ni-NTA-containing liposomes, the exact experiment proposed as the test — or by the L834R activation-loop mutation, establishing that the WT/L834R gap reflects missing dimer cross-activation context rather than a fixed intrinsic ceiling; Petrova et al. (Structure 2025) quantifies this, showing engineered kinase-domain dimerization raises activity several-hundred-fold versus the 15–30-fold of L858R in the monomeric domain. Because at least one retrieved source states this explanation for this phenomenon, the status is established; note that Shan et al. (Cell 2012) argues against the second half of the prediction, since L834R acts largely by promoting dimerization rather than being dimerization-independent.

hypotheses.statement: The autoinhibited state measured for wild-type is an artifact of the construct boundary: the juxtamembrane segment immediately N-terminal to residue 672 (containing T669) is an activating element whose removal locks wild-type in a low-activity state that L834R bypasses.
hypotheses.mechanism: lake2016:findings:000 places the major regulatory Ser/Thr site T669 just outside the 672–998 construct and reports that its phosphorylation lowers EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation by impairing cross activation within the dimer, implying this segment is mechanistically coupled to kinase activation. li2019:findings:015 independently shows the EGFR juxtamembrane region is a distinct protein-interaction element (TRAF4 binds it upon EGF, versus the C-terminal tail upon IL-17A), consistent with it being a separable regulatory module rather than a passive linker.
hypotheses.prediction: A wild-type kinase-domain construct extended N-terminally to include the juxtamembrane segment (e.g. starting near residue 645, with T669 unphosphorylated or mutated to Ala) should show markedly higher kcat/KM than the 672–998 wild-type protein, narrowing the gap to L834R, while a T669 phosphomimetic (T669D/E) extended construct should behave like the truncated wild type.
hypotheses.test: Express and purify from the same system four proteins — WT 672–998, WT juxtamembrane-extended (~645–998), the same extended construct with T669A, and with T669D — plus L834R in both boundaries, and compare kcat/KM in the identical coupled peptide assay; a boundary-dependent activity increase for WT that is reversed by T669D, and little boundary effect for L834R, distinguishes juxtamembrane-dependent activation from intrinsic kinase-domain autoinhibition.

citations.title: Mechanism for activation of the EGF receptor catalytic domain by the juxtamembrane segment.
The juxtamembrane region of the EGF receptor functions as an activation domain.
Inverse correlation between Thr-669 and constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation in the asymmetric epidermal growth factor receptor dimer conformation.

novelty.note: I searched for the juxtamembrane segment as an EGFR activation domain, for construct-boundary effects on purified kinase-domain activity (672–998 vs 645–998), and for T669 phosphorylation/phosphomimetic effects on kinase activation within the asymmetric dimer. Jura et al. (Cell 2009) report exactly the predicted boundary effect with purified protein in a solution kinase assay: the 672–998 kinase core has kcat/KM = 0.0049 s⁻¹mM⁻¹, the JM-extended 645–998 wild-type construct is ~70-fold higher (0.33 s⁻¹mM⁻¹), whereas L834R raises the kinase core only ~14-fold — i.e. the JM segment (containing T669 in JM-B, 664–682) is an activating element whose absence accounts for the measured wild-type autoinhibition. Red Brewer et al. (Mol Cell 2009) independently define the JM activation domain (664–682), note that prior crystal structures used constructs beginning at residue 672, show T669A does not impair activity while the T669D phosphomimetic suppresses activation, and show L834R remains JM-dependent (blocked by L680A); Sato et al. supply the T669-in-receiver negative-feedback mechanism. All three components of the hypothesis are therefore already published.

hypotheses.statement: The wild-type preparation appears autoinhibited because it is largely dephosphorylated at activating sites, so the 20-fold difference measures a phosphorylation-state difference rather than a difference in the unphosphorylated enzymes' intrinsic catalytic power.
hypotheses.mechanism: lake2016:findings:001 states that EGFR phosphorylation at Y1068 is required for its activity and is removed by cdc25c, and kholodenko2006:findings:001 attributes the rapid collapse of cellular EGFR phosphorylation to unprotected phosphotyrosines being stripped by phosphatases; both imply EGFR catalytic output is set by the occupancy of activating phosphosites, which is not controlled in a Sf9-expressed purified preparation. If wild type requires activating autophosphorylation that it cannot efficiently achieve at assay dilution while L834R does not, the measured kcat/KM ratio would overstate intrinsic autoinhibition.
hypotheses.prediction: Preincubating purified wild-type kinase domain with Mg-ATP at high protein concentration before dilution into the assay should raise its kcat/KM toward L834R, and phosphatase pretreatment should lower wild-type activity much more than L834R activity.
hypotheses.test: Split each purified protein three ways — untreated, Mg-ATP preincubated at high concentration then diluted, and lambda-phosphatase treated then inhibitor-quenched — quantify site occupancy by anti-phosphotyrosine immunoblot or intact-mass/LC-MS, and measure kcat/KM for each; a wild-type-specific coupling of kcat/KM to measured phosphosite occupancy supports the phosphorylation-state explanation, while equal kcat/KM across all three states argues for genuine intrinsic autoinhibition.

citations.title: Structures of lung cancer-derived EGFR mutants and inhibitor complexes: mechanism of activation and insights into differential inhibitor sensitivity.
An allosteric mechanism for activation of the kinase domain of epidermal growth factor receptor.
Analysis of the Role of the C-Terminal Tail in the Regulation of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (purified EGFR kinase domain activity set by phosphorylation-site occupancy; dephosphorylated preparation underestimating intrinsic activity), for the entities together (Sf9-expressed EGFR kinase domain, WT vs L834R/L858R, kcat/KM, lambda phosphatase, Mg-ATP preincubation), and for the prediction (autophosphorylation raising wild-type catalytic rate). The general idea that EGFR autoinhibition is modulated by phosphorylation state of purified, Sf9-expressed protein is published (reversible, phosphatase-sensitive biphasic autophosphorylation and an autoinhibitory proximal C-tail; MCB 2015), but the specific explanation here is directly contradicted rather than supported: Yun et al. measured Sf9-purified WT, G719S and L858R kinase domains and state that 'autophosphorylation of the kinase activation loop does not appreciably alter the catalytic rate in our experiments with the wild-type or mutant enzymes', with ~50–100-fold higher kcat/KM for L858R, and Zhang et al. report that the activation-loop leucine's phosphorylation is not required for activation and that the WT kinase domain is intrinsically autoinhibited. Hence partial: the phosphorylation-state mechanism exists in the EGFR literature in general, but the claim that it accounts for the WT/L834R kcat/KM gap has been tested and excluded rather than asserted.

hypotheses.statement: The in vitro/in vivo discrepancy arises because JNK isoform contribution to c-Jun phosphorylation in cells is set by isoform-specific substrate and pathway coupling — JNK1 being the isoform functionally wired into TNF signalling while JNK2 is preferentially engaged by other substrates — rather than by the intrinsic catalytic preference measured with purified kinase and c-Jun.
hypotheses.mechanism: One cited claim shows that JNK2, not JNK1, is the isoform that phosphorylates p53 at Ser6/Ser36, establishing that the two isoforms partition onto different substrates inside cells. Another shows that the TNF-triggered branch producing ferritin degradation and labile-iron/ROS elevation is specifically JNK1-dependent, indicating JNK1 is the isoform recruited by TNF-receptor-proximal signalling. If in cells TNF preferentially routes signal through JNK1 while JNK2 is occupied by alternative substrates, then deleting JNK1 lowers c-Jun phosphorylation and autoinduction even though isolated JNK2α2 out-performs JNK1α1 on c-Jun in a reconstituted assay.
hypotheses.prediction: In TNF-stimulated fibroblasts, c-Jun should be found in complex predominantly with JNK1 and JNK2 predominantly with alternative substrates such as p53, and the specific activity of immunopurified JNK2 assayed on recombinant c-Jun in vitro should equal or exceed that of immunopurified JNK1 from the same lysates — i.e. the isoform ranking should invert between the in-cell and cell-free readouts of the same protein pool.
hypotheses.test: From TNF-stimulated wild-type, JNK1-/- and JNK2-/- fibroblasts, immunoprecipitate JNK1 and JNK2 separately with isoform-specific antibodies; (i) blot the immunoprecipitates for co-associated c-Jun and p53 to quantify substrate partitioning, and (ii) split each immunoprecipitate into an in vitro kinase assay on equal amounts of recombinant c-Jun, normalising to immunoprecipitated active (phospho-JNK) kinase. Substrate partitioning toward JNK1 combined with equal-or-higher normalised in vitro c-Jun activity of JNK2 supports the coupling hypothesis, whereas a JNK1 advantage in the normalised cell-free assay would instead indicate that the original in vitro isoform ranking (or simple JNK1 hyperactivation in JNK2-/- cells) accounts for the data.

citations.title: c-Jun N-terminal protein kinase 1 (JNK1), but not JNK2, is essential for tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced c-Jun kinase activation and apoptosis.
Distinct roles for JNK1 and JNK2 in regulating JNK activity and c-Jun-dependent cell proliferation.
JNK2 contains a specificity-determining region responsible for efficient c-Jun binding and phosphorylation.

novelty.note: I searched for the plain-language mechanism (JNK isoform coupling to TNF signalling vs intrinsic in vitro c-Jun preference), for the entities together (JNK1/JNK2 knockout fibroblasts, TNF, c-Jun phosphorylation, p53), and for the prediction (isoform-specific c-Jun association and immunopurified isoform activity). Liu, Minemoto & Lin (Mol Cell Biol 2004) directly states the explanation for this phenomenon: in Jnk1-/- and Jnk2-/- fibroblasts, TNF-alpha activates JNK1 while JNK2 activation is negligible, so c-Jun expression/activation is impaired without JNK1 and enhanced without JNK2 — i.e. pathway coupling, not intrinsic catalytic preference, sets the in-cell isoform contribution; Sabapathy et al. (Mol Cell 2004) states the substrate-partitioning half, with JNK2 preferentially bound to c-Jun in resting cells (promoting degradation) and JNK1 becoming the dominant c-Jun-interacting kinase after stimulation, explicitly reconciling the cell-free JNK2 advantage (Kallunki et al. 1994) with the in-cell JNK1 requirement. Status is established for the explanation, although the hypothesis's specific sub-prediction that immunopurified JNK2 would show equal-or-higher c-Jun activity is argued against by Liu et al.'s 'futile phosphorylation' finding, and the p53-as-alternative-sink variant is not itself documented.

hypotheses.statement: JNK phosphorylation of Ser295 in the PDZ2–PDZ3 linker acts as a valency/conformation switch that increases PSD-95 partitioning into the multivalent PDZ–PDZ-binding-motif condensate of the postsynaptic density, rather than creating a new binding site.
hypotheses.mechanism: PSD-95 phase separates with SynGAP purely through multivalent PDZ–PBM contacts, so the effective avidity of its tandem PDZ array — set by the spacing and flexibility of the interdomain linkers — determines how strongly it partitions into the dense phase (case2019a:findings:014). Tomography shows PSD-95 held in an extended, membrane-perpendicular arrangement with PDZ1/2 fixed ~15 nm from the membrane, i.e. linker geometry dictates domain presentation in situ (lisman2012:findings:015), and PSD-95 is present in large molar excess over NMDARs (~300 copies, 7:1 over NR1), so occupancy of discrete receptor slots cannot by itself account for graded enrichment (lisman2012:findings:009). A phospho-group in the PDZ2–PDZ3 linker would therefore enhance synaptic accumulation by shifting the partition coefficient of a phase-separating scaffold.
hypotheses.prediction: Phospho-Ser295 (or a phosphomimetic S295D/E) PSD-95 will lower the concentration threshold for droplet formation with SynGAP and show a higher partition coefficient into preformed SynGAP/PSD-95 droplets than WT, while S295A behaves like or worse than WT; affinity of isolated PDZ domains for individual PBM peptides will be unchanged.
hypotheses.test: Purify recombinant PSD-95 WT, S295A and S295D (and WT phosphorylated in vitro with active JNK, verified by phospho-blot or mass shift), mix each with purified SynGAP coiled-coil trimer across a concentration series, and measure turbidity thresholds and fluorescence partition coefficients into droplets; in parallel measure single PDZ–PBM binding affinity for the same variants by fluorescence polarization or ITC. Increased partitioning with unchanged one-to-one PDZ affinity supports the valency/condensate mechanism; unchanged partitioning argues against it.

citations.title: Site-specific phosphorylation of PSD-95 dynamically regulates the postsynaptic density as observed by phase separation.
Bidirectional protein-protein interactions control liquid-liquid phase separation of PSD-95 and its interaction partners.
Synaptic accumulation of PSD-95 and synaptic function regulated by phosphorylation of serine-295 of PSD-95.

novelty.note: I searched for PSD-95 Ser295/JNK1 phosphorylation and synaptic accumulation, for phosphorylation-regulated PSD-95/SynGAP condensate partitioning, and for linker/valency control of PDZ-driven phase separation. The general mechanism is published: multivalency of the PSD-95 PDZ1-2 tandem (not single-site affinity) sets whether and how strongly PSD-95 enters PDZ–PBM condensates (Christensen et al. 2022), and site-specific phosphorylations of PSD-95 bidirectionally tune its LLPS — that work even produced phospho-Ser295 full-length PSD-95 and noted Ser295 lies in the PDZ2–PDZ3 linker, but reported no effect on phase separation (tested with GluN2B, not SynGAP, and the site could not be confirmed by MS), and nowhere frames pS295 as a valency/partition-coefficient switch. Kim et al. 2007 establish the JNK1–Ser295 → synaptic accumulation phenomenon without any condensate/avidity explanation, so the specific hypothesis and its prediction remain unstated (and partly contradicted) in the literature.

hypotheses.statement: Ser295 phosphorylation enhances synaptic PSD-95 by blocking its MDM2-dependent ubiquitylation and proteasomal turnover, so the apparent gain in localization reflects a longer-lived local pool rather than active targeting.
hypotheses.mechanism: PSD-95 is a substrate of the associated E3 ligase MDM2, and its ubiquitylation/degradation is the step that breaks the scaffold–receptor link and removes PSD-95 from the synapse (wong2004:findings:008). Because synaptic PSD-95 is maintained in large molar excess over its receptor partners (lisman2012:findings:009), steady-state synaptic content is set largely by the balance of delivery and degradation rather than by saturable receptor binding, so a phosphorylation event in an exposed interdomain linker that occludes the ubiquitylation/degradation route would raise synaptic levels without altering PDZ-mediated binding.
hypotheses.prediction: S295D/phospho-PSD-95 will show reduced polyubiquitylation and a longer half-life than WT when co-expressed with MDM2, and its enrichment will collapse toward WT when the proteasome is inhibited; S295A will be ubiquitylated and degraded faster.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293 or cultured cell lines co-expressing HA-ubiquitin, MDM2 and FLAG-PSD-95 WT/S295A/S295D (± JNK activation by anisomycin and ± JNK inhibitor), perform denaturing immunoprecipitation to quantify PSD-95 ubiquitylation and a cycloheximide chase to measure half-life, with and without proteasome inhibitor. A phospho-dependent difference in ubiquitylation/half-life supports stabilization; identical turnover with unchanged total protein — combined with redistribution in the phase-separation assay — favours the partitioning explanation instead.

citations.title: Ubiquitination regulates PSD-95 degradation and AMPA receptor surface expression.
Proline-directed phosphorylation and prolyl isomerization oppose each other to regulate PSD-95 ubiquitination and excitatory synaptic plasticity.
Synaptic accumulation of PSD-95 and synaptic function regulated by phosphorylation of serine-295 of PSD-95.
Ca2+-PP2B-PSD-95 axis: A novel regulatory mechanism of the phosphorylation state of Serine 295 of PSD-95.
Posttranslational Modifications Regulate the Postsynaptic Localization of PSD-95.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) the mechanism in words (phosphorylation stabilizing PSD-95 against MDM2 ubiquitylation/proteasomal turnover), (2) the entities together (PSD-95 Ser295/S295D, JNK1, MDM2, ubiquitination, half-life), and (3) the prediction (reduced polyubiquitylation and collapse of S295D enrichment under proteasome inhibition), via PubMed/NCBI, PMC, PLOS, Frontiers and publisher pages. The component mechanisms are published — MDM2-dependent ubiquitylation drives PSD-95 removal from synapses and AMPAR endocytosis (Colledge 2003), phospho-regulation of PSD-95 ubiquitination exists but at N-terminal proline-directed sites T19/S25 where phosphorylation *promotes* ubiquitylation, and PP2B/calcineurin dephosphorylates pS295 — yet no source attributes the Ser295-dependent gain in synaptic PSD-95 to blocked ubiquitylation or a longer protein half-life; Kim et al. frame S295 as enhancing synaptic accumulation/retention without testing turnover, and the S295 ubiquitylation link is explicitly flagged as unresolved. Hence partial: mechanism published in general, specific S295–MDM2 stabilization prediction not.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B directly antagonizes TGF-β signaling output, acting as a negative regulator that limits the amplitude and duration of TGF-β-induced, Smad-dependent transcription.
hypotheses.mechanism: The claims about GSK3B state that it phosphorylates the linker region of activated Smad2 and Smad3, generating a Nedd4L-recognition motif that drives Smad ubiquitylation and degradation and inhibiting Smad nuclear accumulation (derynck2019:findings:042, hata2016:findings:024). The claims about TGF-β state that its transcriptional induction is executed through defined promoter elements (the CAGA boxes of the PAI-1 promoter) that lie in the regions mediating TGF-β responsiveness (dennler1998:findings:000), and that TGF-β-driven functional outputs track with the level of phosphorylated Smad2/3 (chen2003:findings:011). If the activated, nuclear Smad2/3 pool is the limiting transducer of TGF-β transcription, then a kinase that degrades and denuclearizes that pool should set the gain of the TGF-β response itself, independent of any change in ligand or receptor.
hypotheses.prediction: Loss or pharmacological inhibition of GSK3B should increase TGF-β-induced CAGA-box-dependent transcription and endogenous TGF-β target gene expression, prolong nuclear residence and extend the half-life of activated Smad2/3 after ligand addition, while GSK3B overexpression should blunt the same readouts and accelerate Smad3 turnover; the effect should be lost on a Smad3 mutant whose linker GSK3 phospho-acceptor sites are substituted with alanine.
