hypotheses.test: In a cultured reporter line (e.g. HEK293T or HaCaT) transfected with a CAGA-box luciferase reporter, compare TGF-β dose-response and time-course after GSK3B siRNA/CRISPR knockout or a selective GSK3 inhibitor versus control, reading out luciferase and endogenous PAI-1 mRNA by qPCR; in parallel, track Smad3 linker phosphorylation, total Smad3 level with cycloheximide chase, and nuclear versus cytoplasmic Smad3 by fractionation and immunofluorescence, and repeat the whole panel with wild-type versus linker phospho-site-mutant Smad3 re-expressed in Smad3-depleted cells. A direct in vitro kinase reaction with recombinant GSK3B and recombinant Smad3, followed by phospho-site mapping, distinguishes direct action on the TGF-β transducer from an indirect effect.

citations.title: Axin and GSK3-β control Smad3 protein stability and modulate TGF-β signaling
Ubiquitin Ligase Nedd4L Targets Activated Smad2/3 to Limit TGF-β Signaling

novelty.note: I searched for GSK3-mediated Smad3 linker phosphorylation/Nedd4L degradation, for GSK3 inhibition effects on TGF-β reporter activity, and for the specific prediction about Smad3 stability and nuclear accumulation. Guo et al. (Genes Dev 2008) report that GSK3β phosphorylates Smad3 and negatively controls its protein stability, with GSK3β-null cells or LiCl/shRNA-treated cells showing elevated Smad3, greater C-terminal phosphorylation/nuclear translocation, and higher TGF-β-induced reporter activity — the same explanation and essentially the same prediction. Gao et al. (Mol Cell 2009) establish the GSK3-primed linker phosphodegron recognized by Nedd4L that limits amplitude and duration of TGF-β responses.

hypotheses.statement: ERK2 directly phosphorylates EGFR on one or more Ser/Thr sites in its cytoplasmic region, constituting a negative-feedback phosphorylation that limits EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation and shortens EGFR signalling output.
hypotheses.mechanism: ERK2 is shown to act directly on an upstream receptor tyrosine kinase of the same pathway architecture — recombinant ERK1 and ERK2 phosphorylate FGFR1 on S777, and loss of that site prolongs FGF-induced FGFR1 tyrosine phosphorylation (lake2016:findings:002) — and ERK2 likewise directly phosphorylates the upstream components SOS1 and Raf-1 to desensitise them (lake2016:findings:003, lake2016:findings:007). EGFR sits upstream of exactly this ERK module, since ERK pathway output collapses when EGFR is inhibited (albeck2013:findings:000), yet under a constant saturating EGF stimulus EGFR's own tyrosine phosphorylation is markedly transient, peaking within seconds and falling to a low pseudo-stationary level (kholodenko2006:findings:001) — a decay that a direct ERK2-on-EGFR feedback phosphorylation, analogous to the FGFR1 S777 event, would produce.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active ERK2 should phosphorylate the EGFR cytoplasmic domain in vitro on mappable Ser/Thr site(s) with a proline-directed context; in cells, EGF should induce that site's phosphorylation in a MEK/ERK-dependent manner, and blocking ERK activity or mutating the site to alanine should prolong and elevate EGF-induced EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation and sustain the ERK-pathway reporter output instead of letting it decay.
hypotheses.test: Two-part biochemistry in cultured cells: (1) in vitro kinase assay with recombinant active ERK2 and a purified recombinant EGFR intracellular domain (kinase-dead EGFR variant as substrate to exclude autophosphorylation), read out by ³²P incorporation and LC-MS/MS site mapping, with a kinase-dead ERK2 and Raf-1/MEK1 substrates as negative and positive controls; (2) in an EGFR-expressing epithelial line, stimulate with EGF ± MEK inhibitor and blot the mapped site with a phospho-specific antibody, then compare EGF-induced pY-EGFR time courses between wild-type EGFR and the Ser/Thr-to-Ala mutant re-expressed after EGFR knockdown — loss of in vitro phosphorylation plus no change in pY-EGFR kinetics in the mutant would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Inverse correlation between Thr-669 and constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation in the asymmetric epidermal growth factor receptor dimer conformation.
ERK-dependent threonine phosphorylation of EGF receptor modulates receptor downregulation and signaling.
Feedback control of ErbB2 via ERK-mediated phosphorylation of a conserved threonine in the juxtamembrane domain.

novelty.note: I searched for ERK-mediated negative feedback phosphorylation of EGFR, for MAP kinase phosphorylation of EGFR threonine 669 and its effect on receptor tyrosine phosphorylation, and for the prediction (Thr→Ala mutant altering EGF-induced pY-EGFR). This explanation is long-published: ERK1/2 phosphorylate EGFR on the proline-directed juxtamembrane site Thr-669 (the receptor's major Ser/Thr site, originally identified as a growth-factor-stimulated 'MAP kinase' activity), this phosphorylation is EGF-induced and MEK/ERK-dependent, and it suppresses receptor tyrosine phosphorylation — with T669A mutants showing elevated/enhanced tyrosine autophosphorylation and loss of ligand-induced dephosphorylation; the same conserved-threonine feedback was then shown for ErbB2/ErbB3. Since sources state exactly the hypothesised mechanism, the site's context, and the mutant prediction for EGFR itself, the status is established rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: EGFR activity negatively regulates TGFBR1 (TβRI) by driving ERK-dependent, ADAM17/TACE-mediated cleavage of the TβRI ectodomain, thereby lowering cell-surface TβRI and TGF-β/Smad3 responsiveness.
hypotheses.mechanism: Claims about EGFR establish that EGFR is the upstream driver of sustained ERK pathway output: the FIRE live-cell ERK reporter decays upon EGFR inhibition (albeck2013:findings:000), and pharmacological EGFR inhibition with erlotinib modulates p-ERK in EGFR-driven tumours (chen2016:findings:016). Independently, claims about TβRI state that ADAM17/TACE cleaves TβRI but not TβRII specifically in response to ERK (or p38) MAPK signalling, reducing cell-surface TβRI and down-regulating Smad3 activation, antiproliferation and EMT (hata2016:findings:007; derynck2019:findings:009). If EGFR sets ERK activity and ERK activity sets TβRI shedding, then EGFR occupancy should directly set the steady-state amount of intact TβRI at the cell surface, making TβRI an EGFR-controlled node rather than a merely co-regulated one.
hypotheses.prediction: EGF stimulation of cells co-expressing EGFR and TGF-β receptors should cause a rapid (tens of minutes) loss of cell-surface full-length TβRI with appearance of soluble TβRI ectodomain in the medium and no comparable loss of TβRII, accompanied by blunted TGF-β-induced Smad3 phosphorylation and target-gene induction; conversely, EGFR kinase inhibition (erlotinib/gefitinib) should raise basal surface TβRI and potentiate TGF-β/Smad3 signalling. Both effects should be abolished by ADAM17 inhibition or ADAM17 knockdown and by MEK/ERK inhibition, placing TβRI downstream of EGFR→ERK→ADAM17.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured epithelial or fibroblast line expressing EGFR and TGF-β receptors, tag TβRI (or use a surface-specific antibody) and quantify cell-surface TβRI versus TβRII by surface biotinylation/streptavidin pulldown plus immunoblot and by flow cytometry after 0–120 min of EGF, EGF + erlotinib, erlotinib alone, or vehicle; in parallel immunoblot shed TβRI ectodomain in conditioned medium and measure TGF-β1-induced phospho-Smad3 and a Smad-responsive reporter after each pretreatment. Repeat the EGF arm with ADAM17 siRNA/TAPI-1 and with a MEK inhibitor: loss of the EGF-dependent surface-TβRI decrease and of the pSmad3 blunting under these conditions confirms a direct EGFR→ERK→ADAM17→TβRI regulatory link, while an unchanged surface TβRI and unchanged pSmad3 across all EGFR manipulations rules it out.

citations.title: TACE-mediated ectodomain shedding of the type I TGF-beta receptor downregulates TGF-beta signaling.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (ERK/MAPK-driven TACE/ADAM17 cleavage of the TGF-β type I receptor ectodomain), the entities together (EGF + ADAM17 + surface TβRI + Smad3), and the prediction (EGFR kinase inhibition raising surface TβRI and potentiating TGF-β responsiveness). Liu et al., Mol Cell 2009 (retrieved via PMC) states exactly this explanation: EGF addition, which enhances Erk MAPK signaling, decreases cell-surface TβRI but not TβRII; the HA-tagged TβRI ectodomain is released into the medium by active TACE; TAPI-1/metalloprotease inhibition and the MEK inhibitors PD98059/U0126 block the surface loss and restore TGF-β-induced Smad3 phosphorylation; and TACE silencing raises surface TβRI with enhanced TGF-β antiproliferative and EMT responses. Only the narrow pharmacological arm (erlotinib/gefitinib specifically, rather than MEK inhibitors, as the upstream block) is not explicitly reported, which does not change the explanation, so the status is established rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: AKT directly inhibits JNK1, phosphorylating it so that JNK1 catalytic activity and JNK1-dependent apoptotic signalling are suppressed when AKT is active.
hypotheses.mechanism: The AKT claims show that AKT enforces survival by direct phosphorylation of pro-death effectors on basic RxRxx[S/T]-type motifs — it phosphorylates FKHRL1 at T32/S253 in vitro and in cells, excludes it from the nucleus and blocks its transcriptional output (brunet1999:findings:000, brunet1999:findings:001, brunet1999:findings:007) — and that AKT already acts as a negative regulator of a stress-activated MAPK arm, suppressing p38α activation via phosphorylation of ASK1 Ser83 (cuadrado2010:findings:037). The JNK1 claims show JNK1 is the corresponding stress-MAPK requirement for death: loss of JNK1/JNK2 makes fibroblasts resistant to DNA-damage- and UV-induced apoptosis and blocks cytochrome c release (cargnello2011:findings:008), and JNK1 activity is read out by c-Jun phosphorylation, which is lost in JNK1-/- cells after TNF-α (zeke2016:findings:016). If AKT's survival program includes direct restraint of stress-kinase signalling, JNK1 itself — not only the p38 arm — is a predicted direct AKT target, and the two kinases should stand in a direct inhibitory relationship.
hypotheses.prediction: Constitutively active AKT should lower stress-induced JNK1 activation (reduced phospho-JNK1 p46 and reduced c-Jun phosphorylation/autoinduction) and blunt JNK1-dependent apoptosis with reduced cytochrome c release, while kinase-dead AKT or AKT inhibition should raise JNK1 activity and restore death; recombinant JNK1 should be phosphorylated in vitro by active but not inactive AKT at one or more basic-motif Ser/Thr residues, and alanine substitution of those residues should render JNK1 refractory to AKT-mediated inhibition.
hypotheses.test: Run a two-part assay in a standard cell line: (1) an in vitro kinase assay with HA-AKT immunoprecipitated from transfected 293T cells in constitutively active versus kinase-inactive form incubated with bacterially expressed recombinant JNK1 and 32P-ATP (the exact format used for GST-FKHRL1), followed by phosphosite mapping and alanine-substitution of the mapped residues; (2) in cells, co-express constitutively active or kinase-dead AKT (or add an AKT inhibitor), stimulate with anisomycin/UV/TNF-α, and immunoblot phospho-JNK1 and phospho-c-Jun alongside a JNK1 immunoprecipitation-kinase assay on GST-c-Jun, testing whether the phospho-site-mutant JNK1 escapes AKT-dependent suppression.

citations.title: Akt phosphorylates and negatively regulates apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1.
Akt (protein kinase B) negatively regulates SEK1 by means of protein phosphorylation.
Negative regulation of mixed lineage kinase 3 by protein kinase B/AKT leads to cell survival.
Akt negatively regulates the cJun N-terminal kinase pathway in PC12 cells.

novelty.note: I searched for direct AKT phosphorylation of JNK1 (phrase searches on Europe PMC for 'Akt phosphorylates JNK1' / 'JNK1 is a direct substrate of Akt' returned zero hits), for AKT as a negative regulator of the JNK arm, and for the cellular prediction (constitutively active vs kinase-dead AKT suppressing stress-induced JNK/c-Jun and JNK-dependent death). The cellular half of the prediction is firmly established, but always via direct AKT phosphorylation of kinases upstream of JNK1 — ASK1 Ser83 (where the authors explicitly conclude the effect is at ASK1, not downstream of it), SEK1/MKK4 Ser78 (with the S78A mutant refractory to AKT inhibition, the exact experimental logic proposed here but one step above JNK1), MLK3 Ser674, and JIP-1 induction. No retrieved source reports JNK1 itself being phosphorylated in vitro by active AKT or phospho-site mutants of JNK1 escaping AKT suppression, so the specific direct AKT→JNK1 relationship remains unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: SYK directly binds and tyrosine-phosphorylates STAT3, acting as a receptor-proximal activating kinase for STAT3 in ITAM-coupled myeloid cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: SYK is already shown to couple to a cytokine receptor (IFNAR) and amplify STAT activation (STAT1) in primed macrophages, indicating that activated SYK can feed directly into STAT tyrosine phosphorylation at a receptor complex (ivashkiv2014:findings:003). Mechanistically SYK offers the docking chemistry STAT3 requires: STAT3 is recruited through its SH2 domain to specific receptor phosphotyrosine motifs (phospho-YXXQ in gp130/LIFR; heinrich2003:findings:006), and activated SYK displays phosphorylated linker tyrosines (Tyr342/Tyr346) that recruit SH2 domains of effectors such as VAV1 and PLCγ1 (mcsai2010:findings:012), with ten autophosphorylation sites available as docking surfaces (mcsai2010:findings:008). If STAT3's SH2 domain engages these SYK phosphotyrosines, SYK would phosphorylate STAT3 directly rather than only through JAKs.
hypotheses.prediction: Activated (ITAM- or pervanadate-stimulated) SYK should co-immunoprecipitate with STAT3 in a manner requiring SYK Tyr342/Tyr346 phosphorylation and an intact STAT3 SH2 domain; recombinant active SYK should phosphorylate recombinant STAT3 on its activating C-terminal tyrosine in vitro; and SYK inhibition or knockdown in a myeloid/B-cell line should reduce ITAM-receptor-induced phospho-STAT3 (and STAT3-dependent reporter activity) even when JAK activity is held constant or JAK-independent stimuli are used, while SYK overexpression should increase it.
hypotheses.test: Two-part in vitro experiment: (1) a purified kinase assay incubating recombinant active SYK with recombinant STAT3 (± the SYK inhibitor R406 and ± a JAK inhibitor as controls), blotting for phospho-STAT3 Tyr705 and confirming site assignment with a Y705F STAT3 mutant; (2) in a SYK-expressing cell line (e.g. a macrophage or B-cell line), stimulate the ITAM/Dectin-1 pathway and measure phospho-STAT3 and STAT3-driven luciferase reporter output after SYK knockdown or inhibitor treatment, alongside co-immunoprecipitation of STAT3 with wild-type versus Y342F/Y346F SYK and with SH2-domain-mutant STAT3 to test whether the interaction is phosphotyrosine/SH2 dependent.

citations.title: STAT3 is a substrate of SYK tyrosine kinase in B-lineage leukemia/lymphoma cells exposed to oxidative stress.
Dexamethasone induced inhibition of Dectin-1 activation of antigen presenting cells is mediated via STAT-3 and NF-κB signaling pathways.

novelty.note: I searched for SYK as a direct STAT3 kinase, for Syk-dependent STAT3 phosphorylation downstream of ITAM/Dectin-1 receptors in myeloid cells, and for JAK-independent STAT3 tyrosine phosphorylation. Uckun et al. (PNAS 2010) already states essentially this explanation and performs nearly the proposed test: native STAT3 co-immunoprecipitates with SYK in pervanadate-challenged B-lineage cells, purified recombinant SYK binds recombinant STAT3 and phosphorylates it exclusively on tyrosine in vitro (read out with anti-phospho-STAT3 Y705), SYK loss (DT40 syk-/-) or SYK inhibition abolishes STAT3 activation while JAK inhibitors do not, establishing JAK-independent, receptor-proximal SYK-driven STAT3 phosphorylation. The myeloid/ITAM arm of the prediction is supported by Dectin-1 stimulation inducing STAT3 phosphorylation that is blocked by the SYK inhibitor R406; only the specific docking claim (STAT3 SH2 engaging SYK phospho-Tyr342/346) is unaddressed — and that paper reports SYK's own tandem SH2 domains are dispensable for STAT3 signalling.

hypotheses.statement: mTOR activity directly restrains JNK activation, such that catalytic inhibition of mTOR de-represses JNK and the resulting sustained JNK/c-Jun signalling is the proximal executor of mTOR-inhibitor-induced apoptosis.
hypotheses.mechanism: Evidence about C shows that pharmacological inhibition of the PI3K–mTOR axis in AML cells does not merely arrest growth but launches a bona fide apoptotic programme, with downstream markers such as DNA-PK activation arising as a consequence of that apoptosis and with the magnitude of phosphoproteome and proliferative response differing between lines (casado2013:findings:006, casado2013:findings:017). Independently, evidence about A shows that when JNK activation becomes enhanced, delayed and persistent rather than transient, it is sufficient to drive caspase-3 and PARP cleavage and loss of clonogenic survival, and that sustained phospho-JNK/phospho-c-Jun at late time points is the common signature preceding death under both gain and loss of a negative regulator (keusekotten2013:findings:026, keusekotten2013:findings:031). If mTOR output normally holds JNK in the transient regime, removing mTOR activity should convert JNK signalling into the sustained, death-competent mode already shown to be sufficient for caspase-3/PARP cleavage, which would make JNK the missing mechanistic step between mTOR blockade and apoptosis.
hypotheses.prediction: Catalytic mTOR inhibition should produce a delayed but progressively rising phospho-JNK and phospho-c-Jun signal (minimal at 30–60 min, strong at 8–24 h) that tracks the appearance of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP; JNK inhibition or JNK1/2 depletion should blunt caspase-3/PARP cleavage and rescue viability after mTOR inhibition without restoring S6K/4EBP1 phosphorylation, and cells whose phosphoproteome responds most strongly to mTOR inhibitors should show the largest JNK induction.
hypotheses.test: Treat two cultured cell lines with a catalytic mTOR inhibitor (torin1 or Ku-0063794) versus vehicle and collect a time course to 24 h, immunoblotting phospho-JNK(T183/Y185), phospho-c-Jun(S63/S73), phospho-S6K/4EBP1 (to confirm on-target mTOR blockade), cleaved caspase-3 and PARP; then repeat in the presence of a JNK inhibitor (SP600125) and, independently, with siRNA knockdown of JNK1/JNK2, scoring caspase-3/PARP cleavage and viability. Loss of mTOR-inhibitor-induced apoptosis upon JNK blockade with unchanged S6K/4EBP1 dephosphorylation supports the hypothesis; unchanged phospho-JNK after mTOR inhibition, or undiminished death despite full JNK blockade, rules it out.

citations.title: Sustained activation of the JNK cascade and rapamycin-induced apoptosis are suppressed by p53/p21(Cip1).
Inhibition of mammalian target of rapamycin activates apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 signaling by suppressing protein phosphatase 5 activity.
Inhibition of JNK-mediated autophagy enhances NSCLC cell sensitivity to mTORC1/2 inhibitors.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in plain words (mTOR inhibition de-represses JNK / mTOR restrains JNK), the entities together (rapamycin or catalytic mTOR inhibitor + phospho-JNK + phospho-c-Jun + caspase-3/PARP), and the prediction (JNK inhibition or JNK1/2 siRNA rescuing mTOR-inhibitor-induced apoptosis). Huang et al. (Mol Cell 2003) already state exactly this explanation: mTOR inhibition triggers rapid and sustained ASK1–JNK activation with elevated phospho-c-Jun as the lethal response executing apoptosis, and the companion JBC study supplies the de-repression mechanism (mTOR blockade inactivates PP5, releasing ASK1–JNK), so mTOR output normally holding JNK in check is published. Remaining unmatched details are peripheral rather than the core explanation — those studies used rapamycin rather than torin1/Ku-0063794, saw early-onset rather than delayed-onset JNK, and a later report (Sci Rep 2016) found catalytic mTORC1/2 inhibitors do activate JNK but pro-survival via autophagy, so the directionality in the proposed AML setting is contested.

hypotheses.statement: SYK acts directly upstream of TNF production, being required for induction and accumulation of TNF upon ITAM-coupled C-type lectin (CLEC7A/CLEC6A/CLEC4E–FcRγ) stimulation of myeloid cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The SYK evidence states that SYK signalling downstream of CLEC7A ligation drives chemokine and cytokine production through ERK, NFAT and NF-κB (via CARD9–BCL10–MALT1), and that SYK-deficient DCs have a profound block in cytokine synthesis (IL-2, IL-10, IL-23) after yeast stimulation, i.e. SYK is a general proximal controller of the cytokine output of this receptor module. The TNF evidence states that TNF output is set by exactly these kinds of inputs: NF-κB-coupled signalling and MAPK-activated kinase-dependent stabilisation/translation of its ARE-containing mRNA (MK2 phosphorylation of TTP creating 14-3-3 sites, blocking ARE-mRNA degradation and supporting TNF expression). Because TNF is an NF-κB/ERK-MAPK-dependent, ARE-regulated cytokine of the same myeloid receptor programme that SYK controls, SYK activity should be a direct requirement for TNF induction rather than incidental to it.
hypotheses.prediction: In macrophages/DCs stimulated with a Dectin-1/ITAM-coupled ligand (zymosan, curdlan, heat-killed yeast), loss or pharmacological inhibition of SYK will sharply reduce TNF mRNA induction, shorten TNF mRNA half-life, and abolish most secreted TNF protein, with a parallel loss of ERK phosphorylation and NF-κB (IκB degradation/p65 nuclear entry); SYK re-expression or bypassing SYK with a direct NF-κB/MAPK agonist (PMA, or TNF-R1 ligation itself) will restore TNF output, and TNF induction by TLR ligands such as LPS that do not run through the ITAM–SYK module will be largely SYK-independent.
hypotheses.test: In a macrophage/DC line (e.g. RAW264.7 or human monocyte-derived/THP-1 macrophages) generate SYK-knockout clones by CRISPR alongside control clones, and in parallel pretreat wild-type cells with a selective SYK inhibitor (R406/entospletinib) versus vehicle; stimulate with curdlan/zymosan (and LPS as a SYK-independent control) and measure secreted TNF by ELISA, TNF mRNA by qPCR over a time course, TNF mRNA decay after actinomycin D chase, and phospho-ERK/IκB loss by Western blot; rescue SYK-knockout cells with wild-type SYK versus kinase-dead SYK to show the effect is kinase-activity dependent, which would directly confirm or rule out SYK as a required upstream driver of TNF production.

citations.title: CR3 and Dectin-1 Collaborate in Macrophage Cytokine Response through Association on Lipid Rafts and Activation of Syk-JNK-AP-1 Pathway.
Syk kinase is required for collaborative cytokine production induced through Dectin-1 and Toll-like receptors.
Syk signaling in dendritic cells orchestrates innate resistance to systemic fungal infection.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (SYK required upstream of TNF after Dectin-1/ITAM C-type lectin ligation), for the entities together (Syk + zymosan/curdlan/Mincle/FcRγ + TNF + NF-κB/IκB/ERK), and for the prediction (Syk inhibitor or Syk-knockout abolishing TNF while LPS-driven TNF persists). Published primary work already states this explanation: Huang et al. show Syk inhibitors abolish and Syk knockdown almost completely abolishes TNF production by macrophages stimulated with depleted zymosan/β-glucan via a Syk–JNK–AP-1 route, Dennehy et al. show Syk-/- macrophages lose Dectin-1-driven TNF/MIP-1α/MIP-2 and the sustained IκB degradation underlying it (with the TLR/MyD88 arm separable), and Whitney et al. state that fungal induction of TNF along with IL-2/IL-6/IL-12/IL-23 in DCs and macrophages is Syk-dependent. Hence established, though the literature also contains the qualification (e.g., Syk-independent Raf-1/TLR2 contributions to Dectin-1-induced TNF) that the prediction's 'abolish most secreted TNF' framing does not capture.

hypotheses.statement: TGF-β negatively regulates SYK-dependent signalling output in myeloid cells, suppressing the CLEC7A–SYK–CARD9–NF-κB axis and the cytokine programme it drives.
hypotheses.mechanism: SYK downstream of CLEC7A ligation induces chemokine and cytokine production through ERK, NFAT and NF-κB, with the NF-κB arm transduced via CARD9–BCL10–MALT1, and this axis yields a characteristic IL-2/IL-10/IL-23 output (mcsai2010:findings:019, mcsai2010:findings:021). Independently, TGF-β is reported to disrupt NF-κB signalling in fibroblasts (davidson2021:findings:012) and to blunt cytokine production (IL-2, IFN-γ, IL-4) in TCR-stimulated cells while leaving pharmacologically driven activation intact (chen2003:findings:002). If TGF-β acts on the shared NF-κB node, it should intersect the SYK pathway itself, imposing a direct inhibitory relationship on SYK-driven signalling rather than merely coexisting with it.
hypotheses.prediction: Exposing SYK-competent myeloid cells to TGF-β before β-glucan/yeast stimulation should sharply reduce SYK-dependent IL-10 and IL-23 (and IL-2) output and reduce NF-κB p65 nuclear translocation/CARD9-dependent reporter activity, while proximal SYK activation itself (ITAM-driven SYK autophosphorylation at the linker tyrosines) and PMA/ionomycin-driven cytokine release remain largely intact — i.e. the block sits at or below the SYK→CARD9→NF-κB step, is Smad2/3-dependent, and is reversed by TGF-β neutralisation.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate a SYK-expressing myeloid line (e.g. THP-1-derived macrophages or human monocyte-derived DCs) with curdlan/zymosan ± pre-incubation with recombinant TGF-β1, ± neutralising anti-TGF-β antibody or an ALK5/Smad inhibitor, and ± the SYK inhibitor R406 as a pathway-dependence control; read out phospho-SYK (Tyr342/346) and phospho-p65 by Western blot, p65 nuclear translocation by immunofluorescence or an NF-κB luciferase reporter, and IL-10/IL-23/IL-2 by ELISA. TGF-β-dependent loss of the NF-κB and cytokine readouts that phenocopies R406 while sparing phospho-SYK supports direct downstream inhibition; unchanged readouts rule the relationship out.

citations.title: Transforming Growth Factor-β1 Modulates Lipopolysaccharide-Induced Cytokine/Chemokine Production and Inhibits Nuclear Factor-κB, Extracellular Signal-Regulated Kinases and p38 Activation in Dendritic Cells in Mice
Human Dendritic Cells Activated via Dectin-1 Are Efficient at Priming Th17, Cytotoxic CD8 T and B Cell Responses

novelty.note: I searched for TGF-β inhibition of the Dectin-1/CLEC7A–SYK–CARD9–NF-κB axis, for TGF-β suppression of β-glucan/curdlan-induced IL-10/IL-23, and for TGF-β/Smad-dependent downregulation of SYK or ITAM-proximal signalling in myeloid cells. Published work establishes that TGF-β1 blunts myeloid/DC activation and suppresses NF-κB, ERK and p38 activation with altered cytokine output (shown for LPS/TLR4, not for Dectin-1), and that Dectin-1-activated DCs produce IL-23/IL-1β/IL-6 via Syk; however I found no source stating that TGF-β directly suppresses SYK-dependent CLEC7A signalling output or the specific prediction that the block sits at/below SYK→CARD9→NF-κB while sparing phospho-SYK. In the fungal-sensing literature TGF-β is instead treated as a cooperating factor downstream of Dectin-1-activated DCs for Th17 polarisation, so the connection remains partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: TGF-β directly inhibits mTORC1 signalling in TCR-stimulated CD4+ T cells, and this suppression of mTORC1 output is what enforces the TGF-β–induced anergic state.
hypotheses.mechanism: The independent TGF-β evidence describes anergized T cells that are reduced in cell size and fail to proliferate on TCR restimulation, a defect rescued by exogenous IL-2 (chen2003:findings:008, chen2003:findings:001, chen2003:findings:003). The independent mTORC1 evidence states that in lymphocytes mTORC1 couples exactly these two outputs — cell growth (size) and proliferation — through the 4E-BP/eIF4E axis rather than S6Ks, and that mTORC1 is activated downstream of growth-factor/AKT input via TSC2 inactivation (fruman2017:findings:009, laplante2012:findings:002, haeusler2018:findings:027). A coordinate loss of lymphocyte size and proliferative capacity that is restored by a growth-factor–type cytokine is the phenotypic signature of reduced mTORC1 activity, implying TGF-β acts as a negative input onto mTORC1 upstream of 4E-BP1.
hypotheses.prediction: TCR stimulation in the presence of TGF-β should give markedly lower phospho-4E-BP1 (Ser65) and phospho-S6K1 (Thr389) than TCR stimulation alone, with the drop in 4E-BP1 phosphorylation tracking the reduction in cell size (FSC); adding IL-2 should restore both phospho-4E-BP1 and cell size, and expressing a constitutively active Rag heterodimer (RagB Q99L/RagC S75N), which renders mTORC1 insensitive to upstream negative inputs, should blunt both the mTORC1 shutdown and the proliferative unresponsiveness.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured human T cell line (e.g. Jurkat) or in vitro–activated CD4+ T cells, stimulate with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 ± TGF-β and immunoblot a time course of phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65 and phospho-S6K1 Thr389 (with FSC by flow cytometry as the size readout), then repeat with (i) added IL-2 and (ii) stable expression of RagB Q99L/RagC S75N versus wild-type Rags; TGF-β lowering phospho-4E-BP1 in a dose-dependent way that is reversed by IL-2 and resisted by the active Rag heterodimer supports the direct inhibitory relationship, whereas unchanged mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation under TGF-β rules it out.

citations.title: The TGF-β-Smad3 pathway inhibits CD28-dependent cell growth and proliferation of CD4 T cells.
Transforming growth factor-β-regulated mTOR activity preserves cellular metabolism to maintain long-term T cell responses in chronic infection.
Tumor suppressor TSC1 is critical for T-cell anergy.
TGFβ limits Myc-dependent TCR-induced metabolic reprogramming in CD8(+) T cells.
Regulation of T Cell Activation and Metabolism by Transforming Growth Factor-Beta.

novelty.note: I searched for TGF-β inhibition of mTOR/mTORC1 in T cells, for TGF-β-induced CD4 anergy linked to mTORC1/4E-BP1, for the phospho-4E-BP1/S6K1 readouts under anti-CD3/CD28 ± TGF-β, and for mTORC1-suppression-as-anergy. The two halves of the hypothesis are separately published: TGF-β/Smad3 dampens CD28-driven CD4 T-cell growth and proliferation with an effect resembling rapamycin (Delisle et al.), TGF-β represses mTOR signalling in antigen-stimulated CD8 T cells (Gabriel et al.), and suppression of mTORC1 (via TSC1) is required to enforce T-cell anergy (Park et al.). However, no source states that TGF-β-induced CD4 anergy of the Chen-2003 type is enforced through direct mTORC1 shutdown, none reports the specific 4E-BP1 Ser65/cell-size coupling or IL-2/active-Rag rescue predictions, and at least one primary study reports that TGF-β does not measurably impair TCR-induced mTORC1 activity in T cells — so the specific connection remains unestablished.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR2 (TβRII) is the proximal receptor component that directly drives TGF-β-induced JNK activation, acting as the TRAF6/TAK1 docking platform independently of TβRI's Smad-specifying L45 loop and kinase-mediated substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: derynck2019:findings:030 states that TGF-β activates JNK via TRAF6/TRAF4-scaffolded TAK1 recruited to the receptor complex and explicitly without requiring direct phosphorylation by the type I receptor kinases, and hata2016:findings:011 states that the TβRI L45 loop, which dictates Smad interaction, is dispensable for TGF-β-induced JNK activation; together these place the JNK-activating function in a receptor-complex component other than TβRI's Smad/kinase output. Since TβRII is the ligand-binding, complex-nucleating kinase whose autophosphorylation and kinase activity govern complex function (derynck2019:findings:013; macassilva1996:findings:001), and TRAF6 ubiquitylation is itself sufficient to drive JNK activation (gaffen2014:findings:022), TβRII is the plausible direct upstream partner coupling TGF-β to JNK.
hypotheses.prediction: Loss of TGFBR2 should abolish TGF-β-induced JNK and c-Jun phosphorylation, whereas pharmacological inhibition of TβRI kinase (which blocks Smad phosphorylation) should leave TGF-β-induced JNK activation largely intact; TRAF6 and TAK1 should co-immunoprecipitate with TβRII in a TGF-β-dependent manner, and this recruitment plus JNK activation should be preserved by a TβRII mutant that cannot transphosphorylate TβRI but lost in a TβRII cytoplasmic-domain deletion.
hypotheses.test: In a standard cultured line, generate CRISPR TGFBR2-knockout and control cells, stimulate with TGF-β, and immunoblot phospho-JNK and phospho-c-Jun (with phospho-SMAD2 as a pathway control) alongside cells treated with a TβRI kinase inhibitor; then reconstitute the knockout with wild-type TβRII, kinase-dead TβRII, and cytoplasmic-domain-truncated TβRII and score rescue of TGF-β-induced phospho-JNK, coupled with co-immunoprecipitation of endogenous TRAF6/TAK1 with each TβRII construct.

citations.title: TRAF6 mediates Smad-independent activation of JNK and p38 by TGF-beta.
The type I TGF-beta receptor engages TRAF6 to activate TAK1 in a receptor kinase-independent manner.
TGF-beta receptor-activated p38 MAP kinase mediates Smad-independent TGF-beta responses.
Src phosphorylates Tyr284 in TGF-beta type II receptor and regulates TGF-beta stimulation of p38 MAPK during breast cancer cell proliferation and invasion.
Regulation of TGF-β receptor activity.

novelty.note: I searched for kinase-independent TRAF6/TAK1-mediated TGF-β activation of JNK, for TRAF6/TAK1 docking on TGFBR2 specifically, for TβRI L45-loop/Smad-independence of p38-JNK, and for TβRII as a non-Smad MAPK docking platform (PubMed/Europe PMC/PMC full texts). The general mechanism is published: TGF-β activates JNK/p38 via receptor-recruited TRAF6 auto-ubiquitylation and TAK1 independently of receptor kinase activity and of the Smad-specifying L45 loop, and Yamashita et al. explicitly report TRAF6 binding to both TβRI and TβRII 'with slightly higher affinity towards TβRII' — yet all published work assigns the functional TRAF6 docking motif to TβRI (Sorrentino et al.), and TRAF6 recruitment there required heteromeric complex formation rather than TβRII alone. No source states that TGFBR2 is the proximal driver of JNK independent of TβRI, nor tests the predicted dissociation (TGFBR2 loss abolishing p-JNK while TβRI kinase inhibition spares it, with rescue by transphosphorylation-dead TβRII), so the specific attribution and prediction remain unpublished; the closest TβRII-centred non-Smad result is Grb2/Shc docking at TβRII Tyr284 driving p38, not TRAF6/JNK.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B directly phosphorylates the cytoplasmic domain of TGFBR1 (TβRI), acting as a priming-dependent kinase that creates a phospho-degron limiting TβRI abundance and signalling output.
hypotheses.mechanism: The claims about GSK3B establish it as a phospho-primed kinase (it prefers pSer/pThr at fixed motif positions) that acts directly on already-phosphorylated receptor cytoplasmic domains at the membrane — it phosphorylates the LRP6 PPPSP motifs, and in other substrates its phosphorylation generates ubiquitin-ligase recognition motifs (β-Trcp on β-catenin, Nedd4L on the Smad linker) that drive degradation. The claims about TGFBR1 independently show its cytoplasmic region is a heavily Ser/Thr-phosphorylated module (four of five GS-domain S/T residues suffice for activation) and that this same cytoplasmic domain is a substrate for ubiquitylation prior to proteolytic processing. Together these imply that TβRI's receptor-activation phosphorylations could serve as priming sites for GSK3B, coupling TβRI to the same phospho-degron logic GSK3B imposes on LRP6, β-catenin and PHLPP.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant GSK3B should phosphorylate the isolated TβRI cytoplasmic domain in vitro, and much more efficiently when the domain has first been phosphorylated (by TβRII or a phosphomimetic/pre-phosphorylated GS domain) than when unprimed or when the priming Ser/Thr are mutated to Ala; in cells, GSK3 inhibition or GSK3α/β loss should raise steady-state TβRI protein and lengthen its half-life, with correspondingly stronger TGF-β-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation, while a TβRI mutant lacking the GSK3-target sites should be insensitive to GSK3 inhibition.
hypotheses.test: Perform an in vitro kinase assay with purified GSK3B and GST-TβRI cytoplasmic domain, comparing unprimed substrate, substrate pre-phosphorylated by recombinant TβRII kinase, and GS-domain Ser/Thr→Ala variants, reading out ³²P incorporation and mapping sites by phosphopeptide mass spectrometry; in parallel, treat cultured cells with a GSK3 inhibitor (or use GSK3α/β-null cells) and measure TβRI phosphorylation (Phos-tag/phospho-specific immunoblot), TβRI level and half-life by cycloheximide chase with immunoprecipitation-ubiquitin blotting, and TGF-β-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation, then test whether the non-phosphorylatable TβRI mutant abolishes these GSK3-dependent differences.

citations.title: Post-translational regulation of TGF-β receptor and Smad signaling.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: GSK3 phosphorylating the TβRI/ALK5 cytoplasmic domain directly, GSK3 effects on TGFBR1 protein stability/half-life and Smad2/3 output, and GSK3 phospho-degron logic applied to TGF-β receptors. All retrieved sources place GSK3 downstream of the receptor — Axin/GSK3β-mediated Smad3 MH1 and linker phosphorylation driving Smad degradation — and the authoritative review of post-translational TGF-β receptor regulation lists Smurf2, USP4/USP15 and TRAF6 as receptor-level regulators but no GSK3 phosphorylation of TβRI. No source states the priming-dependent TβRI phospho-degron, and none reports a direct negative test of it, so the claim is unanticipated rather than refuted.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly activates MTOR by tyrosine-phosphorylating it, so that Src-family kinase activity is an upstream positive input into mTORC1 catalytic output.
hypotheses.mechanism: The SRC evidence shows Src is a broadly acting tyrosine kinase that switches on other protein kinases by direct tyrosine phosphorylation: it phosphorylates Tyr residues on the Ser/Thr kinase RSK2 to stabilize its ERK1/2 partnership and promote its activation (cargnello2011:findings:059), and tyrosine phosphorylation by Src enhances TβRII kinase activity (derynck2019:findings:013). On the MTOR side, mTOR substrate-group phosphorylation is a measurable, inhibitor-sensitive output in AML cells (casado2013:findings:004), and in the same cell type high phosphorylation of Src/Lck/Abl substrate groups marks the cells whose viability is most dependent on PI3K–mTOR pathway inhibition (casado2013:findings:009) — consistent with Src activity feeding, rather than bypassing, mTOR catalytic output.
hypotheses.prediction: Immunopurified mTOR should acquire phosphotyrosine when incubated with active SRC and ATP in vitro, and in cells, expression of constitutively active SRC should raise mTOR tyrosine phosphorylation and mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1), while Src-family inhibition or SRC knockdown should lower mTOR pTyr and mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation without lowering total mTOR; a phospho-null Tyr→Phe mTOR mutant should be refractory to SRC-driven activation.
hypotheses.test: Immunoprecipitate FLAG-mTOR from HEK-293T lysate, incubate with recombinant active SRC ± a Src inhibitor (PP2/dasatinib) and ATP, then blot with 4G10 anti-phosphotyrosine and map sites by LC-MS/MS; in parallel, express constitutively active SRC or knock down/inhibit SRC in the same cells and measure mTOR immunoprecipitate pTyr alongside S6K1 Thr389 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation by immunoblot, using in vitro mTOR kinase assays on GST-4E-BP1 with SRC-treated versus mock-treated mTOR, and repeating with the Tyr→Phe mTOR mutant to test whether the identified site is required.

citations.title: Regulation of mTORC1 signaling by Src kinase activity is Akt1-independent in RSV-transformed cells.
Src regulates amino acid-mediated mTORC1 activation by disrupting GATOR1-Rag GTPase interaction.
Tyrosine phosphorylation of DEPTOR functions as a molecular switch to activate mTOR signaling.

novelty.note: I searched for direct Src tyrosine phosphorylation of mTOR, for Src-family regulation of mTORC1 output (S6K1/4E-BP1), and for mTOR tyrosine-phosphosite mapping. Published work firmly establishes Src-family kinase activity as a positive upstream input into mTORC1 catalytic output (Src inhibition reduces mTOR, S6K1, S6 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation; Src acts upstream of the Rag GTPases via GATOR1 dissociation), and tyrosine phosphorylation of the mTOR-regulatory protein DEPTOR (Tyr289, by SYK) is a known switch activating mTOR — but no source states that mTOR itself is a direct Src substrate bearing an activating phosphotyrosine, and the Nat Commun authors explicitly leave the relevant Src target unidentified. Hence partial: the upstream-positive-input half is anticipated, the direct-phosphorylation prediction is not.

hypotheses.statement: JNK directly phosphorylates MEK1 on the inhibitory Thr292 feedback site, acting as a cross-cascade brake that lowers MEK1 kinase activity toward ERK1/2.
hypotheses.mechanism: lake2016:findings:010 establishes that MEK1 carries a single MAPK-type feedback site, T292, whose phosphorylation inhibits MEK1 catalytic activity toward ERK1/2, weakens MEK1–ERK2 binding and blocks PAK-mediated S298 phosphorylation — an inhibitory input normally supplied by a proline-directed MAPK. regot2014:findings:000 shows that JNK phosphorylates substrate Ser/Thr sites (c-Jun S63/S73) that are presented together with a JNK docking site, i.e. JNK uses the same docking-plus-proline-directed chemistry that MEK1 T292 offers. johnson2023:findings:014 shows that in LPS-stimulated dendritic cells JNK and the other stress kinases are activated first and are followed by net suppression of MAPK (ERK-cascade) motif activity, the temporal order expected if active JNK imposes an inhibitory mark on MEK1 itself.
hypotheses.prediction: Stress stimuli that activate JNK (e.g. anisomycin, sorbitol) will raise MEK1 phospho-T292 and lower MEK1 activity toward ERK1/2 even when ERK1/2 activity is blocked; the increase will be abolished by a JNK inhibitor or JNK1/2 knockdown, absent on a MEK1 T292A mutant, and MEK1 T292A cells will retain higher ERK1/2 phosphorylation under JNK-activating stress than MEK1 wild-type cells; active JNK and MEK1 should also co-precipitate through a docking interaction.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with recombinant active JNK1/JNK2 and purified kinase-dead MEK1 (wild type vs T292A) using γ-32P-ATP and a phospho-T292-specific antibody, with ERK2 as a positive-control kinase and no-kinase controls; in parallel, treat cultured cells expressing FLAG-MEK1 WT or T292A with anisomycin in the presence of a MEK/ERK inhibitor (to exclude ERK-derived phosphorylation) with or without SP600125 or JNK1/2 siRNA, then blot phospho-T292 and assay immunoprecipitated MEK1 activity toward recombinant ERK2, and co-immunoprecipitate JNK with MEK1 to test for a direct docking interaction.

citations.title: Cross-talk between JNK/SAPK and ERK/MAPK pathways: sustained activation of JNK blocks ERK activation by mitogenic factors.
Negative feedback regulation of the ERK1/2 MAPK pathway.
Mitogen-activated protein kinase feedback phosphorylation regulates MEK1 complex formation and activation during cellular adhesion.

novelty.note: I searched for JNK phosphorylating MEK1 Thr292, for the identity of kinases acting on the MEK1 T292 feedback site, and for JNK-to-ERK negative crosstalk mechanisms. The literature consistently assigns T292 phosphorylation to ERK1/2 (and Cyclin B-Cdc2 at T286/T292), with no source proposing JNK as the T292 kinase or a JNK-MEK1 docking interaction; the closest published work shows sustained JNK activation does block ERK activation downstream of MEK, but attributes it to Jun-dependent transcription and explicitly uncouples ERK from MEK rather than to an inhibitory mark on MEK1. No source tested and negated the specific claim, so the status is open.

hypotheses.statement: MAPK signalling directly activates mTOR (mTORC1) output in EGF-stimulated cells by routing through MAPK-activated protein kinases that phosphorylate the mTORC1 inhibitor TSC2 and the mTOR-shared translational substrate rpS6, making mTOR-motif phosphorylation partly MEK/ERK-dependent.
hypotheses.mechanism: cargnello2011 states that the MAPK-activated protein kinase MK2 phosphorylates TSC2 at Ser1210 to promote 14-3-3 binding and thereby may regulate mTOR-dependent protein synthesis, and that RSK1/2 phosphorylate rpS6 Ser235/236 in response to Ras/MAPK activation, feeding the same preinitiation-complex assembly step that mTOR-dependent S6K controls. bekkerjensen2020 shows that in one EGF-stimulated cell system the ERK1/2 arm (MEK-inhibitor-sensitive, ERK1/2-motif sites) and the mTOR arm (mTOR-inhibitor-sensitive mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate sites) are both engaged by the same EGF stimulus, with the highest-stoichiometry EGF-regulated sites enriched for RTK/MAPK signalling. If MAPK-activated kinases relieve TSC2 inhibition of mTOR and duplicate its substrate output, then MAPK activity should be an upstream determinant of mTOR activity itself, not merely a parallel branch.
hypotheses.prediction: In EGF-stimulated cells, MEK/ERK inhibition should lower canonical mTORC1 readouts (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1, mTOR-motif site occupancy) in addition to ERK1/2-motif sites, and MAPK pathway activation should raise TSC2 Ser1210 phosphorylation with increased TSC2–14-3-3 association; conversely, blocking the MAPKAPK step (MK2 loss or a TSC2 S1210A mutant) should blunt EGF-driven mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation while leaving direct ERK substrates intact, and rpS6 Ser235/236 should remain partly phosphorylated under mTOR inhibition whereas Ser240/244 does not.
hypotheses.test: In cultured cells, serum-starve and stimulate with EGF under four conditions (vehicle, MEK inhibitor, mTOR inhibitor, both) and immunoblot a fixed panel: phospho-ERK1/2, phospho-S6K1 Thr389, phospho-4E-BP1, phospho-rpS6 Ser235/236 versus Ser240/244, and phospho-TSC2 Ser1210, with anti-TSC2 immunoprecipitation blotted for 14-3-3 to test stimulus- and MEK-dependent complex formation; then repeat in cells with siRNA knockdown of MK2 (or RSK1/2) and in TSC2-null cells reconstituted with wild-type versus S1210A TSC2, so that loss of EGF-driven mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation specifically in the MAPKAPK-blocked or S1210A conditions supports the direct MAPK→mTOR link, while unchanged mTORC1 readouts under MEK inhibition and MK2 loss rule it out.

citations.title: The p38 and MK2 kinase cascade phosphorylates tuberin, the tuberous sclerosis 2 gene product, and enhances its interaction with 14-3-3.
Phosphorylation and functional inactivation of TSC2 by Erk implications for tuberous sclerosis and cancer pathogenesis.
Oncogenic MAPK signaling stimulates mTORC1 activity by promoting RSK-mediated raptor phosphorylation.
RAS/ERK signaling promotes site-specific ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation via RSK and stimulates cap-dependent translation.

Pharmacological and genetic evaluation of proposed roles of mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase kinase (MEK), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and p90(RSK) in the control of mTORC1 protein signaling by phorbol esters.

novelty.note: I searched for (a) RSK/ERK-mediated phosphorylation of TSC2 and mTORC1 activation, (b) MK2 phosphorylation of TSC2 Ser1210 and 14-3-3 binding, and (c) MEK-inhibitor dependence of canonical mTORC1 readouts (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1, rpS6 Ser235/236 vs Ser240/244) in growth-factor-stimulated cells. Each element of the proposed explanation is already published as a mechanism for exactly this phenomenon: MK2 directly phosphorylates TSC2 Ser1210 to create a 14-3-3 site (Li et al. 2003), ERK phosphorylates and functionally inactivates TSC2 to relieve mTOR inhibition (Ma et al. 2005), RSK1/2 phosphorylate raptor to activate mTORC1 downstream of Ras/MAPK (Carriere et al. 2008), and RSK phosphorylates rpS6 Ser235/236 mTOR-independently while Ser240/244 remains mTOR/S6K-dependent (Roux et al. 2007). The predicted experiment (MEK-inhibitor sensitivity of S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1 and rpS6, plus RSK/TSC2 site mutants) has also been performed explicitly, with the caveat that MEK/RSK dependence of mTORC1 output is cell-type variable (PMID 21659537); the only unpublished increment is the phosphoproteome-wide EGF/MEK/mTOR site-occupancy framing, which does not change the underlying explanation.

hypotheses.statement: JNK1 catalytic activity directly restrains cell growth, so that active JNK1 imposes a kinase-activity-dependent growth (proliferation/fitness) cost that is relieved by loss of JNK1 or by catalytic inactivation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Systematic expression of human kinases showed that several S/T kinases, Y kinases and all v-SRC variants reduced growth significantly more than their kinase-dead counterparts, establishing that ectopic kinase catalysis per se can be growth-deleterious in a manner detectable by colony-size and competition assays (bradley2024:findings:011, bradley2024:findings:012). JNK1 is one such stress-activated S/T MAPK whose catalytic output drives cell-death programs — fibroblasts lacking JNK1 (with JNK2) are resistant to DNA-damage- and UV-induced apoptosis and fail to release cytochrome c (cargnello2011:findings:008) — and JNK1 is the dominant kinase supplying c-Jun phosphorylation and c-Jun autoinduction in fibroblasts, with JNK1 hyperactivation alone sufficient to raise c-Jun phosphorylation in unstimulated cells (zeke2016:findings:016). Together these imply that the amount of active JNK1 in a fibroblast sets a direct, catalysis-dependent brake on net growth rather than acting only as a passive stress marker.
hypotheses.prediction: Inducible expression of wild-type JNK1 should lower proliferation rate/colony size and lose competitions against an empty-vector control, while an identically expressed kinase-dead JNK1 should be near-neutral; conversely, JNK1-deficient or JNK1-depleted fibroblasts should show increased net growth (larger area under the growth curve, more colonies) relative to matched controls, especially under mild stress, and the growth difference should track the level of c-Jun phosphorylation rather than expression level of the protein.
hypotheses.test: In an isogenic fibroblast line (or the yeast landing-pad format), place doxycycline-inducible wild-type JNK1 and a catalytically dead JNK1 (ATP-site mutant) at the same locus, confirm equal protein levels by immunoblot, then run parallel growth-curve/colony-size assays and a direct co-culture competition against a fluorescently marked empty-vector control read by flow cytometry; in the reciprocal arm, compare proliferation and colony formation of JNK1-knockdown versus control fibroblasts, with c-Jun phosphorylation measured in every condition. A growth deficit specific to the catalytically active allele, mirrored by a growth gain on JNK1 loss and correlated with c-Jun phosphorylation, supports the relationship; equal growth for wild-type and kinase-dead JNK1 and no effect of knockdown rules it out.

citations.title: Distinct roles for JNK1 and JNK2 in regulating JNK activity and c-Jun-dependent cell proliferation.
Role of JNK in mammary gland development and breast cancer.

novelty.note: I searched for JNK1 overexpression vs kinase-dead effects on fibroblast growth, for Jnk1-/- fibroblast proliferation phenotypes, and for JNK1/c-Jun phosphorylation and cell-cycle progression. Sabapathy et al. (Mol Cell 2004) directly tested this in matched Jnk1-/-, Jnk2-/- and wild-type fibroblasts and found the opposite of the prediction: JNK1 loss reduces c-Jun phosphorylation/stability and slows G1-S progression and proliferation, while ectopic JNK1 expression augments proliferation (in Jnk2-/- cells); a review of JNK in fibroblasts likewise reports that compound JNK deficiency causes p53 induction and senescence rather than a growth gain. Because the specific claim — that JNK1 catalytic activity imposes a growth cost relieved by JNK1 loss — was tested in the very cell system proposed and did not hold, the status is refuted.

hypotheses.statement: mTOR directly and positively regulates TNF protein output by driving translation of TNF mRNA through its p70S6K/eIF4 translational arm, such that mTOR kinase inhibition reduces TNF secretion without a proportional loss of TNF transcript.
hypotheses.mechanism: The evidence about TNF states that its production is set post-transcriptionally, at the level of translation and/or stability of its ARE-containing mRNA (cargnello2011:findings:072), so TNF output is rate-limited by translational control rather than transcript abundance alone. The evidence about mTOR states that mTOR signalling selectively promotes translation of particular mRNAs via p70 S6 kinase and eIF4 initiation factors (ivashkiv2014:findings:026), and that catalytic mTOR inhibitors demonstrably collapse p70S6K/mTOR substrate phosphorylation in cells (casado2013:findings:004). If the translational machinery that mTOR controls is the same machinery that limits TNF synthesis, mTOR should act as a direct upstream positive regulator of TNF protein production.
hypotheses.prediction: In stimulated myeloid or T cell lines, acute mTOR kinase inhibition (or RAPTOR depletion) should lower secreted and intracellular TNF protein several-fold while TNF mRNA levels remain largely unchanged, with TNF transcripts shifting from heavy polysomes to light/monosomal fractions and reduced nascent TNF labelling; conversely, constitutive mTORC1 activation should raise TNF protein per unit TNF mRNA.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate THP-1/RAW264.7 macrophages (or activated Jurkat cells) with LPS/PMA in the presence of vehicle, rapamycin, or an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor (e.g. Torin1), and in parallel with siRNA knockdown of RAPTOR versus control; quantify secreted TNF by ELISA and intracellular TNF by immunoblot/flow cytometry, TNF mRNA by qRT-PCR, translational engagement by polysome-gradient fractionation with qRT-PCR of TNF transcripts, and new TNF synthesis by puromycin/SUnSET or short metabolic labelling followed by TNF immunoprecipitation, confirming on-target mTOR blockade via phospho-S6K/phospho-S6 immunoblots. A drop in TNF protein and polysome loading with preserved TNF mRNA supports the direct translational regulation; unchanged TNF protein, or a fall in TNF protein matched by an equal fall in TNF mRNA, rules it out.

citations.title: mTOR-dependent translation amplifies microglia priming in aging mice.
mTOR signaling during T cell activation promotes cytokine production in T cells through 3' UTR-mediated translation control.
Cot/tpl2-MKK1/2-Erk1/2 controls mTORC1-mediated mRNA translation in Toll-like receptor-activated macrophages.
Differential Role of Rapamycin and Torin/KU63794 in Inflammatory Response of 264.7 RAW Macrophages Stimulated by CA-MRSA.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (mTOR/rapamycin controlling TNF translation vs transcription in LPS-stimulated myeloid cells), the entities together (mTORC1, 4E-BP1/p70S6K, TNF polysome loading, Raptor knockdown), and the prediction (TNF protein falls while TNF mRNA is preserved). Published work already states this explanation: Keane et al. (JCI) show that in microglia Torin1 and Rheb deletion reduce TNF and other cytokine protein while their mRNAs are unchanged or even elevated, i.e. mTOR sets cytokine output translationally; Jurgens et al. (Mol Cell) show mTOR/Raptor-dependent, ARE/3'UTR-mediated translational control of T cell cytokines including TNF; López-Peláez et al. show mTORC1-dependent polysomal recruitment of TNFα mRNA in TLR-activated macrophages; and Torin/KU63794 dose-dependently lower TNF secretion in RAW264.7. The main unanticipated details are the specific attribution to the p70S6K arm (published work implicates 4E-BP1/eIF4E and DDX21) and the fact that rapamycin alone often fails to lower — or even raises — TNF (e.g. PMID 20828737), so the effect is specific to catalytic mTOR blockade.

hypotheses.statement: ERK2 activity is a direct, rate-limiting positive driver of proliferative growth in receptor tyrosine kinase-driven cells, such that the level of active ERK2 sets the growth rate.
hypotheses.mechanism: Independent evidence shows that Gab1–SHP2 association activates ERK2 and that a Gab1-PH–active-SHP2 fusion drives constitutive MEK1/ERK2 activation (heinrich2003:findings:010, heinrich2003:findings:011), while in RTK-altered cancer lines SHP2 depletion or SHP099 inhibition suppresses colony formation and confluence growth, and an SHP099-insensitive SHP2 allele preserves both p-ERK signalling and growth in the same cells (chen2016:findings:002, chen2016:findings:013). The concordance of p-ERK level and growth across these perturbations, combined with the demonstration that SHP2 output is ERK2 activation, implies ERK2 activation itself is the growth-determining step rather than a correlated bystander; ERK2's own substrate repertoire includes proliferation-relevant nodes such as FGFR1 S777, whose mutation raised proliferation and migration (lake2016:findings:002).
hypotheses.prediction: Restoring active ERK2 downstream of a blocked upstream node should restore growth: SHP2-depleted or SHP099-treated RTK-driven cells expressing constitutively active MEK1 or a phosphomimetic/activated ERK2 will regain near-normal proliferation and colony formation despite loss of SHP2 function, whereas selectively silencing or inhibiting ERK2 in cells with intact SHP2 (or expressing the SHP099-resistant SHP2 allele) will suppress growth to the same extent as SHP2 loss, with growth rate scaling monotonically with measured p-ERK2.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured RTK-driven line (e.g. the EGFR-amplified/SHP2-dependent cells used with doxycycline-inducible PTPN11 shRNA), run a 2x2 epistasis experiment entirely in vitro: (i) induce SHP2 knockdown or add SHP099 with and without doxycycline-inducible constitutively active MEK1/activated ERK2, and (ii) in parallel deplete ERK2 by siRNA or inhibit it with an ERK inhibitor in SHP2-intact cells; read out growth by crystal-violet colony formation and live-cell confluence over 7-10 days and quantify p-ERK2 by western blot at each condition. Rescue of growth by active ERK2 under SHP2 blockade, plus growth loss on ERK2 depletion alone, establishes the direct ERK2→growth relationship; failure of active ERK2 to rescue, or growth persisting after ERK2 loss, rules it out.

citations.title: Frequency-modulated pulses of ERK activity transmit quantitative proliferation signals.
Shp2-dependent ERK signaling is essential for induction of Bergmann glia and foliation of the cerebellum.
SHP2 Inhibition Prevents Adaptive Resistance to MEK Inhibitors in Multiple Cancer Models.
Resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibition in FGFR-driven cancers through rapid feedback activation of FGFR.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (i) the quantitative mechanism ('ERK activity level sets proliferation rate', single-cell ERK dose–proliferation studies), (ii) the entities together ('SHP2/PTPN11 knockdown or SHP099 growth arrest rescued by constitutively active MEK1/ERK2', 'MEK1DD rescue', 'MAP2K1 bypass of SHP2 dependency'), and (iii) the prediction (epistasis/rescue and ERK2-specific depletion in RTK-driven lines). The two halves are published separately: Albeck et al. show that in EGF/RTK-driven cells proliferation rate is a steep monotonic function of total ERK pathway output (≈95% inhibition needed for 10-fold growth loss), and Lin et al. show formal epistasis in which constitutively active MEK1 (MEK1DD) rescues Shp2-loss phenotypes, establishing ERK as the limiting output of Shp2 — but in cerebellar development, not RTK-driven cancer growth. In the cancer setting the nearest work (Fedele et al.; the FGFR feedback-resistance study, where p-ERK rebound tracks retained growth under SHP099) only correlates p-ERK with growth and explicitly lacks the constitutively active MEK/ERK2 rescue under SHP2 blockade plus paired ERK2-selective depletion, so the specific prediction is unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: ERBB2 acts directly upstream of AKT, activating it: receptor-derived phosphotyrosine sites on ERBB2 drive PI3K-dependent AKT activation, so ERBB2 levels/activity set the amount of active AKT and AKT-motif substrate phosphorylation in ERBB2-amplified cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The AKT-side evidence shows that ErbB-ligand (EGF) stimulation produces a MEK-independent wave of phosphorylation on the AKT substrate motif RxRxx[s/t] (bekkerjensen2020:findings:010) and that AKT is activated by membrane recruitment, with membrane-localizing AKT1-E17K mutations found in 4-8% of breast cancers (fruman2017:findings:003). The ERBB2-side evidence shows ERBB2 phosphosites are unusually promiscuous docking hubs, binding more than 17 SH2/PTB proteins on average with pY1139 alone binding 24 (jones2006:findings:008), that ERBB2-containing heterodimers are the most mitogenic and transforming ErbB complexes (yarden2001:findings:001), that ERBB2 is endocytosis-impaired and slows internalization of its partners (yarden2001:findings:004), and that ERBB2 is amplified in 15-30% of invasive ductal breast cancers (yarden2001:findings:013) — the same tumour type in which membrane-localizing AKT1 mutations recur. Together these imply that a long-lived, docking-rich ERBB2 platform is a direct source of the membrane signal that activates AKT, and that AKT1-E17K would be a receptor-independent substitute for it.
hypotheses.prediction: In an ERBB2-amplified line, depleting or inhibiting ERBB2 should lower AKT Ser473 phosphorylation and globally reduce phosphorylation on RxRxx[S/T]-motif AKT substrates while leaving MEK-dependent Px[S/T]P/ERK-motif sites comparatively less affected; conversely, heregulin-driven ERBB2 heterodimerization should raise AKT Ser473 and RxRxx[S/T] site phosphorylation, and this dependence should be abolished by expressing membrane-localized AKT1-E17K, which should keep AKT substrate phosphorylation high after ERBB2 loss.
hypotheses.test: In an ERBB2-amplified cell line versus an ERBB2-low control, apply inducible ERBB2 shRNA (and, separately, acute ERBB2 kinase inhibition) and immunoblot for AKT Ser473/Thr308, a phospho-RxRxx[S/T] motif antibody, and ERK Thr202/Tyr204 as a pathway-specificity control; in parallel do a gain-of-function arm (ERBB2 overexpression or heregulin stimulation, time course 1-30 min) and an epistasis arm in which AKT1-E17K or wild-type AKT1 is expressed before ERBB2 knockdown. Complement with a pull-down using immobilized ERBB2 phosphopeptides (including pY1139) versus their non-phosphorylated counterparts from the same lysates, blotting for PI3K p85 and other SH2 effectors, to test whether the ERBB2 site itself provides the AKT-activating docking step; loss of AKT Ser473/substrate signal on ERBB2 removal that is rescued by AKT1-E17K supports the hypothesis, while unchanged AKT phosphorylation rules it out.

citations.title: Intrinsic and acquired resistance to HER2-targeted therapies in HER2 gene-amplified breast cancer: mechanisms and clinical implications.

novelty.note: I searched for ERBB2 knockdown/inhibition effects on AKT Ser473, HER2-amplification driving PI3K/AKT, and AKT1-E17K/PI3K-pathway activation bypassing HER2 blockade. The retrieved review explicitly states that HER2 (especially HER2-HER3 heterodimers) potently activates PI3K-AKT, that the antitumor activity of HER2 inhibitors depends on inhibiting PI3K-AKT downstream of HER2, and that gain-of-function AKT1 mutations confer resistance — i.e. AKT activation downstream of ERBB2 and its receptor-independent substitution are both published. Only the specific global phosphoproteomic RxRxx[S/T]-versus-Px[S/T]P motif readout is not directly stated, but the explanation itself is standard.

hypotheses.statement: JAK1 kinase activity directly promotes cell growth (proliferation), such that receptor-coupled, dimerization-dependent JAK1 activation is a growth driver whose loss arrests proliferation in cells whose growth depends on JAK-coupled receptor signaling.
hypotheses.mechanism: Cells carrying JAK1 (or JAK2/RTK) alterations lose viability upon SHP2 inhibition while RAS/BRAF-mutant cells do not (chen2016:findings:012), and in the same system SHP2 blockade suppresses growth only when the proliferative signal is generated upstream, at the receptor-proximal level, in a p-ERK-coupled manner (chen2016:findings:013) — implying that an activated receptor-proximal JAK1 module is itself the proliferative input. Independently, JAK1 is shown to be a receptor-anchored kinase whose activation requires box1/box2 engagement and productive dimerization to become signaling-competent (glassman2022:findings:002), and cells lacking JAK1 fail to transduce gp130/IL-6 receptor signals at all (heinrich2003:findings:022). Together these imply that JAK1 catalytic output, licensed by receptor binding, is a required and sufficient-when-activated generator of the growth signal, rather than an incidental bystander of it.
hypotheses.prediction: Depleting JAK1 or blocking its catalytic activity should reduce proliferation/colony formation specifically in lines whose growth is receptor-proximal (JAK1-altered, SHP099-sensitive) and not in RAS/BRAF-mutant lines; re-expression of wild-type JAK1 should restore growth, kinase-dead JAK1 should not, and a constitutively dimerizing/activated JAK1 (e.g. V657F) should increase growth rate and raise proliferative signaling output (p-STAT3/p-ERK) above wild type.
hypotheses.test: In a JAK1-altered, SHP099-sensitive cell line, perform doxycycline-inducible shRNA or CRISPR knockdown of JAK1 with rescue constructs (wild-type, kinase-dead, and V657F JAK1, plus a box1-binding-deficient variant), and read out growth by colony formation and continuous confluence/growth-curve imaging alongside immunoblots for JAK1 activation-loop phosphorylation, p-STAT3 and p-ERK; a matched BRAF/KRAS-mutant line serves as the specificity control. Growth loss on JAK1 depletion that is rescued by wild-type but not kinase-dead JAK1, and enhanced by V657F, establishes the direct JAK1→growth relationship; unchanged growth across all arms rules it out.

citations.title: Oncogenic JAK1 and JAK2-activating mutations resistant to ATP-competitive inhibitors.
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia-associated JAK1 mutants activate the Janus kinase/STAT pathway via interleukin-9 receptor alpha homodimers.
Structural modeling of JAK1 mutations in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia reveals a second contact site between pseudokinase and kinase domains.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (JAK1 catalytic output as the proliferative signal, receptor-anchored/dimerization-licensed), the entities together (JAK1 V658F, box1/FERM receptor binding, kinase-dead rescue, JAK1 knockdown), and the prediction (JAK1 depletion or catalytic blockade arresting growth; activating JAK1 raising p-STAT output and growth rate). The core explanation is long-published: activating JAK1 pseudokinase mutations (V658F, A634D) confer cytokine-independent autonomous proliferation and constitutive STAT/MAPK signalling, ATP-competitive JAK inhibitors block that growth (resistance requires gatekeeper mutations, i.e. catalytic activity is the growth-generating step), and JAK1 mutant activation strictly requires receptor anchoring via the JAK1 FERM domain and an intact receptor BOX1, with receptor-driven JAK1 homodimerization as the licensing event. Status is established for the JAK1-kinase-activity-as-growth-driver explanation; only the added specificity contrast against SHP099-sensitive versus RAS/BRAF-mutant lines appears untested in the sources retrieved.

hypotheses.statement: ERK2 directly phosphorylates SRC on proline-directed Ser/Thr site(s), attenuating SRC tyrosine-kinase output as a negative-feedback step in the ERK cascade.
hypotheses.mechanism: The ERK2 claims show a consistent pattern in which activated ERK2 directly phosphorylates Ser/Thr residues on the upstream activators that drive it — FGFR1 S777, SOS1 at multiple sites, five Raf-1 residues, MEK1 T292 — and in each case the phosphorylation desensitises the target (shortened FGFR1 tyrosine phosphorylation, loss of SOS1–Grb2/Shc association, loss of Raf-1 membrane/Ras engagement, reduced MEK1 activity and MEK1–ERK2 binding) (lake2016:findings:002, lake2016:findings:003, lake2016:findings:010). The SRC claims place SRC upstream of the same cascade — SRC activation drives RSK2 tyrosine phosphorylation that stabilises ERK1/2–RSK2 binding and RSK2 activation (cargnello2011:findings:059) — and show that SRC's functional output is a large, quantifiable pool of tyrosine-phosphorylated substrates whose number scales with SRC activity (bradley2024:findings:002, bradley2024:findings:014). An upstream activator of the cascade that itself carries Ser/Thr sites is exactly the class of protein ERK2 is documented to phosphorylate back, so ERK2 is predicted to act directly on SRC rather than only through intermediates.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active ERK2 should incorporate phosphate into purified SRC at one or more Ser/Thr-Pro sites in vitro; SRC pre-phosphorylated by ERK2 should show reduced tyrosine-kinase activity toward a generic substrate, and in cells MEK1/2 inhibition should raise SRC-dependent phosphotyrosine signal while a Ser-to-Ala mutant of the ERK2 site should give elevated and prolonged phosphotyrosine output relative to wild-type SRC.
hypotheses.test: Perform an in vitro kinase assay with purified active ERK2 plus recombinant SRC (and kinase-dead SRC to exclude autophosphorylation) using [γ-32P]ATP, map the labelled residues by LC-MS/MS phosphosite mapping, then run a coupled assay in which ERK2-treated versus mock-treated SRC is assayed for tyrosine-kinase activity on a peptide or p130cas-derived substrate; in parallel, express wild-type versus phospho-site-alanine SRC in cultured cells, stimulate, and compare anti-phosphotyrosine (4G10) immunoblot output with and without a MEK1/2 inhibitor.

citations.title: Cdk5 targets active Src for ubiquitin-dependent degradation by phosphorylating Src(S75).
Phosphorylation of Ser-42 and Ser-59 in the N-terminal region of the tyrosine kinase p56lck.
ERK positive feedback regulates a widespread network of tyrosine phosphorylation sites across canonical T cell signaling and actin cytoskeletal proteins in Jurkat T cells.
Modification of Ser59 in the unique N-terminal region of tyrosine kinase p56lck regulates specificity of its Src homology 2 domain.

novelty.note: I searched for ERK/MAPK phosphorylation of SRC on Ser/Thr-Pro sites, for Src serine sites (S17, S72, S75) and their kinases, for ERK-mediated negative feedback on upstream tyrosine kinases, and for MEK-inhibitor feedback activation of SRC. No source states that ERK2 directly phosphorylates SRC itself or that such a phosphorylation attenuates SRC tyrosine-kinase output as ERK-cascade feedback; the documented SRC S75 proline-directed site is assigned to Cdk1/Cdk5, with ERK explicitly absent from that work. Two halves of the idea are published separately: MAP kinase directly phosphorylates the Src-family kinase Lck at the Ser-Pro site Ser59 in vitro (and in cells this acts as ERK-dependent positive, not negative, feedback on tyrosine phosphorylation), and proline-directed phosphorylation of SRC S75 by Cdk5 does restrain SRC Y419 phosphorylation and kinase activity via degradation — hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly tyrosine-phosphorylates p38 on the activation-loop TGY tyrosine, providing a MAP2K-independent route to p38 activation.
hypotheses.mechanism: p38 activity is gated by dual phosphorylation of the Thr and Tyr of the activation-loop Thr-Gly-Tyr motif, canonically installed by MKK3/MKK6 (and MKK4 for p38alpha), so the activating Tyr is an available tyrosine-kinase site (cargnello2011:findings:005, cuadrado2010:findings:000), and p38alpha is already known to acquire activation-loop phosphate non-canonically via TAB1-induced autophosphorylation, showing the site is accessible outside the MAP2K cascade (cuadrado2010:findings:008). Independently, SRC is documented to tyrosine-phosphorylate another protein kinase's catalytic machinery and thereby enhance its activity (derynck2019:findings:013), and active SRC has an unusually broad substrate range, generating over 2000 regulated phosphosites in a heterologous proteome (bradley2024:findings:002). Together these imply SRC could place the activating phosphotyrosine directly on p38, partially activating it without MKK3/6.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC should phosphorylate recombinant unphosphorylated p38alpha specifically on the activation-loop Tyr (Tyr182, the Y of the TGY motif) in vitro, yielding measurable p38 catalytic activity toward a substrate such as ATF2 or MK2 that is increased further by adding MKK6 (Thr180) and abolished in a Y182F mutant; in cells, SRC inhibition or knockdown should reduce basal/stimulated p38 Tyr182 phosphorylation and MK2 phosphorylation even when MKK3/MKK6 are depleted, and SRC gain-of-function should raise p38 Tyr182 phosphorylation without raising Thr180 proportionally.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with purified recombinant active SRC plus bacterially expressed unphosphorylated p38alpha (WT vs Y182F vs T180A), and detect site-specific modification by phospho-Tyr182 immunoblot and by LC-MS/MS mapping of the tryptic activation-loop peptide; couple this to a coupled activity assay measuring p38-dependent phosphorylation of recombinant ATF2 or MK2 with and without SRC and with and without MKK6. Confirm in cultured cells by immunoprecipitating p38alpha after SRC overexpression or PP2/dasatinib treatment (and after siRNA knockdown of MKK3/MKK6) and blotting for Tyr182 versus Thr180 phosphorylation, with a co-immunoprecipitation/in-cell proximity check for SRC-p38 association; absence of Tyr182 labelling in vitro and no loss of Tyr182 signal upon SRC inhibition would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Alternative p38 activation pathway mediated by T cell receptor-proximal tyrosine kinases.
The stress-activated kinase p38 mediates non-canonical activation of Src and tyrosine phosphorylation of the adapter protein TAB1.

novelty.note: Searched for Src phosphorylating p38 activation-loop Tyr182, MAP2K-independent p38 activation, and Src-family/p38 in vitro kinase assays. The published non-canonical tyrosine-kinase route runs through Src-family/Zap70 phosphorylation of p38alpha at Tyr323 (outside the activation loop) followed by autophosphorylation, and one recent study tests the Src-p38 pair but in the reverse direction (p38 phosphorylates Src at Ser75), with no report of SRC placing phosphate directly on Tyr182. So the general idea of a tyrosine kinase driving MAP2K-independent p38 activation is established, but the specific claim of direct SRC phosphorylation of the TGY tyrosine is neither stated nor directly tested and refuted.

hypotheses.statement: SHP2 acts directly upstream of RAS, with its phosphatase activity required to load RAS with GTP at the plasma membrane in receptor-driven signalling, so that SHP2 positively regulates RAS activation.
hypotheses.mechanism: SHP2 loss collapses p-ERK in RTK-driven lines and is rescued only by catalytically active SHP2, while expressing KRASG12V restores p-ERK and abolishes the requirement for SHP2 entirely — an epistasis pattern that places SHP2's action at or above RAS rather than at MEK/ERK (chen2016:findings:003, chen2016:findings:004). Conversely, tethering active SHP2 to membranes via a Gab1-PH fusion is sufficient to drive constitutive MEK1/ERK2 activation (heinrich2003:findings:011), and since ERK1/2 are phosphorylated by MEK1/2 only downstream of Ras-mediated Raf activation (cargnello2011:findings:002), that gain-of-function signal must pass through RAS. Together these imply SHP2 catalytic output converts into increased RAS-GTP, with the plasma membrane the relevant compartment where active RAS accumulates (gest2024:findings:215).
hypotheses.prediction: In an EGFR-amplified, SHP2-dependent line, SHP2 knockdown or SHP099 treatment should reduce RAS-GTP within minutes of growth-factor stimulation and deplete plasma-membrane active-RAS sensor signal, with rescue by wild-type but not SHP2C459S; expressing the Gab1-PH–active-SHP2 fusion should raise RAS-GTP without receptor stimulation, whereas cells expressing KRASG12V should show RAS-GTP and p-ERK that are unchanged by SHP2 inhibition.
hypotheses.test: In MDA-MB-468 (or another EGFR-amplified line), quantify RAS-GTP by GST-Raf1-RBD pulldown followed by pan-RAS/KRAS western blot, and in parallel image translocation of a GFP-tandem-Raf1-RBD sensor, under four conditions: vehicle, SHP099, dox-induced SHP2 shRNA with re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type SHP2 versus SHP2C459S, and transfection of the Gab1-PH–active-SHP2 fusion; run the same panel in cells expressing KRASG12V as the epistasis control. SHP2 inhibition lowering RAS-GTP in a catalysis-dependent manner, and the fusion raising it, supports the relationship; unchanged RAS-GTP with suppressed p-ERK would place SHP2's action below RAS and rule it out.

citations.title: RAS nucleotide cycling underlies the SHP2 phosphatase dependence of mutant BRAF-, NF1- and RAS-driven cancers.
Protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP-2: a proto-oncogene product that promotes Ras activation.
Inhibition of SHP2-mediated dephosphorylation of Ras suppresses oncogenesis.
Mutant KRAS-driven cancers depend on PTPN11/SHP2 phosphatase.

novelty.note: I searched three ways — the mechanism in plain words ("SHP2 catalytic activity required for growth-factor-induced Ras-GTP loading at the plasma membrane"), the entities together (SHP099/SHP2 knockdown + RBD pulldown + EGFR-amplified lines), and the prediction (SHP2 inhibition lowers RAS-GTP; KRASG12V epistasis). The positive, upstream-of-RAS placement of SHP2 with catalysis-dependent promotion of RAS-GTP loading is standard published doctrine: Nichols et al. show RMC-4550 reduces RAS-GTP by disrupting SOS1-mediated RAS-GTP loading and that non-nucleotide-cycling oncogenic RAS (e.g. G12V-type, GAP-insensitive) is refractory to SHP2 inhibition — i.e. the exact epistasis result predicted; Matozaki's review states SHP-2 uniquely promotes Ras-MAPK activation upstream of Ras, and Bunda et al. report SHP2 as a direct activator of Ras, while Ruess et al. confirm SHP2 dependence in KRAS-driven models. Hence established, with the caveat that a 2026 bioRxiv preprint (SHP2–SOS1 binding) disputes the catalytic-activity requirement specifically, so only that sub-clause remains contested rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: SRC kinase activity negatively regulates IFNG (IFNγ) production by T cells, acting as an upstream potentiator of TGF-β receptor signalling that enforces the IFNγ-low, hyporesponsive state.
