hypotheses.test: In serum-starved, EGF-stimulated cultured cells (e.g. HEK-293T or RPE1) expressing FLAG-c-RAF WT, S259A or S259D, treat ±TORKi (and ±rapamycin as an mTORC1-selective control) for 30–120 min, then immunoprecipitate FLAG-c-RAF and read out (i) pS259 by phospho-specific immunoblot, (ii) co-precipitated endogenous 14-3-3, and (iii) in vitro kinase activity of the immunoprecipitate on recombinant kinase-dead MEK1 with anti-pMEK detection, alongside whole-lysate pMEK/pERK; a selective decrease in pS259/14-3-3 with increased RAF activity only in the WT construct supports the hypothesis, while unchanged pS259 and 14-3-3 binding under full mTOR catalytic inhibition rules it out.

citations.title: The PP242 mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor activates extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) in multiple myeloma cells via a target of rapamycin complex 1 (TORC1)/eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF-4E)/RAF pathway and activation is a mechanism of resistance.
The mTOR pathway controls phosphorylation of BRAF at T401.

novelty.note: I searched for (a) mTOR inhibition lowering c-RAF S259/B-RAF S364 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding, (b) mTOR-inhibitor-induced RAF/ERK feedback activation via loss of inhibitory RAF phosphorylation, and (c) mTOR-pathway control of inhibitory RAF sites. The general mechanism is published: Hoang et al. show that the TORKi PP242 (more than rapamycin) increases immunoprecipitated RAF kinase activity and MEK/ERK phosphorylation in myeloma cells, and that this tracks with decreased phosphorylation of the inhibitory RAF residues Ser-289/296/301 — but that same paper explicitly tested the 14-3-3 sites and reports Ser-259 and Ser-621 phosphorylation were unaffected, which contradicts the specific prediction here; a separate study shows the mTORC1/S6K axis sustains a different inhibitory/degron BRAF site (T401) without affecting ERK, and notes S365 as the AKT/14-3-3 site but does not test it under mTOR inhibition. Hence the 'mTOR as negative regulator of RAF via relief of inhibitory phosphorylation' claim is anticipated, while the S259/S364–14-3-3–specific version is not established (and is partly negated).

hypotheses.statement: SYK acts directly upstream of RAS, driving GTP loading of RAS at the plasma membrane in ITAM/C-type-lectin-stimulated myeloid and B cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: SYK signalling downstream of CLEC7A is reported to induce chemokine and cytokine production via ERK (mcsai2010:findings:019), and ERK1/2 are activated only by MEK1/2 phosphorylation of their TEY motif downstream of Ras-mediated Raf activation (cargnello2011:findings:002), so a SYK-initiated ERK response implies SYK-dependent RAS activation. The route is plausible because activated SYK autophosphorylates linker tyrosines (Tyr342/Tyr346) that serve as SH2 docking sites for effectors such as VAV1 and PLCγ1 (mcsai2010:findings:012) and Tyr624 for SLP65 (mcsai2010:findings:013), i.e. SYK's known output is the assembly of SH2-based effector complexes at the membrane, the compartment where active RAS accumulates as reported with tandem-RBD sensors (gest2024:findings:215).
hypotheses.prediction: Receptor stimulation of SYK-competent cells should produce a rapid, SYK-dependent rise in RAS-GTP and plasma-membrane recruitment of a Raf1-RBD sensor that precedes ERK TEY phosphorylation; SYK inhibition, SYK deficiency, kinase-dead SYK, or Y342F/Y346F linker mutants should abolish both the RAS-GTP rise and downstream ERK activation, whereas constitutively active RAS should restore ERK signalling in SYK-null cells.
hypotheses.test: In a SYK-expressing hematopoietic line (or HEK293 reconstituted with an ITAM receptor plus wild-type, kinase-dead, or Y342F/Y346F SYK), stimulate the receptor and quantify RAS-GTP by GST-Raf1-RBD pulldown/immunoblot over a 0–15 min time course alongside live-cell imaging of the tandem GFP-Raf1-RBD translocation sensor, comparing vehicle versus a SYK inhibitor or SYK knockout; blot phospho-ERK TEY in parallel, and rescue SYK-null cells with constitutively active RAS to place RAS downstream of SYK.

citations.title: CARD9 mediates Dectin-1-induced ERK activation by linking Ras-GRF1 to H-Ras for antifungal immunity.
A Ras activation pathway dependent on Syk phosphorylation of protein kinase C.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (SYK acting upstream of RAS-GTP loading), the entities together (Dectin-1/CLEC7A + SYK + Ras + ERK; SYK + Fc receptor + Ras-GTP), and the prediction (SYK inhibition/deficiency abolishing Ras activation and ERK in myeloid and B cells). Two primary papers already state exactly this explanation: Jia et al. (J Exp Med 2014) show that Dectin-1 engagement triggers SYK-dependent Ras-GRF1 phosphorylation which recruits and activates H-Ras (GTP-Ras pulldown assays, piceatannol SYK inhibition blocking both complex formation/Ras activation and ERK phosphorylation) in myeloid antifungal immunity, and Kawakami et al. (PNAS 2003) show SYK phosphorylates conventional PKC isoforms in the membrane compartment of FcεRI-stimulated mast cells, creating a Grb2 SH2 docking site that recruits Grb2/Sos to the plasma membrane for full Ras/ERK activation. Because the SYK→RAS-GTP→ERK causal ordering in ITAM- and C-type-lectin-stimulated cells is published with direct Ras activation assays and SYK loss-of-function, the hypothesis is established rather than novel; only the specific tandem-RBD live-imaging readout is unaddressed.

hypotheses.statement: IFNγ directly activates mTOR (mTORC1) signalling in responding cells, so that mTOR-dependent S6K/4EBP1 translational control is required for the full protein-level output of IFNγ-induced genes.
hypotheses.mechanism: IFNγ priming of macrophages couples SYK to IFNAR to amplify STAT1 activation (ivashkiv2014:findings:003), and signalling through that same IFNAR arm activates PI3K–AKT–mTOR and uses mTOR to promote translation of select interferon-stimulated genes via p70 S6 kinase and eIF4 initiation factors (ivashkiv2014:findings:026); independently, mTOR is shown to act as a selective translational switch for individual proteins through S6K and 4EBP1 (haeusler2018:findings:007), and mTOR activity is directly readable as loss of mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate phosphorylation when the kinase is inhibited (bekkerjensen2020:findings:016). If IFNγ engages the receptor module that feeds mTOR, then IFNγ itself should raise mTOR catalytic output, and IFNγ target genes whose induction is transcriptional should nonetheless depend on mTOR for their protein accumulation.
hypotheses.prediction: IFNγ stimulation should increase phosphorylation of mTOR-motif substrates, p70S6K (T389) and 4EBP1 within minutes to an hour, in a manner reduced by IFNAR blockade or SYK inhibition; rapamycin or an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor should sharply lower IFNγ-induced protein levels of targets such as CXCL9/CXCL10 and STAT1 itself while leaving their STAT1-driven mRNA induction and STAT1 Tyr701 phosphorylation largely intact, i.e. a translational rather than transcriptional block.
hypotheses.test: Treat a cultured macrophage line (e.g. THP-1-derived or immortalized bone-marrow macrophages) with IFNγ over a 0–120 min time course and immunoblot p-mTOR S2448, p-S6K T389, p-S6 and p-4EBP1 alongside p-STAT1, with parallel arms pretreated with torin/rapamycin, an IFNAR-blocking antibody, or a SYK inhibitor; then at 6–24 h compare IFNγ-induced target mRNA (qPCR) against secreted/intracellular protein (ELISA, immunoblot) ± mTOR inhibitor, and confirm the translational step by puromycin-incorporation or polysome fractionation of the target transcripts. Loss of IFNγ-induced mTOR substrate phosphorylation, or equal mRNA with selectively lost protein under mTOR inhibition, supports the relationship; unchanged mTOR substrate phosphorylation after IFNγ plus proportional mRNA/protein loss rules it out.

citations.title: Interferon γ (IFNγ) Signaling via Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 2 (mTORC2) and Regulatory Effects in the Generation of Type II Interferon Biological Responses.
Interferon-γ regulates cellular metabolism and mRNA translation to potentiate macrophage activation.

novelty.note: Searched for IFNγ-driven mTOR activation, mTOR-dependent translation of interferon-stimulated genes, and mTOR inhibitor effects on IFNγ target protein vs mRNA. Kaur/Platanias (JBC 2016) show the type II IFN receptor directly engages mTORC2/AKT and downstream mTORC1 effectors (S6K, 4E-BP1, eIF4F) as required for translation of type II ISGs, and Su et al. (Nat Immunol 2015) show IFNγ targets mTORC1 and MNK to reprogram the macrophage translatome — i.e. the core explanation is published. A PLOS One study qualifies the selectivity claim, finding mTOR inhibition lowers ISG protein mainly via global translational repression rather than ISG-selective control, so the specific CXCL9/CXCL10 selectivity prediction is less firmly established than the general mechanism.

hypotheses.statement: Prolonged rapamycin exposure indirectly de-represses GSK3B, i.e. rapamycin acts as an activator of GSK3β activity in cells by removing AKT-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation of GSK3β, with destabilization of PHLPP as the downstream consequence.
hypotheses.mechanism: The claims about GSK3B state that AKT-mediated inhibition of GSK3β is what keeps GSK3β from phosphorylating PHLPP and triggering its degradation, and that PHLPP translation itself requires mTOR-dependent S6K/4EBP1 signalling (haeusler2018:findings:007). The claims about rapamycin state that FKBP12–rapamycin acutely inhibits mTORC1 but not mTORC2 (laplante2012:findings:001), whereas chronic rapamycin disrupts mTORC2 integrity and blocks mTORC2–AKT output (laplante2012:findings:018). Joining these, chronic rapamycin should lower AKT Ser473-dependent activity and therefore raise GSK3β activity — a time-dependent effect that would be absent in the acute setting, consistent with the observation that simple mTORC2 depletion left GSK3β phosphorylation unaffected (laplante2012:findings:008).
hypotheses.prediction: Acute (1–2 h) rapamycin leaves GSK3β inhibitory Ser9 phosphorylation and GSK3β substrate phosphorylation unchanged while suppressing S6K/4EBP1 readouts, but chronic (24–72 h) rapamycin reduces AKT Ser473 and GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation and increases phosphorylation of GSK3β substrates (e.g. β-catenin Ser33/37/Thr41); PHLPP protein should fall under chronic rapamycin and be partially restored by a selective GSK3 inhibitor or proteasome block, but not by GSK3 inhibition under acute rapamycin.
hypotheses.test: In a standard cell line, run a rapamycin time course (0, 1, 6, 24, 48, 72 h) and immunoblot pAKT-Ser473, pGSK3β-Ser9, pS6K/p4E-BP1, pβ-catenin Ser33/37/Thr41 and total PHLPP; confirm the activity change by immunoprecipitating GSK3β at each time point and assaying it in vitro against a primed peptide substrate, and test causality by repeating the 48 h treatment with a selective GSK3 inhibitor (or GSK3B siRNA) and with constitutively active AKT — the hypothesis requires that chronic-rapamycin-induced substrate phosphorylation and PHLPP loss be reversed by GSK3 inhibition and by AKT rescue, and it is ruled out if GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation and in vitro GSK3β activity are unchanged at all time points.

citations.title: GSK3 is required for rapalogs to induce degradation of some oncogenic proteins and to suppress cancer cell growth.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: prolonged/chronic rapamycin → mTORC2 disruption → Akt Ser473 → GSK3β Ser9 (Sarbassov-type work, podocyte and NSCLC time courses), the GSK3β→PHLPP degradation arm (β-TrCP/CK1 axis), and the joint prediction (rapamycin + PHLPP + GSK3 + proteasome). The component arms are published separately — rapalogs engage GSK3 to drive proteasomal degradation of substrates 'secondary to mTORC2 inhibition' (Koo et al., though they measured slightly *increased* p-GSK3 Ser21/9, not the predicted decrease), and Akt-mediated GSK3β inhibition is known to stabilise PHLPP1 against β-TrCP degradation (Li/Gao) — but no source joins them for rapamycin: the one paper that tested rapamycin on PHLPP attributes the loss to mTOR/S6K/4EBP1-dependent translation and explicitly reports that rapamycin did not change PHLPP degradation kinetics, which is the nearest work and partly counter-indicative. The specific acute-vs-chronic dissociation and GSK3-inhibitor/proteasome rescue of PHLPP under chronic rapamycin appears unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: ERK1 directly phosphorylates EGFR on a proline-directed Ser/Thr site in its cytoplasmic region, acting as a negative-feedback kinase that attenuates EGFR tyrosine autophosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: ERK1 is documented to phosphorylate a receptor tyrosine kinase directly — recombinant ERK1 phosphorylates FGFR1 on S777, and loss of that site prolongs FGF-induced FGFR1 tyrosine phosphorylation and increases proliferation/migration (lake2016:findings:002) — and ERK1 similarly phosphorylates its own upstream activator MEK1 on T292 to dampen the cascade (lake2016:findings:010), showing a general pattern of ERK1 back-phosphorylating upstream components. EGFR is likewise a substrate for Ser/Thr phosphorylation by a MAPK family member, since p38alpha phosphorylates EGFR itself to drive its internalization (cuadrado2010:findings:054), and EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation is sharply transient under constant EGF, decaying to a low pseudo-steady level within minutes (kholodenko2006:findings:001) — kinetics consistent with a fast-acting downstream feedback. Because EGFR activity is required to sustain ERK pathway output (the FIRE reporter decays on EGFR inhibition; albeck2013:findings:000), an ERK1→EGFR phosphorylation event would close this loop directly rather than through the bridge intermediates.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active ERK1 will phosphorylate the purified EGFR cytoplasmic domain in vitro on one or more S/T-P sites; in cells, MEK/ERK inhibition will reduce phosphorylation of that site and prolong/elevate EGF-induced EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation, while a phospho-null (S/T→A) EGFR mutant will show sustained receptor tyrosine phosphorylation and sustained downstream ERK reporter output after EGF, and a phosphomimetic (S/T→D/E) mutant will show blunted, faster-decaying EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Perform an in vitro kinase assay with purified recombinant active ERK1 and the recombinant EGFR intracellular domain (kinase-dead EGFR to exclude autophosphorylation, ±ERK inhibitor control), and map incorporated sites by phosphopeptide LC-MS/MS; then reconstitute EGFR-null or EGFR-knockdown cells with wild-type versus site-alanine and site-phosphomimetic EGFR, stimulate with EGF over a time course ±MEK inhibitor, and quantify EGFR pTyr (anti-pY1068/pY1173 immunoblot) plus site-specific phospho-EGFR antibody signal; an anti-ERK1 co-immunoprecipitation/GST-EGFR-tail pulldown tests direct association. Absence of in vitro site incorporation and no change in EGFR pTyr kinetics in the alanine mutant would rule out the direct relationship.

citations.title: ERK-dependent threonine phosphorylation of EGF receptor modulates receptor downregulation and signaling.
Inverse correlation between Thr-669 and constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation in the asymmetric epidermal growth factor receptor dimer conformation.
Feedback control of ErbB2 via ERK-mediated phosphorylation of a conserved threonine in the juxtamembrane domain.

novelty.note: Searched for ERK-mediated Ser/Thr phosphorylation of EGFR, EGFR Thr669 feedback, and conserved juxtamembrane threonine phosphorylation across ErbB receptors. The published literature already establishes that ERK1/2 directly phosphorylates EGFR on the proline-directed juxtamembrane site Thr669 (an S/T-P site) in an ERK-dependent, MEK-inhibitor-sensitive manner, that this suppresses EGFR tyrosine (auto)phosphorylation and kinase activity, and that T669A mutation removes the feedback — matching the hypothesis statement and core prediction; the mechanism is conserved in ErbB2 (T677) and ErbB4. Status is therefore established.

hypotheses.statement: p38 (p38α) directly activates MTOR-complex signaling as an upstream stress-responsive input, acting through MK2-catalyzed TSC2 Ser1210 phosphorylation, so that p38 activity sets the level of mTOR substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: One line of evidence states that MK2 phosphorylates TSC2 at Ser1210 to promote 14-3-3 binding and may thereby regulate mTOR-dependent protein synthesis (cargnello2011:findings:077), and an independent line establishes that MK2 activation is completely dependent on p38α, which phosphorylates MK2 at Thr222/Ser272/Thr334 (cargnello2011:findings:068). Separately, mTOR pathway activity is read out quantitatively as a coherent set of mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate sites that collapse when mTOR is inhibited (bekkerjensen2020:findings:016). If p38α is the obligate activator of the kinase that inactivates the mTOR inhibitor TSC2, then p38 activity should itself be a determinant of mTOR substrate phosphorylation, i.e. a direct positive regulatory relationship from p38 to mTOR signaling output.
hypotheses.prediction: Stress stimuli that activate p38 should raise mTOR-motif/p70S6K substrate phosphorylation (S6K1 Thr389, rpS6, 4EBP1), and this rise should be abolished by the p38-specific inhibitor SB203580 or by loss of p38α; conversely, expression of constitutively active MKK6 (which activates p38) should increase mTOR substrate phosphorylation. The effect should require the MK2 site on TSC2, i.e. cells expressing TSC2 S1210A should show p38-insensitive mTOR substrate phosphorylation, while TSC2-null cells should show p38-insensitive, constitutively high mTOR output.
hypotheses.test: In cultured cells (e.g. HEK-293T or RPE1), stimulate p38 with sorbitol or anisomycin ± SB203580, and in parallel compare p38α-deficient versus control cells, then immunoblot the mTOR readouts p-S6K1 Thr389, p-rpS6 and p-4EBP1 alongside p-MK2 Thr222 and p-TSC2 Ser1210 as pathway controls; a phosphoproteomic run scored for mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate enrichment gives the same readout globally. Decisive discrimination comes from reconstituting TSC2-null cells with wild-type TSC2 versus TSC2 S1210A: if p38 activation raises mTOR substrate phosphorylation only in the wild-type reconstitution, the direct p38→mTOR regulatory link via Ser1210 is supported; if mTOR readouts are unchanged by p38 activation or inhibition in all backgrounds, the hypothesis is ruled out. A co-immunoprecipitation of TSC2 with 14-3-3 ± SB203580 provides the corresponding interaction test.

citations.title: The p38 and MK2 kinase cascade phosphorylates tuberin, the tuberous sclerosis 2 gene product, and enhances its interaction with 14-3-3.
A role for p38 stress-activated protein kinase in regulation of cell growth via TORC1.
p38 regulates the tumor suppressor PDCD4 via the TSC-mTORC1 pathway.

novelty.note: I searched for the MK2→TSC2 Ser1210→14-3-3 mechanism, for p38/MKK6/SB203580 effects on mTORC1 readouts (S6K1 Thr389, rpS6, 4EBP1), and for p38 as a positive stress input to TORC1. The explanation is already published: Li et al. (2003) identified the p38–MK2 cascade as the kinase pair phosphorylating tuberin Ser1210 to create a 14-3-3 site that sequesters TSC2 from its substrate, thereby relieving inhibition of mTOR; Cully et al. (2010) showed directly that p38-activating stresses (H2O2, anisomycin) activate TORC1 in mammalian and Drosophila cells, that this requires MKK3/6 and p38, and that p38 cascade knockdown blocks the TSC2-depletion growth phenotype; and a 2021 study explicitly frames and tests a p38→MK2→TSC→mTORC1 axis using p38α-deficient cells, catalytically dead MK2 and TSC1/TSC2-null cells with phospho-S6 as the mTORC1 readout. Only the specific discriminating test — reconstitution with TSC2 S1210A — appears untested, and note that Cully et al. attributed the p38→TORC1 step to Rag GTPases rather than TSC2, while a p38β–PRAK route is inhibitory, so the Ser1210 dependence of the p38→mTOR output remains the unsettled part of an otherwise established explanation.

hypotheses.statement: EGFR activity directly dampens IL-17-induced target gene expression by supplying the ERK activity that phosphorylates C/EBPβ downstream of IL-17RA.
hypotheses.mechanism: Live-cell reporter work shows that ERK pathway output in epithelial cells is sustained by EGFR and decays within minutes of EGFR inhibition (albeck2013:findings:000), so EGFR sets the ambient ERK activity available to IL-17-responsive cells. Independently, ERK-mediated (with GSK3β) phosphorylation of C/EBPβ, dependent on the IL-17RA CBAD, correlates with decreased IL-17-induced gene expression, while C/EBP elements are strictly required for IL-17 responsiveness of the Il6 and Lcn2 promoters (gaffen2014:findings:030, gaffen2014:findings:024). If EGFR is the upstream source of that ERK input, EGFR ligand engagement should act as a negative regulator of the IL-17 transcriptional output rather than being neutral to it.
hypotheses.prediction: Co-stimulation with EGF should reduce IL-17-induced Il6/Lcn2/CXCL1 mRNA induction and increase inhibitory phospho-C/EBPβ, while EGFR kinase inhibition during IL-17 stimulation should lower phospho-C/EBPβ and augment IL-17 target gene induction; the effect should be lost in cells expressing a C/EBPβ phospho-site mutant or lacking the IL-17RA CBAD.
hypotheses.test: In an IL-17-responsive adherent line (e.g., HeLa or 3T3/ST2 fibroblasts expressing IL-17RA), treat with IL-17A alone, IL-17A + EGF, and IL-17A + EGFR inhibitor (erlotinib/gefitinib), with an ERK/MEK inhibitor as a positive control; read out IL-17 target genes (IL6, LCN2, CXCL1) by qPCR and reporter assay at 2–6 h, and phospho-ERK and phospho-C/EBPβ by immunoblot at 15–60 min. Decisive controls: repeat in cells reconstituted with a non-phosphorylatable C/EBPβ mutant or with a CBAD-deleted IL-17RA — if EGFR acts through this node, EGF/erlotinib should no longer shift IL-17 target gene output in those cells.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (IL-17RA CBAD / ERK+GSK3β phosphorylation of C/EBPβ as a negative regulator), the entities together (EGF/EGFR + IL-17 + C/EBPβ + ERK in epithelial cells/keratinocytes), and the prediction (EGFR inhibitor or EGF co-stimulation shifting IL-17-induced IL6/LCN2/CXCL1). The ERK→C/EBPβ-Thr188/Thr179 inhibitory arm of IL-17RA signaling is fully published (Shen et al., Sci Signal 2009, the primary source behind the corpus claims), but no source attributes that ERK input to EGFR or frames EGFR as a brake on IL-17 transcriptional output; the closest direct test of the prediction (Dai et al. 2022) reports the opposite direction — EGFR ligands synergize with IL-17A to increase psoriasis signature gene expression via IκBζ and Bcl3, with EGFR inhibition reducing rather than augmenting induction, and no involvement of C/EBPβ phosphorylation. Hence partial: the downstream mechanism is established, the EGFR-as-ERK-source connection and its predicted negative-regulatory consequence are not (and are empirically challenged).

hypotheses.statement: IL-17 activates EGFR in trans by driving p38-dependent ADAM17/TACE phosphorylation and shedding of EGFR ligands.
hypotheses.mechanism: IL-17 signalling through ACT1/TRAF6 activates the canonical MAPK module including p38 (gaffen2014:findings:022). Separately, p38 MAPKs phosphorylate TACE/ADAM17 at Thr735 in response to inflammatory stimuli, and this phosphorylation is required for ectodomain shedding of TGFα-family ligands and consequent EGFR signalling and proliferation (cuadrado2010:findings:029); inflammatory cytokines also drive p38α-dependent phosphorylation and internalization of EGFR itself (cuadrado2010:findings:054). Together these imply that IL-17, as a p38-activating inflammatory input, should be sufficient to transactivate EGFR through the TACE/ligand-shedding route.
hypotheses.prediction: IL-17A stimulation of IL-17RA-expressing epithelial cells should produce a delayed (15–60 min) rise in EGFR autophosphorylation and EGFR-dependent ERK activity that is abolished by p38 inhibition, by ADAM17 inhibition/knockdown, or by an EGFR ligand-neutralizing antibody, and conditioned medium from IL-17-treated cells should activate EGFR in naive reporter cells; ACT1-deficient cells should show no such EGFR transactivation.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate IL-17RA-positive epithelial cells with IL-17A ± SB203580 (p38), ± TAPI-1/ADAM17 siRNA, ± erlotinib, and immunoblot for pEGFR (Y1068), pERK and TACE Thr735 phosphorylation over a 0–90 min time course; in parallel, ELISA the conditioned medium for shed TGFα/amphiregulin and transfer it onto serum-starved reporter cells to test whether the pEGFR response is ligand-mediated, using ACT1-knockdown cells to confirm the signal originates from the IL-17 receptor complex.

novelty.note: I searched for IL-17/EGFR transactivation, IL-17 with ADAM17/TACE and EGFR-ligand shedding, and p38-Thr735-ADAM17 shedding, using Google/PubMed (eutils) and Europe PMC, and opened the primary hits. Both halves are published separately: p38α phosphorylates TACE on Thr735 to drive TGFα-family shedding and EGFR-dependent proliferation (PMID 20188673), and IL-17A does transactivate EGFR in an Act1-dependent manner — but the published mechanism is Act1-recruited c-Src acting on the IL-17R–EGFR complex, not p38/ADAM17-mediated ligand shedding (PMID 30578323); the closest IL-17→sheddase link activates ADAM17 through Nox1/H2O2 in Paneth progenitors without invoking p38 or EGFR-ligand shedding (PMID 41844615), while a psoriasis review only asserts in passing that IL-17A accelerates amphiregulin cleavage and that IL-17R can activate EGFR via TGF-α/HB-EGF, with no ADAM17/p38 machinery or transfer/conditioned-medium test. Hence the p38→ADAM17 Thr735→shed-ligand→trans-EGFR route for IL-17, and the predicted p38/ADAM17/ligand-neutralization dependence, appear unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly tyrosine-phosphorylates SOS1, and this modification weakens the GRB2–SOS1 association that nucleates pLAT–GRB2–SOS1 condensates.
hypotheses.mechanism: SOS1 is already established as a multi-site phospho-substrate whose modification acts as a switch on adaptor binding: ERK2 phosphorylation of SOS1 at multiple sites disrupts its association with Grb2 and Shc (lake2016:findings:003), and SOS1's function in LAT clustering depends strictly on its GRB2-mediated engagement, since clustering in vitro requires both Grb2 and Sos1 (su2016:findings:001). SRC is characterised in this corpus as an exceptionally promiscuous tyrosine kinase, with v-SRC generating over 2000 regulated phosphosites in a heterologous proteome (bradley2024:findings:002), and Src-family kinases are shown to phosphorylate the cytoplasmic regions of scaffold/adaptor-coupled proteins on multiple tyrosines to control SH2/SH3 adaptor engagement (case2019a:findings:011). Together these imply SOS1's proline-rich/adaptor-binding region is a direct SRC substrate whose tyrosine phosphorylation should tune GRB2 occupancy in the same way serine/threonine phosphorylation does.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified recombinant SRC plus ATP will incorporate phosphate into SOS1 at mappable tyrosine residues (4G10-reactive band, MS-identified pY sites, absent with kinase-dead SRC or ATP omission), and SRC-phosphorylated SOS1 will show reduced GRB2 binding in pulldown and reduced partitioning into pLAT–GRB2–SOS1 clusters on supported bilayers; tyrosine-to-phenylalanine substitution of the mapped sites, or SRC inhibition, will restore both GRB2 binding and clustering.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with purified recombinant SRC (WT vs kinase-dead) and purified full-length SOS1 (or its C-terminal proline-rich fragment), detect phosphorylation by anti-phosphotyrosine immunoblot and map sites by LC-MS/MS; then take mock- and SRC-phosphorylated SOS1 into (i) a GST-GRB2 pulldown/co-IP quantified by immunoblot and (ii) the reconstituted His-pLAT + GRB2 + fluorescent SOS1 supported-lipid-bilayer assay imaged by TIRF, comparing SOS1 recruitment and cluster area against non-phosphorylatable Y→F SOS1 as the specificity control.

novelty.note: I searched for SRC phosphorylation of SOS1, SOS1 tyrosine phosphosites affecting Grb2 binding, and tyrosine phosphorylation regulating LAT/EGFR–Grb2–SOS condensates. Tyrosine phosphorylation of SOS1 is established (Y1196 by BCR-ABL, promoting RAC GEF activity, not reducing Grb2 binding), and phosphorylation-driven disruption of the Grb2–SOS1 interaction is established only for ERK/MAPK serine-threonine sites; I found no source stating that SRC phosphorylates SOS1 to weaken GRB2 binding or to dissolve pLAT–GRB2–SOS1 condensates. Hence partial: the component mechanisms are published separately but not this connection or prediction.

hypotheses.statement: S6K1 (RPS6KB1) negatively regulates JNK activation, such that high S6K1 activity dampens stress-induced JNK/c-Jun phosphorylation and loss of S6K1 activity potentiates it.
hypotheses.mechanism: The S6K1 evidence states that S6K1 output feeds back onto AKT: S6K1 phosphorylates Rictor (T1135) and Sin1 (T86/T398) to decrease mTORC2-dependent AKT S473 phosphorylation (manning2017:findings:021), and S6K-dependent translation of PHLPP further lowers AKT S473, with AKT in turn restraining GSK3β (haeusler2018:findings:007). The JNK evidence independently states that GSK3β suppresses JNK activation by phosphorylating the MAPKKK MEKK4 (cuadrado2010:findings:036), and that MEKK-class MAPKKKs are the proximal activators feeding JNK (jaffe2005:findings:008). Combining only what each side states, higher S6K1 activity should lower AKT S473, leave GSK3β more active, and thereby hold MEKK-dependent JNK activation down — i.e. S6K1 acts as a negative regulator of JNK.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic loss of S6K1 activity (PF-4708671 or siRNA) should increase the amplitude and/or duration of anisomycin- or TNFα-induced phospho-JNK and phospho-c-Jun (S63/S73), accompanied by increased AKT S473 and increased inhibitory GSK3β Ser9 phosphorylation; conversely, expressing constitutively active/rapamycin-resistant S6K1 should blunt JNK and c-Jun phosphorylation. The potentiation should be occluded when GSK3β is independently inhibited (e.g. CHIR-99021), placing the S6K1 effect on JNK in the same arm as GSK3β rather than in parallel.
hypotheses.test: In HEK-293 or 3T3 cells, knock down S6K1 (or treat with PF-4708671) versus control, stimulate with anisomycin or TNFα over a 0–120 min time course, and quantify phospho-JNK (T183/Y185), phospho-c-Jun (S63/S73), AKT S473 and GSK3β S9 by quantitative immunoblot; in parallel, read JNK activity in single living cells with the Jun(29-84)-Clover translocation reporter, which reports JNK activity without perturbing endogenous c-Jun signalling (regot2014:findings:000, regot2014:findings:001). Repeat the S6K1 perturbation in the presence of a GSK3β inhibitor and with a non-phosphorylatable MEKK4 background: if the S6K1-dependent change in JNK activation disappears under GSK3β inhibition, the proposed S6K1→AKT/GSK3β→JNK regulation is supported; if S6K1 loss leaves JNK and c-Jun phosphorylation unchanged at all time points, the relationship is ruled out.

novelty.note: I searched for S6K1/RPS6KB1 as a negative regulator of JNK, for S6K1 knockdown/PF-4708671 effects on phospho-JNK and phospho-c-Jun, and for the proposed AKT-S473→GSK3β→MEKK4 route. The core explanation and its central prediction are already published: Chen et al. show that both S6K1 siRNA knockdown and PF-4708671 increase JNK and c-Jun phosphorylation (dose-dependently), and that S6K1 negatively regulates JNK via TAK1, consistent with Kim et al., where S6K1-knockdown cells show increased TAK1 phosphorylation and downstream p38/JNK activation. The published route is TAK1–TAB1, not the hypothesised AKT/GSK3β/MEKK4 arm; indeed Zhang et al. report that S6K1 directly phosphorylates GSK3 Ser9 (inhibiting GSK3) under mTORC1-dependent AKT feedback, the opposite sign to the proposed mechanism, so the specific GSK3β-occlusion prediction remains untested.

hypotheses.statement: 14-3-3 directly antagonizes GSK3B activity on shared substrates by occupying and burying the priming phosphoserine/phosphothreonine that GSK3B requires for substrate recognition, making 14-3-3 and GSK3B mutually competitive binders of the same phosphosite.
hypotheses.mechanism: The corpus states that 14-3-3 proteins act by masking substrate phosphosites (bollen2010:findings:022) and that binding buries the phosphoserine deep in the dimer channel through salt bridges to Arg-56, Arg-127 and Lys-49 and a hydrogen bond to Tyr-128 (yaffe1997:findings:009), so an occupied phosphosite is sterically and electrostatically unavailable to other readers. GSK3 is explicitly a phospho-priming kinase that selects an upstream phosphorylated Thr/Ser as its preferred motif residue (johnson2023:findings:003), and isolated phospho-PPPSPxS peptides are sufficient to directly inhibit GSK3 phosphorylation of β-catenin in vitro (macdonald2009:findings:017), showing that GSK3B engagement depends on a free, accessible priming phosphate. Two proteins that read the same phosphate with high affinity must compete, predicting that 14-3-3 loading onto a primed site blocks GSK3B catalysis and, conversely, that 14-3-3 can sequester inhibitory phosphopeptides away from GSK3B.
hypotheses.prediction: Adding recombinant 14-3-3 to an in vitro GSK3B reaction on a pre-primed substrate will suppress GSK3B-dependent phosphorylation in a dose-dependent, saturable manner, with the degree of suppression tracking 14-3-3 affinity for the priming site; unprimed or 14-3-3-nonbinding substrates, and phosphate-pocket-dead 14-3-3 (K49/R56/R127 mutant), will show no inhibition, and excess 14-3-3 will relieve the inhibition of GSK3B caused by free primed phosphopeptides.
hypotheses.test: Run parallel in vitro kinase assays with recombinant GSK3B and a primed peptide/protein substrate (e.g. a CK1-preprimed β-catenin fragment and a primed PPPSPxS peptide), titrating recombinant 14-3-3ζ versus the phosphate-binding-pocket mutant, and quantify GSK3B-dependent phosphorylation by phospho-specific immunoblot or 32P incorporation; in parallel, run a fluorescence-polarization competition using a fluorescein-labelled primed phosphopeptide to show that 14-3-3 and catalytically dead GSK3B displace each other from the same phosphosite, and confirm in cells by immunoprecipitating the substrate after 14-3-3 knockdown or difopein expression and blotting the GSK3B-site phosphorylation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (14-3-3 masking a priming phosphate / occluding a phosphosite from a kinase), the entities together (14-3-3 + GSK3 + priming site + competition, incl. PubMed queries that returned zero hits), and the prediction (dose-dependent 14-3-3 inhibition of GSK3 in vitro kinase assays, difopein/knockdown in cells). The general half is published — 14-3-3 occupancy of a phosphosite is an established occlusion/protection mechanism (e.g. 14-3-3γ binding shields DAPK2 pSer318/pThr369 from dephosphorylation and blocks CaM access), and free phosphoprimed peptides are known to inhibit GSK-3 in vitro — and the overlap between mode-II 14-3-3 motifs and the GSK3 (S/T)XXX(pS/T) consensus has been noted (GPSM3 Ser35), but there I found no claim of competition; in that case GSK3-type phosphorylation instead creates the 14-3-3 site. The nearest work on a genuinely shared primed site (tau pSer214) reports the opposite of the hypothesis: 14-3-3 binding scaffolds and stimulates GSK3β phosphorylation of tau rather than blocking it, so the specific mutual-exclusivity prediction is unpublished and partly contradicted.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B directly phosphorylates PTEN on a primed Ser/Thr phosphodegron, destabilizing PTEN protein and lowering its PIP3-phosphatase output, so that AKT-mediated inhibition of GSK3B stabilizes PTEN.
hypotheses.mechanism: The GSK3B evidence shows a recurring mode of action in which GSK3B phosphorylates a substrate to create an E3-ligase recognition site and trigger its proteasomal destruction (β-catenin Ser33/37 → β-Trcp; Smad linker → Nedd4L/Smurf1), and specifically that GSK3B phosphorylates the AKT-opposing phosphatase PHLPP to trigger its degradation, with AKT inhibition of GSK3B stabilizing that phosphatase (haeusler2018:findings:007, macdonald2009:findings:008); GSK3B substrates characteristically require an upstream priming phosphorylation (johnson2023:findings:003). The PTEN evidence independently establishes that PTEN is the PIP3 phosphatase opposing PI3K (manning2017:findings:002) and that PTEN protein abundance is set post-translationally by covalent modification leading to ubiquitination and degradation (fruman2017:findings:048). Placing PTEN in the same GSK3B-phosphodegron class as PHLPP predicts a direct kinase–substrate relationship that would make PTEN levels, like PHLPP levels, an AKT→GSK3B-controlled negative feedback node on PI3K signaling.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant GSK3B should phosphorylate purified PTEN in vitro on one or more primed Ser/Thr sites; in cells, GSK3 inhibition or GSK3A/GSK3B deletion should raise steady-state PTEN protein and lengthen its half-life while reducing its polyubiquitination, whereas GSK3B overexpression should lower PTEN protein and raise PIP3-dependent AKT phosphorylation, and a PTEN mutant with the GSK3B site(s) mutated to Ala should be stable and insensitive to GSK3B manipulation.
hypotheses.test: Two-part biochemical/cell assay: (1) in vitro kinase reaction of recombinant GSK3B with purified recombinant PTEN (assay buffer containing 10 mM DTT to keep PTEN intact), with and without pre-priming by CK1, read out by ³²P incorporation and phosphosite mapping by LC-MS/MS, using kinase-dead GSK3B and a GSK3 inhibitor as controls; (2) in HeLa or RPE1 cells, treat with a selective GSK3 inhibitor or knock down GSK3B by siRNA and perform cycloheximide-chase immunoblotting of endogenous PTEN plus anti-PTEN immunoprecipitation/anti-ubiquitin blotting, then repeat with re-expressed wild-type versus phosphosite-Ala PTEN to confirm the mapped site(s) account for the stability change and for the accompanying change in phospho-AKT Ser473.

citations.title: Cooperative phosphorylation of the tumor suppressor phosphatase and tensin homologue (PTEN) by casein kinases and glycogen synthase kinase 3beta.
PTEN is destabilized by phosphorylation on Thr366.
A partnership with the proteasome; the destructive nature of GSK3.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (GSK3β phosphorylating PTEN to trigger its degradation), for the entities together (GSK3β + PTEN + CK2 priming + Thr366), and for the prediction (GSK3 inhibition/mutation raising PTEN protein levels and ubiquitination-dependent turnover). Al-Khouri et al. (JBC 2005) show recombinant GSK3β directly phosphorylates purified PTEN at Ser362 and Thr366, that prior CK2 phosphorylation of Ser370 strongly primes Thr366 phosphorylation, that GSK3 phosphorylates PTEN in intact cells (RNAi), and explicitly propose GSK3β as feedback regulation of PTEN; Maccario et al. (Biochem J 2007) show that blocking Thr366 phosphorylation by mutation or GSK3 inhibition stabilizes PTEN protein, i.e. the phosphorylation destabilizes PTEN. Together these state the same primed-site, GSK3B-dependent PTEN destabilization explanation, including the phosphosite-Ala stability prediction, so the hypothesis is already published (only the specific β-TrCP-type phosphodegron/polyubiquitination step and the explicit AKT→GSK3→PTEN loop quantification remain less directly demonstrated).

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR1 (TβRI) kinase activity directly and negatively regulates IFNG production in activated CD4+ T cells, i.e. TGFBR1 is the signal-transducing node required for suppression of IFNγ.
hypotheses.mechanism: TGF-β pretreatment of antigen-specific CD4+ T cells blunts IFN-γ production without increasing apoptosis, and TGF-β-conditioned suppressor T cells reduce antigen-specific IFN-γ output (chen2003:findings:002, chen2003:findings:019). The receptor claims establish that TGF-β signal transduction is executed by TβRI: TGF-β1/β3 are captured by TβRII, which then recruits the low-affinity TβRI, and phosphorylation of the TβRI GS domain is itself sufficient to activate downstream signalling (derynck2019:findings:004, hata2016:findings:004). Together these imply that the cytokine-level repression of IFNG is carried specifically by TβRI kinase engagement rather than by ligand binding to TβRII alone.
hypotheses.prediction: In T cells stimulated through the TCR, adding TGF-β will lower IFNG mRNA and secreted IFNγ, and this suppression will be abolished by TβRI kinase inhibition, TGFBR1 knockout, or a GS-domain phosphorylation-deficient TβRI, while ligand binding to TβRII remains intact; conversely, expression of a constitutively active GS-domain TβRI mutant will suppress IFNG even without added TGF-β.
hypotheses.test: In a TCR-responsive T cell line (e.g. Jurkat or EL4) stimulated with plate-bound anti-CD3/anti-CD28 with or without TGF-β1, compare parental cells, CRISPR TGFBR1-knockout cells, cells treated with the TβRI kinase inhibitor SB-431542, and knockout cells reconstituted with either wild-type TβRI or a GS-domain (T204D-type constitutively active, or phospho-deficient) mutant; read out IFNG transcription by qRT-PCR and an IFNG-promoter luciferase reporter and secreted IFNγ by ELISA, with anti-pSmad2/3 immunoblot confirming receptor status. Loss of TGF-β-dependent IFNG repression in TGFBR1-null or kinase-inhibited cells, and repression by the constitutively active receptor alone, would establish the direct regulatory link; retained repression in TGFBR1-null cells would rule it out.
