novelty.note: I searched for direct TβRI/ALK5 phosphorylation of Smad1, for the L45–L3 receptor–Smad interface and the two-residue L3 swap, and for the prediction that constitutively active TβRI engages and C-terminally phosphorylates Smad1. Wrighton et al. (JBC 2009) report exactly this explanation: constitutively active ALK5 co-precipitates with FLAG-Smad1, directly phosphorylates GST-Smad1 at the SXS motif in vitro (SB431542-sensitive, BMP-receptor-independent), and the authors explicitly note ALK5 can contact Smad1 'despite the assumed incompatible L45–L3 pairing'; Liu et al. (EMBO J 2009) independently show kinase- and L45-loop-dependent (D266A) direct ALK5 phosphorylation of GST-Smad1/5, and Lo et al. (EMBO J 1998) established that swapping the two L3 residues between Smad1 and Smad2 gains/loses TGF-β receptor association and switches which receptor phosphorylates them. Since the mechanism, the interface determinant and the key prediction are all already published, the status is established; an alternative indirect route (TβRI phosphorylating ACVR1, which then phosphorylates SMAD1/5) is cited as the nearest competing account.

hypotheses.statement: TSC2 negatively regulates RICTOR phosphorylation at Thr1135 and thereby restrains mTORC2-dependent AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, so loss of TSC2 function directly suppresses RICTOR-dependent mTORC2 output.
hypotheses.mechanism: Depletion of TSC2 raises basal and insulin-stimulated S6K phosphorylation and activity without changing AKT Ser473 input signals (inoki2002:findings:004, inoki2002:findings:005), and S6K1 phosphorylation of RICTOR at Thr1135 selectively lowers mTORC2-dependent AKT Ser473 phosphorylation while sparing other mTORC2 substrate sites such as AKT Thr450 (manning2017:findings:021). Since RICTOR is the mTORC2-specific subunit required for AKT Ser473 phosphorylation in every cell line tested (sarbassov2005:findings:003, sarbassov2005:findings:005), the TSC2 status of a cell should set the phosphorylation state of RICTOR and hence mTORC2 activity toward AKT. The converse direction is not proposed, because mTORC2 loss leaves TSC2 phosphorylation unaffected (liu2020:findings:008).
hypotheses.prediction: TSC2-depleted or TSC2-null cells should show increased RICTOR Thr1135 phosphorylation and reduced AKT Ser473 (but not Thr450) phosphorylation relative to TSC2-replete controls, with both changes reversed by blocking S6K activity and abolished when RICTOR Thr1135 is mutated to alanine.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293 cells (and TSC2-null versus wild-type MEFs), knock down TSC2 by siRNA and immunoblot phospho-RICTOR Thr1135, phospho-AKT Ser473, phospho-AKT Thr450 and phospho-S6K Thr389 under serum-starved and insulin-stimulated conditions; then repeat with rapamycin or the S6K1 inhibitor PF-4708671, and in cells whose endogenous RICTOR is replaced by shRNA-resistant wild-type or T1135A RICTOR, to test whether the TSC2-dependent change in AKT Ser473 requires the RICTOR Thr1135 site.

citations.title: Characterization of Rictor phosphorylation sites reveals direct regulation of mTOR complex 2 by S6K1.
mTORC1-activated S6K1 phosphorylates Rictor on threonine 1135 and regulates mTORC2 signaling.
The TSC1-TSC2 complex is required for proper activation of mTOR complex 2.

novelty.note: I searched for the S6K1–Rictor Thr1135 feedback mechanism, for the combination of TSC2 loss with Rictor T1135 and AKT S473, and for the prediction that TSC2-deficient cells have impaired mTORC2 output. Dibble, Asara & Manning (2009) explicitly show that stable TSC2 knockdown produces constitutive, growth-factor-independent Rictor T1135 phosphorylation, that this site is phosphorylated by S6K1 (S6K1 siRNA and rapamycin reduce it), and that the T1135A mutant increases AKT S473 phosphorylation without affecting AKT T450, SGK1 or PKCα; Julien et al. (2010) independently report the same S6K1→Rictor T1135→reduced mTORC2-dependent AKT phosphorylation axis, and Huang et al. (2008) report that TSC2-null cells have impaired mTORC2 kinase activity toward AKT S473. The explanation and its component predictions are therefore already published, with the caveat that Huang et al. and Dibble et al. conclude the bulk of the mTORC2 defect in TSC2-deficient cells is mTORC1/S6K-independent rather than attributable to T1135.

hypotheses.statement: PKC directly phosphorylates the TGFBR2 (TβRII) cytoplasmic kinase domain on an inhibitory serine/threonine site, attenuating TβRII autophosphorylation-dependent kinase activity and thereby dampening TGF-β signaling.
hypotheses.mechanism: The corpus states that PKC directly phosphorylates the cytoplasmic regions of other receptor kinases to shut them down — Thr654 in the EGFR juxtamembrane domain, abolishing high-affinity ligand binding, and Thr1160 in the insulin receptor activation loop, impairing IR autophosphorylation — establishing PKC as a negative-feedback kinase acting on receptor kinase domains (lemmon2010:findings:021, haeusler2018:findings:003). Independently, TβRII kinase output is set by serine phosphorylation of its cytoplasmic domain, with Ser213/Ser249 (Ser409) phosphorylation enhancing and Ser416 phosphorylation attenuating activity, and additional activity control by heterologous kinases such as Src, so TβRII is intrinsically phospho-regulatable by a Ser/Thr kinase (derynck2019:findings:013, hata2016:findings:002). PKC is moreover placed at the TGF-β receptor complex itself, since TRAF6 recruits PKC-ζ to TβRI where it controls receptor localization, giving PKC physical access to the partner receptor TβRII (hata2016:findings:008).
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant PKC should phosphorylate the purified TβRII cytoplasmic domain in vitro at one or more Ser/Thr residues matching PKC's basic (R/K at −2/−3) site preference; in cells, PKC activation (e.g. phorbol ester or DAG analogue) should increase TβRII phosphostoichiometry at an inhibitory site, reduce TβRII autophosphorylation at the activating Ser213/Ser409 sites and reduce TβRII-dependent transphosphorylation of TβRI and downstream Smad3 phosphorylation, while PKC inhibition or knockdown should raise them — all without the loss of cell-surface TβRII that would indicate an indirect trafficking or shedding effect (TβRII being the receptor the corpus reports is not TACE-cleaved).
hypotheses.test: Two-part in vitro/cell-based assay: (1) incubate purified recombinant active PKC with a bacterially expressed GST-TβRII cytoplasmic domain (kinase-dead K277R version to exclude autophosphorylation) plus [γ-32P]ATP, and map sites by phosphopeptide LC-MS/MS; then mutate identified sites to Ala and confirm loss of PKC-dependent 32P incorporation. (2) In transfected HEK293/COS-1 cells co-expressing tagged TβRII and TβRI, treat with PMA versus a specific PKC inhibitor (or PKCζ siRNA), immunoprecipitate TβRII and assay (a) site-specific phosphorylation by phospho-MS, (b) TβRII kinase activity as transphosphorylation of co-precipitated TβRI, and (c) TGF-β-induced Smad3 phosphorylation by Western blot, with surface biotinylation as a control for receptor abundance; the phospho-site Ala mutant should be refractory to the PMA effect if the relationship is direct.

citations.title: Regulation of Smad signaling by protein kinase C.
Post-translational regulation of TGF-β receptor and Smad signaling.

novelty.note: I searched for PKC phosphorylation of the TβRII cytoplasmic domain, for PKC/Ser416/TGFBR2 kinase attenuation, and for phorbol-ester suppression of TβRII-dependent Smad3 phosphorylation. Published work places PKC downstream of the receptor — PKC directly phosphorylates Smad3/Smad2 in their MH1 domain and blocks DNA binding (Yakymovych et al.), and reviews of TβRII phospho-regulation attribute Ser213/Ser409/Ser416 to autophosphorylation and tyrosine sites to Src, with no report of PKC acting on the TβRII kinase domain. No source states this explanation and none reports a direct negative test of it, so the claim remains open.

hypotheses.statement: TSC2 is a direct substrate of the ubiquitin–26S proteasome catabolic pathway, and its degradation is gated not by ubiquitylation alone but by loss of TSC1 occupancy, which exposes a degradation-initiation region in TSC2.
hypotheses.mechanism: Phosphomimetic substitution of the Akt sites in TSC2 both weakens TSC1 binding (inoki2002:findings:012) and renders TSC2 short-lived in cycloheximide chase with elevated ubiquitin conjugation under MG132 (inoki2002:findings:013), so the same modification that dissociates the complex is what commits TSC2 to proteolysis. Independently, efficient 26S degradation is reported to require both a ubiquitin chain and a loosely folded initiation region of ≥30 varied, hydrophobic-biased residues (collins2017:findings:001, collins2017:findings:011), and a tightly folded/ligand-bound substrate can be ubiquitylated and proteasome-bound yet fail to progress to the committed, degraded state (collins2017:findings:010). Together these imply TSC1 acts on TSC2 the way a stabilizing ligand acts on DHFR: it does not prevent ubiquitylation but occludes or rigidifies the unstructured segment the proteasome needs to engage.
hypotheses.prediction: TSC1 co-expression (or added recombinant TSC1) should prolong TSC2 half-life and slow its in vitro proteasomal turnover without proportionally reducing TSC2 ubiquitylation or its ubiquitin-dependent binding to the 26S; conversely, phosphomimetic or TSC1-binding-deficient TSC2 should be degraded faster, and deleting a candidate ≥30-residue unstructured hydrophobic-biased stretch in TSC2 should stabilize it even when fully ubiquitylated.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293 cells, express HA-TSC2 (wild type, Akt-site alanine, Akt-site phosphomimetic, and an internal unstructured-segment deletion) with or without Myc-TSC1 and Flag-ubiquitin; measure half-life by cycloheximide chase, ubiquitylation by anti-HA IP/anti-Flag blot ± MG132, and then reconstitute the step directly: immunopurify ubiquitylated HA-TSC2 and incubate with purified 26S proteasomes ± recombinant TSC1, scoring substrate loss and proteasome association separately. Faster degradation with unchanged proteasome binding upon TSC1 removal, and rescue of stability by deleting the unstructured segment, supports the hypothesis; equal in vitro degradation rates across all conditions rules it out.

citations.title: Degron masking outlines degronons, co-degrading functional modules in the proteome.
An unstructured initiation site is required for efficient proteasome-mediated degradation.
The tuberous sclerosis-1 (TSC1) gene product hamartin suppresses cell growth and augments the expression of the TSC2 product tuberin by inhibiting its ubiquitination.
TSC1 stabilizes TSC2 by inhibiting the interaction between TSC2 and the HERC1 ubiquitin ligase.
WD40 protein FBW5 promotes ubiquitination of tumor suppressor TSC2 by DDB1-CUL4-ROC1 ligase.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (a) TSC1/hamartin stabilization of TSC2/tuberin via the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, (b) the biophysical mechanism (ubiquitin chain plus an unstructured ≥30-residue degradation-initiation region, ligand-stabilized DHFR bound but not degraded), and (c) the prediction in terms of partner-mediated masking of a disordered proteasome-engagement segment. Both halves are separately published: TSC2 is an established ubiquitin–proteasome substrate whose turnover is suppressed by TSC1 binding (Benvenuto 2000; Chong-Kopera 2006 via HERC1 exclusion; Hu 2008 via FBW5–DDB1–CUL4, where TSC1 co-expression abrogates degradation), and the requirement for an accessible unstructured initiation site, plus the general idea that partner binding stabilizes substrates by masking the 'tertiary degron' (disordered proteasomal entry site), is stated by Prakash 2004 and Guharoy 2022. No source applies the initiation-region/occlusion model to TSC2, and the existing TSC2 papers attribute TSC1's protection to reduced ubiquitylation (TSC1-bound tuberin is reportedly unubiquitinated), i.e. the specific prediction of unchanged ubiquitylation with blocked post-ubiquitylation commitment is neither stated nor tested — hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: JAK1 acts directly upstream of AKT, with receptor-bound JAK1 kinase activity required for TGF-β-induced PI3K/AKT activation in fibroblasts.
hypotheses.mechanism: JAK1 is described as constitutively associated with TβRI and as directly driving STAT3 signalling from that receptor in fibroblasts (derynck2019:findings:034), while AKT activation downstream of the same receptor is reported to proceed through p85/PI3K association with TβRII/TβRI (derynck2019:findings:032) — placing an active tyrosine kinase and the p85 recruitment step on the same receptor complex. The JAK1 structure shows the FERM-SH2 module clamped on the receptor Box1/Box2 segment with the tyrosine kinase domains positioned at the base of the assembly with outward-facing, accessible catalytic clefts (glassman2022:findings:003, glassman2022:findings:004), i.e. geometrically able to phosphorylate receptor-proximal substrates other than the receptor tail itself, such as tyrosines that create p85 SH2 docking sites. If so, loss of JAK1 should blunt AKT output, readable as loss of the AKT-dependent phosphorylation and cytoplasmic retention of FKHRL1/FOXO3a that occurs in fibroblasts only when Akt is active (brunet1999:findings:007).
hypotheses.prediction: In fibroblasts, JAK1 depletion or catalytic inhibition should reduce TGF-β- (and IL-6/gp130-) stimulated AKT Ser473/Thr308 phosphorylation and p85 co-precipitation with the receptor complex, and should keep FKHRL1 nuclear after stimulation; JAK1 re-expression in JAK1-deficient cells should restore AKT phosphorylation and FKHRL1 nuclear exclusion, whereas kinase-dead JAK1 should not. If JAK1 and AKT are not directly coupled, TGF-β-induced pAKT should be unchanged by JAK1 loss even where STAT3 activation is abolished.
hypotheses.test: Use JAK1-deficient human fibrosarcoma cells versus the JAK1-reconstituted line (and siRNA knockdown plus a JAK1-selective inhibitor in normal fibroblasts): stimulate with TGF-β, immunoblot pAKT S473/T308, pSTAT3 and total AKT over a time course, and immunoprecipitate TβRI to quantify associated p85 and phosphotyrosine. In parallel, score AKT output functionally by anti-HA immunofluorescence of transfected HA-FKHRL1 (wild type versus the T32A/S253A/S315A mutant control) for nuclear versus cytoplasmic localization, and by anti-phospho-T32/S253 immunoblot; rescue with wild-type versus kinase-dead JAK1 discriminates a catalytic requirement from a scaffolding one.

citations.title: Ruxolitinib Alleviates Renal Interstitial Fibrosis in UUO Mice.
Functional involvement of Akt signaling downstream of Jak1 in v-Abl-induced activation of hematopoietic cells.
Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) Directly Activates the JAK1-STAT3 Axis to Induce Hepatic Fibrosis in Coordination with the SMAD Pathway.
Noncanonical JAK1/STAT3 interactions with TGF-β modulate myofibroblast transdifferentiation and fibrosis.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the plain-language mechanism (JAK1 kinase activity required for TGF-β-induced PI3K/AKT in fibroblasts), the entities together (JAK1 + TβRI + p85/PI3K + AKT; JAK1-deficient U4A fibrosarcoma reconstitution), and the prediction (JAK1 depletion/JAK inhibition blunting TGF-β-stimulated pAKT S473/T308 and keeping FKHRL1/FOXO3a nuclear). The two papers establishing JAK1's constitutive association with TβRI and its role in TGF-β-driven STAT3 signalling in stellate cells and lung fibroblasts (PMID 28154170, PMID 36283961) examine only STAT3/SMAD outputs and never test AKT, PI3K, p85 recruitment or kinase-dead rescue; the closest positive evidence is pharmacological — the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib suppresses TGF-β1-induced Akt/mTOR phosphorylation in renal fibroblasts without isolating JAK1 or showing receptor-level p85 coupling (PMID 31929748) — plus older work placing Jak1 upstream of PI3K/Akt in a non-TGF-β, hematopoietic v-Abl context (PMID 12130510). So the generic JAK-to-AKT link and a JAK-dependence of TGF-β-induced pAKT are published, but the specific direct coupling at the TβR complex, the catalytic-requirement rescue experiment, and the FKHRL1 readout are not, making this partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: ERK1 directly inhibits Ras activation, acting as a retrograde negative-feedback kinase that lowers the GTP-loaded fraction of Ras after growth-factor stimulation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The claims about ERK1 show it phosphorylates components lying upstream of itself in its own activating cascade — FGFR1 on S777, where loss of the site prolongs FGF1-induced receptor tyrosine phosphorylation and increases proliferation/migration (lake2016:findings:002), and MEK1 on T292, which inhibits MEK1 catalytic output and disrupts its docking with ERK (lake2016:findings:010) — so ERK1 has demonstrated access to, and inhibitory action on, the receptor and MEK tiers. The claims about Ras place it immediately between that receptor/adaptor tier and Raf: Ras is activated by receptor-recruited ShcA–Grb2–SOS complexes (derynck2019:findings:028) and Ras-mediated Raf activation is what feeds MEK1/2 phosphorylation of the ERK1/2 TEY motif (cargnello2011:findings:002). Because receptor tyrosine phosphorylation is the step that nucleates the Grb2–SOS complex that loads Ras, ERK1's established ability to damp that step predicts that ERK1 activity itself sets the level and duration of active Ras.
hypotheses.prediction: Removing ERK1 activity (or blocking its activation) should increase and prolong GTP-loaded Ras and the plasma-membrane pool of active Ras after EGF/FGF stimulation, rather than leaving it unchanged; conversely, sustaining ERK1 activity should shorten the active-Ras pulse, and the effect should track with phosphorylation of the ERK1-dependent upstream sites (e.g. receptor serine phosphorylation) rather than with total Ras levels.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa or U2OS cells, stimulate with EGF or FGF1 over a time course under (i) ERK1 siRNA/ERK1-2 knockdown, (ii) MEK inhibition to remove ERK activation, and (iii) control, and quantify active Ras in parallel by GST–Raf1-RBD pulldown followed by anti-Ras western blot and by live-cell imaging of a GFP-tandem-RBD translocation sensor scoring plasma-membrane recruitment (gest2024:findings:215); an increase in amplitude or duration of RBD-bound Ras when ERK1 activity is absent supports the feedback relationship, while an unchanged active-Ras profile rules it out. Specificity can be confirmed by rescuing with wild-type versus kinase-dead ERK1 and by testing whether the FGFR1 S777A mutant, which cannot receive the ERK1 phosphorylation, abolishes the ERK1-dependent difference in Ras loading.

citations.title: Negative feedback regulation of the ERK1/2 MAPK pathway.
Feedback activation of neurofibromin terminates growth factor-induced Ras activation.

novelty.note: I searched for ERK-to-Ras retrograde feedback (ERK phosphorylation of SOS1/Grb2 uncoupling, RTK serine phosphorylation such as EGFR T669), for the prediction that MEK/ERK inhibition or ERK1/2 knockdown prolongs Ras-GTP, and for GAP-side feedback. Both retrieved sources state exactly this explanation: the review documents ERK1/2 negative feedback onto receptors/adaptors/SOS1 limiting the transient Ras-GTP pulse and notes that inhibition or knockdown of MEK1/2 or ERK1/2 yields sustained Ras GTP loading, while the primary paper directly measures prolonged EGF-induced Ras-GTP (RBD-based readouts) upon MEK/ERK inhibition and attributes termination to ERK/RSK-driven activation of the RasGAP neurofibromin in addition to SOS feedback. The hypothesis's mechanism and its central prediction are therefore already published, so the status is established (the specific FGFR1 S777 contribution is an untested variant of an established loop).

hypotheses.statement: EGFR activity directly suppresses TGF-β-induced SMAD3 activation, with EGFR acting as an upstream negative regulator of SMAD3 C-terminal phosphorylation and transcriptional output via ERK-driven ADAM17 shedding of TβRI.
hypotheses.mechanism: EGFR is the proximal driver of sustained ERK pathway output, since ERK reporter signal decays when EGFR is inhibited (albeck2013:findings:000), and ERK activation causes TACE/ADAM17 to cleave TβRI, lowering cell-surface TβRI and down-regulating SMAD3 activation and its antiproliferative/EMT outputs (hata2016:findings:007). Because ADAM17 also sheds TGFα-family ligands to feed EGFR signalling (cuadrado2010:findings:029), tonic EGFR activity should maintain the ERK–ADAM17 arm that strips TβRI, placing SMAD3 phosphorylation and CAGA-box-dependent transcription (dennler1998:findings:008) under direct negative control by EGFR.
hypotheses.prediction: EGF stimulation (or EGFR overexpression) will reduce steady-state cell-surface TβRI and blunt TGF-β-induced SMAD3 C-terminal phosphorylation, nuclear SMAD3 accumulation and (CAGA)9-luciferase activity, whereas EGFR inhibition or EGFR knockdown will raise surface TβRI and amplify the same SMAD3 readouts; the EGF-driven suppression will be abolished by ADAM17 knockdown/inhibition or by MEK inhibition, and will not occur in cells expressing a cleavage-resistant TβRI.
hypotheses.test: In a TGF-β-responsive epithelial line (e.g. HepG2 or MCF-10A) carrying the (CAGA)9-MLP-Luc reporter, pretreat with EGF, with an EGFR kinase inhibitor (erlotinib/gefitinib), or with EGFR siRNA, then stimulate with TGF-β and quantify (i) phospho-SMAD3 (SXS) by immunoblot, (ii) SMAD3 nuclear translocation by immunofluorescence, (iii) reporter luciferase, and (iv) cell-surface TβRI by surface biotinylation/flow cytometry; repeat each arm with ADAM17 siRNA, a TACE inhibitor, or MEK inhibition to establish whether the EGFR effect on SMAD3 runs through ERK-dependent receptor shedding, and confirm the EGFR-dependent change in SMAD3 occupancy at a CAGA-containing promoter by ChIP-qPCR.

citations.title: TACE-mediated ectodomain shedding of the type I TGF-beta receptor downregulates TGF-beta signaling.
Post-translational regulation of TGF-β receptor and Smad signaling.
Targeting Stat3 and Smad7 to restore TGF-β cytostatic regulation of tumor cells in vitro and in vivo.

novelty.note: I searched for (i) ERK/TACE-ADAM17 cleavage of TβRI and Smad3 downregulation, (ii) EGFR as a negative regulator of TGF-β-induced SMAD3 phosphorylation/nuclear translocation/reporter output, and (iii) whether EGF stimulation lowers surface TβRI in an ADAM17/MEK-dependent way. Liu et al. (Mol Cell 2009) already states exactly this explanation: EGF-enhanced Erk signalling decreases cell-surface TβRI via TACE/ADAM17-mediated ectodomain shedding, thereby reducing TGF-β-induced Smad3 activation and cytostasis, with the MEK inhibitor PD98059 restoring surface TβRI and Smad3 activation and TACE silencing/catalytically dead TACE blocking the shedding; the Xu/Derynck FEBS Letters review restates it as growth-factor-driven ERK/p38-dependent loss of TβRI. Only peripheral details of the prediction (EGFR-kinase-inhibitor or EGFR-siRNA arms, a cleavage-resistant TβRI, CAGA-box ChIP) are untested, and an independent line of work shows EGFR overexpression desensitising Smad2/3 output through Stat3/Smad7 instead, so the core explanation is published rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: MEK1 directly associates with the actin cytoskeleton, docking onto the F-actin/IQGAP-tethered ERK pool so that it phosphorylates ERK1/2 in situ on actin filaments.
hypotheses.mechanism: In vascular smooth muscle an actin-associated pool of ERK1/2 is held on actin by IQGAP and caveolin and becomes phosphorylated and activated upon PKC stimulation, with upstream C-raf activation required (brozovich2016:findings:030). The only described activating event for ERK1/2 is MEK1/2 phosphorylation of the TEY activation-loop motif (cargnello2011:findings:002), a reaction whose specificity is set by MEK1 docking rather than by the site sequence, since the ERK activation-loop site is selected against by nearly every other human kinase (johnson2023:findings:009) and depends on a MEK1–ERK2 binding interface that is regulated by MEK1 T292 phosphorylation (lake2016:findings:010). Activation of an actin-bound, ERK therefore requires MEK1 itself to be recruited to the actin/IQGAP scaffold, implying a direct MEK1–actin association.
hypotheses.prediction: MEK1 should be recoverable in the F-actin fraction of smooth muscle or fibroblast lysates and should co-localize with actin by proximity ligation; this actin-associated MEK1 should increase upon PKC stimulation, be lost on IQGAP knockdown, and be reduced by mutations or T292 phosphorylation that weaken MEK1–ERK binding, with phosphorylation of the actin-bound ERK pool abolished by PD0325901/U0126 but total cytosolic ERK unaffected in the IQGAP-knockdown condition.
hypotheses.test: Perform (i) an F-actin co-sedimentation assay with purified recombinant MEK1 (wild type versus T292D and ERK-docking-site mutants) and polymerized rabbit muscle actin, scoring MEK1 in the pellet by immunoblot, and (ii) in cultured vascular smooth muscle cells or fibroblasts, a MEK1–actin proximity ligation assay plus co-immunoprecipitation of MEK1 with actin and IQGAP under control versus IQGAP siRNA and ± PKC activation, with Triton-insoluble cytoskeletal fractionation blotted for phospho-MEK1/phospho-ERK ± U0126 to confirm that the actin-bound ERK pool is MEK1-dependent.

citations.title: The biology of IQGAP proteins: beyond the cytoskeleton.

novelty.note: I searched for MEK1 association with the actin cytoskeleton, for IQGAP1 as a scaffold binding B-Raf/MEK1/2/ERK1/2, and for the prediction that MEK1 co-fractionates with actin and is required for phosphorylating the actin-bound ERK pool. Published work already shows IQGAP1 binds MEK1 and MEK2 directly (in vitro and in cells) alongside ERK1/2 and B-Raf, recruiting the cascade to actin filaments, which is the core of the proposed explanation; the reviewed literature states MEK is scaffolded onto the same actin-associated IQGAP1 platform where ERK is tethered and activated. The T292-dependent and PKC-stimulated smooth-muscle specifics are not individually demonstrated, but the mechanism itself (MEK1 docked to the F-actin/IQGAP-tethered ERK pool) is published, so I mark it established with the nearest scaffold review cited.

hypotheses.statement: S6K1 (RPS6KB1) directly phosphorylates STAT3 on Ser727, acting as a negative regulator of STAT3 DNA binding and transactivation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The cited claims establish S6K1 as a serine/threonine kinase that directly phosphorylates regulatory serine/threonine sites on non-ribosomal signalling proteins to dampen their output — Rictor T1135 and Sin1 T86/T398 to reduce mTORC2-dependent AKT S473 phosphorylation, and IRS1 to promote its degradation and blunt upstream signalling. Independently, STAT3 carries a regulatory Ser727 site whose phosphorylation by an associating serine kinase (PKCδ) inhibits STAT3 DNA binding and transcriptional activity, and STAT3 transcriptional output is read out at the α2M promoter, which requires an intact STAT3 consensus site. If S6K1 engages STAT3 as it engages Rictor/Sin1/IRS1, S6K1 activity should impose Ser727 phosphorylation on STAT3 and suppress its promoter activity, making STAT3 a direct S6K1 substrate and a feedback-inhibited transcription factor.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active S6K1 should phosphorylate purified STAT3 on Ser727 in vitro and co-precipitate with STAT3 in cells; in IL-6-stimulated hepatoma cells, S6K1 knockdown or S6K1-selective inhibition should lower STAT3 Ser727 phosphorylation (without lowering Tyr705 phosphorylation) and increase STAT3 DNA binding and α2M-promoter reporter activity, while constitutively active S6K1 should raise Ser727 phosphorylation and suppress the reporter; a STAT3 S727A mutant reporter should be insensitive to S6K1 manipulation.
hypotheses.test: Perform an in vitro kinase assay with purified active S6K1 and recombinant wild-type versus S727A STAT3, detecting incorporation with a phospho-Ser727 antibody and 32P, then in HepG2 cells stimulated with IL-6 compare siRNA knockdown of S6K1 and the S6K1-selective inhibitor PF-4708671 against controls by immunoblot for STAT3 pSer727 and pTyr705, co-immunoprecipitation of S6K1 with STAT3, EMSA for STAT3 DNA binding, and an α2M-promoter luciferase reporter assayed with wild-type versus S727A STAT3 to confirm the effect is site-dependent.

citations.title: S6K1 Modulates STAT3 Activation to Promote Resistance to Radiotherapy in Lung Cancer.
Serine phosphorylation and maximal activation of STAT3 during CNTF signaling is mediated by the rapamycin target mTOR.

novelty.note: I searched for S6K1/p70S6K as a STAT3 Ser727 kinase, for mTORC1–S6K1 control of STAT3 serine phosphorylation, and for the specific prediction (co-IP, in vitro kinase assay, PF-4708671, α2M reporter, S727A) via web search, PubMed and Europe PMC. A 2026 study (PMC12940830, full text read) does link S6K1 activity to STAT3 Ser727 phosphorylation and STAT3 transcriptional activity, using S6K1 knockout and PF-4708671, but it reports S6K1 as a *positive* regulator, performs no co-IP or in vitro kinase assay, and explicitly states it remains unclear whether S6K1 phosphorylates STAT3 directly; the older rapamycin/mTOR work likewise places this pathway as positively required for Ser727 phosphorylation and maximal transactivation. Thus the S6K1→pSer727 dependence is published in part, while the direct kinase–substrate relationship and the negative-regulation/α2M-reporter prediction (including site-dependence via S727A and selective loss of Ser727 but not Tyr705) are unpublished and of opposite polarity to existing reports.

hypotheses.statement: AKT directly phosphorylates RSK2 (RPS6KA3) on a basophilic RxRxxS/T-type site, acting as an upstream positive regulator of RSK2 activation and its growth-factor-induced nuclear accumulation rather than merely running in parallel with it.
hypotheses.mechanism: In AML cells, Akt Ser473 and p90RSK Ser380 are co-elevated and the Akt and RSK substrate groups are co-enriched, and motif-based analysis shows both are associated with the same basic RxRxxS/KxRxxS motifs; PI3K/mTOR-axis inhibitors (PI-103, AZ123, Ku-794) dose-dependently collapse the p90RSK substrate group together with the Akt group, placing RSK output downstream of this axis (casado2013:findings:002, :003, :004). AKT is a bona fide kinase for basophilic R-x-R-x-x-S/T sites, as shown by direct in vitro phosphorylation of GST-FKHRL1 at T32/S253 by immunoprecipitated active but not inactive Akt (brunet1999:findings:001), and EGF induces AKT-motif (RxRxx[s/t]) phosphorylation in a MEK-independent manner (bekkerjensen2020:findings:010) in the same stimulus window in which RPS6KA3 is imported into the nucleus (itzhak2016:findings:011). Since RSK2 activation is known to be built up by additional non-ERK priming phosphorylations that stabilize ERK1/2 binding and permit full activation (cargnello2011:findings:059), an AKT-catalyzed basophilic site on RSK2 is a concrete candidate for the MEK-independent input.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active AKT will phosphorylate recombinant kinase-dead RSK2 in vitro at one or a few R-x-R-x-x-S/T sites (loss on alanine substitution, no signal with kinase-inactive AKT), and in EGF-stimulated cells AKT inhibition or AKT knockdown will reduce the RSK2 phospho-motif signal, lower RSK2 Ser380 and RSK2-dependent substrate phosphorylation (e.g. BAD Ser112), and blunt EGF-induced nuclear accumulation of RPS6KA3, all without reducing ERK1/2 Thr202/Tyr204 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Two-part standard-bench experiment: (1) in vitro kinase assay with recombinant constitutively active HA-AKT immunoprecipitated from transfected 293T cells (kinase-inactive AKT as control) plus bacterially expressed kinase-dead GST-RSK2 and [γ-32P]ATP, followed by SDS-PAGE/autoradiography, phospho-RxRxxS/T immunoblot and phosphosite mapping by LC-MS/MS, with alanine mutants of each mapped site retested to confirm site identity; (2) in EGF-stimulated HeLa or RPE1 cells, treat with an allosteric AKT inhibitor or siRNA against AKT1/2 (MEK inhibitor as a specificity comparator) and measure RSK2 phospho-motif and Ser380 signal, RSK2 immunokinase activity toward BAD Ser112, and nuclear versus cytosolic RPS6KA3 by subcellular fractionation/immunoblot and immunofluorescence; rescue with a phospho-mimetic RSK2 mutant at the mapped site should restore nuclear accumulation and substrate phosphorylation under AKT inhibition, while failure of AKT to phosphorylate RSK2 in vitro and no change in RSK2 readouts after AKT loss would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Novel wiring of the AKT-RSK2 signaling pathway plays an essential role in cancer cell proliferation via a G(1)/S cell cycle transition.
Akt regulates RSK2 to alter phosphorylation level of H2A.X in breast cancer.

novelty.note: I searched for direct AKT phosphorylation of RSK2/RPS6KA3, for AKT as an upstream activator of p90RSK Ser380, for RSK2 basophilic RxRxxS/T sites and MEK-independent AKT–RSK crosstalk, and for AKT-dependent RSK2 nuclear translocation. A 2023 BBRC paper states exactly this explanation: AKT1-3 bind the RSK2 N-terminal kinase domain and phosphorylate RSK2 at Thr115, a conserved site matching the AKT consensus RxRxxS/T, confirmed by in vitro kinase assays (NTKD deletion and T115A abolish it), and this AKT-catalyzed site is required for EGF/IGF-1-driven proliferation and G1/S transition — i.e. AKT acts as an upstream positive regulator of RSK2, not merely a parallel pathway. An earlier study independently reports Akt-mediated phosphorylation of RSK2 (Ser19) altering RSK2 substrate phosphorylation, with p-RSK2 reduced by LY294002 or dominant-negative Akt. Only the subsidiary prediction about growth-factor-induced nuclear accumulation of RPS6KA3 and RSK2 Ser380 appears untested, so the core mechanism is established rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: BRAF is a direct negative regulator of mTORC1 activity: sustained BRAF (or downstream Raf/MEK) inhibition de-represses mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation, and mTOR/AKT activity in turn feeds back onto BRAF via inhibitory S364 phosphorylation, forming a reciprocal cross-pathway loop.
hypotheses.mechanism: Claims about BRAF state that mutant B-Raf signalling holds an ERK1/2-dependent negative feedback on upstream receptors, and that Raf or MEK1/2 inhibition relieves this feedback to raise IGF-1R and EGFR/ERBB3 activity and Akt phosphorylation, with PI3K co-inhibition then killing B-Raf-inhibitor-resistant cells (lake2016:findings:025). Claims about mTOR place it as the measurable output arm of exactly that PI3K–AKT axis, since PI3K/mTOR inhibitors coordinately collapse mTOR, Akt and p70S6K substrate groups (casado2013:findings:004) and type I IFN-type inputs signal through PI3K–AKT–mTOR to S6K (ivashkiv2014:findings:026); therefore the Akt arm released by BRAF inhibition should register as increased mTORC1 output. The loop closes in the reverse direction because AKT phosphorylates B-RAF at S364 to promote 14-3-3 binding and suppress RAF signalling (manning2017:findings:024), so lowering mTOR/AKT-arm activity should relieve this inhibitory mark on BRAF.
hypotheses.prediction: In BRAF-V600E cells, vemurafenib or MEK inhibition will produce a delayed (6–48 h) rise in mTORC1-specific readouts (p-S6K1 T389, p-S6 S235/236, p-4EBP1 T37/46) above the acute drop, BRAF knockdown will reproduce it, and a TORKi will be synergistic with the BRAF inhibitor; conversely, mTOR/PI3K inhibition will reduce BRAF S364 phosphorylation and BRAF–14-3-3 co-immunoprecipitation, and this relief will be absent in cells expressing BRAF S364A.
hypotheses.test: In BRAF-V600E melanoma/colon lines, run a vemurafenib and trametinib time course (plus doxycycline-inducible BRAF shRNA as a drug-free arm) and immunoblot p-ERK alongside p-S6K1 T389/p-4EBP1, with rapamycin and a TORKi as specificity controls and a checkerboard viability assay for BRAFi+TORKi synergy; in the reverse direction, treat the same cells with a TORKi or PI3K inhibitor and quantify endogenous BRAF S364 phosphorylation and BRAF/14-3-3 co-immunoprecipitation, comparing wild-type BRAF with an S364A mutant to test whether that site is required for the mTOR-arm effect on BRAF output.

citations.title: The mTOR pathway controls phosphorylation of BRAF at T401.
BRAFV600E Negatively Regulates the AKT Pathway in Melanoma Cell Lines

novelty.note: I searched for BRAF as a negative regulator of mTORC1, for delayed mTORC1 rebound after vemurafenib/MEK inhibition, and for AKT-mediated BRAF S364/S365–14-3-3 phosphorylation under mTOR/PI3K inhibition. Published work supports parts of the loop separately: BRAF-V600E negatively regulates AKT signalling in melanoma via mTORC2/rictor (PLOS One 2012), and the mTOR pathway does control a specific BRAF phosphosite (T401, a degron) with mTOR inhibitors suppressing it — but that paper found no reciprocal effect of BRAF T401 on mTOR signalling and does not address S364/14-3-3. No source states BRAF as a direct negative regulator of mTORC1 with the predicted delayed de-repression of S6K1/4E-BP1, nor mTOR-inhibition-dependent relief of BRAF S364 phosphorylation, so this is partial.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3β directly phosphorylates the TGFBR2 (TβRII) cytoplasmic domain, creating a phosphodegron that promotes TβRII ubiquitylation and turnover, making GSK3β a direct negative regulator of TβRII abundance downstream of AKT.
hypotheses.mechanism: The cited claims describe GSK3β as a priming-dependent kinase whose substrate phosphorylation generates E3-ligase recognition motifs that drive degradation — creating the β-Trcp site on β-catenin, the Nedd4L/Smurf1 motif on R-Smad linkers, and the degradation signal on PHLPP that AKT-mediated GSK3β inhibition removes (macdonald2009:findings:008, hata2016:findings:024, haeusler2018:findings:007), with GSK3 preferring an already-phosphorylated Thr/Ser at a fixed motif position (johnson2023:findings:003). TβRII is precisely the kind of substrate this logic predicts: it carries multiple autophosphorylated cytoplasmic serines (Ser213, Ser249, Ser416) that could serve as priming sites (derynck2019:findings:013), and its steady-state level is set by a ubiquitylation-versus-neddylation balance that determines receptor stability and TGF-β responsiveness (derynck2019:findings:011). The same AKT node connects the two: AKT inhibits GSK3β (haeusler2018:findings:007) while insulin/AKT signaling raises cell-surface TβRII (derynck2019:findings:010), consistent with GSK3β being the AKT-suppressed kinase that otherwise marks TβRII for destruction.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant GSK3β should phosphorylate the TβRII cytoplasmic domain in vitro, strongly preferring a pre-autophosphorylated (primed) substrate, and the two proteins should co-immunoprecipitate; in cells, GSK3 inhibition or GSK3α/β loss should lengthen TβRII protein half-life, reduce its ubiquitylation, and raise total and surface TβRII with increased TGF-β-induced SMAD2/3 phosphorylation, while alanine substitution of the GSK3-target serines should render TβRII stable and insensitive to GSK3 inhibition (TβRI levels should be comparatively unaffected, as for neddylation).
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with purified GSK3β and the recombinant TβRII cytoplasmic domain, comparing kinase-dead/non-autophosphorylated versus autophosphorylated (primed) substrate, and map sites by phosphopeptide mass spectrometry; in parallel, in cultured cells co-immunoprecipitate GSK3β with TβRII and measure TβRII half-life by cycloheximide chase, ubiquitylation by IP-western, and surface levels by biotinylation, comparing GSK3 inhibitor-treated versus control cells and wild-type versus phospho-site-alanine TβRII mutants, with loss of the GSK3-dependent difference in the mutant as the decisive read-out.

citations.title: FAF1 phosphorylation by AKT accumulates TGF-β type II receptor and drives breast cancer metastasis.
Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) regulates TGF-β₁-induced differentiation of pulmonary fibroblasts.

novelty.note: I searched for GSK3β phosphorylation/degradation of TGFBR2, for GSK3-generated phosphodegrons on TGF-β receptors, and for GSK3 inhibition effects on TβRII protein level/half-life/surface abundance. Published work places GSK3 phosphodegron control on TGF-β pathway components downstream of the receptor (Smad3, Smad4) and attributes AKT-dependent stabilization of TβRII to AKT phosphorylation of FAF1 (which otherwise recruits VCP/βTRCP to ubiquitylate surface TβRII) rather than to GSK3; a GSK-3 study in TGF-β1-driven fibroblast differentiation explicitly did not examine or implicate receptor stability. Nothing found states GSK3β phosphorylates the TβRII cytoplasmic domain, and nothing reports a direct negative test of it, so the claim is open with the AKT–FAF1–TβRII axis as the nearest published work.

hypotheses.statement: IFNγ acts as an upstream negative regulator of mTORC1, suppressing mTORC1 signalling in IFNγ-responsive myeloid cells and in T cells sharing their medium by driving STAT1-dependent arginase/iNOS induction that depletes extracellular arginine, thereby cutting off the Rag-GTPase amino-acid input to mTORC1.
hypotheses.mechanism: The IFNγ evidence states that IFNγ, via STAT1, is required for upregulation of ARG1 and iNOS in myeloid suppressor cells and that IFNγ blockade abolishes their ability to suppress T-cell responses (gabrilovich2009:findings:007), with IFNγ-driven STAT1/IRF1 occupancy providing the transcriptional arm of this program (ivashkiv2014:findings:013). Independently, the mTORC1 evidence states that mTORC1 activation requires amino acid sensing through the Rag GTPases and lysosomal translocation (balla2013:findings:096), that arginine withdrawal inhibits mTORC1 through a SAMTOR-independent route (gu2017:findings:011), and that a dominant-active RagB Q99L/RagC S75N heterodimer renders mTORC1 refractory to upstream amino-acid inputs (barpeled2013:findings:007). Together these imply that an IFNγ-induced arginine-consuming enzymatic program should read out as a direct, Rag-dependent loss of mTORC1 activity.
hypotheses.prediction: IFNγ treatment of arginase/iNOS-competent macrophages should lower phospho-S6K1 Thr389 and phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65 and disperse mTOR from LAMP2+ lysosomes within hours-to-days of cytokine exposure, in proportion to medium arginine consumption; this suppression should be reversed by arginine repletion or by an arginase inhibitor, and should be abolished in cells expressing dominant-active RagB Q99L/RagC S75N, whereas IFNγ should not further inhibit mTORC1 in cells already deprived of arginine.
hypotheses.test: Treat THP-1-derived (or RAW264.7) macrophages ± IFNγ in defined medium, then immunoblot phospho-S6K1 Thr389 and phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65 over a time course while measuring medium arginine/ornithine by a colorimetric or HPLC assay; repeat with (i) arginine add-back, (ii) an arginase inhibitor or STAT1 knockdown, and (iii) stable expression of dominant-active RagB Q99L/RagC S75N versus wild-type Rags, scoring mTOR/LAMP2 colocalization by immunofluorescence. A transwell co-culture in which anti-CD3-activated T cells are exposed to conditioned medium from IFNγ-treated versus untreated macrophages, with T-cell phospho-S6K1 as readout ± arginine repletion, tests the trans arm; loss of the IFNγ effect under arginine add-back plus its persistence with dominant-active Rags would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Interferon-γ regulates cellular metabolism and mRNA translation to potentiate macrophage activation.
Regulatory T cells use arginase 2 to enhance their metabolic fitness in tissues.

novelty.note: I searched for IFN-γ-driven mTORC1 suppression, for arginase/iNOS arginine depletion acting on mTORC1 in myeloid and T cells, and for the Rag/lysosomal-translocation arm. Su et al. (Nat Immunol 2015) already establish the core logic in the same cell type and phenomenon — IFN-γ physiologically downregulates mTORC1 in human macrophages by inducing an amino-acid-consuming enzyme (IDO) whose depletion of the amino acid prevents mTOR recruitment to lysosomes, plus PI3K–Akt–TSC suppression — but the depleted amino acid is tryptophan, not arginine, and arginase/iNOS, STAT1-dependence of the mTORC1 effect, the trans arm to co-cultured T cells, and the dominant-active RagB Q99L/RagC S75N epistasis test are not addressed. Lowe et al. independently show that arginase-mediated consumption of extracellular arginine attenuates mTORC1 (phospho-S6) in T cells, reversibly with arginase inhibition and arginine-low media, but this is T-cell-intrinsic ARG2 and not IFN-γ/STAT1-driven; hence partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: JNK1 directly phosphorylates STAT3 on the inhibitory Ser727 site, acting as a negative regulator that reduces STAT3 DNA binding and transactivation of STAT3-dependent promoters.
hypotheses.mechanism: JNK1 is a conventional stress-activated MAPK that shuttles constitutively into the nucleus and acts there as an inducible serine kinase on transcription factors, phosphorylating specific residues of NFAT2/NFAT4 with isoform selectivity to drive their export and switch off their transcriptional output (hogan2003:findings:005; zeke2016:findings:010; cargnello2011:findings:000). STAT3 is negatively regulated by precisely this kind of event: Ser727 phosphorylation blocks its DNA binding and transactivation, and the pathway assigned to producing it runs through the stress-kinase module component MKK-4 (Vav→Rac-1→MKK-4→PKCδ) in IL-6-stimulated HepG2 cells (heinrich2003:findings:023). A nuclear, MKK-4-coupled serine kinase with demonstrated activity against transcription-factor regulatory serines is therefore a candidate for phosphorylating STAT3 Ser727 directly rather than only via PKCδ.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active JNK1 should phosphorylate STAT3 on Ser727 in vitro and co-immunoprecipitate with STAT3; in IL-6-stimulated cells, JNK1 loss or inhibition should lower STAT3 pSer727 while increasing STAT3 DNA binding and STAT3-dependent promoter activity (e.g. α2M), and JNK1 activation (e.g. by anisomycin or osmotic stress) should raise pSer727 and suppress that promoter output without requiring a change in STAT3 Tyr705/Tyr-phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In vitro kinase assay with purified active JNK1 and recombinant full-length STAT3 (plus a S727A mutant as control), read out by phospho-Ser727 immunoblot and 32P incorporation, paired in HepG2 cells with JNK1 siRNA/knockout or a selective JNK inhibitor versus JNK1 overexpression: measure STAT3 pSer727 by immunoblot, STAT3 DNA binding by EMSA/ChIP on the α2M STAT3 site, α2M luciferase reporter activity, and JNK1–STAT3 association by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation; loss of Ser727 phosphorylation with the S727A mutant and failure of JNK1 manipulation to move pSer727 or reporter activity would rule the relationship out.

citations.title: Serine phosphorylation and negative regulation of Stat3 by JNK.
MSK1 and JNKs mediate phosphorylation of STAT3 in UVA-irradiated mouse epidermal JB6 cells.
JNK mediates serine phosphorylation of STAT3 in response to fatty acids released by lipolysis.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words ("JNK negative regulation of STAT3 serine phosphorylation"), the entities together (JNK1 + STAT3 + Ser727 + DNA binding), and the prediction (in vitro kinase assay / JNK1 knockout effects on pSer727). Lim & Cao (JBC 1999) state exactly this explanation: JNK induces Stat3 Ser-727 phosphorylation (by stress or by upstream MKK7), and JNK1 negatively regulates Stat3 DNA binding and transcriptional activity, including serine phosphorylation occurring without tyrosine phosphorylation; Zhang et al. (JBC 2001) show active JNKs directly phosphorylate STAT3 Ser727 in vitro and that Jnk1-/- cells lose UVA-induced pSer727, and a recent study assigns JNK1 as the Ser727 kinase in intact cells. The only element not covered is the specific IL-6/α2M-promoter HepG2 readout and the JNK1–STAT3 co-immunoprecipitation, but the mechanism and its negative-regulatory consequence are published for this phenomenon.

hypotheses.statement: MEK1 negatively regulates insulin (INS) signalling at the receptor-proximal level, so that insulin-stimulated MEK1–ERK activity acts as a feedback brake limiting insulin's own IR/IRS–AKT output.
hypotheses.mechanism: The MEK1 claims show that MEK1/2 activity imposes ERK-dependent feedback on receptor-proximal signalling components — MEK1/2 inhibition relieves this feedback, raising IGF-1R and EGFR/ERBB3 phosphorylation and activating PI3K/AKT (lake2016:findings:025), and MEK1/2-dependent phosphorylation of the adaptor FRS2a on Thr-Pro sites suppresses its tyrosine phosphorylation and Grb2 binding (lake2016:findings:004). The insulin claims show that the insulin receptor is governed by exactly this class of brake: insulin-driven serine/threonine phosphorylation of IRS1 and of the IR pseudosubstrate GRB10 forms negative feedback loops whose loss improves insulin sensitivity (haeusler2018:findings:009, haeusler2018:findings:002), and insulin receptor levels themselves are rebound-regulated when the PI3K arm is blocked (fruman2017:findings:013). If insulin engages MEK1 like other receptor inputs, MEK1 should feed back onto IR/IRS the way it does onto FRS2a, IGF-1R and EGFR, making MEK1 a direct suppressor of insulin's downstream AKT signal.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic loss of MEK1 should potentiate insulin action: higher insulin-stimulated IR and IRS1 tyrosine phosphorylation and AKT Ser473 phosphorylation, with reduced inhibitory Ser/Thr phosphorylation of IRS1 and GRB10; conversely, expression of constitutively active MEK1 should blunt insulin-stimulated AKT phosphorylation without reducing insulin receptor abundance, and should increase IRS1 inhibitory-site phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In serum-starved insulin-responsive cultured cells (e.g. 3T3-L1 adipocytes or HepG2), pretreat with the recommended MEK1/2 inhibitors PD0325901 or PD184352 with U0126 as verification (cargnello2011:findings:003), or knock down MEK1 by siRNA, then stimulate with a submaximal insulin dose over a time course and immunoblot for IR and IRS1 phosphotyrosine, IRS1 inhibitory Ser sites, GRB10 phosphorylation and AKT Ser473/Thr308; in parallel express constitutively active MEK1 (MEK1-DD) versus kinase-dead MEK1 and repeat the insulin time course. A reciprocal arm measures whether insulin alone raises MEK1-dependent ERK TEY phosphorylation in the same cells. Potentiated insulin-stimulated AKT and IR/IRS phosphorylation on MEK1 loss, mirrored by suppression with MEK1-DD, supports the relationship; no change in either direction rules it out.

citations.title: Modulation of insulin receptor substrate-1 tyrosine phosphorylation and function by mitogen-activated protein kinase.
Phosphorylation of Grb10 by mitogen-activated protein kinase: identification of Ser150 and Ser476 of human Grb10zeta as major phosphorylation sites.
Inhibition of MEK1 Signaling Pathway in the Liver Ameliorates Insulin Resistance.

novelty.note: I searched for MEK/ERK negative feedback on receptor-proximal insulin signalling, for MEK inhibition potentiating insulin-stimulated IRS-1 tyrosine/AKT phosphorylation, and for ERK phosphorylation of the IR pseudosubstrate GRB10; PubMed/PMC records retrieved show this explanation is long published. De Fea & Roth showed MAP kinase serine-phosphorylates IRS-1 and thereby reduces insulin-receptor-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation and PI3K association; Langlais et al. showed p42/44 MAPK phosphorylates GRB10 at Ser150/Ser476 as a feedback inhibitory mechanism on insulin signalling; and a MEK1-focused in vivo study states MEK inhibition increases Akt phosphorylation, lowers IRS-1 Ser307 phosphorylation and improves insulin sensitivity. The only parts not confirmed are details of the prediction — that same MEK1 paper notes constitutively active MEK in liver was insulinotropic without altering insulin sensitivity, and other work reports MEK inhibitors impairing insulin-stimulated glucose uptake without changing Akt — so the direction of the brake is established while the CA-MEK1 arm remains contested.

hypotheses.statement: LPS activates SYK through ITAM-containing adaptors coupled to the CD14/MD2 recognition cascade, and SYK activity is required for LPS-induced CD14/TLR4 endocytosis.
hypotheses.mechanism: The LPS evidence shows that LPS engagement proceeds through an upstream transfer cascade (LBP → CD14 → MD2 → TLR4 dimerization) and that the resulting endocytosis of CD14 and TLR4 is strictly dependent on CD14 and MD2-mediated dimerization rather than on TLR4's own cytosolic signaling — LPS-induced CD14 endocytosis even occurs in TLR4-deficient cells, so a TLR4-signaling-independent kinase must transduce the receptor-proximal step (fitzgerald2020:findings:004, fitzgerald2020:findings:011). The SYK evidence shows SYK is recruited and activated by non-classical surface receptors (β2 integrins, PSGL1) through the ITAM-containing adaptors DAP12 and FcRγ in macrophages and neutrophils, and that its linker-tyrosine-dependent coupling to VAV1/PLCγ1 governs cytoskeletal and internalization-related functions in these same myeloid cells (mcsai2010:findings:016, mcsai2010:findings:012, mcsai2010:findings:014). Together these imply LPS-loaded CD14 acts as another ITAM-adaptor-coupled trigger of SYK, with SYK providing the cytoskeletal output that internalizes the CD14/TLR4 cargo.
hypotheses.prediction: LPS should induce rapid SYK tyrosine autophosphorylation (including the linker sites Tyr342/Tyr346) in macrophages, and this should still occur in TLR4-deficient cells but be lost in CD14-deficient cells or when ITAM adaptors are absent; conversely, SYK inhibition or knockout should block LPS-induced loss of surface CD14 and TLR4 (and TRIF-dependent output) while leaving the initial MD2-dependent TLR4 dimerization and the plasma-membrane NF-κB response largely intact.
hypotheses.test: In a macrophage line (e.g. immortalized BMDM or THP-1), stimulate with picomolar-to-nanomolar LPS and immunoblot SYK phospho-Tyr342/Tyr346 plus SYK immunoprecipitation over 0–30 min, comparing wild type with CRISPR CD14-knockout and TLR4-knockout clones; in parallel, measure LPS-induced endocytosis of CD14 and TLR4 by surface antibody staining/flow cytometry and confocal imaging in cells pretreated with a SYK inhibitor (R406/piceatannol) or in SYK-knockout clones rescued with wild-type versus kinase-dead or Tyr342/346-mutant SYK. SYK phosphorylation that is CD14-dependent but TLR4-independent, together with a SYK-dependent block of CD14/TLR4 internalization rescued only by wild-type SYK, would confirm the direct relationship; absence of LPS-induced SYK phosphorylation and normal endocytosis without SYK would rule it out.

citations.title: CD14 controls the LPS-induced endocytosis of Toll-like receptor 4.

CD14 mediates Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) endocytosis and spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) and interferon regulatory transcription factor 3 (IRF3) activation in epithelial cells and impairs neutrophil infiltration and Pseudomonas aeruginosa killing in vivo.
Early innate immune responses to bacterial LPS.

novelty.note: I searched for (a) SYK requirement in LPS-induced TLR4/CD14 endocytosis, (b) CD14/ITAM-adaptor (DAP12, FcRγ) coupling to SYK by LPS, and (c) the prediction that SYK activation by LPS is CD14-dependent but TLR4-signalling-independent while sparing plasma-membrane MyD88/NF-κB output. Zanoni et al. (Cell 2011) reports exactly this explanation: LPS induces phospho-SYK in BMDM in a CD14-dependent manner, SYK activation persists in signalling-defective TLR4 (C3H/HeJ) cells, SYK inhibitors (including piceatannol) and DAP12/FcεRIγ double deficiency impair TLR4/CD14 endocytosis and TRIF-dependent IFN while leaving MyD88-dependent TNFα intact; this 'inflammatory endocytosis' SYK/PLCγ2–ITAM-adaptor mechanism is restated in later primary work (epithelial cells, PMID 24275652) and reviews. Only the specific SYK linker-tyrosine (Tyr342/346) requirement is not directly addressed, so the framework itself is anticipated rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: LPS transactivates EGFR: LPS/TLR4 engagement drives p38-dependent ADAM17/TACE phosphorylation and ectodomain shedding of TGFα-family ligands, producing ligand-dependent EGFR autophosphorylation and downstream ERK output in the stimulated cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The EGFR-side evidence states that p38 MAPKs phosphorylate TACE/ADAM17 on Thr735 specifically in response to inflammatory stimuli and that this phosphorylation is required for shedding of TGFα-family ligands and consequent EGFR signalling and proliferation (cuadrado2010:findings:029), and the same corpus shows LPS is a stimulus that engages the p38 module in macrophages, where p38 phosphorylation/dephosphorylation is actively regulated after LPS exposure (cuadrado2010:findings:011). Independently, the LPS-side evidence shows that even picomolar LPS, delivered through the LBP/CD14/MD2 transfer cascade, triggers TLR4 dimerization and full inflammatory signalling in macrophages (fitzgerald2020:findings:004), so LPS supplies exactly the inflammatory input the ADAM17–EGFR axis is described as responding to. Together these imply a direct, cell-autonomous route from LPS to EGFR activation that does not require any of the bridge entities beyond the shed-ligand step, and that should be readable as EGFR/ERK pathway output using an EGFR-inhibitor-sensitive reporter (albeck2013:findings:000).
hypotheses.prediction: Adding LPS to TLR4/CD14/MD2-competent cells should produce a delayed (10–60 min) rise in EGFR Tyr1068/Tyr1173 phosphorylation and in ERK-pathway output that is abolished by an EGFR kinase inhibitor, by an ADAM17/metalloprotease inhibitor or ADAM17 knockdown, by a p38 inhibitor, and by a neutralizing anti-EGFR-ligand antibody; conditioned medium from LPS-treated cells should activate EGFR in untreated reporter cells, and soluble TGFα/amphiregulin should appear in the LPS-treated supernatant. If the relationship is false, LPS will induce NF-κB/p38 readouts with no EGFR phosphorylation, no shed ligand, and no EGFR-inhibitor-sensitive reporter change.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate a TLR4/CD14/MD2-expressing line (or MD2/CD14-reconstituted epithelial cells) with LPS and immunoblot a time course for phospho-EGFR, phospho-p38 and phospho-ERK, in parallel with ELISA of shed TGFα/amphiregulin in the supernatant; repeat under pretreatment with erlotinib/gefitinib, TAPI-1 or ADAM17 siRNA, a p38 inhibitor, and ligand-neutralizing antibody, and cross-check with the live-cell FIRE (YFP–Fra-1 PEST) ERK-output reporter, which should rise after LPS and decay upon EGFR inhibition; a conditioned-medium transfer onto naive reporter cells distinguishes ligand-shedding-mediated transactivation from an intracellular, ligand-independent mechanism.

citations.title: Helicobacter pylori-induced gastric mucosal TGF-α ectodomain shedding and EGFR transactivation involves Rac1/p38 MAPK-dependent TACE activation.
Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-Induced Biliary Epithelial Cell NRas Activation Requires Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR).
Erlotinib protects against LPS-induced endotoxicity because TLR4 needs EGFR to signal.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (LPS/TLR4 → p38 → ADAM17/TACE → TGFα-family shedding → EGFR), the entities together (LPS, ADAM17/TAPI-1, amphiregulin/TGFα, EGFR phosphorylation, macrophages/epithelium), and the prediction (delayed EGFR phosphorylation abolished by EGFR/TACE inhibition). Published work states exactly this explanation: Slomiany & Slomiany report that H. pylori LPS drives gastric mucosal TGF-α ectodomain shedding and EGFR transactivation through Rac1/p38 MAPK-dependent TACE/ADAM17 activation, and Cheung et al. show LPS produces EGFR phosphorylation in cholangiocytes that is undetectable at 0–15 min but evident at 30–60 min, with TACE-sensitive amphiregulin release and blockade by an EGFR inhibitor and TAPI-1 — matching the mechanism, kinetics and inhibitor-sensitivity predicted. A further PNAS study establishes that TLR4 signalling to NF-κB requires EGFR in vivo (erlotinib-sensitive), though by a LYN-binding route rather than shed-ligand transactivation, so it is the nearest alternative account.

hypotheses.statement: Activated NTRK1 directly activates MAPK (ERK) and, because its output is unusually long-lived, drives MAPK into a self-sustaining active state that persists after ligand removal, unlike short or weak EGF-type input.
hypotheses.mechanism: The NTRK1 claims state that ligand-activated NTRK1 assembles a long-lived FRS2–Crk–C3G complex giving sustained Rap1→B-Raf activation (in contrast to transient EGFR-driven Rap1), that APPL recruitment to endosomal NTRK1 is required for ERK1/ERK2 activation, and that lowering TrkA receptor number in PC12 cells converts ERK activation from sustained to transient — i.e. NTRK1 kinase output quantitatively sets ERK amplitude and duration. The MAPK claims independently state that MAPK sits in a bistable feedback loop with PKC having a basal state, a threshold and an active state, and that only inputs of sufficient strength and duration (5 nM EGF for 100 min, but not 2 nM or 10 min) leave MAPK active after the stimulus is withdrawn. Combining them, NTRK1 is positioned as an upstream activator whose sustained, receptor-number-dependent drive should push MAPK above that threshold, whereas reduced NTRK1 drive should leave MAPK in the transient/basal regime.
hypotheses.prediction: NGF-stimulated cells expressing high NTRK1 should show phospho-ERK that remains elevated for tens of minutes to hours after ligand washout and after NTRK1 kinase inhibition, while cells with knocked-down, kinase-dead or briefly stimulated NTRK1 show only transient phospho-ERK that decays promptly; the transition between the two behaviours should be abrupt with respect to NTRK1 activity level (all-or-none per cell) rather than graded, and loss of NTRK1 kinase activity before the threshold is crossed should abolish MAPK activation entirely.
hypotheses.test: In PC12 cells, titrate NTRK1 (doxycycline-inducible NTRK1, plus siRNA knockdown and a kinase-dead control) and stimulate with NGF for varying durations, then wash out ligand and add a selective NTRK1 kinase inhibitor at defined times; measure phospho-ERK1/2 by immunoblot time course and by single-cell flow cytometry/immunofluorescence to test (i) whether MAPK activation strictly requires NTRK1 kinase activity (loss-of-function arm), and (ii) whether pERK persists after NTRK1 is inhibited and shows bimodal single-cell distributions only above a critical NTRK1 level, with a chemically dimerizable NTRK1 kinase domain as the gain-of-function arm.

citations.title: Growth factor-induced MAPK network topology shapes Erk response determining PC-12 cell fate.
Untangling the signalling wires.
Frequency modulation of ERK activation dynamics rewires cell fate.
Kinetics of receptor tyrosine kinase activation define ERK signaling dynamics.

novelty.note: I searched for NGF/TrkA sustained ERK with positive feedback and bistability, for persistence of pERK after TrkA kinase inhibition or ligand washout, and for single-cell bimodal pERK in PC-12 cells. Santos, Verveer & Bastiaens (Nat Cell Biol 2007) already state exactly this explanation: NGF-activated TrkA engages positive feedback (PKCδ→Raf) giving switch-like, bistable Erk activation that remains largely active even after complete TrkA inhibition, in contrast to EGF/EGFR, which engages only negative feedback and gives transient Erk — as summarised in Kholodenko's accompanying commentary; Ryu et al. (Mol Syst Biol 2015) further show at single-cell level that a brief 10-min NGF pulse leaves sustained ERK activity in a cell subpopulation, i.e. the bimodal/all-or-none behaviour the prediction posits, with heterogeneity in component levels setting which cells cross the threshold. The receptor-number titration arm (graded vs abrupt dependence on NTRK1 level per cell) is less directly tested, and Shindo-type receptor-kinetics work (Sci Signal 2020) argues ERK dynamics instead track RTK phosphorylation kinetics, so that specific quantitative arm remains contested rather than unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: TGF-β directly induces PTEN transcription through Smad-dependent CAGA-type promoter elements, so that TGF-β signaling lowers PIP3 and dampens PI3K/AKT output in the responding cell.
hypotheses.mechanism: TGF-β's transcriptional program operates through repeated AG(C/A)CAGACA "CAGA" elements that mediate direct TGF-β induction of target promoters such as PAI-1 (dennler1998:findings:000), so a CAGA-containing PTEN promoter would place PTEN among such direct targets; PTEN is a PIP3 phosphatase that opposes PI3K (manning2017:findings:002), and loss of PTEN elevates PI3K signaling strongly enough to redirect lymphocyte fate in a Foxo1-reversible manner (fruman2017:findings:008). The TGF-β phenotype of hyporesponsiveness is itself reversed by exogenous IL-2, a strong activator of the PI3K axis, added during or after the TGF-β culture (chen2003:findings:003), which is what would be expected if TGF-β imposes its state partly by raising PTEN and thereby holding PIP3/AKT low rather than by killing cells.
hypotheses.prediction: TGF-β exposure should raise PTEN mRNA and protein within hours and reduce phospho-AKT(S473)/phospho-FOXO1; this induction should require Smad3/Smad4 and intact CAGA-like elements in the PTEN promoter, with Smad3 detectable at that promoter; and knocking down PTEN should specifically abolish TGF-β's ability to suppress AKT signaling without abolishing other TGF-β responses such as PAI-1 induction.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa cells (TGF-β/Smad-responsive and PTEN-expressing), (1) treat ± TGF-β and immunoblot PTEN, p-AKT(S473) and p-FOXO1 over 0–24 h with qPCR for PTEN and PAI-1 as a positive control; (2) transfect luciferase reporters carrying the PTEN promoter with wild-type versus point-mutated CAGA-like boxes, ± TGF-β and ± SMAD3/SMAD4 siRNA, and run Smad3 ChIP-qPCR at those sites versus the PAI-1 CAGA boxes; (3) test necessity by siRNA knockdown of PTEN (or expression of catalytically dead PTEN-C124S) and asking whether TGF-β still lowers p-AKT. Loss of TGF-β-driven PTEN induction, absence of Smad3 occupancy/CAGA dependence, or persistence of full AKT suppression after PTEN knockdown would rule out the direct link.

citations.title: A Smad3-PTEN regulatory loop controls proliferation and apoptotic responses to TGF-β in mouse endometrium.
Activin/TGF-beta induce apoptosis through Smad-dependent expression of the lipid phosphatase SHIP.

novelty.note: I searched for TGF-β induction of PTEN via Smads, for Smad3/Smad4 occupancy and CAGA/SBE elements in the PTEN promoter, and for TGF-β-driven suppression of PI3K/AKT in lymphocytes. The core explanation is already published: Eritja et al. (Cell Death Differ 2017) show TGF-β raises PTEN mRNA within hours in a Smad3-dependent way, with Smad3 ChIP occupancy across the −1 to −1500 bp PTEN promoter and consequent loss of AKT phosphorylation, while Smad3- or PTEN-null cells instead show elevated PI3K/AKT; an older analogue shows Smad-dependent induction of the PIP3-degrading phosphatase SHIP lowering AKT in hematopoietic cells. However, no retrieved work identifies CAGA-type boxes in the PTEN promoter or tests reporter/point-mutant CAGA dependence, none places this in the lymphocyte TGF-β-hyporesponsiveness/IL-2-reversal setting, and opposing reports (TGF-β lowering PTEN via NF-κB or miR-216a/217) show the direction is context-dependent — hence partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B directly and negatively regulates IFNG production in activated T cells by driving NFAT nuclear export and thereby limiting NFAT-dependent transcription of IFNG.
hypotheses.mechanism: In T cells, CD28/Akt signalling inhibits GSK3, and this inhibition is what blocks NFAT nuclear export and prolongs NFAT nuclear residence (hogan2003:findings:006), so active GSK3B should shorten NFAT's time on target promoters. Independently, IFNγ secretion by T cells falls when NFATC1 activity is disrupted (de2024:findings:016), placing IFNG output downstream of NFAT residence, and GSK3 is already reported to act as a negative regulator of interferon production in the type I arm (ivashkiv2014:findings:038). Together these imply GSK3B activity itself sets the ceiling on IFNG expression in stimulated T cells rather than acting only through a bridge pathway.
hypotheses.prediction: Inhibiting or deleting GSK3B in anti-CD3-stimulated T cells should increase IFNG mRNA and secreted IFNγ per cell with concomitant prolonged NFAT nuclear residence, while expressing a constitutively active, Akt-insensitive GSK3B (S9A) should shorten NFAT nuclear dwell time and suppress IFNG induction; the GSK3B-driven change in IFNG should be abolished when NFAT nuclear translocation is blocked.
hypotheses.test: In primary CD4+/CD8+ T cells or Jurkat cells stimulated with anti-CD3 (±anti-CD28), compare GSK3B knockdown/CRISPR knockout or selective GSK3 inhibitor treatment against GSK3B-S9A overexpression, and in each arm measure (i) IFNG mRNA by qPCR, secreted IFNγ by ELISA and intracellular IFNγ by flow cytometry, (ii) NFATC1 nuclear versus cytoplasmic localization by immunofluorescence and nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation with immunoblot, and (iii) NFAT occupancy at the IFNG promoter/enhancer by ChIP-qPCR; epistasis with cyclosporin A or an NFAT-translocation-blocking peptide determines whether the GSK3B effect on IFNG requires NFAT.

The component links are published: Ohteki et al. show constitutively active GSK-3β suppresses, and GSK-3 inhibition enhances, T-cell cytokine output (IL-2, not IFNG) precisely through NFATc nuclear export/dwell time; Taylor/Rudd show GSK-3 inhibition raises IFN-γ in CD8 T cells but attribute it to a T-bet/PD-1 axis and explicitly do not place NFAT in that pathway; Fu et al. directly test the GSK3→NFAT nuclear-export axis in CD8 T cells and measure IFNγ, but report the opposite sign (GSK3α/β deletion increased NFAT nuclear import and markedly lowered IFNγ, TNFα and GzmB via an exhaustion program). So no source states this specific GSK3B→NFAT-residence→IFNG ceiling explanation, and the nearest direct test contradicts the predicted direction.

hypotheses.statement: Activated TGFBR1 (TβRI) kinase acts directly upstream of Rho, so that TβRI catalytic activity is required for the rapid, Smad-independent RhoA activation triggered by TGF-β.
hypotheses.mechanism: The A-side evidence states that TGF-β induces transient RhoA activation in epithelial cells within ~5 min and can also locally repress RhoA at tight junctions, placing Rho control on the same fast timescale as receptor-proximal events rather than transcription (derynck2019:findings:035); the C-side evidence states that TβRI is the ligand-activated kinase of the complex, switched on by GS-domain phosphorylation (four of five Ser/Thr sufficient) and requiring TβRI/TβRII kinase activity for its own modifications (hata2016:findings:004, hata2016:findings:005). Since Rho activity is read out by effector-binding biosensors within minutes of receptor stimulation (avet2022:findings:014, gest2024:findings:216), the simplest direct link consistent with both sides is that the activated TβRI kinase itself is the node that sets Rho nucleotide state, rather than TβRII ligand binding or downstream transcription.
hypotheses.prediction: TGF-β-induced RhoA activation at 2–10 min should be abolished by a TβRI kinase inhibitor or by kinase-dead/GS-domain-unphosphorylatable TβRI, and a constitutively active TβRI should raise Rho-GTP and effector binding without any ligand; blocking transcription or Smad recruitment should leave the early Rho response intact, and the TβRI-dependent Rho signal should be spatially resolvable (plasma membrane versus junctional loss).
hypotheses.test: In TβRI-null or TβRI-knockdown epithelial cells (e.g. MCF10A/NMuMG) expressing a Rho activity biosensor (PKN-RBD-RlucII/rGFP-CAAX BRET or dimericTomato-2xrGBD translocation) plus doxycycline-inducible wild-type, kinase-dead, GS-domain S/T→A, or constitutively active TβRI, measure Rho activation kinetics over 0–15 min of TGF-β with and without SB-431542, and confirm by GST-rhotekin-RBD pulldown of Rho-GTP; loss of the early Rho signal only when TβRI kinase activity is absent, and ligand-free Rho activation by constitutively active TβRI, supports the relationship, while an unchanged Rho response rules it out.

Two components are already published: Fleming et al. state that TGF-β-mediated RhoA activation depends on ALK5 kinase activity and occurs independently of Smad2/3/4, and Papadimitriou et al. show that the early (minutes-scale) TGF-β-induced RhoA/RhoB activation is Smad2/3-independent — but they route it through Src and the GEF Vav2 rather than establishing TβRI as a direct Rho-proximal node, and neither tests GS-domain-unphosphorylatable TβRI or resolves the response with Rho biosensors in space/time. hypotheses.statement: MEK1 negatively regulates KRAS nucleotide state, such that loss of MEK1 activity raises KRAS-GTP loading and thereby shifts KRAS-G12C out of the GDP-bound conformation that state-selective inhibitors require.
hypotheses.mechanism: lake2016:findings:006 shows that inhibition or knockdown of MEK1/2 produces sustained Ras-GTP loading attributable to relief of a Ras-GAP (NF1) step rather than a change in exchange rate, placing MEK1 activity upstream of the GTP/GDP balance of Ras; lake2016:findings:020 independently shows Ras-GTP is low under intact MEK1/2 feedback and rises when that feedback is disrupted. simanshu2017:findings:026 states that covalent G12C compounds such as ARS-853 engage KRAS only in its GDP-bound state in the switch-II pocket, and simanshu2017:findings:013 shows KRAS alleles that accumulate GTP without upstream input escape this state dependence; combining these, MEK1 activity should be a direct determinant of how much KRAS sits in the drug-competent GDP state.
hypotheses.prediction: In KRAS-G12C cells, MEK1 inhibition or MEK1 knockdown should increase GTP-bound KRAS (RAF-RBD pulldown) within hours and correspondingly decrease the rate and extent of covalent ARS-853 adduct formation on KRAS-G12C and of ARS-853-mediated block of downstream signalling, whereas a nucleotide-cycling-independent allele such as KRAS A146T should show high KRAS-GTP that MEK1 inhibition does not further change.
hypotheses.test: In KRAS-G12C cell lines, pretreat with a MEK1/2 inhibitor (PD0325901 or U0126 as confirmation) or transfect MEK1-selective siRNA, then (i) quantify KRAS-GTP by GST-RAF1-RBD pulldown/immunoblot and (ii) measure covalent engagement of KRAS-G12C by ARS-853 over a time/dose series using intact-protein gel-shift or mass-spectrometric adduct quantification plus phospho-ERK readout; run the same panel in isogenic cells expressing KRAS A146T as the cycling-independent control, and rescue with MEK1 re-expression to confirm the effect maps to MEK1.

Lito et al. 2016 (retrieved via PMC) establishes the core logic: ARS-853 traps GDP-bound KRAS-G12C, exchange-promoting mutants (Y40A, N116H, A146V) attenuate its effect, and the authors note that relieving downstream feedback (MEK/ERK/PI3K-AKT inhibition) reactivates receptors and is likely to blunt mutant-KRAS inhibition; secondary literature attributes a trametinib-increases-KRAS-GTP/decreases-ARS-853 observation to the Patricelli 2016 work, but I could not retrieve that page to cite it. Thus the general mechanism is published, while the specific MEK1-selective attribution (NF1/GAP-based rather than SOS-based, MEK1 knockdown, A146T control) is not stated in any source I could verify.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B directly restrains type I interferon secretion, so that loss of GSK3B activity increases the amount of IFNβ released by cytosolic-DNA/STING-activated cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: One line of evidence places GSK3 as a negative regulator of IFNβ production in immune cells, alongside other IFN-pathway modifiers such as HDAC3 and PTPN22 (ivashkiv2014:findings:038). Independently, cGAMP-triggered STING signalling is read out quantitatively as secreted IFNβ from THP-1 monocytic cells, a response that can be pharmacologically scaled up or down at the level of the STING module (decout2021:findings:016). If GSK3B is the negative regulator acting on this axis, its activity should set the ceiling on the secreted IFNβ output of that same pathway rather than only on intracellular transcript levels.
hypotheses.prediction: GSK3B knockdown or catalytic inhibition in THP-1 cells should raise cGAMP-induced IFNβ protein in the supernatant (leftward/upward shift of the dose–response), while GSK3B overexpression or expression of a constitutively active GSK3B (S9A) should lower secreted IFNβ without blocking STING ligand binding; the STING-site inhibitor should still suppress secretion in GSK3B-depleted cells, placing GSK3B on the output arm of the same pathway.
hypotheses.test: In THP-1 cells, compare secreted IFNβ by ELISA after cGAMP (or transfected dsDNA) stimulation across four conditions — control siRNA, GSK3B siRNA/CRISPR knockout, GSK3B-S9A overexpression, and a selective GSK3 inhibitor (e.g. CHIR-99021) — with a parallel intracellular readout (IFNB1 qPCR plus TBK1/IRF3 phospho-blot) to distinguish an effect on induction from an effect on release; include the STING CDN-site inhibitor as an epistasis arm to confirm the GSK3B effect requires STING.
