novelty.note: Searched for GSK3 as a negative regulator of IFN-β, for GSK3β with cGAS/STING/cGAMP, and for GSK3 inhibition effects on DNA-sensing IFN-β secretion in THP-1 cells. Wang et al. (PMID 18981097) already establish the core mechanism and nearly the exact predicted experimental pattern — GSK3 inhibitor, siRNA and kinase-dead mutant raise secreted IFN-β while GSK3β-S9A attenuates it — but in TLR4/LPS-stimulated macrophages via c-Jun/ATF-2, not via cytosolic DNA/STING; a dedicated review (PMID 32272583) explicitly notes that whether GSK-3 positively or negatively regulates cGAS/STING-driven IFN-β is unresolved. So the mechanism is published but not the STING-axis connection or the cGAMP-dose/epistasis prediction.

hypotheses.statement: GSK3B negatively regulates NFAT-dependent cytokine secretion by T cells, acting as a direct brake on IFNγ release.
hypotheses.mechanism: In T cells, GSK3 drives NFAT nuclear export, and its inhibition downstream of CD28/Akt prolongs NFAT nuclear residence (hogan2003:findings:006). Separately, IFNγ secretion by T lymphocytes is reduced when NFATC1 activity is disrupted, identifying NFAT activity as a limiting input to that secretory output (de2024:findings:016). Together these imply that the duration of nuclear NFAT set by GSK3B activity should directly scale how much IFNγ a stimulated T cell secretes.
hypotheses.prediction: GSK3B inhibition or knockdown in stimulated T cells should increase secreted IFNγ per cell and extend the window of secretion, tracking with longer nuclear NFAT dwell time; conversely, constitutively active GSK3B-S9A should shorten nuclear NFAT residence and cut secreted IFNγ, and this suppression should be rescued by a constitutively nuclear NFAT mutant lacking the GSK3 phosphorylation sites.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate a T cell line (e.g. Jurkat) or in vitro-activated T cells with anti-CD3 ± anti-CD28 and measure supernatant IFNγ (and IL-2) by ELISA at several timepoints under control, GSK3 inhibitor, GSK3B siRNA, and GSK3B-S9A conditions, in each case quantifying nuclear/cytoplasmic NFAT by imaging or fractionation in the same samples; epistasis with a GSK3-site-mutant constitutively nuclear NFAT distinguishes a GSK3B→NFAT→secretion route from a GSK3B effect on the secretory machinery itself.

novelty.note: I searched for GSK3 as a brake on NFAT nuclear residence, for GSK3 inhibition/knockdown effects on IFNγ secretion, and for the GSK3B-S9A prediction. The core mechanism is long published — Ohteki et al. showed GSK3 inhibition (Li+) keeps NF-ATc nuclear after antigen stimulation while retroviral GSK-3β-S9A reduces proliferation and IL-2, and Fu et al. reformulated this as GSK3 controlling NFAT nuclear traffic in T cells — and GSK-3β inhibition with 9-ING-41 has been reported to raise IFN-γ secretion from patient CD8+ T cells, but with no NFAT link measured. The specific claim that nuclear-NFAT dwell time set by GSK3B scales secreted IFNγ per cell is not established and is partly contested: GSK3-deficient CD8+ T cells showed reduced IFN-γ in vivo, and a human CD4+ T cell study found GSK-3β facilitates (rather than restrains) IFN-γ production through T-bet, explicitly independent of NFAT. Hence partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly phosphorylates 14-3-3 on tyrosine within its phosphopeptide-binding channel (notably the Tyr-128 that contacts the ligand phosphate), thereby disrupting 14-3-3 binding to its phospho-Ser clients.
hypotheses.mechanism: Structural work on the 14-3-3 dimer places Tyr-128 in the conserved amphipathic channel where it hydrogen-bonds the ligand phosphoserine alongside the basic Arg-56/Arg-127/Lys-49 cluster (yaffe1997:findings:009), so adding a bulky negative charge at this position should electrostatically and sterically antagonize the same phosphate coordination that drives client binding, which the corpus shows requires a phospho-Ser with strong Arg preference at pS-4 (yaffe1997:findings:002). v-SRC is exceptionally promiscuous, generating over 2000 phosphosites in a heterologous proteome with substrate overlap approaching two-thirds with another tyrosine kinase (bradley2024:findings:002), so a solvent-accessible channel tyrosine in an abundant protein is a plausible direct substrate. Because client capture is the sole output of 14-3-3 (e.g., growth-factor-dependent capture of FKHRL1 via phospho-T32/S253, brunet1999:findings:009), such a modification would act as a direct off-switch for 14-3-3 rather than a change in its expression.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active SRC will incorporate phosphate into purified 14-3-3 on tyrosine (with Tyr-128 among the mapped sites), and tyrosine-phosphorylated 14-3-3 will show markedly reduced affinity for a phospho-Ser/Thr client peptide or protein, while a Y128F 14-3-3 mutant will be phosphorylated less and retain client binding; in cells, SRC activation will reduce co-immunoprecipitation of 14-3-3 with phospho-clients such as FKHRL1 without lowering client phosphorylation at T32/S253.
hypotheses.test: Incubate purified GST-14-3-3 (wild type and Y128F) with recombinant active SRC and ATP in vitro, confirm and map tyrosine phosphorylation by 4G10 immunoblot and LC-MS/MS, then quantify binding of the phosphorylated versus mock-treated protein to a fluorescein-labeled phospho-Ser client peptide (e.g., an RxxpSxP-type motif) by fluorescence polarization or ITC; in parallel, co-transfect 293T or HeLa cells with tagged 14-3-3 (WT or Y128F) plus a phospho-client such as HA-FKHRL1 with or without active SRC and compare anti-tag co-immunoprecipitation of the client while blotting the client's own phospho-sites as a control.

novelty.note: I searched for tyrosine phosphorylation of 14-3-3 itself disrupting phospho-Ser client binding, for the groove tyrosine specifically (Tyr-128/Tyr-130 numbering), and for Src/tyrosine-kinase phosphorylation of 14-3-3 plus loss of client (e.g., FOXO3/FKHRL1) co-immunoprecipitation. The general mechanism is published: a tyrosine kinase (IGF1R) phosphorylates maize 14-3-3 GF14-6 on Tyr-137, a binding-groove tyrosine, and this lowers affinity for a 14-3-3-binding phosphopeptide and reduces association with the H+-ATPase in planta; independently, genetically encoded nitration of the homologous groove tyrosine Y130 in human 14-3-3β abolishes client binding, confirming that bulky modification of this residue is inactivating. I found nothing reporting SRC (or any kinase) phosphorylating mammalian 14-3-3 on Tyr-128/Y130, no mapping of such a site by MS, and no link to loss of phospho-client capture such as FKHRL1/FOXO3 in cells, so the specific kinase–residue–client prediction remains unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: EGFR directly recruits and activates SYK by binding the SYK tandem SH2 domains to a pair of phosphorylated tyrosines in the EGFR cytoplasmic tail, making SYK an EGFR-proximal substrate/effector.
hypotheses.mechanism: The EGFR tail carries ~12 verified phosphotyrosines, several of which (notably Y998 and Y1016) engage many SH2/PTB domains with high affinity, and EGFR's binding repertoire expands markedly as the affinity threshold is relaxed, i.e. it is a promiscuous multi-site phospho-scaffold (jones2006:findings:009, jones2006:findings:010, jones2006:findings:014). SYK, in turn, is switched on precisely by bidentate engagement of its tandem SH2 domains with two phosphotyrosines, and the structure of that module is unusually flexible, accommodating phosphotyrosine pairs with a broad range of spacing rather than a strict ITAM geometry (mcsai2010:findings:007, mcsai2010:findings:006). A closely spaced, doubly phosphorylated EGFR tyrosine pair should therefore be a competent, non-ITAM ligand that both docks and de-autoinhibits SYK, in the same way the integrin β-tail engages SYK SH2 surfaces outside the canonical ITAM mode (mcsai2010:findings:015).
hypotheses.prediction: Purified SYK tandem SH2 domains should bind doubly phosphorylated EGFR tail peptides (e.g. spanning Y998/Y1016-containing pairs) with measurable affinity, with singly phosphorylated or non-phosphorylated versions binding much more weakly; in EGFR-expressing cells, EGF stimulation should increase SYK association with EGFR and SYK autophosphorylation at its activating linker tyrosines (Tyr342/Tyr346), and both should be abolished by EGFR kinase inhibition or by phosphotyrosine-binding mutations in the SYK SH2 domains.
hypotheses.test: Two-part in vitro/cell assay: (1) fluorescence-polarization or SPR titration of recombinant SYK tandem-SH2 protein against a panel of synthetic EGFR tail peptides — unphosphorylated, singly phosphorylated, and doubly phosphorylated pairs — to obtain KD values, with a doubly phosphorylated CD3ε ITAM peptide as positive control and an SH2 phospho-binding-pocket mutant as negative control; (2) in an EGFR-high epithelial line transfected with SYK, co-immunoprecipitate EGFR after 0/2/10 min EGF and blot for SYK plus phospho-SYK Tyr342/346, repeating with an EGFR inhibitor and with SYK SH2 mutants, and confirm direct phosphorylation by incubating purified full-length SYK with recombinant active EGFR kinase domain and ATP in vitro.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (Syk tandem SH2 bidentate binding to a non-ITAM receptor tail / ITAM-independent Syk activation), the entities together (EGFR + SYK association, co-IP, EGF-induced Syk phosphorylation, gefitinib sensitivity), and the prediction (SYK SH2 domain affinity for EGFR pY998/pY1016 phosphopeptides in SH2 domain–peptide arrays and FP interactomes). The functional half is already published: EGFR activation induces Syk phosphorylation in keratinocytes with reciprocal Syk requirement for EGFR phosphorylation (PMID 26763439), and SYK is reported to interact with EGFR/ERBB2 and enhance their phosphorylation in ovarian cancer (PMID 31492560); large-scale SH2 domain–phosphopeptide datasets have measured SYK's individual N- and C-SH2 domains against EGFR/ErbB phosphopeptides (PMID 32540967), and a time-resolved SH2 profiling of EGF-stimulated cells explicitly excluded SYK for data quality (10.7554/eLife.11835). I found nothing stating the specific structural claim — that a doubly phosphorylated EGFR tail tyrosine pair is a bidentate, ITAM-mimicking ligand for the SYK tandem SH2 module that both docks and de-autoinhibits SYK, with the interaction abolished by SH2 phospho-pocket mutation — so the mechanism is partially anticipated but the specific bidentate-recruitment prediction is not.

hypotheses.statement: ATM kinase activity directly restrains cellular catabolic flux, acting as a negative regulator of lysosomal/autophagic protein degradation through phosphorylation of degradation machinery, such that loss of ATM activity accelerates bulk protein catabolism.
hypotheses.mechanism: The evidence about ATM states that it phosphorylates the vacuolar ATPase subunit ATP6V1G1 and that blocking this phosphorylation with the ATM inhibitor KU-60019 restores lysosomal activity and enhances autophagic flux (di2021:findings:046), and independently that ATM signalling blocks autophagy and thereby preserves mitochondria and suppresses ROS (kastenhuber2017:findings:008). The evidence about catabolic degradation establishes that kinase phosphorylation of a substrate is itself a switch setting that substrate's degradation rate — removal of MNK1 phosphosites on Spry2, or MNK inhibition, sends Spry2 to degradation (cargnello2011:findings:066) — and that the bulk of cellular protein catabolism runs through defined, saturable degradative machinery whose throughput can be measured (collins2017:findings:000). Together these imply a direct, kinase-activity-dependent relationship in which ATM phosphorylation sets the operating rate of the catabolic machinery rather than merely correlating with stress state.
hypotheses.prediction: Acute ATM kinase inhibition or ATM knockdown, without any DNA-damaging stimulus, should increase the rate of bulk long-lived protein turnover and shorten the half-lives of labile reporter substrates; the increase should be abolished by lysosomal/v-ATPase blockade (bafilomycin A1 or chloroquine) and be reproduced by a non-phosphorylatable ATP6V1G1 mutant but not by a phosphomimetic one, whereas kinase-dead ATM should fail to suppress catabolic flux when re-expressed in ATM-depleted cells.
hypotheses.test: In a single cell line, measure bulk protein catabolic flux by metabolic pulse-chase (SILAC heavy-to-light chase or 35S-methionine release of acid-soluble counts) plus degradation of a short-lived fluorescent reporter, comparing vehicle, KU-60019/ATM inhibitor, and ATM siRNA arms, each crossed with bafilomycin A1 and with a proteasome inhibitor to partition lysosomal versus proteasomal contributions; in parallel, rescue ATM-depleted cells with wild-type versus kinase-dead ATM, and express wild-type, S→A, and S→D/E ATP6V1G1 while reading out lysosomal cathepsin/v-ATPase acidification activity and LC3-II flux. ATM inhibition raising lysosome-dependent flux, phenocopied by non-phosphorylatable ATP6V1G1 and reversed by wild-type but not kinase-dead ATM, supports the relationship; no change in flux, or a change insensitive to both lysosomal blockade and the ATP6V1G1 phosphosite state, rules it out.

novelty.note: I searched for ATM phosphorylation of ATP6V1G1 / v-ATPase and lysosomal acidification, for ATM as a negative regulator of autophagic-lysosomal degradation (KU-60019/KU-55933, bafilomycin, LC3-II flux), and for ATM inhibition increasing bulk protein turnover. The kinase-activity-dependent arm is already published: Kang et al. show ATM directly phosphorylates the V-ATPase subunit ATP6V1G1, reducing V1–V0 assembly and lysosomal acidification, so that ATM inhibition reacidifies lysosomes and restores autophagy — i.e. ATM activity restrains lysosomal degradation. What is not published is the generalisation to bulk protein catabolic flux or the specific predictions (non-phosphorylatable vs phosphomimetic ATP6V1G1, kinase-dead ATM rescue, pulse-chase long-lived protein turnover without DNA damage); indeed the nearest work on bulk turnover reports the opposite direction — ATM loss impairs proteasome-mediated degradation via ISG15, and ATM loss disrupts (rather than accelerates) the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, with ATM inhibitors reported to block autolysosome formation. Hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly phosphorylates STAT5 on its activating C-terminal tyrosine (Y694/Y699), driving SH2-mediated STAT5 dimerization and transcriptional activation independently of JAK.
hypotheses.mechanism: v-SRC is an exceptionally promiscuous tyrosine kinase, generating >2000 regulated phosphosites in a heterologous system (bradley2024:findings:002), and SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation of a downstream effector is already documented to stabilize SH2/partner binding and drive that effector's activation (cargnello2011:findings:059). On the STAT5 side, the activating Y699 site is set by a cytoplasmic non-JAK tyrosine kinase (BCR::ABL1) together with the Grb2/Crkl/Cbl adaptor phosphosites and is lost within minutes of kinase inhibition (oliinyk2024:findings:016), and STAT5 activation depends on SH2-domain-mediated dimerization that pY engagement provides (philips2022:findings:014) — so the site is accessible to, and functionally sufficient for, phosphorylation by a soluble tyrosine kinase such as SRC.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC will phosphorylate recombinant STAT5 on Y694/Y699 in vitro with stoichiometry detectable by phospho-specific antibody and MS, the signal disappearing with a Y694F/Y699F substrate or a kinase-dead SRC; in cells, gain of SRC activity will raise pY-STAT5 and STAT5-reporter output even under JAK inhibition, and SRC inhibition will lower basal pY-STAT5 in SRC-active lines.
hypotheses.test: Two-part bench test: (1) in vitro kinase reaction of recombinant active SRC (and kinase-dead control) with purified full-length STAT5A/B WT versus Y694F, read out by anti-pY694 immunoblot and by LC-MS/MS site mapping to confirm the phosphorylated residue and measure stoichiometry; (2) in HEK293 cells co-expressing STAT5 with inducible v-SRC (WT versus kinase-dead), measure pY694-STAT5, STAT5 dimerization by co-IP of differentially tagged STAT5, and a STAT5-responsive luciferase reporter in the presence of a JAK inhibitor and of a SRC inhibitor, so that a JAK-independent, SRC-inhibitor-sensitive pSTAT5 signal confirms and its absence rules out the direct relationship.

novelty.note: I searched for direct SRC phosphorylation of STAT5 Y694/Y699, JAK-independent STAT5 activation by Src-family kinases, and in vitro kinase assays with recombinant STAT5. Okutani et al. (Oncogene 2001) report exactly this explanation: co-expression of Src with STAT5 in COS7 cells phosphorylates STAT5A mainly on Tyr694, an in vitro kinase assay shows Src phosphorylates GST-STAT5 bearing the conserved C-terminus but not the Tyr694-lacking truncation, and Src inhibition (PP1/PP2, dominant-negative Src, Src knockdown in K562) lowers pY-STAT5 — the same in vitro and cellular readouts the prediction proposes. Klejman et al. (EMBO J 2002) show the SFK Hck phosphorylates STAT5B on Y699 downstream of BCR/ABL, and Berger et al. (Cell Commun Signal 2015) confirm v-Src/Hck/Lyn-driven Y694 phosphorylation while adding the caveat that the SFK pY416–STAT5 SH2 interaction actually impairs STAT5A dimerization and nuclear accumulation, qualifying the dimerization half of the hypothesis.

hypotheses.statement: ZAP70 directly phosphorylates tyrosines in the CD28 cytoplasmic tail, making CD28 a ZAP70 substrate in addition to an Lck substrate and providing a second route to phospho-CD28-dependent p85/PI3K docking.
hypotheses.mechanism: The CD28 tail is a bona fide membrane-proximal tyrosine-kinase substrate: Lck phosphorylates it with measurable Michaelis–Menten kinetics on liposomes, and phosphorylation of the CD28/ICOS tails specifically creates an SH2 docking site for the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 at the pYMNM motif (hui2017:findings:008, hui2017:findings:004, smithgarvin2009:findings:021). ZAP70, once released from its autoinhibited conformation by SH2 engagement of phosphorylated ITAMs, phosphorylates tyrosine motifs on other membrane-proximal molecules (LAT, SLP-76) precisely to create SH2-protein docking sites (mcsai2010:findings:005, good2011:findings:006). Since CD28's tail presents the same class of substrate motif in the same membrane compartment where active ZAP70 operates, ZAP70 is predicted to act on CD28 directly rather than only downstream of it.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified, activated ZAP70 plus ATP should phosphorylate the CD28 cytosolic tail on liposomes in the complete absence of Lck activity, generating phospho-CD28 that recruits the p85 SH2 domain; conversely, inhibiting or deleting ZAP70 in cells should reduce CD28 tail phosphorylation and p85 association beyond what loss of Lck-driven phosphorylation alone accounts for, while a kinase-dead ZAP70 should give no CD28 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute His-tagged CD28 cytosolic tail on large unilamellar vesicles or supported lipid bilayers with either (i) ZAP70 pre-activated by a synthetic doubly phosphorylated CD3ζ ITAM peptide or (ii) kinase-dead ZAP70, add ATP with no Lck present (and in parallel with Lck plus a Src-family inhibitor as a specificity control), and read out CD28 phosphotyrosine by anti-pTyr Western blot and phospho-site-specific mass spectrometry of the YMNM tyrosine, with functional confirmation by FRET-based recruitment of labeled p85 SH2 to the bilayer; ZAP70 knockdown/knockout Jurkat lines stimulated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 and blotted for CD28 pTyr and CD28–p85 co-immunoprecipitation provide the cellular loss-of-function counterpart.

citations.title: p56Lck and p59Fyn regulate CD28 binding to phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, growth factor receptor-bound protein GRB-2, and T cell-specific protein-tyrosine kinase ITK: implications for T-cell costimulation.

novelty.note: I searched for ZAP-70 as a direct CD28-tail kinase, for CD28 YMNM/p85 recruitment kinase identity, and for in vitro/coexpression tests of Syk-family kinases on CD28. Raab et al. (PNAS 1995) directly compared kinases in coexpression assays and found Lck and Fyn phosphorylate CD28 Tyr-191 and increase p85/GRB-2 SH2 binding, while 'ZAP-70 and ITK failed to induce these events' — a stated negative result for exactly this claim. Reviews of CD28 signaling likewise attribute CD28 tail phosphorylation solely to Src-family kinases, with ZAP70 acting downstream.

hypotheses.statement: JAK1 directly phosphorylates STAT5 on its activating tyrosine when JAK1 is engaged at a cytokine receptor Box1/Box2 site, making STAT5 a direct JAK1 substrate.
hypotheses.mechanism: The JAK1 claims show JAK1 is a receptor-bound active kinase whose dimer at an IFNλR1 Box1/Box2 site is signaling-competent with outward-facing, accessible TK catalytic clefts, and that receptor-associated JAK1 directly activates a STAT family member (STAT3) downstream of TβRI without intermediates; JAK1-deficient cells lose gp130/IL-6 signal transduction, placing JAK1 upstream of STAT activation at these receptors. The STAT5 claims show STAT5 tyrosine phosphorylation tracks the activity of a closely related JAK family kinase (JAK2 V617F in BaF3 cells) and that STAT5 is activated through an SH2 domain of the same type that mediates STAT3 recruitment to phosphorylated receptor/kinase sites. Together these imply the kinase activity of JAK1, not only JAK2, can be the proximal source of STAT5 Y694 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.prediction: Cytokine stimulation of cells reconstituted with catalytically active JAK1 will produce STAT5 tyrosine phosphorylation that is abolished by kinase-dead JAK1 or by JAK1 loss, and purified active JAK1 kinase domain will phosphorylate recombinant STAT5 on its C-terminal tyrosine in vitro in the absence of any other kinase.
hypotheses.test: In JAK1-deficient human fibrosarcoma cells, reconstitute with vector, wild-type JAK1, or a kinase-dead JAK1 mutant, stimulate with a gp130-family cytokine, and immunoblot phospho-STAT5 (Y694) versus total STAT5; in parallel, run an in vitro kinase assay with purified recombinant JAK1 kinase domain, ATP, and recombinant STAT5, reading out pY694 by immunoblot with a JAK1-inhibitor and no-ATP control to confirm direct, JAK1-catalysed phosphorylation.

citations.title: Jak1 has a dominant role over Jak3 in signal transduction through γc-containing cytokine receptors.
Jak1 plays an essential role for receptor phosphorylation and Stat activation in response to granulocyte colony-stimulating factor.

Differential substrate recognition capabilities of Janus family protein tyrosine kinases within the interleukin 2 receptor (IL2R) system: Jak3 as a potential molecular target for treatment of leukemias with a hyperactive Jak-Stat signaling machinery.

novelty.note: I searched for JAK1 kinase-dead reconstitution with STAT5 phosphorylation, for in vitro phosphorylation of recombinant STAT5 by purified JAK1, and for JAK1-deficient fibrosarcoma (U4A) reconstitution experiments, retrieving records via PubMed/eutils and publisher pages. Both halves of the prediction are already published: Haan et al. showed in a reconstituted γc receptor system that kinase-inactive JAK1 (but not kinase-inactive JAK3) completely abolishes STAT5 phosphorylation, Shimoda et al. showed that JAK1-deficient human fibrosarcoma cells lose cytokine-induced receptor and Stat (including Stat5) phosphorylation and are rescued by wild-type but not kinase-inactive JAK1, and Witthuhn et al. used baculovirus-expressed recombinant components to show JAK1 directly phosphorylates STAT5 among other STATs. JAK1 as a direct upstream kinase for STAT5 activating-tyrosine phosphorylation at cytokine receptor Box1/Box2 sites is therefore standard, experimentally supported knowledge rather than a novel proposal.

hypotheses.statement: AKT directly phosphorylates ERK5/MAPK7 on a basic (RxRxxS/T-type) site in its C-terminal half, acting as an inhibitory input that restrains ERK5 nuclear accumulation and C-terminal transactivation activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: brunet1999 establishes AKT as a kinase whose direct phosphorylation of discrete residues on a partner protein (FKHRL1 T32/S253/S315) is both necessary and sufficient to shift that partner out of the nucleus and to suppress its transcriptional output, and bekkerjensen2020 shows the AKT substrate motif RxRxx[S/T] is driven by EGF independently of MEK, i.e. AKT is active on basic-motif sites under the same growth-factor stimulation that engages ERK5. plotnikov2011 shows ERK5's own localization is governed by phosphorylation-dependent disruption of an intramolecular N/C-terminal fold that unmasks its NLSs over its NES, and that phosphorylation of the C-terminal half tunes its intrinsic transactivation activity — the same class of regulatory node AKT acts on in FKHRL1. Together these imply ERK5 itself could be a direct AKT substrate, with AKT-placed phosphate stabilizing the closed/NES-exposed state and damping transactivation.
hypotheses.prediction: Constitutively active AKT should label recombinant ERK5 C-terminal-half protein in vitro at one or more mappable Ser/Thr residues in a basic consensus, and in cells active AKT should hold stimulus-activated ERK5 cytoplasmic and lower MEF2-site-dependent reporter/Nur77 induction, while AKT inhibition should increase ERK5 nuclear accumulation and transactivation; an ERK5 mutant with the identified site(s) changed to alanine should be phosphorylated poorly or not at all by AKT and should become insensitive to AKT status in both localization and reporter assays, without change in its TEY-motif phosphorylation by MEK5.
hypotheses.test: Immunoprecipitate HA-tagged constitutively active versus kinase-inactive AKT from transfected 293T cells and run in vitro 32P-ATP kinase assays on bacterially produced GST-ERK5 fragments (full-length, N-terminal kinase domain, C-terminal half), then map sites by alanine-substitution series exactly as done for GST-FKHRL1; in parallel, co-express wild-type or phospho-site-mutant ERK5 with active AKT (or treat with an AKT inhibitor) in a cell line where ERK5 is cytoplasmic at rest, and score ERK5 nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution by immunofluorescence plus MEF2-site luciferase activity and anti-phospho-TEY blots.

citations.title: A crucial role for p90RSK-mediated reduction of ERK5 transcriptional activity in endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis.
Phosphorylation of ERK5 on Thr732 is associated with ERK5 nuclear localization and ERK5-dependent transcription.
VEGF Stimulates Activation of ERK5 in the Absence of C-Terminal Phosphorylation Preventing Nuclear Localization and Facilitating AKT Activation in Endothelial Cells.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: AKT directly phosphorylating ERK5/MAPK7 and holding it cytoplasmic; basic/RxRxxS-motif (AGC-kinase) phosphorylation of the ERK5 C-terminal half as an inhibitory input on transactivation; and the prediction side (AKT inhibition raising ERK5 nuclear accumulation and MEF2-reporter/Nur77 output). No source states that AKT itself phosphorylates ERK5, and no mapped AKT site on ERK5 exists in the literature or in the sites catalogued for its C-terminal tail. The general mechanism class is, however, published: an AGC-family kinase with the same RxRxxS/T consensus (p90RSK) binds the ERK5 C-terminus (aa 571–807) and directly phosphorylates Ser496, suppressing ERK5 transcriptional activity independently of TEY/kinase activation, and other kinases (ERK1/2 at Thr732) are known to tune ERK5 nuclear localization and MEF2-dependent transcription through C-terminal phosphorylation — so the inhibitory-phosphorylation node exists, but the specific AKT connection and the localization prediction are unclaimed.

hypotheses.statement: SYK binds directly, via its tandem SH2 domains, to the Lck-phosphorylated cytoplasmic tail of CD28, and this engagement relieves SYK autoinhibition to activate the kinase.
hypotheses.mechanism: The CD28 tail is a bona fide Lck substrate whose tyrosine phosphorylation creates SH2-docking sites that recruit SH2-domain proteins such as PI3K p85, and its phosphorylation state is tuned by CD45 and PD-1-bound Shp2 (hui2017:findings:004, hui2017:findings:006, hui2017:findings:008, smithgarvin2009:findings:021). SYK is held in a compact autoinhibited conformation that is released by phosphotyrosine engagement of its SH2 pair, and its tandem SH2 module is unusually flexible, accommodating phosphotyrosine motifs with a broad range of tyrosine spacing; SYK can moreover be engaged and activated ITAM-independently through direct association of a receptor cytoplasmic tail (integrin β-chain) with non-ITAM-binding surfaces of its N-terminal SH2 domain (mcsai2010:findings:006, mcsai2010:findings:007, mcsai2010:findings:015). Together these properties predict the phospho-CD28 tail, a non-ITAM but Lck-phosphorylated costimulatory tail, as a direct SYK ligand and activator.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified SYK (full-length and its tandem SH2 module) should bind the Lck-phosphorylated CD28 cytoplasmic tail with measurable affinity but not the unphosphorylated tail, binding should be lost when the CD28 tail tyrosines (including the YMNM tyrosine) are mutated to phenylalanine, and CD28-tail binding should increase SYK catalytic activity and autophosphorylation of the linker tyrosines (Tyr342/Tyr346/Tyr624) relative to SYK alone; conversely, Shp2- or CD45-mediated dephosphorylation of the CD28 tail should release SYK.
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute His-tagged CD28 cytoplasmic tail (wild type versus tyrosine-to-phenylalanine mutants) on liposomes with His-Lck and ATP as in the established CD28 phosphorylation system, then add fluorescently labeled recombinant SYK tandem SH2 domains and measure recruitment by FRET or fluorescence polarization, with a doubly phosphorylated CD3ε ITAM peptide as positive control and unphosphorylated CD28 tail as negative control; in parallel run phospho-CD28 peptide pulldowns from T cell lysates blotted for SYK, and assay recombinant SYK kinase activity plus anti-pTyr342/pTyr624 blots with and without phospho-CD28 tail peptide to test activation. Lack of phosphorylation-dependent binding above the unphosphorylated control, or no change in SYK activity, would rule out the direct interaction.

citations.title: Crystal Structures and Thermodynamic Analysis Reveal Distinct Mechanisms of CD28 Phosphopeptide Binding to the Src Homology 2 (SH2) Domains of Three Adaptor Proteins.
The mechanism of allosteric activation of SYK kinase derived from multiple phospho-ITAM-bound structures.

novelty.note: I searched for direct SYK/ZAP70 binding to the phosphorylated CD28 tail, for SH2-domain specificity screens against the CD28 pYMNM motif, and for ITAM-independent SYK activation by costimulatory tails. Published work on phospho-CD28 SH2 ligands covers only Grb2, Gads and PI3K p85 (structures and thermodynamics), and SYK tandem-SH2 activation work is restricted to phospho-ITAMs; no source states or directly tests SYK binding/activation by the Lck-phosphorylated CD28 tail. Hence open, with the nearest published studies cited.

hypotheses.statement: NGF stimulation directly regulates MEK1 at its inhibitory feedback site, producing weaker/short-lived ERK1/2-dependent phosphorylation of MEK1 Thr292 than EGF does, so MEK1 is the node through which NGF sustains ERK1/2 activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: MEK1 Thr292 is phosphorylated by ERK1/2 in an ERK-dependent manner in intact cells and this modification inhibits MEK1 kinase activity toward ERK1/2 and disrupts MEK1–ERK2 binding, making T292 the principal MEK-level negative feedback brake on the cascade (lake2016:findings:010). In the same cell system, NGF and EGF differ precisely in feedback wiring: EGF engages only negative feedback onto the ERK module and gives transient ERK, whereas NGF adds positive feedback and yields switch-like, sustained ERK activation and differentiation (lemmon2010:findings:024, lake2016:findings:016, purvis2013:findings:002, ryu2015:findings:000). If sustained NGF-driven ERK activity coexists with a functional MEK1 T292 brake, either NGF must attenuate phosphorylation of that site or NGF-sustained ERK is mechanistically incompatible with the ERK→MEK1 brake — a direct, testable relationship between NGF and MEK1.
hypotheses.prediction: In PC-12 cells, EGF should induce rapid, pronounced MEK1 Thr292 phosphorylation coincident with ERK adaptation within 10–15 min, whereas NGF should induce markedly less or only briefly elevated Thr292 phosphorylation despite comparable or greater initial ERK activation; conversely, expressing non-phosphorylatable MEK1 T292A should prolong EGF-stimulated phospho-ERK1/2 toward the NGF-like sustained profile and increase neurite outgrowth, while a phosphomimetic/ERK-docking-competent MEK1 should blunt the sustained phase of the NGF response.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate PC-12 cells with saturating EGF versus NGF and immunoblot a matched time course (0–120 min) for phospho-MEK1 Thr292, phospho-MEK1 Ser217/221, and phospho-ERK1/2, with MEK1/2 or ERK inhibitor controls to confirm the site is feedback-dependent; in parallel co-immunoprecipitate MEK1 and blot for ERK2 to test whether NGF preserves the MEK1–ERK2 complex that T292 phosphorylation disrupts. Then stably express FLAG-MEK1 wild type versus T292A in the same cells and quantify phospho-ERK1/2 duration by immunoblot plus neurite outgrowth after EGF or NGF; a T292A-dependent conversion of the EGF response to a sustained, differentiating one, together with low NGF-induced Thr292 phosphorylation, supports the hypothesis, whereas equal Thr292 phosphorylation under both ligands and no effect of T292A rules it out.

citations.title: Negative feedback regulation of the ERK1/2 MAPK pathway.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: MEK1 Thr292 phosphorylation in NGF vs EGF PC12 signalling; MEK1 T292 as an ERK negative-feedback site generally; and the prediction (MEK1 T292A effects on sustained ERK/neurite outgrowth). The T292 feedback mechanism itself is well published (Lake et al. review: ERK1/2 phosphorylates MEK1 T292, inhibiting MEK1 and disrupting MEK–ERK complex formation; T292A is more strongly activated), and the differential NGF/EGF feedback wiring in PC12 cells is also published (positive ERK→Raf feedback under NGF vs negative under EGF), but I found no source that connects the two — no report of ligand-specific T292 phosphorylation kinetics, no MEK1 T292A experiment converting EGF responses to sustained/differentiating ones, and no negative test of this specific claim. Hence open, with the nearest published work cited.

hypotheses.statement: RIPK1 directly activates NF-κB by serving as the ubiquitinated scaffold that recruits NEMO to the TNF receptor signalling complex, independently of RIPK1 kinase activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: Evidence about A states that RIP/RIPK1 is critical for TNF-induced NF-κB activation without requiring its kinase activity, and that NEMO is the essential regulator of IKK complex activation by upstream signals (chen2002:findings:003, chen2002:findings:005). Independently, evidence about C shows that endogenous NEMO co-precipitates ubiquitinated RIPK1 after TNF stimulation and that this NEMO–RIPK1 complex is destroyed by the Met1-Ub-specific DUB OTULIN, whose depletion increases Met1-linked RIPK1 ubiquitination in the TNF-RSC (keusekotten2013:findings:021, keusekotten2013:findings:029). Together these imply the direct relation is ubiquitin-dependent physical coupling: RIPK1's ubiquitin chains, not its catalytic output, are the docking site that loads NEMO/IKK and thereby switches on NF-κB.
hypotheses.prediction: In TNF-stimulated cells, loss of RIPK1 should abolish NEMO recruitment, IKK activation, IκBα degradation and NF-κB nuclear translocation; re-expression of kinase-dead RIPK1 should restore all of these, whereas a RIPK1 mutant that cannot be ubiquitinated should bind NEMO poorly and fail to restore NF-κB activation. Conversely, conditions that increase RIPK1 ubiquitination (OTULIN depletion) should increase NEMO–RIPK1 complex and NF-κB output, while OTULIN overexpression should reduce both.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa or U2OS cells, delete RIPK1 (CRISPR) and stably reconstitute with wild-type, kinase-dead, or ubiquitin-acceptor-mutant RIPK1; stimulate with TNF and read out (i) endogenous NEMO immunoprecipitation followed by blotting for Ub-RIPK1 and for associated IKKα/β, and (ii) NF-κB activation by IκBα degradation/IKK phosphorylation blots, NF-κB reporter assay and nuclear RelA immunofluorescence. Parallel arms with OTULIN knockdown and OTULIN overexpression test whether NF-κB output tracks the amount of ubiquitinated RIPK1 bound to NEMO.

citations.title: Activation of IKK by TNFalpha requires site-specific ubiquitination of RIP1 and polyubiquitin binding by NEMO.
Sensing of Lys 63-linked polyubiquitination by NEMO is a key event in NF-kappaB activation [corrected].
The kinase activity of Rip1 is not required for tumor necrosis factor-alpha-induced IkappaB kinase or p38 MAP kinase activation or for the ubiquitination of Rip1 by Traf2.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (ubiquitinated RIPK1 as scaffold recruiting NEMO/IKK to TNFR1), for the entities together (RIP1 + NEMO + polyubiquitin + IKK activation), and for the kinase-independence prediction (kinase-dead RIP1 restoring NF-κB). The explanation is long-published: Ea et al. (Mol Cell 2006) showed TNF-induced K377 ubiquitination of RIP1 is required for IKK/NF-κB activation and that polyubiquitinated RIP1 recruits the IKK complex through NEMO's polyubiquitin binding, with K377R RIP1 failing to restore IKK activation in RIP1-deficient cells; Wu et al. (Nat Cell Biol 2006) showed NEMO point mutants that cannot bind K63 polyubiquitin lose RIP binding, IKK recruitment to TNFR1, and NF-κB activation; and Lee et al. (JBC 2004) showed kinase-inactive RIP1 (D138N) supports normal TNF-induced IKK activation and RIP1 ubiquitination. Together these state the same ubiquitin-dependent, kinase-independent scaffold explanation the hypothesis proposes, so the status is established (only the OTULIN-titration arm is an untested add-on).

hypotheses.statement: NF-κB transcriptional activity directly restrains RIPK1-dependent cell death downstream of TNF, so that the protection NF-κB confers is executed by suppressing RIPK1 function.
hypotheses.mechanism: Evidence about A states that loss of NF-κB activity increases susceptibility to TNF-induced death while enforced NF-κB activation protects, and that NF-κB drives resynthesis of inhibitory gene products including IκB and the cIAPs that limit the amplitude and duration of TNF signalling (chen2002:findings:006, chen2002:findings:007). Independently, evidence about C shows RIPK1 is required for TNF-induced necroptotic death and its lipid signalling step, since RIPK1−/− Jurkat cells fail to accumulate ceramide and are protected from TNF-induced necroptosis, and tissue-specific RIPK1 loss unleashes spontaneous CASP8- or necroptosis-driven death and inflammation (vandenabeele2010:findings:019, galluzzi2018:findings:013). If NF-κB-induced inhibitors act on the same TNF-receptor node where RIPK1 operates, then the death that appears when NF-κB is blocked should be RIPK1-executed rather than a separate pathway.
hypotheses.prediction: Blocking NF-κB (IKK inhibitor or IκBα super-repressor) in TNF-treated cells should convert TNF into a cytotoxic stimulus, and that added death should be largely abolished by RIPK1 deletion or by a RIPK1 inhibitor, whereas enforced NF-κB activation should suppress death to the same extent as removing RIPK1; markers of RIPK1 engagement (RIPK1 phosphorylation, complex formation, ceramide accumulation) should rise when NF-κB is blocked and fall when NF-κB is enforced.
hypotheses.test: In L929 and Jurkat cells (including RIPK1−/− Jurkat as the genetic arm), express IκBα super-repressor or apply an IKK inhibitor, then treat with TNF and quantify death (viability, LDH release, live-cell imaging) with and without necrostatin-1 or RIPK1 knockout; in parallel immunoblot RIPK1 phosphorylation and assay ceramide accumulation, and confirm that NF-κB-dependent inhibitor proteins (IκB, cIAPs) are lost under NF-κB blockade. Epistasis — NF-κB blockade increasing death only in RIPK1-proficient cells — would establish or rule out the direct suppression of RIPK1 by NF-κB output.

citations.title: NEMO Prevents RIP Kinase 1-Mediated Epithelial Cell Death and Chronic Intestinal Inflammation by NF-κB-Dependent and -Independent Functions.
NF-κB inhibition in keratinocytes causes RIPK1-mediated necroptosis and skin inflammation.
NF-κB regulated expression of A20 controls IKK dependent repression of RIPK1 induced cell death in activated T cells.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (NF-κB transcriptional output restraining RIPK1-dependent death downstream of TNF), for the key entities together (NF-κB/IKK/NEMO + RIPK1 + TNF + necroptosis/apoptosis), and for the prediction (blocking NF-κB converts TNF into a cytotoxic stimulus that is rescued by RIPK1 deletion/kinase inhibition). Multiple primary papers state exactly this explanation: NEMO loss in intestinal epithelium kills via a RIPK1-kinase-dependent RIPK1/FADD/caspase-8 complex with an explicitly NF-κB-dependent component (Vlantis 2016); epidermal IKK2 or RelA/c-Rel deletion unleashes TNFR1-driven, RIPK1-kinase-dependent necroptosis, with the authors framing it as NF-κB-dependent transcription restraining RIPK1 (Kumari 2021); and IKK2-deficient activated T cells die by TNF-induced RIPK1-dependent death because they fail to induce the NF-κB target A20, with RIPK1 kinase inactivation rescuing the phenotype (Webb 2024). The literature also documents the two-checkpoint framing (direct IKK/TBK1/MK2 phosphorylation of RIPK1 plus NF-κB-dependent prosurvival genes) and notes that some in vitro settings give RIPK1-independent TRADD-driven death, so the epistasis proposed here has already been performed and partly qualified.

hypotheses.statement: JNK1 negatively regulates IFNG expression in activated T cells by phosphorylating NFAT2/NFATC1 and driving its nuclear export, so that loss of JNK1 activity increases IFNγ production.
hypotheses.mechanism: hogan2003:findings:005 states that JNK1 acts as an inducible NFAT export kinase with isoform selectivity, phosphorylating NFAT2 and NFAT4 (but not NFAT1/NFAT3). de2024:findings:016 states that in T lymphocytes, disruption of NFATC1 (NFAT2) activity accompanies reduced effector function including IFNγ secretion, tying NFATC1 activity to the amount of IFNγ a T cell makes. If the nuclear dwell time of NFAT2 sets IFNγ output, then the kinase that exports NFAT2 — JNK1 — should be a direct upstream negative regulator of IFNG, a relation the corpus already states in kinase→substrate→output form (e.g. JNK1→NLRP3 phosphorylation controlling activation in swanson2019:findings:028).
hypotheses.prediction: In TCR-stimulated T cells, JNK1 depletion or selective JNK inhibition will prolong nuclear retention of NFATC1 and raise IFNG transcript and secreted IFNγ, whereas constitutively active JNK1 (or MKK7-JNK1 fusion) will accelerate NFATC1 nuclear exit and lower IFNγ; an NFATC1 mutant lacking the JNK1 target serines will retain IFNγ output even when JNK1 is hyperactivated, and IFNγ should be comparatively insensitive to p38 inhibition, which targets NFAT1/NFAT3 rather than NFAT2.
hypotheses.test: In a T cell line (e.g. Jurkat or a CD4+ T hybridoma) stimulated with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 or PMA/ionomycin, compare CRISPR/siRNA JNK1 knockout, JNK1 re-expression, and constitutively active JNK1 against control: quantify NFATC1 nuclear/cytoplasmic distribution by subcellular fractionation immunoblot and by GFP-NFATC1 live imaging of export kinetics after stimulation, and in parallel measure IFNG mRNA by qPCR, secreted IFNγ by ELISA, and IFNG-promoter reporter activity; confirm directness with an in vitro kinase assay using recombinant active JNK1 and purified NFATC1 plus phospho-site mapping, and rescue the knockout with wild-type versus phospho-site-mutant NFATC1 to show the IFNγ change tracks the JNK1 phosphorylation sites.

citations.title: c-Jun NH(2)-terminal kinase inhibits targeting of the protein phosphatase calcineurin to NFATc1.
Defective T cell differentiation in the absence of Jnk1.
JNK knockdown enhances CAR-T cell cytotoxicity through elevated NFATc1-dependent transcription in preclinical ovarian cancer models.
JNK2 negatively regulates CD8+ T cell effector function and anti-tumor immune response.
c-Jun NH(2)-terminal kinase (JNK)1 and JNK2 have distinct roles in CD8(+) T cell activation.

novelty.note: I searched for JNK1-mediated NFATc1/NFAT2 phosphorylation and nuclear export, for Jnk1-/- T cell cytokine phenotypes, and for JNK inhibition/knockdown effects on IFN-γ output. The kinase→substrate→localization half is fully published: Chow et al. show JNK phosphorylates the calcineurin-targeting (PxIxIT) domain of NFATc1, blocking its nuclear accumulation, and that Jnk1-/- T cells have greatly increased NFATc1-dependent nuclear responses, while Dong et al. link JNK1 loss to increased nuclear NFATc and elevated cytokine output (Th2 skewing, i.e. more IL-4 rather than more IFN-γ). The specific prediction — that removing JNK1 raises IFNG through prolonged NFATc1 nuclear dwell time — is not stated anywhere I found, and the nearest direct tests point the other way or are null: a 2025 CAR-T study found JNK knockdown enhanced NFATc1 nuclear localization and transcription yet left IFN-γ unaffected, JNK1 is reported to promote (not restrain) IFN-γ in CD8 T cells, and it is JNK2 whose deletion raises IFN-γ. Hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: SYK kinase activity in dendritic cells is a direct upstream positive regulator of IL-17 production, such that SYK inhibition or loss suppresses IL-17 expression by responding T cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: SYK signalling downstream of CLEC7A drives an ERK/NFAT/NF-κB–CARD9 program in DCs whose hallmark output is robust IL-23 (and IL-2/IL-10) and potent TH17 responses (mcsai2010:findings:021, mcsai2010:findings:019), and SYK-deficient DCs show an even deeper cytokine block than CLEC7A-deficient DCs, placing SYK as the non-redundant node (mcsai2010:findings:022). Independently, IL-23 is a sufficient and necessary driver of IL-17: exogenous IL-23 induces infiltration of IL-17-producing T cells and IL-23 inhibition lowers IL-17 levels (gaffen2014:findings:033), while human loss of the IL-17 axis phenocopies CARD9 mutation in chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (gaffen2014:findings:032) and CARD9 deficiency defines the same antifungal axis as SYK (mcsai2010:findings:020). Together these imply that IL-17 output is set quantitatively by DC SYK catalytic activity, not merely correlated with it through shared context.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic loss of SYK in DCs stimulated with a CLEC7A ligand should reduce IL-23 secretion and, in co-culture, proportionally reduce IL-17A produced by CD4+ T cells; adding recombinant IL-23 back to SYK-inhibited DC cultures should restore IL-17A, whereas SYK inhibition applied only to the T cells (or to IL-17-responsive reporter cells downstream of the IL-17 receptor) should leave IL-17A production and IL-17-induced Il6/Lcn2-type target gene induction unchanged.
hypotheses.test: Treat human monocyte-derived DCs (or a DC-like myeloid line) with a SYK inhibitor or SYK siRNA/CRISPR knockout, stimulate with zymosan/curdlan (CLEC7A ligand), quantify IL-23 and IL-10 by ELISA, then co-culture the DCs with allogeneic or polyclonally activated naive CD4+ T cells and measure IL-17A by ELISA and intracellular flow cytometry; run parallel arms with recombinant IL-23 add-back (rescue) and with SYK inhibitor added only to purified T cells or to an IL-17-responsive fibroblast reporter line, which distinguishes a SYK requirement upstream of IL-17 induction from any effect on IL-17 signalling itself.

citations.title: Syk- and CARD9-dependent coupling of innate immunity to the induction of T helper cells that produce interleukin 17.
The active metabolite of spleen tyrosine kinase inhibitor fostamatinib abrogates the CD4⁺ T cell-priming capacity of dendritic cells.
Neutrophils produce interleukin 17A (IL-17A) in a dectin-1- and IL-23-dependent manner during invasive fungal infection.
Human dendritic cells activated via dectin-1 are efficient at priming Th17, cytotoxic CD8 T and B cell responses.

novelty.note: I searched the mechanism in plain words (Dectin-1/Syk/CARD9 DC signalling instructing IL-17-producing T cells), the entities together (Syk inhibitor + DC + IL-23 + Th17 co-culture), and the prediction (IL-23 add-back rescuing IL-17A when the DC pathway is blocked). LeibundGut-Landmann et al. state exactly this explanation: CLEC7A(dectin-1)–Syk–CARD9 signalling in DCs drives IL-23-skewed cytokine output and 'instructs' differentiation of CD4+ IL-17-producing T cells, with Th17 responses to Candida lost in CARD9-deficient animals; the fostamatinib/R406 study shows that pharmacological SYK inhibition of DCs abrogates their CD4+ T cell-priming capacity with loss of IL-17 production in DC–T cell interaction, i.e. the predicted quantitative dependence. The IL-23 add-back arm is supported in a related fungal model where recombinant IL-23 dose-dependently restores IL-17A when the dectin-1 arm is missing; only the negative-control arm (SYK inhibition applied to T cells or to IL-17R-responsive reporter cells) is not directly addressed in the sources found, but the central explanation is published.

hypotheses.statement: MEK1 acts as a direct upstream activator of mTORC1, its catalytic activity being required for full mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation through MEK1-driven ERK1/2 activation and consequent inactivation of the TSC1/TSC2 complex.
hypotheses.mechanism: MEK1/2 is the kinase that phosphorylates ERK1/2 on the activation-loop TEY motif with near-exclusive specificity for that site (cargnello2011:findings:002; johnson2023:findings:009), so ERK1/2 activity in cells is set by MEK1 output. Independently, ERK1/2 (with Akt and RSK1) directly phosphorylates and inactivates the TSC1/TSC2 Rheb-GAP, thereby switching mTORC1 on (laplante2012:findings:002), and mTORC1 activation is gated on the Rheb nucleotide state controlled by TSC2 (haeusler2018:findings:027). Joining only what these claims state, MEK1 kinase activity should be a positive determinant of mTORC1 activity, with the caveat that acute MEK1/2 inhibition also relieves ERK-dependent negative feedback and raises PI3K/Akt signalling (lake2016:findings:025), which can mask or invert the readout unless Akt is held constant.
hypotheses.prediction: Expression of constitutively active MEK1 in serum-starved cells should raise phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrates S6K1 Thr389 and 4E-BP1 Ser65 in a rapamycin-sensitive manner, accompanied by increased TSC2 phosphorylation; conversely, MEK1/2 inhibition with PD0325901 (or MEK1 knockdown) should lower these marks when Akt is simultaneously blocked, and neither manipulation should change S6K1/4E-BP1 phosphorylation in TSC2-null cells.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293T or HeLa cells, compare (i) doxycycline-induced constitutively active MEK1 versus kinase-dead MEK1 and (ii) PD0325901 plus a pan-Akt inhibitor versus either alone, immunoblotting phospho-S6K1 Thr389, phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65, phospho-ERK1/2 (TEY) and phospho-TSC2, with rapamycin as a specificity control; repeat the identical panel in isogenic TSC2-knockout cells (CRISPR) — MEK1-dependent shifts in mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation that persist without TSC2 would refute the proposed TSC2-routed MEK1→mTORC1 link, while loss of the shift in TSC2-null cells would confirm it.

citations.title: Phosphorylation and functional inactivation of TSC2 by Erk implications for tuberous sclerosis and cancer pathogenesis.
TSC2/Rheb signaling mediates ERK-dependent regulation of mTORC1 activity in C2C12 myoblasts.
ERK and Akt signaling pathways function through parallel mechanisms to promote mTORC1 signaling.
Single serine on TSC2 exerts biased control over mTORC1 activation mediated by ERK1/2 but not Akt.

novelty.note: I searched for ERK/MEK-dependent TSC2 phosphorylation and mTORC1 activation, for constitutively active MEK1 driving S6K1 Thr389/4E-BP1, and for MEK1/2-inhibitor plus Akt-inhibitor effects on mTORC1, and retrieved the primary papers. The MEK1/2→ERK1/2→TSC2-inactivation→Rheb-GTP→mTORC1 route is explicitly published: Ma et al. (Cell 2005) show Erk phosphorylation of TSC2 (S664/S540) dissociates TSC1-TSC2 and relieves inhibition of mTOR signalling; Miyazaki et al. show MEK1/2 inhibition (U0126) blocks TSC2 S664 phosphorylation and S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation with Rheb/TSC2 dependence (and no MEK-inhibitor effect where mTORC1 is constitutively active without functional TSC2); Winter et al. show ERK and Akt phosphorylate distinct TSC2 sites and converge synergistically on mTORC1, which covers the stated Akt-confound caveat. Since the mechanism, the MEK1/2-dependence and the TSC2-routing prediction are all already stated, the status is established rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: TGF-β induces T cell anergy in part by directing the phosphatase SHP2 onto CD28, i.e. SHP2 phosphatase activity is a required downstream effector of TGF-β-driven CD28 costimulatory shutdown and the resulting IL-2 loss.
hypotheses.mechanism: The SHP2 evidence shows that in T cells SHP2 is recruited to inhibitory receptor clusters and preferentially dephosphorylates CD28 rather than the TCR (case2019a:findings:010), and that SHP2's cellular effects require its catalytic activity and are blockable by the selective allosteric inhibitor SHP099 (chen2016:findings:003, chen2016:findings:006). The TGF-β evidence describes exactly a CD28/IL-2-selective lesion: TGF-β-pretreated T cells are unresponsive to anti-CD3 or antigen with blunted IL-2 production yet respond normally to PMA/ionomycin, which bypasses receptor-proximal tyrosine signalling (chen2003:findings:002), and the anergy is both prevented and reversed by exogenous IL-2 (chen2003:findings:003). A TGF-β-driven increase in SHP2 engagement of CD28 would produce this precise signature — loss of costimulation-dependent IL-2 with intact distal machinery — rather than a global TCR block.
hypotheses.prediction: In TGF-β-conditioned T cells restimulated through TCR/CD28, phosphotyrosine on the CD28 cytoplasmic tail should be reduced and CD28–SHP2 co-association increased relative to controls, while TCR/CD3ζ phosphorylation is comparatively spared; SHP099 treatment, SHP2 knockdown, or replacement of SHP2 with the catalytically dead C459S mutant should restore CD28 phosphorylation, IL-2 secretion and proliferation upon restimulation (phenocopying the exogenous IL-2 rescue), without altering TGF-β-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Culture human CD4+ T cells (or Jurkat cells) with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 ± TGF-β for the anergy-inducing period, then restimulate with anti-CD3/anti-CD28 in the presence or absence of 0.25–1 µM SHP099, or in cells carrying SHP2 shRNA reconstituted with shRNA-resistant wild-type versus C459S SHP2. Read out (i) CD28 immunoprecipitation followed by anti-phosphotyrosine blot and SHP2 co-immunoprecipitation (with CD3ζ phosphorylation as the selectivity control), (ii) IL-2 by ELISA and proliferation by CFSE/thymidine, and (iii) p-Smad2/3 by western blot to confirm TGF-β receptor signalling itself is unchanged. Rescue of CD28 phosphorylation and IL-2 by SHP2 inhibition or catalytic-dead SHP2, together with increased CD28–SHP2 association after TGF-β, supports the hypothesis; absence of any change in CD28 phosphorylation or SHP2 association after TGF-β, or failure of SHP2 loss to relieve the anergy, rules it out.

citations.title: T cell costimulatory receptor CD28 is a primary target for PD-1-mediated inhibition.
TGFβ limits proximal CD8+ TCR signaling via PTPN22 following strong and moderate agonism.
TGF-beta abrogates TCR-mediated signaling by upregulating tyrosine phosphatases in T cells.

Altered T-cell receptor + CD28-mediated signaling and blocked cell cycle progression in interleukin 10 and transforming growth factor-beta-treated alloreactive T cells that do not induce graft-versus-host disease.
TGFβ-dependent expression of PD-1 and PD-L1 controls CD8(+) T cell anergy in transplant tolerance.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words ("TGF-β induces T cell anergy via a phosphatase acting on CD28"), the entities together (TGF-β + SHP2 + CD28 + IL-2/anergy; SHP099 + TGF-β + T cells), and the prediction (reduced CD28 phosphotyrosine / increased CD28–SHP2 association after TGF-β, with spared CD3ζ). The SHP2→CD28 half is firmly published but only downstream of PD-1 (Hui et al., Science 2017: SHP2 strongly prefers CD28 over the TCR, and PD-1 inhibits chiefly by inactivating CD28), and TGF-β is published as acting through tyrosine phosphatases in T cells — but the documented ones are SHP-1 upregulation and a TGFβRII–PTPN22–Zap70 module, both aimed at TCR-proximal kinases, while Boussiotis et al. found TGF-β/IL-10-tolerized T cells have defective TCR-ζ phosphorylation, contrary to the predicted TCR sparing. I found no source that places SHP2 on CD28 as a required effector of TGF-β-induced anergy or that tests SHP2 inhibition/catalytic-dead SHP2 for rescue of TGF-β-blunted IL-2, so the specific linkage remains unstated.

hypotheses.statement: S6K1 (RPS6KB1) acts as a direct negative-feedback regulator of EGFR, damping EGF-stimulated EGFR phosphorylation/adaptor loading and hence EGFR-driven ERK output.
hypotheses.mechanism: The S6K1 evidence states that S6K1, once activated by mTORC1, directly phosphorylates IRS1 to trigger its degradation and thereby reduces growth-factor signalling downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, with the same arm of the pathway lowering RTK-proximal components (Grb10 phosphorylation, reduced PDGFR levels) (laplante2012:findings:011). The EGFR evidence shows that EGFR is the upstream determinant of ERK pathway output in epithelial cells, since the FIRE reporter decays when EGFR is inhibited (albeck2013:findings:000), and that EGF-stimulated signalling flux is set by the amount of adaptor loaded onto the receptor, with GRB2 recruited to EGFR at roughly 1:1 stoichiometry (itzhak2016:findings:025). If S6K1's documented suppression of RTK-proximal signalling extends to EGFR itself, then S6K1 activity should directly set the level of phosphorylated, adaptor-loaded EGFR and thus the amplitude of EGFR-dependent ERK output.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic loss of S6K1 should raise EGF-stimulated EGFR autophosphorylation, increase GRB2/SHC1 co-precipitation with EGFR, and elevate the amplitude/duration of the FIRE ERK-output signal at a fixed EGF dose; conversely, expressing a constitutively active, rapamycin-resistant S6K1 should lower pEGFR, reduce receptor-bound GRB2, and blunt FIRE induction, with these changes abolished if EGFR is already saturated or inhibited.
hypotheses.test: In MCF-10A FIRE cells and HeLa cells, compare vehicle, the S6K1 inhibitor PF-4708671, and S6K1 siRNA against expression of a rapamycin-resistant active S6K1: after serum starvation and a graded EGF pulse, quantify live-cell FIRE intensity time courses and, in parallel lysates, immunoblot pEGFR (Y1068/Y1173) and total EGFR and perform anti-EGFR immunoprecipitation with GRB2/SHC1 blots; a reciprocal shift in pEGFR and receptor-bound GRB2 with matching FIRE amplitude changes supports the direct feedback, while unchanged pEGFR and adaptor loading despite altered S6K1 activity rules it out.

citations.title: mTORC1 phosphorylates and stabilizes LST2 to negatively regulate EGFR.
S6K1 blockade overcomes acquired resistance to EGFR-TKIs in non-small cell lung cancer.

novelty.note: I searched for S6K1/p70S6K negative feedback onto EGFR, PF-4708671 effects on EGFR/ERK output, and S6K1 knockdown effects on EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation and GRB2 loading. Published work establishes mTORC1-driven negative feedback onto growth-factor receptors (S6K1→IRS1 degradation; mTORC1→LST2 stabilization causing EGFR degradation and reduced EGFR signaling), and separate ERK→EGFR T669 feedback, but no source states that S6K1 itself directly sets EGF-stimulated EGFR autophosphorylation, receptor-bound GRB2/SHC1 stoichiometry, or ERK-reporter (FIRE) amplitude. Hence the general mechanism is published while this specific S6K1→EGFR-adaptor-loading→ERK-output link is not.

hypotheses.statement: 14-3-3 proteins act as positive upstream regulators of RPS6KB1 (S6K1) activation, such that phospho-dependent 14-3-3 engagement of TSC2 (and other mTORC1 repressors) is required for full stimulus-induced S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: On the 14-3-3 side, phosphorylation of TSC2 at Ser1210 creates a 14-3-3-binding site proposed to control mTOR-dependent protein synthesis (cargnello2011:findings:077), and 14-3-3 complex formation with PI3KC2beta relieves repression of mTORC1 signalling (posor2022:findings:014); i.e. 14-3-3 binding neutralizes mTORC1 brakes. On the S6K1 side, TSC1-TSC2 inhibits nutrient- and insulin-stimulated S6K Thr389 phosphorylation without binding S6K directly (inoki2002:findings:014), and this inhibition is weakened when the TSC2 phosphosites are made phosphomimetic and strengthened when they are mutated to alanine (inoki2002:findings:011), while mTORC1 itself is the direct S6K1 kinase (laplante2012:findings:005). Combining these, the phosphosite-dependent partner that converts TSC2 phosphorylation into loss of inhibition — 14-3-3 — should be a required determinant of S6K1 activation.
hypotheses.prediction: Blocking 14-3-3 phosphopeptide binding (difopein/R18 expression) or depleting the major 14-3-3 isoforms should lower basal and insulin/nutrient-stimulated S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation and downstream rpS6 phosphorylation, with a parallel increase in TSC2-associated inhibition; conversely, 14-3-3 overexpression should raise pT389. The effect should be largely abolished in TSC2-null cells and in cells expressing the alanine (non-14-3-3-binding) TSC2 phosphosite mutant, and 14-3-3 should co-immunoprecipitate with TSC2 in a stimulus- and phosphorylation-dependent manner but not with S6K1 itself.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293/HEK293T cells, express difopein (or scrambled control) or siRNA-deplete 14-3-3 beta/epsilon/zeta, serum-starve and restimulate with insulin or amino acids, and immunoblot phospho-S6K1 Thr389, phospho-rpS6 Ser240/244 and phospho-AKT Ser473 as a specificity control; in parallel, immunoprecipitate TSC2 to quantify stimulus-dependent 14-3-3 co-precipitation, and repeat the difopein experiment in TSC2-null cells and in TSC2-null cells reconstituted with wild-type versus phosphosite-alanine TSC2 to test whether the 14-3-3 requirement for S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation is TSC2- and phosphosite-dependent.

citations.title: Regulation of TSC2 by 14-3-3 binding.
14-3-3beta binds to and negatively regulates the tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (TSC2) tumor suppressor gene product, tuberin.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in plain words (phospho-dependent 14-3-3 binding to TSC2 relieving mTORC1 inhibition), for the entities together (14-3-3 + TSC2 + S6K1 Thr389), and for the loss-of-function prediction (difopein/R18, 14-3-3 knockdown and S6K phosphorylation). Two JBC papers from 2002 already state this explanation: Li et al. show TSC2 binds 14-3-3 in a Ser1210-phosphorylation-dependent manner and that this association inhibits TSC2 function, with 14-3-3β co-expression elevating S6K Thr389 (and 4E-BP1) phosphorylation, while Shumway et al. show the phospho-dependent 14-3-3β–TSC2 interaction compromises the ability of the TSC1–TSC2 complex to reduce S6K phosphorylation. Because the causal claim (14-3-3 as a phosphosite-dependent, TSC2-mediated positive determinant of S6K Thr389) is explicitly published, the status is established, even though the specific difopein/isoform-depletion loss-of-function format of the prediction was not found as such.

hypotheses.statement: MEK1 kinase activity negatively regulates mTOR (mTORC1) signalling output, such that loss of MEK1 activity raises mTOR substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: MEK1/2 activity sustains ERK1/2-dependent negative feedback onto upstream receptors — MEK1/2 inhibition reduces phosphorylation of the EGFR feedback site T669, increases EGFR/ERBB3 activity and activates PI3K/Akt, and prolonged pathway inhibition raises IGF-1R and Akt phosphorylation (lake2016:findings:025). Independently, AKT-proximal PI3K signalling drives mTOR activity toward p70 S6K and eIF4-dependent translation (ivashkiv2014:findings:026), and mTOR pathway activity is directly readable as a coherent mTOR-motif/p70S6K substrate group in phosphoproteomes (casado2013:findings:004, bekkerjensen2020:findings:016). Together these imply that MEK1 output acts as a brake on mTOR, so removing MEK1 activity should release mTOR substrate phosphorylation rather than merely collapse the ERK1/2 motif cluster.
hypotheses.prediction: Selective MEK1/2 inhibition (or MEK1 knockdown) in growth-factor-stimulated cells will collapse ERK1/2-motif phosphorylation while increasing mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate phosphorylation (S6K1 T389, S6 S235/236, 4EBP1), with the increase appearing at later time points and being abolished by co-inhibition of PI3K/AKT or of mTOR itself.
hypotheses.test: In a single cell line (e.g. RPE1 or HEK-293T), stimulate with EGF and treat in parallel with PD0325901 or PD184352 (with U0126 as a confirmatory non-ATP-competitive MEK1/2 inhibitor, per cargnello2011:findings:003), siRNA against MEK1 alone, or vehicle, then immunoblot a time course (0–6 h) for phospho-ERK1/2 (TEY), phospho-S6K1 T389, phospho-S6 and phospho-4EBP1; run the same conditions by LC-MS/MS phosphoproteomics with motif/KSEA scoring to test whether the mTOR and p70S6K substrate groups move up as the ERK1/2 group moves down. Epistasis arms adding a PI3K/AKT inhibitor or rapamycin/TORKi distinguish a MEK1-dependent release of mTOR activity from a MEK1-independent drift; no change in mTOR substrate groups after MEK1 loss rules the hypothesis out.

citations.title: MEK1 is required for PTEN membrane recruitment, AKT regulation, and the maintenance of peripheral tolerance.
S6K1 and 4E-BP1 are independent regulated and control cellular growth in bladder cancer.
Dual PI3K/mTOR Inhibitors Induce Rapid Overactivation of the MEK/ERK Pathway in Human Pancreatic Cancer Cells through Suppression of mTORC2.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: MEK-inhibition feedback relief onto PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MEK1-specific negative regulation of mTOR/AKT with loss-of-function, and the prediction itself (increased S6K1 T389 / 4E-BP1 / S6 after MEK1/2 inhibitors in phosphoproteomic and immunoblot studies). Zmajkovicova et al. directly anticipate the core claim — MEK1 ablation stabilises AKT activation by blocking MAGI1-dependent PTEN membrane recruitment and produces enhanced EGF-stimulated phosphorylation of mTOR, GSK3β and S6K — but they show this MEK1 function is kinase-activity-independent (requiring ERK-mediated MEK1 T292 phosphorylation), so the hypothesis' attribution to MEK1 kinase output and to receptor-level ERK feedback is not what is published, and no source states the predicted phosphoproteome-level swap of ERK1/2-motif down / mTOR-and-p70S6K-motif up. The nearest direct test of the prediction reports the opposite for mTORC1 readouts: U0126 in bladder carcinoma cells abolished pERK1/2 and raised pAKT S473/T308 while leaving S6K1 (and 4E-BP1) phosphorylation unchanged, so the specific prediction remains unpublished/contested.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly tyrosine-phosphorylates the PKA catalytic subunit, increasing PKA catalytic activity toward its consensus substrates.
hypotheses.mechanism: In a yeast system where human kinases were expressed in an otherwise tyrosine-kinase-naive proteome, kinase-substrate enrichment detected activation of PKA substrate phosphorylation specifically in tyrosine kinase conditions, and v-SRC was among the most catalytically productive of those kinases (>2000 upregulated sites), implying that SRC-type tyrosine kinase activity is sufficient to raise PKA output in the absence of the usual cAMP-generating machinery. The independent SRC evidence shows this is a mode of action SRC already uses on other serine/threonine kinases: SRC-driven tyrosine phosphorylation of the AGC-family kinase RSK2 stabilizes its activating partner interaction and promotes its activation, and tyrosine phosphorylation by SRC enhances the intrinsic kinase activity of TβRII. Taken together, the simplest direct relationship is SRC acting as an upstream tyrosine kinase for PKA itself rather than through cAMP.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC should phosphorylate the PKA catalytic subunit on one or more tyrosine residues in vitro, and this phosphorylation should increase PKA's specific activity on a PKA consensus peptide; in cells, SRC activation should raise PKA-substrate phosphorylation without a corresponding rise in cAMP, and SRC inhibition or mutation of the modified tyrosine(s) to phenylalanine should abolish that increase while leaving cAMP-driven PKA activation intact.
hypotheses.test: Incubate recombinant PKA catalytic subunit with active recombinant SRC and ATP in vitro, detect tyrosine phosphorylation by anti-phosphotyrosine (4G10) blotting and map the sites by LC-MS/MS; in parallel assay PKA activity on a consensus substrate peptide (radiometric or phospho-specific antibody readout) with and without prior SRC treatment, and repeat with Tyr-to-Phe mutants of the mapped sites. Complement in cultured cells by expressing a PKA activity reporter (e.g. AKAR/ExRai-AKAR) plus a cAMP indicator, then activating or inhibiting SRC: a SRC-dependent rise in reporter signal without a cAMP change, lost in the Tyr-to-Phe PKA background, supports direct phosphorylation, whereas no in vitro pY incorporation and no SRC-dependent activity shift rules it out.

citations.title: Fyn Regulates Binding Partners of Cyclic-AMP Dependent Protein Kinase A.
Direct modulation of the protein kinase A catalytic subunit α by growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases.

novelty.note: I searched for Src/Fyn tyrosine phosphorylation of the PKA catalytic subunit, for tyrosine-phosphorylation-driven (cAMP-independent) PKA activation, and for the specific residues reported (Y69, Y330). The Proteomes 2018 study by Deming/Ballif colleagues states exactly this explanation: Fyn and Src directly phosphorylate Y69 of human PKA-Cα, which increases PKA catalytic activity in vitro and in cells, and Fyn expression increases phosphorylation of cellular proteins bearing the PKA consensus motif — i.e. tyrosine kinase activity raising PKA output without invoking cAMP. An earlier primary paper independently shows receptor tyrosine kinases (EGFR/PDGFR) directly tyrosine-phosphorylate PKA-C at Y330 and lower the Km for a PKA peptide substrate, so the general mechanism of PKA-C activation by tyrosine phosphorylation is also established; hence 'established' rather than 'partial'.

hypotheses.statement: MAPKAPK2 (MK2) directly phosphorylates canonical AKT consensus (RxRxxS/T) substrate sites, making it a stress-activated kinase functionally redundant with AKT at those sites — e.g. the AKT sites T32 and S253 of FKHRL1/FOXO3.
hypotheses.mechanism: The AKT-attributed substrate signature is the basophilic RxRxxS/KxRxxS motif, which the corpus assigns jointly to AKT and RSK (casado2013:findings:003, bekkerjensen2020:findings:010), and the mapped in vitro AKT sites on FKHRL1 (T32, S253) are exactly such basic-motif sites (brunet1999:findings:001). MK2's kinase domain is most closely related to CAMK and to the RSK C-terminal kinase domain (cargnello2011:findings:067), and MK2 is documented to phosphorylate a basophilic site also used by PKA and RSK2 (CREB Ser133), albeit with higher Km (cargnello2011:findings:043). If MK2 shares this basophilic specificity, it should be able to phosphorylate AKT-consensus sites directly, independently of PI3K/AKT activity.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active MK2 will incorporate 32P into bacterially produced GST-FKHRL1 and generate anti-phospho-T32 and anti-phospho-S253 signal, with that signal lost in the T32A/S253A mutants and absent for the triple mutant; in cells, p38/MK2-activating stress will raise T32/S253 (and general RxRxxS-motif) phosphorylation in a way that persists under PI3K/AKT inhibition but is abolished by MK2 depletion, and should drive partial cytoplasmic relocalization of FKHRL1. If MK2 is not basophilic in this sense, no site-specific phosphorylation above kinase-dead/no-kinase controls will be seen.
hypotheses.test: Side-by-side in vitro kinase assays on bacterially expressed GST-FKHRL1 (wild type and T32A, S253A, T32A/S253A/S315A) using recombinant active MK2 versus immunoprecipitated constitutively active AKT and kinase-inactive controls, read out by 32P autoradiography and immunoblot with anti-phospho-T32/anti-phospho-S253, with Km determination for MK2; followed in cultured cells by anisomycin or sorbitol stimulation of the p38–MK2 arm with or without PI3K/AKT inhibitor and with siRNA/CRISPR knockdown of MK2, scoring phospho-T32/S253 immunoblot and anti-HA immunofluorescence localization of tagged FKHRL1.

citations.title: The substrate specificity and structure of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase-activated protein kinase-2.
MAPKAP Kinase-2 phosphorylation of PABPC1 controls its interaction with 14-3-3 proteins after DNA damage: A combined kinase and protein array approach.
MK5 activates Rag transcription via Foxo1 in developing B cells.
The PI3K and MAPK/p38 pathways control stress granule assembly in a hierarchical manner.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) MK2/MAPKAPK2 phosphorylating FOXO3/FKHRL1 at the AKT sites T32/S253, (2) MK2 substrate-specificity/consensus motif and its overlap with the basophilic AKT RxRxxS motif, and (3) the prediction that p38–MK2 stress signalling raises AKT-consensus (RxRxxS) phosphorylation under PI3K/AKT inhibition. The general premise is published — Stokoe et al. defined MK2's Arg-directed consensus (Hyd-X-R-X-X-S) and noted it shares the Arg at n−3 with MAPKAP kinase-1/RSK and resembles CaMKII (but requires a bulky hydrophobic, not Arg, at n−5, i.e. not canonical RxRxxS), MK2 is described as sharing an optimal motif with Chk1 and generating 14-3-3-binding phosphosites (PABPC1 Ser470), and MK2 can phosphorylate Akt-S473 when PI3K is inactive. However, no source states that MK2 phosphorylates canonical AKT-consensus substrate sites or FKHRL1/FOXO3 T32/S253; the closest FOXO work assigns AKT-independent MAPKAPK phosphorylation of FoxO1/FoxO3a to MK5 at the non-AKT site Ser215 and reports MK2/MK3 knockdown had no effect, so the specific claim remains unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: IL-17 signaling directly potentiates TGFBR2 (TβRII) function, increasing its cell-surface abundance and TGF-β responsiveness through the ACT1–TRAF6 module that IL-17 receptors engage.
hypotheses.mechanism: The IL-17 claims state that IL-17 receptor engagement via the SEFIR–ACT1 platform causes ACT1 to recruit TRAF6 and catalyze its ubiquitination as the proximal step of IL-17 signaling (gaffen2014:findings:022, li2019:findings:002). Independently, the TGFBR2 claims state that TRAF6-mediated ubiquitylation of the PI3K subunit p85 — which associates constitutively with TβRII — activates PI3K/AKT without needing TβRI kinase activity (derynck2019:findings:032), and that AKT activation phosphorylates the RabGAP AS160 to release intracellular pools of TβRII to the cell surface (derynck2019:findings:010). If IL-17 supplies the TRAF6 ubiquitination event in the same cell, it should feed this p85/AKT/AS160 arm and raise functional surface TGFBR2, making IL-17 a direct positive regulator of TβRII rather than merely a co-inflammatory cytokine.
hypotheses.prediction: Within 1–6 h of IL-17A treatment (alone or with TNFα) of IL-17RA-expressing epithelial cells, cell-surface TβRII protein should rise without a requirement for increased TGFBR2 mRNA, TRAF6–p85 association and AKT phosphorylation should increase, and a subsequent TGF-β pulse should produce greater SMAD2 phosphorylation and higher TGF-β reporter/target-gene output than in untreated cells; the effect should be lost upon ACT1 or TRAF6 knockdown, upon SEFIR-blocking peptide treatment, or upon AKT inhibition, and should be absent in TGFBR2-knockout cells.
hypotheses.test: In a responsive epithelial line (e.g. HaCaT or HeLa stably expressing IL-17RA), treat with IL-17A ± TNFα and quantify surface TβRII by cell-surface biotinylation/streptavidin pulldown and by non-permeabilized flow cytometry, with parallel TGFBR2 qPCR to separate trafficking from transcription; co-immunoprecipitate TRAF6 with p85 and blot p-AKT and p-AS160; then challenge with a TGF-β1 dose series and read p-SMAD2 by immunoblot plus a CAGA-luciferase reporter. Repeat the entire panel under siRNA knockdown of ACT1 or TRAF6, with an ACT1–SEFIR blocking peptide, and with an AKT inhibitor, using TGFBR2-knockout cells as the specificity control; loss of the IL-17-induced surface-TβRII and p-SMAD2 gain in the ACT1/TRAF6/AKT-disrupted arms would confirm the proposed direct link, while no change in surface TβRII or TGF-β responsiveness after IL-17 would rule it out.

citations.title: IL-17A enhances the expression of profibrotic genes through upregulation of the TGF-β receptor on hepatic stellate cells in a JNK-dependent manner.
TGF-β promotes PI3K-AKT signaling and prostate cancer cell migration through the TRAF6-mediated ubiquitylation of p85α.
IL-17A signaling in colonic epithelial cells inhibits pro-inflammatory cytokine production by enhancing the activity of ERK and PI3K.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (IL-17/ACT1/TRAF6 raising surface TβRII via p85–AKT–AS160 trafficking), the entities together (IL-17 + TGFBR2/TβRII surface expression, HaCaT/epithelial, TRAF6 + p85 ubiquitylation), and the prediction (IL-17A pretreatment enhancing SMAD2/3 phosphorylation to a subsequent TGF-β pulse). The core phenotype is already published: Fabre et al. show IL-17A upregulates cell-surface TGF-β-RII on hepatic stellate cells (with receptor stabilization rather than new synthesis) and that IL-17A pretreatment yields robust SMAD2/3 phosphorylation at suboptimal TGF-β doses — but they attribute it to JNK, explicitly not testing ACT1, TRAF6, or AKT, and in a non-epithelial cell at 24 h rather than 1–6 h. The two mechanistic halves exist separately (IL-17A→Act1-dependent PI3K–AKT activation in colonic epithelial cells; TRAF6-mediated K63 ubiquitylation of p85α activating PI3K–AKT downstream of TβRII independent of TβRI kinase), but no source I retrieved joins them into an IL-17-driven ACT1/TRAF6→p85/AKT/AS160 route to functional surface TβRII, so the specific mechanism and its knockdown/inhibitor predictions remain unstated.

hypotheses.statement: JAK1 directly and negatively regulates TGF-β-induced ERK/MAPK activation by occupying the membrane-proximal region of TβRI and thereby limiting p52ShcA docking on the receptor.
