hypotheses.mechanism: JAK1 is reported to be constitutively associated with TβRI, where it drives Smad-independent STAT3 activation (derynck2019:findings:034), and the ERK/MAPK arm of TGF-β signalling is initiated by p52ShcA recruitment to the tyrosine-phosphorylated TβRI, where ShcA competitively displaces another receptor-binding effector (Smad3) and sets the balance between outputs (derynck2019:findings:029). Because JAK1 binding to cytokine receptors strictly requires an intact membrane-proximal box1–2 segment and cannot be rescued by relocating that segment elsewhere (heinrich2003:findings:020), JAK1 must engage a spatially restricted receptor-proximal surface — the same class of site ShcA needs — so the two effectors should compete, making JAK1 occupancy a brake on receptor-initiated ERK/MAPK signalling.
hypotheses.prediction: Loss of JAK1 in fibroblasts should increase TGF-β-induced ShcA–TβRI association and raise/prolong TGF-β-stimulated ERK phosphorylation while reducing STAT3 phosphorylation, and JAK1 re-expression should reverse both; conversely, JAK1 overexpression should reduce ShcA co-immunoprecipitation with TβRI and blunt TGF-β-induced pERK without affecting EGF-induced pERK.
hypotheses.test: In JAK1-deficient versus JAK1-reconstituted human fibroblast/fibrosarcoma lines (or JAK1 siRNA/CRISPR knockdown in normal fibroblasts), stimulate with TGF-β and immunoblot pERK1/2, pSTAT3 and pSmad3 time courses, and in parallel immunoprecipitate TβRI (or tagged TβRI) to quantify co-precipitated p52ShcA and JAK1; a reciprocal titration of JAK1 expression that inversely shifts ShcA–TβRI binding and pERK, with EGF-induced pERK unchanged, supports the competition model, whereas unchanged ShcA–TβRI binding and pERK rules it out.

citations.title: ShcA Protects against Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition through Compartmentalized Inhibition of TGF-β-Induced Smad Activation.

novelty.note: I searched for JAK1–TβRI/ShcA competition, JAK1 as a negative regulator of TGF-β-induced ERK, and the box1–2 membrane-proximal binding requirement applied to TβRI. Published work independently establishes p52ShcA–Smad3 competition at TβRI driving ERK versus Smad output, and separately establishes constitutive JAK1–TβRI association driving Smad-independent STAT3 signalling (including JAK1 silencing promoting myofibroblast transdifferentiation), but no retrieved source proposes or tests JAK1 occupancy of a membrane-proximal TβRI surface as a brake on ShcA docking and ERK activation, and none reports a negative test of it. Hence open, with the ShcA receptor-competition paper as the nearest published work.

hypotheses.statement: MAPK (ERK1/2) pathway activity is required for the protein-synthesis-dependent second wave of JAK1-driven signalling, i.e. MAPK acts upstream of late JAK1 output through MAPK-controlled cap-dependent translation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The late phase of JAK1-STAT3 signalling downstream of TβRI is explicitly dependent on new protein synthesis in fibroblasts and hepatic stellate cells (derynck2019:findings:034), and the same stimulus activates ERK/MAPK within 5–10 min (derynck2019:findings:028), placing MAPK activity in the window that precedes the second wave. Ras/MAPK pathway activation drives RSK1/2 phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 at Ser235/236, which facilitates translation preinitiation complex assembly and increases cap-dependent translation (cargnello2011:findings:034), providing the translational capacity the second JAK1 wave requires.
hypotheses.prediction: MEK/ERK or RSK inhibition applied after the first JAK1-STAT3 wave should selectively abolish the late, synthesis-dependent wave of JAK1/STAT3 phosphorylation (phenocopying cycloheximide) while leaving the immediate early wave intact, and this should coincide with loss of rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate cultured fibroblasts with TGF-β and add U0126/trametinib, an RSK inhibitor, or cycloheximide at 30–60 min post-stimulation; immunoblot pJAK1 and pSTAT3 at early (10–30 min) and late (2–8 h) time points alongside pS6 Ser235/236, with a puromycin-incorporation blot as a translation readout — selective loss of the late but not early pJAK1/pSTAT3 wave under MEK/RSK inhibition supports the relationship, while an unchanged late wave despite abolished pS6 rules it out.

citations.title: Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) Directly Activates the JAK1-STAT3 Axis to Induce Hepatic Fibrosis in Coordination with the SMAD Pathway.
Blocking STAT3 signaling augments MEK/ERK inhibitor efficacy in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

novelty.note: I searched for the TGF-β-induced second, protein-synthesis-dependent wave of JAK1-STAT3 signalling, for MEK/ERK or RSK requirement for late STAT3 activation, and for RSK-driven rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation and cap-dependent translation. The primary source (Tang et al., JBC 2017) attributes the second STAT phosphorylation phase to SMADs plus de novo protein synthesis, with no MEK/ERK/RSK translational requirement proposed; no paper was found stating or directly testing that MEK/ERK-RSK-rpS6-driven translation is required for the late JAK1 wave. Notably, the nearest functional test in another system found the opposite direction — MEK inhibition (U0126) increased delayed STAT3 phosphorylation via loss of ELK1-driven SOCS3 — but this is not a test of the TGF-β/TβRI-JAK1 late wave, so the hypothesis remains open rather than refuted.

hypotheses.statement: MEK1 activity directly and negatively regulates CBL: MEK1-dependent (ERK-mediated) phosphorylation of CBL, or of its EGFR docking interface, restrains CBL recruitment to activated EGFR and thereby limits CBL-mediated receptor ubiquitination and degradation.
hypotheses.mechanism: CBL is recruited to the membrane upon EGF stimulation (itzhak2016:findings:011) and must associate with EGFR at Y1045 to drive receptor ubiquitination, downregulation and degradation, since loss of that association abolishes EGF-induced ubiquitination and degradation even when CBL is overexpressed (levkowitz1999:findings:007). In the same EGFR system, MEK1/2 activity operates as a negative feedback arm on the receptor — MEK1/2 inhibition reduces phosphorylation of the EGFR feedback site T669 and increases EGFR/ERBB3 activity (lake2016:findings:025) — and the corpus repeatedly shows MEK1/2-dependent phosphorylation of receptor-proximal adaptors (SOS1, FRS2a, LAT) that disrupts their protein–protein associations, e.g. with Grb2 and Shc (lake2016:findings:003, lake2016:findings:004). Placing CBL, a membrane-recruited receptor-proximal adaptor/E3, in that same MEK1-controlled feedback layer predicts that MEK1 output sets how much CBL engages EGFR and how fast the receptor is destroyed, offering a degradation-based contribution to the rise in EGFR activity seen when MEK1/2 is inhibited.
hypotheses.prediction: Acute MEK1/2 inhibition during EGF stimulation should decrease Ser/Thr phosphorylation of CBL on MAPK-consensus sites, increase EGF-induced CBL–EGFR co-immunoprecipitation, increase EGFR poly-ubiquitination and accelerate EGFR loss; conversely, expression of constitutively active MEK1 should raise CBL MAPK-site phosphorylation, reduce CBL–EGFR association, and blunt CBL-dependent EGFR ubiquitination and degradation, with these effects absent for a CBL mutant lacking the responsive Ser/Thr sites or for EGFR Y1045F, which cannot recruit CBL at all.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa or CHO cells co-expressing EGFR (wild type or Y1045F), HA-ubiquitin and HA-CBL, stimulate with EGF after 1 h pretreatment with PD0325901 or U0126 versus DMSO, or after transfection of constitutively active MEK1: immunoprecipitate CBL and blot with a phospho-MAPK-substrate (PXS*P/S*P) antibody plus phosphosite mapping by LC-MS/MS to identify MEK1/2-dependent CBL sites; in parallel immunoprecipitate EGFR to quantify co-precipitated CBL and anti-HA ubiquitin smearing, and follow total EGFR by immunoblot over a 0–120 min EGF chase to measure degradation rate. A phospho-null CBL mutant at the mapped sites should render CBL–EGFR association, ubiquitination and receptor turnover insensitive to MEK1 status, which would confirm the relationship, whereas no change in CBL phosphorylation, CBL–EGFR binding or EGFR ubiquitination across MEK1 perturbations would rule it out.

citations.title: ERK-dependent threonine phosphorylation of EGF receptor modulates receptor downregulation and signaling.
Additional Serine/Threonine Phosphorylation Reduces Binding Affinity but Preserves Interface Topography of Substrate Proteins to the c-Cbl TKB Domain
Sprouty2 attenuates epidermal growth factor receptor ubiquitylation and endocytosis, and consequently enhances Ras/ERK signalling.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (a) ERK/MEK-dependent serine-threonine phosphorylation of CBL and its effect on EGFR ubiquitination/degradation (PubMed title searches returned only PKC/phorbol-ester and structural papers, no ERK–CBL substrate report); (b) the key entities together (MEK inhibition + CBL recruitment + EGFR degradation feedback); (c) the prediction itself (does MEK1/2 inhibition increase EGFR ubiquitination and accelerate receptor loss). The prediction's receptor-side half is already published: Li et al. show MEK1/ERK-dependent phosphorylation of EGFR T669 suppresses receptor ubiquitination and downregulation, so U0126/PD98059 or T669A accelerates EGF-induced EGFR loss and markedly enhances ubiquitination; Sun et al. show that additional Ser/Thr phosphorylation flanking the CBL-docking phosphotyrosines (EGFR S1070/S1071, Spry2 T56) reduces c-Cbl TKB-domain binding 26–31-fold, though the implicated kinase is p38 rather than ERK; and the nearest CBL-directed ERK feedback is the ERK-induced Sprouty2 protein, which sequesters c-Cbl and blocks EGFR ubiquitylation. No retrieved source reports MEK1/2-dependent phosphorylation of CBL itself on MAPK-consensus sites, nor an increase in EGF-induced CBL–EGFR co-immunoprecipitation upon acute MEK inhibition, so the specific CBL-phosphorylation link is unanticipated while its consequences are established.

hypotheses.statement: SHP2 directly dephosphorylates components of the IFNγ receptor–JAK–STAT1 module, acting as a negative regulator of IFNγ-induced STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and IFNγ target-gene induction.
hypotheses.mechanism: SHP2 is a phosphotyrosine-activated phosphatase (ligand binding to its tandem SH2 domains relieves autoinhibition and boosts catalysis ~100-fold) that, when recruited to a cytokine receptor, restrains phosphorylation of the receptor, JAK and STAT proteins — dominant-negative SHP2 raises receptor/JAK/STAT phosphorylation (heinrich2003:findings:009, alonso2004:findings:014). IFNγ signalling is transduced by the same kind of tyrosine-phosphorylation cascade onto STAT1, and its amplitude is set by tunable receptor-proximal tyrosine input (SYK–IFNAR coupling amplifies STAT1 activation; ivashkiv2014:findings:003), with downstream output read out as STAT1/IRF1 occupancy and M1-type genes such as Cxcl9/Cxcl10 (ivashkiv2014:findings:013, cui2024:findings:007). If SHP2 engages phosphotyrosines in this complex, IFNγ-driven STAT1 phosphorylation should be under SHP2 control rather than only under nuclear-PTP control.
hypotheses.prediction: Catalytic inhibition or depletion of SHP2 should increase and prolong IFNγ-induced STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and amplify induction of STAT1 targets (e.g. CXCL9/CXCL10), while catalytically active SHP2 should co-immunoprecipitate with the tyrosine-phosphorylated IFNγ receptor/JAK–STAT1 complex after IFNγ stimulation and dephosphorylate phospho-STAT1 in vitro; a catalytically dead SHP2 (C459S-type) should have no such effect.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured macrophage-like or epithelial cell line, pretreat with the selective allosteric SHP2 inhibitor SHP099 (0.1–3 µM) or use doxycycline-inducible SHP2 shRNA with re-expression of shRNA-resistant wild-type versus catalytically inactive SHP2, then stimulate with IFNγ and measure phospho-STAT1 (Tyr701) time courses by immunoblot plus CXCL9/CXCL10 mRNA by qPCR; in parallel, immunoprecipitate SHP2 (and IFNGR1) from IFNγ-stimulated lysates to test complex formation, and run purified activated SHP2 against phospho-STAT1 immunoprecipitates in an in vitro phosphatase assay to test direct substrate use.

citations.title: Shp-2 tyrosine phosphatase functions as a negative regulator of the interferon-stimulated Jak/STAT pathway.
SHP-2 is a dual-specificity phosphatase involved in Stat1 dephosphorylation at both tyrosine and serine residues in nuclei.
SHP2 is overexpressed and inhibits pSTAT1-mediated APM component expression, T-cell attracting chemokine secretion, and CTL recognition in head and neck cancer cells.
SHP2 blockade enhances anti-tumor immunity via tumor cell intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms.

novelty.note: I searched for SHP2 as a negative regulator of IFNγ-induced STAT1 phosphorylation, for direct SHP2-mediated STAT1/JAK dephosphorylation in the IFNγ receptor module, and for the specific prediction that SHP2 inhibition (SHP099) amplifies STAT1 targets CXCL9/CXCL10. The explanation is long-published: You et al. (MCB 1999) showed Shp-2-deficient fibroblasts have markedly elevated and prolonged IFNγ-induced Stat1 (and Jak1) tyrosine phosphorylation, rescued by wild-type Shp-2 re-expression; Wu et al. (JBC 2002) showed SHP-2 associates with Stat1 after IFNγ and directly dephosphorylates Stat1 Tyr701/Ser727, with enhanced and prolonged phosphorylation in SHP-2−/− cells; Leibowitz et al. (Clin Cancer Res 2013) showed SHP2 knockdown raises pSTAT1-Y701 and STAT1-dependent chemokine secretion; and Quintana et al. (Sci Rep 2021) showed allosteric SHP2 inhibition augments tumor-intrinsic IFNγ signalling and CXCR3-ligand (CXCL9/10/11) release. Both the mechanism and the predicted pharmacological readout are therefore already stated in the literature.

hypotheses.statement: SHP2 phosphatase activity negatively controls IFNγ production by activated T cells, by dephosphorylating the CD28 costimulatory tail that drives cytokine output.
hypotheses.mechanism: PD-1 clusters recruit SHP2, which preferentially dephosphorylates CD28 rather than the TCR, placing SHP2 at the costimulatory node of T cell activation (case2019a:findings:010). IFNγ is a synaptically secreted, costimulation-dependent effector cytokine of activated T cells (altanbonnet2019:findings:008, altanbonnet2019:findings:010), and relieving PD-1 engagement in vivo shifts the microenvironment toward IFNγ-induced states, consistent with PD-1-proximal signalling suppressing IFNγ output (cui2024:findings:015). If SHP2 is the enzyme executing that suppression at CD28, its catalytic activity should directly set the amount of IFNγ a T cell makes.
hypotheses.prediction: Selective SHP2 inhibition or knockdown in PD-1-expressing T cells stimulated in the presence of PD-L1 should restore CD28 tyrosine phosphorylation and increase IFNG transcription and IFNγ secretion per cell, with little change in proximal TCR-chain phosphorylation; catalytically inactive SHP2 re-expression should fail to re-impose suppression.
hypotheses.test: Use a PD-1-expressing T cell line (or anti-CD3/anti-CD28 bead-expanded T cell blasts) stimulated on anti-CD3 ± PD-L1-coated surfaces, with SHP099 or inducible SHP2 shRNA (rescued by shRNA-resistant wild-type versus C459S SHP2); read out CD28 phosphotyrosine by immunoprecipitation/immunoblot and IFNγ by supernatant ELISA plus intracellular cytokine staining, comparing against TCR-ζ phosphorylation as the specificity control.

citations.title: T cell costimulatory receptor CD28 is a primary target for PD-1-mediated inhibition.
PD-1/SHP-2 inhibits Tc1/Th1 phenotypic responses and the activation of T cells in the tumor microenvironment.
T cell-specific constitutive active SHP2 enhances T cell memory formation and reduces T cell activation.

novelty.note: I searched for SHP2 inhibition raising T cell IFNγ, for PD-1–SHP2 dephosphorylation of CD28, and for Ptpn11 deletion/gain-of-function effects on IFNγ. The CD28-as-preferential-SHP2-substrate mechanism is firmly published (Hui et al., PMID 28280247), and SHP2 activity is separately shown to negatively regulate Th1/IFNγ output (PMID 25480946; constitutively active SHP2 lowers IFNγ, PMID 35983034), but no retrieved source joins them into the specific prediction that SHP099/SHP2-knockdown restores CD28 phosphotyrosine and raises per-cell IFNG/IFNγ with TCR-ζ unchanged — and in vivo work reports SHP2 is dispensable for PD-1 signalling, leaving the link contested. Hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: MTOR, through its own catalytic activity rather than solely through AKT, directly phosphorylates FOXO1 and thereby restrains FOXO1 nuclear transcriptional activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: Claims about FOXO1 state that loss of mTOR complex (mTORC2) kinase activity selectively impairs FOXO1/3a phosphorylation while leaving other AKT substrates such as TSC2 and GSK3β intact (liu2020:findings:008, laplante2012:findings:008), and that mTOR-complex signalling also controls FoxO1 modification state in an Akt-independent manner (szwed2021:findings:020); a substrate-selectivity pattern that an exclusively AKT-relayed input would not predict. Claims about MTOR independently show that ATP-competitive/catalytic-site inhibition of MTOR collapses phosphorylation of mTOR-motif substrate groups as a distinct, directly attributable signature separable from downstream kinases (bekkerjensen2020:findings:016, casado2013:findings:004), and that catalytic-domain MTOR mutations change inhibitor sensitivity of its own signalling output (fruman2017:findings:023). Together these imply FOXO1 is itself an MTOR substrate rather than only an AKT substrate downstream of MTOR.
hypotheses.prediction: Catalytic MTOR inhibition (Torin1/Ku-0063794), but not rapamycin, should reduce phosphorylation of FOXO1 and drive its nuclear accumulation and target-gene induction even when AKT activity is already fully blocked or bypassed, and immunopurified MTOR should phosphorylate recombinant FOXO1 in vitro in a Torin1-sensitive, kinase-dead-MTOR-insensitive manner, with residual sites distinct from the canonical AKT sites.
hypotheses.test: Two-part cell-culture experiment: (1) in vitro kinase assay with FLAG-immunopurified wild-type versus kinase-dead MTOR (from HEK293T) plus recombinant FOXO1 and [γ-32P]ATP or phospho-specific immunoblot, ± Torin1 and ± rapamycin, to test direct phosphorylation; (2) in cells, treat with an AKT inhibitor (or express an AKT-site-mutant FOXO1) and then add Torin1, rapamycin, or vehicle, and quantify FOXO1 phosphorylation by immunoblot, nuclear/cytosolic FOXO1 by fractionation and immunofluorescence, and FOXO1 target-gene mRNA by qPCR; MTOR-dependent, AKT-independent changes support the hypothesis, while no change beyond the AKT-blocked baseline rules it out.

citations.title: The mTOR Pathway Controls Cell Proliferation by Regulating the FoxO3a Transcription Factor via SGK1 Kinase

novelty.note: I searched for direct mTOR phosphorylation of FOXO1 (in vitro kinase assays, Akt-independent), for Torin1-driven FOXO1 nuclear accumulation, and for mTOR-motif FOXO sites. Published work consistently routes mTOR's control of FOXO1/3 through intermediary AGC kinases: the retrieved PLOS ONE study explicitly attributes mTOR-dependent FoxO3a phosphorylation to Akt (Thr32/Ser253) and SGK1 (Ser314) rather than to mTOR itself, i.e. the Akt-independent-but-still-indirect part of the mechanism is established, while direct mTOR catalytic phosphorylation of FOXO1 with distinct non-AKT sites was not found stated or directly tested and negated.

hypotheses.statement: BRAF kinase activity negatively regulates GRB2, reducing GRB2's recruitment into receptor-proximal complexes (GRB2–SOS1 and GRB2–EGFR at the membrane/endosome), such that constitutively active BRAF V600E holds GRB2 in a cytosolic, complex-free state and RAF inhibition restores GRB2 complex assembly.
hypotheses.mechanism: The BRAF-side claims state that mutant B-Raf is constitutively active and drives MEK/ERK output that is normally restrained by negative feedback, and that relieving this feedback with Raf or MEK1/2 inhibitors immediately upregulates EGFR activity and raises Ras-GTP in B-RafV600E cells (lake2016:findings:019, lake2016:findings:020, lake2016:findings:023). The GRB2-side claims, from independent papers, state that the same MAPK output phosphorylates Sos, impairing Sos/Grb2 interactions and reducing Sos membrane recruitment (lemmon2010:findings:022), and that GRB2 is quantitatively redistributed from cytosol onto EGFR-bearing membranes in roughly 1:1 stoichiometry with EGFR upon receptor activation (itzhak2016:findings:025). Taken together, the amount of GRB2 held in receptor complexes should be a direct read-out of BRAF activity: high BRAF output should strip GRB2 from SOS1 and from activated receptors, and BRAF inhibition should reverse it.
hypotheses.prediction: Inducing BRAF V600E (or its constitutive activity) should decrease co-immunoprecipitation of SOS1 with GRB2 and decrease the EGF-stimulated cytosol-to-membrane shift of GRB2 and its association with EGFR, while treating BRAF V600E cells with a RAF inhibitor should increase GRB2–SOS1 binding and increase the membrane/organellar GRB2 pool, with kinase-dead BRAF producing no change.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa cells, compare doxycycline-inducible BRAF V600E, kinase-dead BRAF and empty vector: after EGF stimulation, perform anti-GRB2 immunoprecipitation blotted for SOS1 and EGFR, plus cytosol/membrane fractionation blotted for GRB2, and repeat in a BRAF V600E line (e.g. A375) ± vemurafenib; a BRAF-activity-dependent loss and inhibitor-dependent restoration of GRB2–SOS1/GRB2–EGFR complexes and membrane GRB2 supports the relationship, while unchanged GRB2 partitioning across all conditions rules it out.

citations.title: Relief of profound feedback inhibition of mitogenic signaling by RAF inhibitors attenuates their activity in BRAFV600E melanomas.
SOS phosphorylation and disassociation of the Grb2-SOS complex by the ERK and JNK signaling pathways.
Multiple decisive phosphorylation sites for the negative feedback regulation of SOS1 via ERK.
EGFR-mediated re-activation of MAPK signaling contributes to insensitivity of BRAF mutant colorectal cancers to RAF inhibition with vemurafenib.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) the mechanism in plain words (ERK/MAPK feedback phosphorylation of SOS1 dissociating the Grb2–SOS complex and reducing SOS membrane recruitment), (2) the entities together (BRAF V600E + GRB2 + SOS1 + EGFR, including interactome/spatial-proteomics angles), and (3) the prediction (RAF/MEK inhibitor restoring GRB2–SOS1 or GRB2–EGFR complexes and membrane GRB2). Both halves are published separately: ERK-dependent phosphorylation of SOS dissociates the Grb2–SOS complex and blocks SOS membrane recruitment (Waters 1996; Kamioka 2010), and BRAF V600E is documented to impose high ERK-dependent negative feedback that suppresses ligand-dependent mitogenic signaling and RAS function, relieved by RAF inhibition with rebound of RTK/EGFR signaling (Lito 2012; Corcoran 2012). I found no source that frames GRB2 itself as the negatively regulated node — i.e. that BRAF activity holds GRB2 in a cytosolic complex-free state, that GRB2 occupancy of GRB2–SOS1/GRB2–EGFR complexes is a direct read-out of BRAF activity, or that RAF inhibition/kinase-dead BRAF comparison restores the membrane GRB2 pool — so the specific prediction and the BRAF-activity-to-GRB2-partitioning link remain unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR1 (TβRI) acts as an upstream activator of MTORC1, with TβRI kinase-initiated PI3K/AKT signaling relieving TSC2 inhibition to increase mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The evidence about TGFBR1 states that TGF-β triggers AKT activation through TβRI, with the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 associating with TβRI upon ligand binding (TβRI-kinase-dependent) as well as through TRAF6-mediated p85 ubiquitylation (derynck2019:findings:032). The independent evidence about mTORC1 states that AKT activation is the growth-factor input that phosphorylates and inactivates TSC2, dissociating it from the lysosome and stabilizing GTP-loaded RHEB to switch mTORC1 on (haeusler2018:findings:027), and that AKT directly phosphorylates the TSC1/TSC2 GAP complex to activate mTORC1 (laplante2012:findings:002). If TβRI feeds the same PI3K/AKT-to-TSC2 node that gates mTORC1, then receptor engagement of TβRI should itself be sufficient to raise mTORC1 output in amino-acid-replete cells.
hypotheses.prediction: TGF-β stimulation of amino-acid-replete cells should raise phospho-S6K1 Thr389 and phospho-4E-BP1 within tens of minutes; this increase should be abolished by TβRI kinase inhibition or TβRI depletion, should be accompanied by AKT activation and increased TSC2 phosphorylation, and should be lost when AKT is inhibited or in TSC2-null cells (where mTORC1 output is already high and TGF-β adds nothing).
hypotheses.test: In serum-starved but amino-acid-replete cultured cells (e.g. HEK-293T or MEFs), stimulate with TGF-β over a 0–120 min time course and immunoblot phospho-S6K1 Thr389, phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65, phospho-AKT and phospho-TSC2, comparing vehicle, a TβRI kinase inhibitor added before ligand, and siRNA/CRISPR TβRI knockout cells; run the same time course with an AKT inhibitor and in TSC2-null versus TSC2-restored cells for epistasis. A TβRI-kinase- and AKT-dependent rise in mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation that is non-additive in TSC2-null cells supports the relationship, whereas unchanged mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation after TGF-β despite intact receptor signaling (Smad2/3 phosphorylation as positive control) rules it out.

citations.title: Cell size and invasion in TGF-beta-induced epithelial to mesenchymal transition is regulated by activation of the mTOR pathway.
Noncanonical TGF-beta pathways, mTORC1 and Abl, in renal interstitial fibrogenesis.
TGFβ acts through PDGFRβ to activate mTORC1 via the Akt/PRAS40 axis and causes glomerular mesangial cell hypertrophy and matrix protein expression.

novelty.note: I searched for TGF-β/TβRI activation of mTORC1 via PI3K-Akt-TSC2, for the predicted phospho-S6K1 Thr389/4E-BP1 response to TGF-β, and for TGF-β-induced TSC2 (tuberin) phosphorylation. Lamouille & Derynck (J Cell Biol 2007) state and largely test this explanation: TGF-β raises phospho-S6K1 Thr389 and phospho-4E-BP1 within ~30–60 min, the response requires TβRI kinase activity (SB431542 blocks the ensuing Akt activation) and PI3K/Akt (wortmannin/LY294002 block S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation), and the paper's Discussion explicitly attributes activation to Akt-mediated inactivation of the TSC1/TSC2 complex with accumulation of GTP-Rheb; a TβRI–p85 association is the proposed receptor-proximal step. Wang et al. independently articulate the same TGF-β→PI3K→Akt→tuberin(TSC2)→mTORC1 chain in fibroblasts with in vivo Akt/TSC2 phosphorylation data, so the mechanism is published; only the explicit TSC2-null epistasis test remains undone, with the nearest receptor-proximal epistasis work (Maity et al.) placing the node at PRAS40 downstream of PDGFRβ transactivation rather than at TSC2.

hypotheses.statement: CDC42 and SRC act as jointly required, synergistic co-activators of the same effector, N-WASP, such that Src-family kinase activity and GTP-loaded CDC42 must converge on N-WASP to drive Arp2/3-dependent actin polymerization.
hypotheses.mechanism: The CDC42 evidence states that CDC42 initiates peripheral actin polymerization indirectly through Arp2/3 by acting via N-WASP/WASP (with Toca-1 required for activation of the N-WASP/WIP complex), and that CDC42 activation produces protrusive actin-rich filopodia. Independently, the SRC evidence states that Src-family kinases phosphorylate the nephrin cytoplasmic tail on pYDXV motifs that recruit the Nck SH2 domain, and that Nck's three SH3 domains engage the six to nine proline-rich motifs of N-WASP. Because the two pathways deposit their inputs on distinct parts of the same autoinhibited effector (GTPase-binding region versus proline-rich motifs), neither input alone should fully relieve N-WASP autoinhibition, making CDC42 loading and Src-generated phosphotyrosine/Nck occupancy mutually dependent rather than parallel.
hypotheses.prediction: Src-phosphorylated, Nck-clustered N-WASP should show only partial Arp2/3-driven actin nucleation that is strongly potentiated by GTP-loaded CDC42 (super-additive relative to either input alone), and conversely CDC42-driven actin/filopodial output should be blunted when Src-family kinase activity or Nck-binding phosphotyrosines are removed; active CDC42 and Src-phosphorylated Nck complexes should be detectable on the same N-WASP molecules.
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute pyrene-actin polymerization in vitro with purified N-WASP/WIP, Arp2/3, and actin, adding in a 2x2 design (i) Nck preloaded with a Src-phosphorylated nephrin tail peptide (phospho-null peptide and kinase-dead/PP2-treated Src as controls) and (ii) GTPγS-loaded versus GDP-loaded recombinant CDC42, and score nucleation rate for synergy; in parallel, in cultured fibroblasts, co-immunoprecipitate N-WASP and probe for bound CDC42 and phospho-Nck complexes after Src activation with and without CDC42 knockdown or a CDC42 inhibitor, quantifying filopodia and cortical F-actin by phalloidin imaging.

citations.title: Cdc42 and the Rho GEF intersectin-1 collaborate with Nck to promote N-WASP-dependent actin polymerisation.
Nck and Cdc42 co-operate to recruit N-WASP to promote FcγR-mediated phagocytosis.
Contingent phosphorylation/dephosphorylation provides a mechanism of molecular memory in WASP.
Nck and phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate synergistically activate actin polymerization through the N-WASP-Arp2/3 pathway.
Differential regulation of WASP and N-WASP by Cdc42, Rac1, Nck, and PI(4,5)P2.

novelty.note: I searched for Cdc42/Nck synergy on N-WASP, for the combined biochemical reconstitution (pyrene-actin with Nck plus GTP-Cdc42), and for Src-phosphorylated receptor tail → Nck → N-WASP plus Cdc42 in cells. The cellular version of this explanation is published: in vaccinia actin tails, Src/Abl phosphorylation of the A36 tail recruits Nck/WIP/N-WASP and Cdc42 (activated by intersectin-1) is jointly required, cooperating with Nck in a feed-forward loop to sustain N-WASP-driven Arp2/3 polymerization (PMID 24284073), and the same Nck+Cdc42-CRIB joint requirement holds for FcγR phagocytosis (PMID 22454526); Torres & Rosen further show coincidence detection of Cdc42 and Src-family kinase inputs on a single WASP molecule (PMID 12769846). Note that the specific in vitro super-additivity prediction has already been tested with the opposite result: GTP-Cdc42 gave no further stimulation of Nck-activated N-WASP/Arp2/3 nucleation, interpreted as redundant rather than synergistic activation (PMID 11340081), consistent with the differential-regulator survey (PMID 17302440).

hypotheses.statement: TNF acts directly on BRAF-mutant (B-RafV600E) tumour cells to antagonize BRAF/MEK-inhibitor-induced cell death, so that TNF–TNF-R1/NF-κB signalling functions as a cell-extrinsic modifier of BRAF-inhibitor sensitivity.
hypotheses.mechanism: The BRAF evidence states that killing B-RafV600E melanoma cells with Raf/MEK1/2 inhibition is incomplete and depends on parallel survival inputs, since cell death only becomes efficient when MEK1/2 inhibition is combined with IGF-1R or PI3K blockade in B-Raf-inhibitor-resistant lines (lake2016:findings:025). Independently, the TNF evidence states that TNF-R1 engagement simultaneously loads an apoptotic caspase-8 arm and an NF-κB arm, that NF-κB activity determines whether TNF-exposed cells die or survive, and that NF-κB induces cIAPs and IκB that damp the death-promoting output (chen2002:findings:001, chen2002:findings:006, chen2002:findings:007). If BRAF-inhibitor lethality is set by the balance of such survival inputs, TNF present in the tumour milieu should shift a BRAF-mutant cell away from drug-induced death through its NF-κB/cIAP arm rather than by restoring ERK signalling.
hypotheses.prediction: Adding recombinant TNF to vemurafenib- or MEK-inhibitor-treated B-RafV600E cells will reduce caspase-3/7 activation, annexin-V positivity and loss of clonogenicity, while leaving the drug-induced suppression of phospho-ERK1/2 intact; the protected cells will show nuclear NF-κB activity with induced cIAP1/2 and resynthesized IκBα, and the protection will be lost (with death restored or exceeding drug alone) when TNF-R1 is knocked down or IKKβ is inhibited.
hypotheses.test: In B-RafV600E melanoma lines, run a 2×2 factorial of vemurafenib (or trametinib) ± recombinant TNF, each arm repeated with control siRNA, TNFR1 siRNA, or an IKKβ inhibitor: read out viability (CellTiter-Glo), caspase-3/7 activity and annexin V/PI flow cytometry at 24–72 h, colony formation at 10–14 days, and immunoblot phospho-ERK1/2, cleaved caspase-8/-3, IκBα and cIAP1/2. TNF-dependent rescue of viability/clonogenicity that is abolished by TNFR1 knockdown or IKKβ inhibition, without recovery of phospho-ERK1/2, supports the hypothesis; no change in drug-induced death across TNF arms rules it out.

citations.title: NF-κB Regulation of c-FLIP Promotes TNFα-Mediated RAF Inhibitor Resistance in Melanoma.
Co-expression of TNF receptors 1 and 2 on melanomas facilitates soluble TNF-induced resistance to MAPK pathway inhibitors.
Increased CD271 expression by the NF-kB pathway promotes melanoma cell survival and drives acquired resistance to BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib.

novelty.note: Searched for TNF/NF-κB-mediated protection against BRAF/MEK inhibitor killing in BRAF-V600E melanoma, TNF-R1 dependence, and rescue of drug-induced apoptosis. Lehraiki et al. (TNFα secretion → NF-κB → CD271 driving vemurafenib resistance), Gray-Schopfer/Smith et al. (TNFα blocks RAF-inhibitor-induced apoptosis via NF-κB, requiring c-FLIP, with NF-κB targeting restoring response), and Vredevoogd-type work on TNFR1/TNFR2 co-expression (solTNF-induced, reversible MAPK-inhibitor resistance, TNFR1 as the main NF-κB mediator) together state exactly this cell-extrinsic mechanism and prediction. The only detail not directly anticipated is the specific cIAP1/2 readout, c-FLIP being the documented NF-κB effector instead.

hypotheses.statement: SYK acts as a direct upstream activator of the JNK/c-Jun pathway in ITAM-coupled cells, with SYK kinase activity required for receptor-induced JNK phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The SYK evidence shows that activated SYK uses its phosphorylated linker tyrosines to recruit VAV1 and PLCγ1 (mcsai2010:findings:012) and that SYK ligation downstream of CLEC7A drives cytokine and chemokine output through ERK, NFAT and NF-κB (mcsai2010:findings:019) — i.e. SYK sits at the head of multiple MAPK/transcription-factor branches and of Rho-family-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling. Independently, the JNK evidence states that Rac/Cdc42 activate JNK through the MAPKKKs MLK2, MLK3 and MEKK4 (jaffe2005:findings:008), and that brief strong calcium bursts give prolonged JNK activation because JNK has low calcium affinity and slow deactivation (purvis2013:findings:008, purvis2013:findings:021). The two branches SYK is documented to nucleate are therefore exactly the inputs the JNK literature assigns to JNK activation, implying SYK activity should be a required upstream determinant of receptor-induced JNK signalling rather than only of the ERK/NFAT/NF-κB arms already recorded.
hypotheses.prediction: ITAM- or Dectin-1-dependent stimulation should produce a phospho-JNK/phospho-c-Jun burst that is abolished or strongly blunted by SYK inhibition or SYK loss, and conversely expression of autoinhibition-released SYK (tandem-SH2-deleted or Tyr130 phosphomimetic) should raise phospho-JNK and c-Jun Ser63/Ser73 phosphorylation without receptor ligation; the SYK linker mutants that cannot bind VAV1/PLCγ1 (Tyr342/Tyr346) should fail to transmit to JNK while still supporting SYK autophosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In a SYK-expressing myeloid or B cell line (e.g. RAW264.7 or Ramos), stimulate with zymosan/curdlan or anti-IgM and compare phospho-JNK (Thr183/Tyr185) and phospho-c-Jun by quantitative Western blot across (i) vehicle versus a SYK ATP-site inhibitor, (ii) SYK-knockdown/knockout versus rescue with wild-type SYK, constitutively active SYK (ΔSH2 or Y130E, per mcsai2010:findings:006 and mcsai2010:findings:009), or the Y342F/Y346F linker mutant; read out single-cell JNK activity in parallel with the Jun(29-84)-Clover translocation reporter, whose movement is JNK-inhibitor- and S73A-sensitive (regot2014:findings:000), so that loss of translocation upon SYK inhibition and gain upon active-SYK expression would establish the relationship, while unchanged JNK activity would rule it out.

citations.title: CR3 and Dectin-1 Collaborate in Macrophage Cytokine Response through Association on Lipid Rafts and Activation of Syk-JNK-AP-1 Pathway.
BLNK required for coupling Syk to PLC gamma 2 and Rac1-JNK in B cells.
Phospholipase Cgamma2 is critical for Dectin-1-mediated Ca2+ flux and cytokine production in dendritic cells.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the plain-language mechanism (Syk required for receptor-induced JNK/c-Jun phosphorylation), the entities together (Dectin-1/zymosan/curdlan + Syk + phospho-JNK; BCR/anti-IgM + Syk + Rac1 + JNK), and the prediction (Syk inhibitor or Syk-/- abolishing phospho-JNK; constitutively active Syk raising p-JNK; Y342/Y346 linker mutants). The Syk→JNK/AP-1 axis in ITAM/Dectin-1-coupled cells is explicitly published: Huang et al. show Syk inhibitors (SykI, Bay 61-3606) and Syk-/- macrophages abolish CR3/Dectin-1-driven JNK and c-Jun/c-Fos phosphorylation and name the 'Syk-JNK-AP-1 pathway', and Ishiai et al. established Syk coupling to Rac1-JNK via BLNK in anti-IgM-stimulated B cells, with the PLCγ2 arm of Dectin-1-induced JNK activation documented separately. Only the accessory details (autoinhibition-released SYK ΔSH2/Y130E raising basal p-JNK, and Y342F/Y346F linker mutants selectively failing to reach JNK) were not found stated, which does not change that the central explanation is already in the literature.

hypotheses.statement: ERK2 directly phosphorylates the cytoplasmic domain of TGFBR1 (TβRI) on Ser/Thr residues, acting as a direct negative-feedback modification that licenses TβRI ectodomain shedding and dampens TβRI-driven Smad signaling.
hypotheses.mechanism: ERK2 is an established direct feedback kinase for receptors and upstream pathway components, phosphorylating FGFR1 on S777 to curtail receptor tyrosine phosphorylation and downstream proliferation/migration, and phosphorylating MEK1 T292 and Raf-1 to desensitize them (lake2016:findings:002, lake2016:findings:010, lake2016:findings:007). Independently, TβRI — but not TβRII — is selectively down-regulated by TACE/ADAM17 cleavage specifically in response to ERK/MAPK signaling, reducing surface TβRI, Smad3 activation, antiproliferation and EMT (derynck2019:findings:009, hata2016:findings:007), and TβRI activity and fate are known to be governed by covalent modification of its cytoplasmic/kinase region (GS-domain phosphorylation, Lys389 sumoylation, ubiquitylation; hata2016:findings:004, derynck2019:findings:014). The selectivity of the ERK-triggered effect for TβRI over TβRII, together with ERK2's demonstrated ability to directly phosphorylate serines on a transmembrane receptor to switch off its signaling, implies TβRI itself is a direct ERK2 substrate rather than only a downstream casualty of protease activation.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active ERK2 should phosphorylate the purified TβRI cytoplasmic domain in vitro at one or more Ser-Pro/Thr-Pro-containing sites (absent or non-conserved in TβRII), phosphorylation of these sites in cells should rise upon EGF/mitogen stimulation and be abolished by MEK1/2 inhibition, and Ser/Thr→Ala substitution of the ERK2 sites should render TβRI resistant to ERK-induced surface loss and preserve TGF-β-induced Smad3 activation, while phosphomimetic substitution should reduce surface TβRI and Smad3 output even without mitogen stimulation.
hypotheses.test: Perform an in vitro kinase assay with purified active ERK2 (and kinase-dead ERK2 plus a MEK/ERK inhibitor as controls) on recombinant GST-TβRI cytoplasmic domain versus the TβRII cytoplasmic domain, mapping incorporated phosphosites by LC-MS/MS; then, in cultured cells, co-immunoprecipitate tagged TβRI with ERK2 and blot TβRI phospho-site occupancy ± EGF ± MEK1/2 inhibitor, and compare wild-type, Ala-mutant and phosphomimetic TβRI for cell-surface levels (surface biotinylation) and TGF-β-induced Smad3 phosphorylation/reporter activity.

citations.title: TACE-mediated ectodomain shedding of the type I TGF-beta receptor downregulates TGF-beta signaling.
ERK-mediated phosphorylation of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 on Ser777 inhibits signaling.

novelty.note: I searched for direct ERK phosphorylation of the TβRI/TGFBR1 cytoplasmic domain, for ERK/MAPK-driven TACE/ADAM17 shedding of TβRI, and for ERK2 Ser/Thr-Pro substrate mapping on TGFBR1. The closest published work is Liu et al., which shows ERK MAPK activation triggers TACE-mediated shedding of TβRI (not TβRII) and reduced Smad3 signaling but attributes this to protease activation and neither tests nor reports direct ERK phosphorylation of the receptor; the receptor-level precedent exists only for FGFR1 Ser777. No source states or refutes ERK2 directly phosphorylating TβRI's cytoplasmic domain as a shedding-licensing feedback mark, so the claim is open.

hypotheses.statement: JNK1 is a direct positive regulator of extracellular ATP/P2RX7-driven IL-1β secretion from myeloid cells, acting upstream of the secretory step by licensing NLRP3 through Ser198 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: TLR priming drives JNK1-mediated phosphorylation of NLRP3 Ser198 (Ser194 mouse), which promotes BRCC3 binding, deubiquitylation and self-association needed for NLRP3 activation in macrophages (swanson2019:findings:028). Independently, extracellular ATP sensed through P2RX7 activates dendritic/myeloid cells specifically via inflammasome signalling to produce IL-1β secretion (de2024:findings:027). If the ATP-triggered secretory output depends on an NLRP3 inflammasome that must first be JNK1-licensed, then JNK1 activity should be a direct determinant of how much IL-1β a myeloid cell secretes, independent of P2RX7 engagement itself.
hypotheses.prediction: In primed macrophages or THP-1 cells, loss or inhibition of JNK1 should sharply reduce ATP-induced mature IL-1β release into the supernatant (with a parallel loss of NLRP3 Ser198 phosphorylation, NLRP3 oligomerization and caspase-1 processing) without reducing pro-IL-1β expression or P2RX7-dependent ion flux; conversely, restoring a phosphomimetic NLRP3 S198 should rescue secretion in JNK1-deficient cells.
hypotheses.test: LPS-prime wild-type and JNK1-knockout/siRNA (plus JNK-inhibitor-treated) human THP-1 or mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages, stimulate with extracellular ATP, and quantify secreted IL-1β by ELISA and cleaved IL-1β/caspase-1 in supernatants by western blot, alongside lysate blots for pro-IL-1β, phospho-NLRP3 Ser198 and NLRP3 self-association (native/crosslink or co-IP); then re-express wild-type, S198A and S198D NLRP3 in NLRP3-null JNK1-deficient cells to test whether the phosphomimetic restores ATP-induced IL-1β secretion, which would establish or exclude JNK1 as a direct upstream requirement for this secretion.

citations.title: NLRP3 Phosphorylation Is an Essential Priming Event for Inflammasome Activation.
NEK7 phosphorylation amplifies NLRP3 inflammasome activation downstream of potassium efflux and gasdermin D.

novelty.note: I searched for JNK1-mediated NLRP3 Ser198/Ser194 phosphorylation as a priming event, for ATP-induced IL-1β secretion in JNK1-deficient (Mapk8−/−) macrophages, and for JNK dependence of P2X7/ATP-triggered IL-1β release. Song et al. (Mol Cell 2017) already reports that JNK1 phosphorylates NLRP3 at S194/S198 as a critical priming event required for BRCC3-dependent deubiquitylation, self-association and inflammasome activation, using S194A knockin mice and phospho-site mutants; Xu et al. (Sci Immunol 2024) independently shows that Mapk8−/− macrophages have impaired caspase-1 activation and IL-1β release after ATP stimulation while TNF-α production and AIM2 responses are intact — i.e. the stated mechanism, the ATP-stimulation prediction and its specificity controls are all published. Status is established, though the specific rescue by a phosphomimetic S198D in JNK1-null cells and the explicit separation from P2RX7 ion flux were not found as such.

hypotheses.statement: JNK1 directly restrains mTORC1 activity in the insulin-responsive branch of the pathway, such that loss or inhibition of JNK1 increases insulin-stimulated mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The mTORC1 claims establish that mTORC1 activation is gated by insulin, which via AKT inactivates TSC2 to stabilize GTP-bound RHEB, and that this insulin arm is subject to negative regulation at the receptor level, since mTORC1-driven GRB10 phosphorylation forms a feedback brake on the insulin receptor and loss of that brake improves insulin sensitivity (haeusler2018:findings:027, haeusler2018:findings:009). The JNK1 claims independently place JNK1 as a negative determinant of metabolic status in the same tissues: JNK1-/- mice resist obesity and obesity-induced metabolic changes, and metabolic homeostasis requires JNK1 more than JNK2 (zeke2016:findings:021, zeke2016:findings:022), with JNK1 expressed and functionally active in fibroblasts (zeke2016:findings:016), the very cell type in which mTORC1 output is read out through S6Ks (fruman2017:findings:009). Together these imply JNK1 acts as an inhibitory input onto the insulin→AKT→TSC2→mTORC1 axis, so that removing JNK1 disinhibits mTORC1 rather than merely altering whole-body physiology.
hypotheses.prediction: In JNK1-deficient or JNK-inhibited fibroblasts, insulin stimulation should produce higher and more sustained phosphorylation of the mTORC1 substrates S6K1 Thr389 and 4E-BP1, with correspondingly increased AKT-dependent TSC2 phosphorylation, while rapamycin should still abolish the signal; conversely, JNK1 gain of function or JNK activation should blunt insulin-stimulated S6K1/4E-BP1 phosphorylation without affecting amino-acid-only stimulation.
hypotheses.test: Compare wild-type and JNK1-null mouse embryonic fibroblasts (and wild-type cells pretreated with a selective JNK inhibitor or JNK1 siRNA) in a standard serum-starvation/insulin time-course, immunoblotting phospho-S6K1 Thr389, phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65, phospho-AKT and phospho-TSC2 alongside total protein; then test dependence on the insulin arm by repeating the comparison under amino-acid-only restimulation and in cells expressing constitutively active RHEB or a phospho-site-mutant TSC2, where JNK1 status should no longer change mTORC1 output if JNK1 acts through this branch. A reciprocal arm expressing active JNK1 (or MKK7-JNK1 fusion) should suppress insulin-stimulated S6K1 phosphorylation; absence of any shift in mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation in either direction rules out the proposed relationship.

citations.title: c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) mediates feedback inhibition of the insulin signaling cascade.
mTORC1 and JNK coordinate phosphorylation of the p70S6K1 autoinhibitory domain in skeletal muscle following functional overloading.
Osmotic stress regulates mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 via c-Jun N-terminal Kinase (JNK)-mediated Raptor protein phosphorylation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (JNK1 as a brake on the insulin→AKT→TSC2→mTORC1 arm), the entities together (JNK1 + S6K1 Thr389 / 4E-BP1 / TSC1-TSC2 / Raptor), and the prediction (JNK1-null or JNK-inhibited fibroblasts showing higher insulin-stimulated mTORC1 output). The restraining half is published: Lee et al. showed in mouse embryo fibroblasts that insulin-activated JNK binds IRS1 and phosphorylates Ser307 as negative feedback, with JNK-deficient cells displaying enhanced insulin-stimulated signalling and glucose uptake — but the readouts are IRS1/AKT-level, not mTORC1 substrates, and no source states that JNK1 loss raises insulin-stimulated S6K1 Thr389/4E-BP1 phosphorylation via TSC2. The nearest work on the JNK–mTORC1 link in fact reports the opposite sign (JNK inhibition lowers S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation after IGF-I/overload; JNK phosphorylates Raptor to activate mTORC1 under osmotic stress), so the specific connection and its direction remain unsettled rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: ERK5/MAPK7 negatively regulates JNK activation, so that engagement of the MEK5–ERK5 branch downstream of the Act1 scaffold dampens JNK/c-Jun signalling in IL-17-responsive cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The corpus states that IL-17 signalling routes through Act1, which recruits TRAF6 as an E3 ligase to drive NF-κB and MAPK (including JNK) activation, with JNK output being the branch most sensitive to feedback attenuation of TRAF6 ubiquitination (gaffen2014:findings:022, gaffen2014:findings:027); independently, the same Act1 hub is stated to recruit TRAF4, which tethers EGFR to the IL-17R complex and drives MEKK3–MEK5–ERK5 activation (li2019:findings:014, li2019:findings:016). Because both branches draw on one limiting scaffold, and scaffolds are stated to become inhibitory when partner stoichiometry is skewed (good2011:findings:001), recruitment into the TRAF4–ERK5 arm should divert Act1 away from the TRAF6–JNK arm; the corpus already states this kind of MAPK-on-JNK negative regulation for p38α acting on the JNK/c-Jun pathway in an EGFR-linked context (cuadrado2010:findings:041).
hypotheses.prediction: Loss of ERK5 or MEK5 should increase and prolong IL-17A-induced phospho-JNK and phospho-c-Jun without a comparable rise in early IκBα degradation, while constitutively active MEK5 (or TRAF4 overexpression) should blunt IL-17A-induced JNK/c-Jun phosphorylation; the shift should be accompanied by reciprocal changes in the amount of TRAF6 versus TRAF4 co-precipitating with Act1 and in TRAF6 ubiquitination.
hypotheses.test: In cultured IL-17-responsive keratinocytes (or HeLa cells reconstituted with IL17RA), compare siRNA knockdown of ERK5/MEK5 and ERK5 kinase inhibition against expression of constitutively active MEK5, then run a time course of IL-17A stimulation with quantitative western blots for phospho-JNK, phospho-c-Jun, phospho-IκBα, and JNK-dependent transcript output; in the same lysates, immunoprecipitate Act1 and blot for bound TRAF6 versus TRAF4 and for TRAF6 polyubiquitination to test whether ERK5-branch activity redistributes the scaffold away from the JNK arm.

citations.title: A novel IL-17 signaling pathway controlling keratinocyte proliferation and tumorigenesis via the TRAF4-ERK5 axis.
Lose and gain: impacts of ERK5 and JNK cascades on each other.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) plain-language mechanism ('ERK5 negatively regulates JNK activation', 'ERK5/BMK1 suppresses JNK', MAPK7 compensatory crosstalk), (2) the entities together (IL-17/Act1/TRAF4/TRAF6/MEK5-ERK5/JNK, Act1 scaffold stoichiometry), and (3) the prediction (ERK5/MEK5 loss increasing IL-17-induced phospho-JNK/c-Jun). The Act1-partitioning half is published: Wu et al. (JEM 2015) show TRAF4 and TRAF6 compete for the same TRAF-binding sites on Act1, that TRAF4 is required specifically for IL-17A-induced MEKK3–MEK5–ERK5 activation, and that TRAF4 deficiency leaves ERK1/2, p38, JNK and NF-κB activation not abolished but enhanced — i.e. diverting the scaffold into the ERK5 arm restrains the TRAF6 arm. What is not published is the distinctive kinase-level claim that ERK5/MEK5 activity itself dampens JNK/c-Jun, nor the predicted dissociation from IκBα degradation (the published TRAF4-null data show IκBα degradation and NF-κB output rise alongside JNK), nor any TRAF6-ubiquitination readout of the redistribution; the closest dedicated treatment of ERK5↔JNK crosstalk is a systems-modelling study that concludes crosstalk between the two cascades has no significant impact on either kinase's activation. Hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: CDK1 acts directly on a canonical Ras/MAPK effector site — phosphorylating ribosomal protein S6 at Ser235/236, the RSK-specific readout of Ras pathway activity — so that CDK1 activity generates Ras-independent phosphorylation at a site otherwise attributed to Ras signalling.
hypotheses.mechanism: Sang et al. show that when Cdk1 is concentrated with substrate in SUMO-SIM condensates it phosphorylates peptides that lack its primary specificity determinants, explicitly including RPS6 Ser235/236 (sang2022:findings:009), indicating the site is chemically accessible to CDK1 when local enzyme-substrate concentration is high. Cargnello & Roux report that Ser235/236 of rpS6 is the site phosphorylated specifically by RSK1/2 downstream of Ras/MAPK activation, in contrast to the broader S6K site set (cargnello2011:findings:034). A precedent for CDK1 cross-phosphorylating ERK-pathway-derived substrate sequences already exists in the EKAR reporter, whose Cdc25-based ERK substrate peptide is phosphorylated by Cdk1 and required mutation to restore specificity (gest2024:findings:192), so CDK1 and the Ras output converge on overlapping phosphoacceptor sequences rather than being read out independently.
hypotheses.prediction: In cells where Ras/MEK/ERK/RSK signalling is fully inhibited, rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation should not fall to background in mitotic (high CDK1-activity) cells but should persist or rise, and that residual signal should be abolished by CDK1 inhibition; conversely, purified CDK1/cyclin B should phosphorylate recombinant rpS6 (or an S235/236 peptide) in vitro in a CDK1-inhibitor-sensitive manner, with the signal enhanced by artificially raising local CDK1-substrate concentration.
hypotheses.test: Two-part assay in a standard cell/biochemistry lab: (1) in vitro kinase reactions with purified CDK1/cyclin B (and, as comparators, RSK1 and CDK2/cyclin A) on recombinant rpS6 or an S235/236 synthetic peptide, ±RO-3306, read out by phospho-S235/236 immunoblot or radiolabel incorporation, including a tethered/high-local-concentration format (e.g., GST-pulldown-immobilised substrate with CDK1 fused to a binding partner) to test the concentration dependence; (2) in HeLa cells, block Ras output with MEK plus RSK inhibitors, synchronise with nocodazole to raise CDK1 activity, and immunoblot phospho-rpS6 S235/236 with and without RO-3306 or CDK1 siRNA — CDK1-dependent residual pS235/236 under complete Ras-pathway blockade supports the relationship, while complete loss of signal with MEK/RSK inhibition alone rules it out.

citations.title: Condensed-phase signaling can expand kinase specificity and respond to macromolecular crowding.
RAS/ERK signaling promotes site-specific ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation via RSK and stimulates cap-dependent translation.

novelty.note: I searched for CDK1 phosphorylation of rpS6 Ser235/236, MEK/RSK-independent S6 phosphorylation in mitosis, and CDK1-inhibitor (RO-3306) effects on pS6, across PubMed, PMC and publisher pages. The condensate paper (Sang et al., Mol Cell 2022) does report Cdk1 phosphorylating an RPS6 S235/236 peptide, but only in synthetic SUMO-SIM condensates and without any claim about Ras-independent pS6 in cells; Roux et al. establish S235/236 as the RSK/Ras-MAPK-specific site. No source found states, or tests and refutes, that CDK1 generates Ras-independent pS235/236 in cells, so the mechanism is partly published but the specific prediction is not.

hypotheses.statement: mTORC2 directly suppresses STAT3-dependent transcription by driving AKT-mediated phosphorylation of FOXO1/FKHR, the STAT3 coactivator, so that loss of mTORC2 activity increases STAT3 target-gene output.
hypotheses.mechanism: mTORC2 is the AKT S473/T450 kinase and its activity is specifically required for AKT-dependent phosphorylation of FOXO1/3a, while being dispensable for other AKT substrates such as TSC2 and GSK3-β (laplante2012:findings:008; liu2020:findings:008; manning2017:findings:006). Independently, FKHR/FOXO1 physically associates with STAT3, co-localizes with it in the nucleus of IL-6-treated HepG2 cells, and selectively enhances STAT3-dependent promoters such as α2M but not a STAT5-responsive promoter (heinrich2003:findings:017). Because phosphorylation is the step that removes FOXO1 from the nucleus, an mTORC2-selective input into FOXO1 phosphorylation predicts that mTORC2 sets the level of nuclear FOXO1 available as a STAT3 cofactor and therefore constrains STAT3 transcriptional activity.
hypotheses.prediction: Depleting RICTOR or mLST8 (or inhibiting mTOR catalytically) in IL-6-stimulated hepatoma cells should reduce FOXO1 phosphorylation, increase nuclear FOXO1–STAT3 co-immunoprecipitation and co-localization, and raise STAT3-dependent α2M promoter-reporter activity and endogenous STAT3 target mRNA without increasing STAT3 Y705-type activation by the receptor; conversely, forcing mTORC2 output (rictor overexpression) should lower nuclear FOXO1 and dampen the same STAT3 reporter, and the whole effect should disappear when FOXO1 is knocked down or replaced with a phosphorylation-site mutant.
hypotheses.test: In HepG2 cells, compare siRNA knockdown of RICTOR/mLST8 versus RAPTOR versus control (with an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor as an orthogonal arm), stimulate with IL-6, and read out in parallel: (i) immunoblot for phospho-FOXO1 and AKT S473/T450, (ii) nuclear/cytoplasmic fractionation plus FOXO1–STAT3 co-immunoprecipitation and immunofluorescence co-localization, and (iii) an α2M-promoter luciferase reporter carrying intact STAT3 sites alongside qPCR of endogenous STAT3 targets. Epistasis arms — FOXO1 knockdown, and re-expression of a non-phosphorylatable FOXO1 mutant — determine whether the transcriptional change requires the FOXO1–STAT3 interaction; a change in STAT3 reporter output that persists after FOXO1 removal, or no change in FOXO1 occupancy at all, rules the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Akt modulates STAT3-mediated gene expression through a FKHR (FOXO1a)-dependent mechanism.
Mammalian target of rapamycin complex 2 (mTORC2) negatively regulates Toll-like receptor 4-mediated inflammatory response via FoxO1.
mTORC2 Is the Major Second Layer Kinase Negatively Regulating FOXO3 Activity.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (mTORC2/Rictor → AKT → FOXO1 phosphorylation → nuclear FOXO1 as STAT3 cofactor), the entities together ("mTORC2"/"rictor" + "FOXO1" + "STAT3", plus FKHR/α2-macroglobulin/IL-6/HepG2), and the prediction (Rictor knockdown or mTOR catalytic inhibition raising STAT3 target-gene output in hepatoma cells). Both halves of the mechanism are published separately: Kortylewski et al. (JBC 2003) show that AKT-mediated FKHR/FOXO1a phosphorylation suppresses STAT3-dependent α2M transcription in IL-6-treated HepG2 cells, and Brown et al. (JBC 2011) show that rictor/mTORC2 loss impairs FoxO1 phosphorylation, raises nuclear FoxO1 and increases FoxO1-dependent inflammatory transcription — explicitly speculating in its discussion only that nuclear FoxO1 might bind and negatively regulate STAT3 (opposite sign to the coactivator model). I found no source assigning the FOXO1 phosphorylation step upstream of STAT3 specifically to mTORC2, nor any test of RICTOR/mLST8 depletion on STAT3-dependent promoter output, so the specific connection and prediction remain unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: The p38 module directly activates RPS6KB1 (S6K1) by phosphorylating its hydrophobic-motif site Thr389, providing an mTORC1-independent route to S6K1 activation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The p38 evidence shows that stress-activated p38 drives activation of the AGC kinase RSK through MK2/3-catalyzed phosphorylation of the RSK hydrophobic-motif site Ser380 (cargnello2011:findings:058), and that p38 substrate selection is governed by KIM/D-domain docking with contiguous basic residues shared across MAPKAPK-family kinases (cargnello2011:findings:017). The S6K1 evidence shows that S6K1 is activated through phosphorylation of the equivalent hydrophobic-motif site Thr389 (inoki2002:findings:003; gu2017:findings:002) and that S6K1 is a close functional counterpart of RSK, with the two kinases phosphorylating overlapping sites on ribosomal protein S6 (cargnello2011:findings:034). Together these imply that the same p38-driven hydrophobic-motif phosphorylation that activates RSK can act directly on the homologous site in S6K1.
hypotheses.prediction: Acute p38 activation (e.g. anisomycin or sorbitol) should increase S6K1 Thr389 phosphorylation and downstream rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation, this increase should be abolished by the p38 inhibitor SB203580 or in p38α-deficient cells, and a residual SB203580-sensitive pool of pThr389 should persist when mTORC1 is fully inhibited; recombinant p38α (or p38-activated MK2) should phosphorylate purified S6K1 on Thr389 in vitro, and a Thr389Ala S6K1 mutant should lose all stress-induced activation.
hypotheses.test: In HEK-293T cells, stimulate with anisomycin/sorbitol with and without SB203580 and with and without an active-site mTOR inhibitor, then immunoblot immunoprecipitated HA–S6K1 for pThr389 and assay its activity on GST–S6; in parallel run an in vitro kinase reaction of activated recombinant p38α (and p38α-activated MK2) with catalytically inactive purified S6K1 wild type versus Thr389Ala, detecting site-specific phosphorylation by phospho-Thr389 immunoblot and [γ-32P]ATP incorporation.

citations.title: A role for p38 stress-activated protein kinase in regulation of cell growth via TORC1.
ERK and p38 pathways regulate amino acid signalling.
Contribution of S6K1/MAPK signaling pathways in the response to oxidative stress: activation of RSK and MSK by hydrogen peroxide.

novelty.note: I searched for direct p38/MK2 phosphorylation of the S6K1 hydrophobic motif (Thr389/Thr412), for stress (anisomycin/sorbitol/H2O2) plus SB203580 effects on pThr389, and for mTORC1-independent S6K1 activation, using PubMed, Europe PMC and publisher pages. Published work establishes that p38 is required for and can drive S6K Thr389 phosphorylation after anisomycin/H2O2 and amino acids (Cully 2010; Casas-Terradellas 2008), but in every case the route is through TORC1/mTORC1, and no paper reports p38α or MK2 phosphorylating purified S6K1 at Thr389 in vitro or an mTORC1-independent pThr389 pool. A directly relevant study instead shows that the stress-induced 'pThr389' signal is largely antibody cross-reactivity with the homologous hydrophobic-motif sites of p38/ERK-activated RSK and MSK rather than S6K1, so the specific direct-phosphorylation mechanism is unpublished and partly contradicted.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR1 (TβRI) acts as a direct negative regulator of NF-κB activation by binding TRAF6 and diverting its K63-linked ubiquitin ligase output onto the TβRI cytoplasmic domain instead of the NF-κB-activating substrates.
hypotheses.mechanism: TRAF6's RING-dependent assembly of K63-linked polyubiquitin chains is strictly required for NF-κB activation, since RING mutants that cannot build those chains also fail to activate an NF-κB reporter (deng2000:findings:009), and receptor-proximal adaptors that engage TRAF6 convert its ubiquitylation activity into canonical NF-κB signalling (gaffen2014:findings:022). TGF-β-bound TβRI recruits TRAF6 and is itself polyubiquitylated by it as part of a receptor-centred TRAF6 complex (derynck2019:findings:036), so an activated TβRI presents a competing, membrane-anchored acceptor for the same limiting pool of TRAF6 ligase activity. This predicts a cell-intrinsic, receptor-level explanation for the observation that TGF-β disrupts NF-κB signalling in inflammatory fibroblasts and drives them to the myCAF state (davidson2021:findings:012).
hypotheses.prediction: In fibroblasts, TGF-β pretreatment (or TβRI overexpression) will increase TβRI–TRAF6 co-association and TβRI K63-ubiquitylation while reducing IL-1β/IL-17-induced TRAF6 auto-K63-polyubiquitylation, IκB degradation, NF-κB nuclear translocation and NF-κB reporter output; TβRI knockdown, or a TβRI carrying a disrupted TRAF6-binding motif, will abolish this suppression and restore full NF-κB activation, and the suppression should persist under TβRI kinase inhibition because the TRAF6 arm is kinase-independent.
hypotheses.test: In cultured fibroblasts (or HEK293 reconstitution), pretreat with TGF-β or express wild-type versus TRAF6-binding-motif-mutant or kinase-dead TβRI, then stimulate with IL-1β/IL-17; read out (i) anti-TβRI and anti-TRAF6 reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation with K63-linkage-specific ubiquitin immunoblot of both TRAF6 and the TβRI cytoplasmic domain, and (ii) NF-κB activity by κB-luciferase reporter plus IκBα degradation and p65 nuclear translocation imaging, comparing siRNA-TGFBR1 against control; a TGF-β-dependent shift of K63 chains from TRAF6 to TβRI that tracks quantitatively with loss of NF-κB output, and is rescued by TGFBR1 knockdown or the TRAF6-binding mutant, supports the hypothesis, whereas unchanged TRAF6 ubiquitylation and NF-κB output rules it out.

citations.title: The type I TGF-beta receptor engages TRAF6 to activate TAK1 in a receptor kinase-independent manner.
IL1-Induced JAK/STAT Signaling Is Antagonized by TGFβ to Shape CAF Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.

novelty.note: I searched for TβRI/TGFBR1–TRAF6 binding and NF-κB suppression, for TRAF6 K63-ubiquitin substrate competition as a negative regulator, and for the mechanism of TGF-β antagonism of NF-κB/inflammatory signalling in fibroblasts (iCAF/myCAF). The TβRI–TRAF6 interaction, TRAF6 autoubiquitylation and TβRI cytoplasmic-domain ubiquitylation in a kinase-independent manner are well published (PMID 18758450), and the published fibroblast/CAF mechanism for TGF-β shutting down inflammatory signalling is transcriptional IL1R1 downregulation via SMAD2/3 (PMID 30366930), not substrate diversion of TRAF6. No source states that TβRI sequesters TRAF6's K63 ligase output away from NF-κB substrates, and none directly tested and refuted it, so the components are established but the specific explanation and prediction are not.

hypotheses.statement: mTORC1 is a direct positive regulator of the LPS/TLR4-triggered inflammatory program in macrophages and monocytes, being activated by LPS stimulation and required for full LPS-induced pro-inflammatory cytokine output and the accompanying glycolytic shift.
hypotheses.mechanism: The LPS-side evidence shows that monocytes trained with BCG mount a markedly larger pro-inflammatory cytokine response to LPS together with a switch to aerobic glycolysis, and that this hyper-inflammatory LPS response is abolished by rapamycin (fitzgerald2020:findings:013). The mTORC1-side evidence establishes that rapamycin, as an FKBP12 gain-of-function complex, directly binds and inhibits mTOR specifically when mTOR is in mTORC1 and not in mTORC2 (laplante2012:findings:001), so the rapamycin-sensitive step in the LPS cytokine response is attributable to mTORC1 catalytic output rather than to mTORC2 or to off-pathway effects. Taken together, the independent claims imply a direct LPS→mTORC1→cytokine axis in which TLR4 ligation feeds into mTORC1 activation and mTORC1 activity is needed to license the transcriptional/metabolic amplification of the LPS response.
hypotheses.prediction: LPS stimulation of macrophages/monocytes should acutely increase canonical mTORC1 substrate phosphorylation (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1 Ser65) in a TLR4-dependent manner, and acute rapamycin treatment or raptor loss during LPS exposure should blunt TNFα/IL-6 production and the rise in glycolytic flux, while rictor/mTORC2 loss should not phenocopy this.
hypotheses.test: In a macrophage line (e.g. RAW264.7 or immortalized BMDMs) and primary human monocytes, stimulate with LPS over a 0–120 min time course and immunoblot phospho-S6K1 Thr389 and phospho-4E-BP1 Ser65 versus total protein; then compare LPS-induced TNFα/IL-6 (ELISA plus qPCR to separate transcript from protein effects) and extracellular acidification/lactate output across four conditions — vehicle, rapamycin, CRISPR/shRNA knockdown of RPTOR (mTORC1-specific subunit), and knockdown of RICTOR (mTORC2-specific control) — with co-immunoprecipitation of mTOR/raptor after LPS to confirm complex integrity; loss of the LPS-induced substrate phosphorylation signal or failure of RPTOR loss to reduce cytokine output would rule the relationship out.

citations.title: mTORC1-S6K activation by endotoxin contributes to cytokine up-regulation and early lethality in animals.
Myeloid-specific Rictor deletion induces M1 macrophage polarization and potentiates in vivo pro-inflammatory response to lipopolysaccharide.
mTOR regulation of metabolism limits LPS-induced monocyte inflammatory and procoagulant responses.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the plain mechanism (LPS/TLR4 → mTORC1 → S6K1/4E-BP1 phosphorylation and cytokine output), the entities together (raptor/rictor deletion in macrophages with LPS-induced TNF/IL-6 and glycolysis), and the prediction (rapamycin blunting LPS-driven glycolytic flux and cytokines in monocytes). Core pieces are already published: Reiling-style endotoxin work shows LPS activates mTORC1-S6K within 30 min in RAW264.7 and peritoneal macrophages in a raptor-dependent manner and that rapamycin lowers several inflammatory cytokines in vivo, and myeloid Rictor deletion produces the opposite (pro-inflammatory) phenotype, matching the mTORC2 control arm. However, the specific prediction that rapamycin or RPTOR loss blunts LPS-induced TNFα/IL-6 is contested rather than established — a direct test in human monocytes found mTOR drives the LPS glycolytic program yet its inhibition fails to suppress TNFα and instead amplifies inflammatory/procoagulant output, and earlier monocyte work reports rapamycin raising IL-6/IL-12. (I deliberately excluded the raptor/HK1 glycolysis-inflammasome paper, which has been retracted.)

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly phosphorylates STAT1 on Tyr701, and this SRC-catalysed phosphorylation is sufficient to drive STAT1 SH2-mediated homodimerization and GAS-element DNA binding independently of JAK activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: STAT1 activation is gated by a single tyrosine, Tyr701, whose phosphorylation converts the monomer into a reciprocal SH2–pTyr701 dimer competent for GAS binding and nuclear entry (darnell1994:findings:009, darnell1994:findings:015), and STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation with SIE/GAS binding is also induced by growth factors such as EGF and PDGF rather than only by interferons (darnell1994:findings:022). Independently, SRC is documented as an unusually promiscuous and highly active tyrosine kinase that generates over 2000 phosphosites at intermediate phosphorylation stoichiometry even in a heterologous cell background lacking its normal receptor context (bradley2024:findings:002, bradley2024:findings:017), and SRC-type reporter substrates show that tyrosine-kinase substrate recognition in this family is broad rather than tightly restricted (gest2024:findings:208). A kinase with that activity and substrate breadth acting on a single critical acceptor tyrosine predicts direct SRC modification of STAT1 Tyr701.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC should phosphorylate recombinant STAT1 in vitro on a single major tryptic phosphopeptide corresponding to Tyr701, converting STAT1 from a monomer to a dimer that binds a GAS probe; a STAT1 Y701F mutant should be nearly unphosphorylated by SRC and show no SRC-induced dimerization or DNA binding, and in cells expressing constitutively active SRC, STAT1 pTyr701 and GAS-complex formation should rise without interferon and fall upon SRC inhibition.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase reaction with recombinant purified active SRC (and a kinase-dead SRC control) plus recombinant STAT1 WT versus STAT1 Y701F, then read out (i) anti-pTyr and phospho-Tyr701-specific immunoblot with phosphopeptide mapping to confirm the site, (ii) gel filtration or native gel to score monomer-to-dimer conversion, and (iii) EMSA with a labelled GAS oligonucleotide; in parallel, transfect HeLa cells with activated SRC versus kinase-dead SRC, treat with a Src-family inhibitor or vehicle, and measure STAT1 pTyr701 by immunoblot and GAS complex formation by EMSA with anti-STAT1 supershift, which together would detect or exclude direct SRC-to-STAT1 Tyr701 phosphorylation.

citations.title: Differential role of Janus family kinases (JAKs) in interferon-gamma-induced lung epithelial ICAM-1 expression: involving protein interactions between JAKs, phospholipase Cgamma, c-Src, and STAT1.
c-Src activates both STAT1 and STAT3 in PDGF-stimulated NIH3T3 cells.
ErbB receptor-induced activation of stat transcription factors is mediated by Src tyrosine kinases.
Activation of Stat3 in v-Src-transformed fibroblasts requires cooperation of Jak1 kinase activity.

novelty.note: I searched for direct SRC phosphorylation of STAT1 Tyr701, for JAK-independent Src-family activation of STAT1 with GAS/DNA binding, and for in vitro purified-Src/STAT1 kinase reactions (PubMed/eutils, publisher pages). Published work already establishes that c-Src activity drives STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and DNA-binding activity (PDGF/NIH3T3, with STAT1 co-immunoprecipitating with c-Src), that ErbB-induced Stat1 phosphorylation is Src-dependent but Jak-independent, and that a PKC→c-Src branch phosphorylates STAT1 on Tyr701 without JAK1/2 activation; however, I found no report of purified active SRC phosphorylating recombinant STAT1 in vitro with phosphopeptide mapping to Tyr701, Y701F loss-of-phosphorylation controls, and monomer-to-dimer/GAS-EMSA readouts demonstrating sufficiency independent of JAKs — and the nearest direct test argues Jak1 cooperation is needed in mammalian cells even though Src activates STATs in JAK-free Sf-9 cells. Hence the mechanism is largely published in cells but the specific direct/sufficiency prediction is not.

hypotheses.statement: p53 acts as a negative regulator of EGFR activation, such that loss of p53 function raises ligand-dependent EGFR phosphorylation and downstream ERK output in the same cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: The corpus states that p38alpha phosphorylates TACE/ADAM17 on Thr735 to drive ectodomain shedding of TGFalpha-family ligands and consequent EGFR signalling and proliferation (cuadrado2010:findings:029), and separately that p53 transcriptionally induces Wip1, which imposes negative feedback on the p38alpha pathway (cuadrado2010:findings:061); p53 should therefore hold down the shedding-dependent arm of EGFR activation. Independently, p53 is described as actively restraining the secretory output of damaged/senescing fibroblasts, whose loss greatly enhances secreted-factor levels and their stimulation of epithelial cells (copp2010:findings:007, copp2010:findings:004), consistent with p53 constraining production of growth-factor-type ligands. Because ERK pathway output is a direct live readout of EGFR activity (albeck2013:findings:000), a p53-imposed brake on EGFR should be visible as reduced basal ERK reporter intensity in p53-proficient versus p53-deficient cells.
hypotheses.prediction: Knockdown or inactivation of p53 in serum-starved epithelial cells will increase basal phospho-EGFR and basal FIRE/ERK reporter intensity, and this increase will be abolished by an EGFR kinase inhibitor, by a TACE/ADAM17 inhibitor, or by p38alpha inhibition; conversely, pharmacological stabilization of p53 will lower basal EGFR phosphorylation and reporter output. Conditioned medium from p53-depleted cells will activate the reporter in naive cells in an EGFR-inhibitor-sensitive manner.
hypotheses.test: In MCF-10A cells stably carrying the FIRE (YFP–Fra-1 PEST) reporter, deplete p53 with shRNA/CRISPR (versus non-targeting control) and, in parallel, stabilize p53 pharmacologically; after serum/growth-factor starvation, measure median FIRE fluorescence by live-cell imaging and phospho-EGFR (Y1068) and phospho-ERK by immunoblot, each in the presence or absence of an EGFR inhibitor, a TACE/ADAM17 inhibitor, or a p38alpha inhibitor, and add a conditioned-medium swap between p53-depleted and control cultures to separate cell-autonomous from secreted-ligand contributions.

citations.title: Inhibition of DYRK1A-EGFR axis by p53-MDM2 cascade mediates the induction of cellular senescence.
Mutant p53 initiates a feedback loop that involves Egr-1/EGF receptor/ERK in prostate cancer cells.
Alterations of EGFR, p53 and PTEN that mimic changes found in basal-like breast cancer promote transformation of human mammary epithelial cells.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: p53 as a negative regulator of EGFR/ERK output; wild-type versus mutant p53 effects on EGFR expression, ligand shedding (ADAM17/amphiregulin/TGFalpha) and autocrine loops; and the specific prediction that p53 depletion raises basal phospho-EGFR/ERK in serum-starved mammary epithelial cells (including MCF10A) reversible by EGFR/ADAM17/p38 inhibition. Published work establishes the general polarity — pharmacologic p53 stabilization (Nutlin-3a) lowers EGFR levels and phospho-ERK via the p53–MDM2–DYRK1A axis, and cells with altered p53 run an Egr-1-driven autocrine loop of HB-EGF/amphiregulin/epiregulin that activates EGFR–MEK/ERK and is blocked by EGFR inhibition — but the latter is a mutant-p53 gain-of-function (p53 knockdown abolished Egr-1, the opposite of the hypothesis' loss-of-function direction), the mechanism runs through receptor stability or Egr-1 transcription rather than p53→Wip1→p38alpha→ADAM17 Thr735 shedding, and the nearest MCF10A test found p53 inactivation (p53DD) alone insufficient to raise EGFR/ERK signalling under starvation. No source states the specific p53-brake-on-shedding explanation or the live-reporter/conditioned-medium prediction, so this is partial rather than established.

hypotheses.statement: SYK directly promotes CD274 (PD-L1) expression in myeloid cells by amplifying the STAT1 signalling that drives interferon-induced PD-L1 transcription, making PD-L1 levels on macrophages SYK-dependent.
hypotheses.mechanism: PD-L1 induction is reported to run through JAK–STAT (preferentially STAT1) signalling with IRF1 as the central downstream mediator, and type I interferons acting via IFNAR induce PD-L1 in monocytes and dendritic cells (sun2018:findings:010, sun2018:findings:011). Independently, SYK is reported to be coupled to IFNAR in IFNγ-primed macrophages, where it amplifies STAT1 activation in an ITAM-dependent manner (ivashkiv2014:findings:003). If SYK sets the gain on STAT1 in macrophages, it should set the gain on the STAT1/IRF1-dependent PD-L1 output in the same cells — which would also account for PD-L1 on tumour-associated macrophages being only partially reduced by IFN-γ blockade, unlike PD-L1 on tumour cells (sun2018:findings:004).
hypotheses.prediction: In macrophages/monocytes, loss of SYK activity should reduce phospho-STAT1 and, downstream, IRF1 and surface PD-L1 after low-dose IFNγ priming plus type I IFN or ITAM-receptor engagement, with PD-L1 falling in proportion to the loss of STAT1 phosphorylation; SYK loss should leave PD-L1 induction largely intact in non-myeloid tumour cells lacking ITAM-adaptor–SYK coupling, and gain of SYK signalling (ITAM/Dectin-1 ligation) should raise PD-L1 above the IFN-only level.
