hypotheses.test: In a macrophage line (e.g. THP-1-derived or immortalized bone marrow-derived macrophages) and a parallel non-myeloid carcinoma line, compare SYK knockdown/knockout (siRNA or CRISPR) and SYK inhibitor (R406/entospletinib) versus control after low-dose IFNγ priming followed by type I IFN or ITAM-coupled receptor stimulation: quantify surface PD-L1 by flow cytometry and CD274 mRNA by qPCR, with immunoblots for phospho-STAT1 (Tyr701) and IRF1 on the same lysates; rescue with a SYK re-expression construct (and a kinase-dead control) to confirm specificity, and test whether forcing STAT1/IRF1 activity restores PD-L1 in SYK-null cells, which would place SYK upstream rather than in a parallel pathway.

citations.title: TREM2 facilitates gastric cancer progression and immune evasion via inhibiting TRIM21-mediated STAT1 degradation in tumor-associated macrophages.
Dectin-1 signaling in neutrophils up-regulates PD-L1 and triggers ROS-mediated suppression of CD4(+) T cells.
Drug repurposing of fostamatinib against cancer via potential cytotoxicity and immune checkpoint regulation.

novelty.note: I searched for SYK-dependent PD-L1 regulation in myeloid cells, SYK/STAT1/IRF1 control of interferon-induced CD274, ITAM/Dectin-1-driven PD-L1, and SYK-inhibitor effects on PD-L1 in macrophages. A 2025 Cell Death & Disease study states exactly this explanation: in tumour-associated macrophages the ITAM/DAP12-coupled receptor TREM2 scaffolds SYK onto STAT1, SYK phosphorylates STAT1 at Tyr701, and phospho-STAT1 transactivates PD-L1 (and CCL8); SYK knockdown abolished both STAT1 phosphorylation and PD-L1 upregulation, and the paper itself notes STAT1 acts on PD-L1 directly or via IRF1. Supporting work shows ITAM-receptor (Dectin-1)/SYK-dependent Cd274 induction in myeloid cells and SYK-inhibitor-mediated PD-L1 loss, so the SYK-sets-the-gain-on-STAT1-for-PD-L1 mechanism is published; only the specific framing as amplification of IFNAR/IFNγ-primed interferon-induced PD-L1, and the myeloid-versus-non-myeloid contrast, remain untested.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR2 signaling negatively regulates STAT1 activation, so loss of TGFBR2 in myeloid/dendritic cells raises STAT1 tyrosine-701 phosphorylation, nuclear STAT1 and STAT1-dependent gene expression, while TGF-β engagement of TGFBR2 suppresses them.
hypotheses.mechanism: TGFBR2-deficient dendritic cells acquire a hyperinflammatory phenotype with increased IFN-γ production and failed Treg induction (massagu2023:findings:011), and IFN-γ is precisely the stimulus that phosphorylates STAT1 at Tyr701, drives its dimerization and nuclear translocation, and makes it the GAS-binding factor GAF (darnell1994:findings:009, darnell1994:findings:008); because basal STAT1 abundance itself sets the gain of this pathway (ivashkiv2014:findings:002) and STAT1 is required for the IFN-γ-driven myeloid effector program including ARG1/iNOS induction (gabrilovich2009:findings:007), an intact TGFBR2 arm should act as a brake on the STAT1 module in the same cells. The proposed direct relationship is therefore TGFBR2 → STAT1 inhibition at the level of STAT1 expression and Tyr701 phosphorylation, with the loss-of-TGFBR2 inflammatory phenotype being read out through STAT1.
hypotheses.prediction: In cultured myeloid/dendritic-like cells, TGFBR2 knockdown or knockout should increase basal and IFN-γ-induced pSTAT1(Y701), total STAT1, nuclear STAT1 and STAT1 target gene output (e.g. GAS-driven reporters, iNOS/ARG1), and conversely TGF-β pretreatment of TGFBR2-competent cells should blunt IFN-γ-induced pSTAT1 and STAT1 target induction; a residual TGFBR2-dependent difference in pSTAT1 should persist even when secreted IFN-γ is neutralized, whereas STAT1 knockdown should collapse the TGFBR2-loss gene signature.
hypotheses.test: In a bone-marrow-derived DC or macrophage line (or THP-1-derived cells), use siRNA/CRISPR to delete TGFBR2 and compare with controls: (i) immunoblot pSTAT1-Y701, total STAT1 and nuclear/cytoplasmic STAT1 fractions at baseline and after graded IFN-γ, (ii) repeat in the presence of an IFN-γ-neutralizing antibody to separate a TGFBR2-intrinsic effect on STAT1 from an autocrine IFN-γ relay, (iii) measure a GAS-luciferase reporter and STAT1 target transcripts by qPCR, and (iv) pretreat wild-type cells with TGF-β1 and score suppression of IFN-γ-induced pSTAT1 and reporter activity; epistasis by STAT1 knockdown in TGFBR2-null cells should abolish the elevated target-gene response if STAT1 is the downstream node.

citations.title: TGF-beta1 suppresses IFN-gamma-induced NO production in macrophages by suppressing STAT1 activation and accelerating iNOS protein degradation.
TGFβ Antagonizes IFNγ-Mediated Adaptive Immune Evasion via Activation of the AKT-Smad3-SHP1 Axis in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
TGF-beta suppresses IFN-gamma-STAT1-dependent gene transcription by enhancing STAT1-PIAS1 interactions in epithelia but not monocytes/macrophages.
Silencing of TGFβ signalling in microglia results in impaired homeostasis.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in plain words (TGF-β inhibition of IFN-γ-induced STAT1 Y701 phosphorylation in macrophages/DCs), the entities together (TGFBR2 + dendritic cells/microglia + STAT1), and the prediction (TGFBR2 knockdown/knockout raising pSTAT1, STAT1 targets iNOS/ARG1, GAS output). The ligand-side half of the hypothesis is clearly published: Takaki et al. show TGF-β1 suppresses IFN-γ-induced STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and iNOS transcription in macrophages and dendritic cells via IFN-γR/TGF-βR receptor cross-talk, and Lu et al. show TGFβ decreases IFNγ-induced JAK1/2 and STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation via an AKT–Smad3–SHP1 axis (in lung adenocarcinoma, not myeloid cells). However, the loss-of-function arm is not published: Bhattacharyya et al. explicitly report that in monocytes/macrophages TGF-β does NOT alter STAT1 Tyr701/Ser727 phosphorylation (acting instead through PIAS1 in epithelia), and the one myeloid Tgfbr2-deletion study that assays IFN-γ responsiveness (Zöller et al., microglia) measures only iNos/Tnfa and TAK1, never STAT1 phosphorylation, nuclear STAT1 or STAT1 epistasis. So the general mechanism exists but the specific TGFBR2-loss → elevated STAT1 module prediction, and STAT1 as the required node for the TGFBR2-null DC inflammatory signature, remain unstated and partly contested.

hypotheses.statement: RSK directly activates the mTOR kinase within mTORC1 — phosphorylating mTOR itself and/or its partner Raptor — making RSK an upstream, MAPK-driven activator of mTOR catalytic output.
hypotheses.mechanism: The claims about RSK state that it phosphorylates Raptor, an mTORC1 subunit, and phosphorylates TSC2 at Ser1798 (and S939/T1462) to disable TSC2's GAP activity toward Rheb, and that RSK can substitute for AKT in driving mTORC1 induction; it also phosphorylates rpS6 at Ser235/236 in a manner independent of S6K1/2 and rapamycin, so RSK acts directly on mTORC1 components and outputs rather than only through them. The claims about mTOR show that its substrate-group activity (mTOR-motif and p70S6K sites) is co-regulated with the p90RSK substrate group under PI3K–mTOR pathway inhibition, i.e. RSK-driven and mTOR-driven phosphorylation collapse together in the same cells. Together these imply a direct RSK→mTOR kinase-substrate/activating relationship on the complex itself, not merely two parallel pathways converging on shared downstream targets.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active RSK should phosphorylate immunopurified mTOR (and Raptor) on mappable Ser/Thr sites and increase mTORC1 kinase activity toward S6K1 in vitro; in cells, RSK inhibition or knockdown should lower mTOR-motif/S6K substrate phosphorylation (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1) and reduce mTOR's association with lysosomal membranes, while a phospho-null mTOR/Raptor mutant at the RSK site should be refractory to RSK-driven mTORC1 activation and a phospho-mimetic should raise basal mTORC1 output.
hypotheses.test: In HeLa or HEK-293T cells, immunoprecipitate mTOR/Raptor and run an in vitro kinase assay with recombinant active RSK plus [γ-32P]ATP or phospho-specific detection, mapping sites by mass spectrometry; in parallel, treat cells with the RSK-selective inhibitors BI-D1870/SL-0101/FMK or RSK1-3 siRNA and immunoblot mTORC1 readouts (S6K1 Thr389, 4E-BP1) alongside mTOR/LAMP2 immunofluorescence colocalization, then test whether alanine substitution of the identified RSK site(s) in re-expressed mTOR or Raptor abolishes the RSK-dependent change — absence of direct phosphorylation and no loss of mTORC1 activity upon RSK inhibition would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Oncogenic MAPK Signaling Stimulates mTORC1 Activity by Promoting RSK-Mediated Raptor Phosphorylation
RSK regulates activated BRAF signalling to mTORC1 and promotes melanoma growth.
ERK1/2 phosphorylate Raptor to promote Ras-dependent activation of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1).

novelty.note: I searched for RSK-mediated Raptor/mTOR phosphorylation, for direct RSK phosphorylation of mTOR (e.g. Ser2448, kinase-domain sites), and for the prediction that RSK inhibition lowers S6K1 Thr389/4E-BP1. Carrière et al. (Curr Biol 2008) already states exactly this explanation: RSK1/2 directly phosphorylate Raptor on RXRXXS/T sites in a conserved region, oncogenic Ras/MEK drives this phosphorylation, and Raptor alleles lacking the RSK sites markedly reduce mTOR phosphotransferase activity — i.e. RSK is an upstream MAPK-driven activator of mTORC1 catalytic output; Romeo et al. (Oncogene 2013) confirms in cells that ERK/RSK inhibition suppresses S6K1 Thr389 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation, and Carrière et al. (JBC 2011) extends Raptor phospho-regulation to ERK1/2. The only parts I found no published support for are phosphorylation of mTOR itself by RSK (Ser2448 is attributed to p70S6K, not RSK) and an RSK effect on mTOR lysosomal localization, but the statement's Raptor arm is fully anticipated.

hypotheses.statement: MTORC1 directly and positively regulates JUN abundance and AP-1 transcriptional output through 4E-BP/eIF4E-dependent cap translation, placing JUN downstream of mTORC1 as the effector of mTOR-driven PD-L1 expression.
hypotheses.mechanism: The corpus states that mTORC1 controls growth and proliferation chiefly through the 4E-BP/eIF4E translational axis (fruman2017:findings:009), i.e. it sets the rate of cap-dependent synthesis of short-lived regulatory proteins, and that persistent mTORC1 activity is what sustains signaling output in PI3K-pathway-mutant tumor cells until everolimus removes it (fruman2017:findings:010). Independently, JUN protein is required for constitutive PD-L1 expression in BRAF-inhibitor-resistant melanoma (sun2018:findings:014), and the same compilation lists JUN and the PTEN-loss/PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis as separate regulators converging on PD-L1 (sun2018:findings:048). If mTORC1 supplies the translational flux that maintains the labile JUN pool, then the PI3K-AKT-mTOR arm and the JUN arm are not parallel inputs but one linear axis in which mTORC1 acts directly upstream of JUN protein levels.
hypotheses.prediction: Acute mTOR kinase inhibition should lower JUN protein and JUN-dependent transcription (AP-1 reporter activity, JUN occupancy at AP-1 target enhancers, PD-L1 mRNA/protein) within one to two JUN half-lives while JUN mRNA and JNK-dependent JUN S63/S73 phosphorylation stoichiometry remain essentially unchanged; ribosome/polysome association of JUN mRNA should drop; and relieving 4E-BP inhibition (4E-BP1/2 knockdown) should restore JUN protein and PD-L1 despite continued mTOR inhibition, whereas a phosphorylation-resistant 4E-BP1 mutant should suppress JUN even with mTORC1 active.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured JUN-dependent, PD-L1-positive line, treat with torin/RapaLink-type mTOR kinase inhibitor and rapamycin over a 0–8 h time course and quantify, in parallel, JUN protein by calibrated western blot, JUN and PD-L1 mRNA by qPCR, and phospho-4E-BP1/phospho-S6 as pathway controls; assay JUN mRNA translation by polysome fractionation plus qPCR (or puromycin-labeling/pulse SILAC of newly synthesized JUN), and JUN transcriptional function by AP-1 luciferase reporter and JUN ChIP-qPCR at AP-1 target promoters. Decisive arms: (i) siRNA knockdown of 4E-BP1/2 or expression of eIF4E should rescue JUN protein and PD-L1 under mTOR inhibition, and (ii) expression of non-phosphorylatable 4E-BP1(4A) should phenocopy mTOR inhibition on JUN without inhibiting mTOR; loss of JUN protein change, or a change explained entirely by JUN mRNA or by altered JUN phosphorylation rather than synthesis rate, rules the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Enhanced bypass of PD-L1 translation reduces the therapeutic response to mTOR kinase inhibitors.
Aberrant expression of c-Jun in glioblastoma by internal ribosome entry site (IRES)-mediated translational activation

novelty.note: I searched for the mTORC1–4E-BP/eIF4E control of JUN protein, for mTOR inhibition lowering JUN and PD-L1, and for JUN mRNA translational control/polysome studies. Direct tests contradict both arms of the prediction: Xu et al. (Cell Reports 2023) show that mTOR kinase inhibition with effective 4E-BP1 dephosphorylation does not lower PD-L1 protein but increases it via eIF4A-dependent IRES translation of the PD-L1 5'UTR, and the PNAS study of c-Jun shows JUN protein accumulates through a potent cap-independent IRES in its 5'UTR (elevated protein with unchanged mRNA and half-life), so JUN is not simply a 4E-BP/eIF4E-dependent cap-translation output. Hence the specific linear mTORC1→cap-translation→JUN→PD-L1 claim is contradicted by stated negative results.

hypotheses.statement: PKC directly phosphorylates MEK1 at a regulatory (non-activation-loop) site, thereby activating MEK1 and constituting the immediate kinase input by which PKC drives MAPK activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: Independent modelling evidence establishes a graded, thresholded concentration-effect relationship in which PKC activity sets MAPK activity (bhalla1999:findings:002, bhalla1999:findings:001), yet the ERK activation-loop TEY motif is phosphorylated essentially exclusively by MEK1/2 (cargnello2011:findings:002, johnson2023:findings:009), so any PKC-driven increase in MAPK output must pass through a change in MEK1 catalytic output. MEK1 is itself a substrate for kinases other than Raf at regulatory sites that tune its activity and partner binding — T292 (ERK1/2) and S298 (PAK) (lake2016:findings:010) — establishing that MEK1's proline-rich regulatory region is a phosphorylation-based control point accessible to a second kinase. PKC is therefore a candidate direct MEK1 kinase at such a site rather than acting only through upstream components.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active PKC will phosphorylate recombinant unphosphorylated MEK1 in vitro on one or more serine/threonine residues outside the S217/S221 activation loop (predicted in the S298-containing proline-rich region), and this phosphorylation will increase MEK1 catalytic activity toward recombinant ERK1/2 in a coupled assay; in cells, PKC activation (phorbol ester) will raise MEK1 site-occupancy at that residue and raise phospho-ERK TEY even when Raf catalytic activity is blocked, while PKC inhibition or an alanine mutant at the identified site will blunt the PKC-dependent component of MEK1 activity without altering basal Raf-driven S217/S221 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Two-step in vitro kinase assay: (1) incubate purified active PKC with recombinant catalytically competent but unphosphorylated MEK1 plus [γ-32P]ATP, resolve by SDS-PAGE and map incorporated sites by phosphopeptide LC-MS/MS, using kinase-dead MEK1 and PKC-inhibitor-treated reactions as controls to exclude autophosphorylation; (2) take PKC-pretreated versus mock-pretreated MEK1, remove PKC, and measure MEK1-catalysed phosphorylation of recombinant kinase-dead ERK2 by phospho-TEY immunoblot to quantify any activity change. Confirm in cells by phorbol-ester stimulation of a MEK1-null or MEK1-knockdown line reconstituted with wild-type versus alanine mutants at the mapped site, under pan-Raf inhibition, blotting phospho-MEK1 (site-specific), phospho-MEK1 S217/S221 and phospho-ERK; absence of PKC-dependent MEK1 phosphorylation in vitro and loss of the phorbol-ester-driven phospho-ERK increment being unaffected by the site mutant would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway by conventional, novel, and atypical protein kinase C isotypes.
Protein kinase C alpha trigger Ras and Raf-independent MEK/ERK activation for TPA-induced growth inhibition of human hepatoma cell HepG2.
Protein kinase C zeta plays a central role in activation of the p42/44 mitogen-activated protein kinase by endotoxin in alveolar macrophages.
Signalling from TPA to MAP kinase requires protein kinase C, raf and MEK: reconstitution of the signalling pathway in vitro.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (i) direct biochemistry ('PKC directly phosphorylates MEK1 in vitro', PubMed/Europe PMC phrase and field searches), (ii) the entities together with the predicted site ('PKC + MEK1 Ser298 / proline-rich region / non-activation-loop site'), and (iii) the prediction ('phorbol ester raises phospho-ERK with Raf blocked / Raf-independent MEK activation'). Published work establishes the general half of the mechanism — all PKC classes activate MEK1, and atypical PKCζ and PKCα raise MEK1 activity without any increase in c-Raf (or Ras) activity, with PKCζ binding MEK and being required for its phosphorylation in cells — which is precisely a PKC-driven, Raf-independent input to MEK1. But no retrieved source demonstrates PKC phosphorylating purified MEK1 directly, maps such a site outside S217/S221 (e.g., in the S298-containing proline-rich region), or shows that this phosphorylation increases MEK1 catalytic output; the only in vitro reconstitution of the phorbol-ester-to-MAPK route instead required c-Raf between PKC and MEK, and S298 is attributed to PAK. Hence partial, not established.

hypotheses.statement: CSF2 (GM-CSF) signals directly through JAK2, which is recruited to and tyrosine-phosphorylated at the GM-CSF receptor and is the kinase step at which SOCS-mediated suppression of GM-CSF responses acts.
hypotheses.mechanism: TLR-induced SOCS1 suppresses GM-CSF signalling and thereby blocks GM-CSF-driven DC development from human monocytes (yoshimura2007:findings:017), implying GM-CSF acts through a SOCS-sensitive JAK; JAK2 is the documented SOCS target in this corpus, since SOCS3 binds the pTyr1007 site in the JAK2 activation loop (heinrich2003:findings:014). JAK2 is also reported to be attached to the IL-3 receptor and tyrosine phosphorylated in response to IL-3 and other haematopoietic cytokines (darnell1994:findings:025), and the JAK2 V617F kinase lowers the IL-3 threshold for proliferation with strongly increased STAT5 phosphorylation (kralovics2005:findings:009, kralovics2005:findings:011) — so a GM-CSF receptor engaging the same JAK2-dependent myeloid growth-factor machinery would place JAK2 immediately downstream of CSF2.
hypotheses.prediction: GM-CSF addition to GM-CSFR-bearing myeloid cells should induce rapid JAK2 tyrosine phosphorylation (including the activation-loop site) followed by STAT5 phosphorylation; loss or pharmacological inhibition of JAK2 should abolish GM-CSF-induced STAT5 phosphorylation and GM-CSF-driven DC/macrophage differentiation without affecting TLR3/TLR4-driven responses, and expression of constitutively active JAK2 V617F should make cells proliferate and differentiate with little or no GM-CSF, while enforced SOCS1/SOCS3 expression should suppress GM-CSF-induced JAK2 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In a GM-CSF-responsive line and in GM-CSF-cultured bone-marrow cells, stimulate with GM-CSF and immunoblot a time course for phospho-JAK2 (pTyr1007/1008) and phospho-STAT5, and test physical coupling by co-immunoprecipitating JAK2 with the GM-CSF receptor chains before and after ligand; then perform loss-of-function with JAK2 siRNA/CRISPR knockout (or a JAK2-selective inhibitor versus a JAK1/JAK3-selective control) and gain-of-function by stably expressing wild-type JAK2 or JAK2 V617F in a GM-CSF-dependent cell line, scoring GM-CSF dose-response curves for STAT5 phosphorylation, proliferation and differentiation marker acquisition; SOCS1/SOCS3 co-transfection should reproduce the block at the phospho-JAK2 step. Absence of GM-CSF-induced JAK2 phosphorylation and unchanged GM-CSF responses after JAK2 removal would rule the hypothesis out.

citations.title: Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor-activated signaling pathways in human neutrophils. Selective activation of Jak2, Stat3, and Stat5b.
Roles of JAK kinases in human GM-CSF receptor signal transduction.

novelty.note: I searched for GM-CSF receptor JAK2 tyrosine phosphorylation, SOCS1 suppression of GM-CSF signalling via JAK2, and the prediction that JAK2 loss abolishes GM-CSF-induced STAT5 phosphorylation. Published work from the 1990s already establishes that GM-CSF selectively induces JAK2 (not JAK1/JAK3/TYK2) tyrosine phosphorylation with STAT5b activation, that JAK2 is coupled to the GM-CSF receptor, and that dominant-negative JAK2 blocks GM-CSF-driven proliferation and gene induction; related literature also documents SOCS1 acting on the JAK2 activation loop and cross-regulating GM-CSF signalling. The explanation is therefore long-standing textbook knowledge rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly phosphorylates ERBB3 on its C-terminal tyrosines, including the Y1276 and Y1289 docking sites, acting as a trans-kinase that supplies phosphorylation this catalytically dead receptor cannot generate itself.
hypotheses.mechanism: ERBB3 lacks intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity, so the eleven experimentally verified phosphotyrosines on it — among which Y1276 and Y1289 are high-affinity hubs engaging many SH2/PTB domains — must be written by a kinase acting in trans (yarden2001:findings:000, jones2006:findings:009, jones2006:findings:014). SRC is an extremely active and promiscuous tyrosine kinase, generating over 2000 phosphosites when expressed in a heterologous system and producing detectable pan-phosphotyrosine signal on the bulk proteome (bradley2024:findings:002, bradley2024:findings:026). Since ERBB3 tyrosine phosphorylation can rise substantially without ERBB3 gaining catalytic activity, as seen in melanoma cells under prolonged vemurafenib treatment (lake2016:findings:026), a non-ERBB tyrosine kinase such as SRC is a candidate direct writer of these sites.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC should phosphorylate recombinant ERBB3 cytoplasmic domain and ERBB3-derived Y1276/Y1289 peptides in vitro with stoichiometry detectable by phospho-blot or MS, and the resulting phosphopeptides should acquire SH2/PTB binding; in cells, SRC inhibition or knockdown should reduce basal and stress-induced ERBB3 tyrosine phosphorylation at these sites and reduce recruitment of SH2-containing partners to ERBB3, without changing ERBB3 protein level.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with recombinant active SRC plus (i) purified ERBB3 cytoplasmic tail and (ii) synthetic unphosphorylated ERBB3 Y1276 and Y1289 peptides, and map phosphorylation by anti-phosphotyrosine blot, site-specific antibodies and LC-MS/MS, using kinase-dead SRC and ATP-free reactions as controls; then in a melanoma or breast line, treat with a SRC-family inhibitor or SRC siRNA and immunoprecipitate ERBB3 to quantify pY at the mapped sites and co-precipitating SH2 adaptors, scoring loss of the ERBB3 pY signal as support and its persistence as refutation.

citations.title: SRC-family kinases are activated in non-small cell lung cancer and promote the survival of epidermal growth factor receptor-dependent cell lines.
Ligand-Independent EGFR Activation by Anchorage-Stimulated Src Promotes Cancer Cell Proliferation and Cetuximab Resistance via ErbB3 Phosphorylation.
c-Src modulates ErbB2 and ErbB3 heterocomplex formation and function.
Transcriptional and posttranslational up-regulation of HER3 (ErbB3) compensates for inhibition of the HER2 tyrosine kinase.

novelty.note: I searched for direct SRC phosphorylation of ERBB3/HER3 (in vitro kinase assays, recombinant cytoplasmic domain, Y1276/Y1289 peptides), for SRC-inhibitor effects on ERBB3 pY in cells, and for kinase-substrate annotations of these sites. The literature repeatedly lists Src among kinases 'implicated in the phosphorylation of HER3' and shows cell-based effects — the SFK inhibitor PP1 lowered ErbB3 pY1289 in EGFR-dependent lung lines (though the authors could not attribute this to c-Src itself), anchorage-stimulated Src raises ErbB3 pY1289 but explicitly via transactivated EGFR, and c-Src promotes ErbB2/ErbB3 heterocomplex formation rather than phosphorylating ErbB3 itself; a HER2-inhibitor study found dasatinib did not block P-HER3 recovery. I found no source demonstrating purified SRC directly phosphorylating the ERBB3 tail or Y1276/Y1289 peptides in trans with consequent SH2/PTB binding, so the general mechanism (SFK involvement in ERBB3 tyrosine phosphorylation) is published but the specific direct-writer claim and its in vitro prediction are not.

hypotheses.statement: SHP2 acts directly upstream of MEK as a positive regulator, with its phosphatase activity required for the Raf-dependent activating phosphorylation of MEK's kinase-subdomain-VIII serines in RTK-driven cells.
hypotheses.mechanism: Claims about SHP2 show that its catalytic activity is necessary for p-ERK and growth in RTK-altered lines (re-expression of wild-type but not C459S SHP2 restores p-ERK; SHP099 lowers p-ERK with an IC50 of ~0.25 µM without touching p-AKT), that KRASG12V expression fully bypasses the SHP2 requirement, and that a Gab1-PH–active-SHP2 fusion is sufficient to drive constitutive MEK1 and ERK2 activation. Claims about MEK show MEK is switched on by Raf phosphorylation of two serines four residues apart and that MEK activity sets ERK amplitude, so a Ras-level input requirement placed by SHP2 should register as a change in the phosphorylation state of MEK itself, not merely of ERK. Together these imply SHP2 activity is an obligatory input to the phosphorylation of MEK, i.e. loss of SHP2 should collapse pMEK upstream of the ERK readouts already measured.
hypotheses.prediction: Acute SHP2 inhibition or catalytic-dead SHP2 replacement in SHP2-dependent, RTK-amplified cells should reduce phospho-MEK1/2 (S218/S222) with kinetics and dose-response matching the fall in p-ERK, while leaving p-AKT unchanged; and expression of a constitutively activated MEK (acidic substitution of the two Raf-target serines) or KRASG12V should restore p-ERK and proliferation despite full SHP2 blockade, whereas active SHP2 delivered to the membrane should raise pMEK without any receptor ligand.
hypotheses.test: In MDA-MB-468 (SHP2-dependent, EGFR-amplified) and A2058 (SHP2-independent) cells, run a SHP099 dose- and time-course and immunoblot pMEK1/2 S218/S222, total MEK, pERK and pAKT; then perform the epistasis arm by stably expressing either constitutively active MEK1 (Raf-site serine-to-acidic mutant) or an empty vector and asking whether p-ERK and colony formation become insensitive to SHP099, with the converse gain-of-function arm transfecting the Gab1-PH–active-SHP2 fusion or catalytically dead SHP2 into serum-starved cells and blotting pMEK1/2.

citations.title: Molecular mechanism for the Shp-2 tyrosine phosphatase function in promoting growth factor stimulation of Erk activity.
Resistance to allosteric SHP2 inhibition in FGFR-driven cancers through rapid feedback activation of FGFR.
Genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 screens reveal shared and cell-specific mechanisms of resistance to SHP2 inhibition.
RAS nucleotide cycling underlies the SHP2 phosphatase dependence of mutant BRAF-, NF1- and RAS-driven cancers.
PTPN11 Is a Central Node in Intrinsic and Acquired Resistance to Targeted Cancer Drugs.

novelty.note: I searched for (a) the plain mechanism ('SHP2 acts upstream of MEK / phosphatase activity required for MEK activation'), (b) the entities together (SHP099/RMC-4550 + phospho-MEK S217/S221 + RTK-driven, pAKT-sparing), and (c) the prediction (bypass of SHP2 inhibition by activated MEK/RAS/SOS). The explanation is already published: Shi et al. showed that in cells expressing catalytically compromised Shp-2, EGF-stimulated Ras, Raf and Mek activation is attenuated, placing SHP2's phosphatase function upstream of MEK activation; the FGFR-driven-cancer study directly blots p-MEK falling within 30 min of 1 µM SHP099 while p-AKT is unchanged; and the JEM CRISPR study states SHP2 works upstream of RAS/SOS1-2 with resistance arising from reactivation at or above MEK, while Nichols et al. show membrane-targeted SOS-F (a downstream bypass analogous to KRASG12V) renders cells insensitive to SHP2 inhibition. Only the narrow experimental arm of rescuing SHP099 with an acidic-substitution MEK1 mutant in MDA-MB-468 appears untested, but the mechanistic claim itself is not novel.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly phosphorylates RSK (notably RSK2) on tyrosine residues, acting as an upstream activating kinase that strengthens the ERK1/2–RSK complex and potentiates RSK activation.
hypotheses.mechanism: One line of evidence states that RSK2 acquires tyrosine phosphorylation upon Src activation and that these pTyr events stabilize ERK1/2 binding to RSK2 and promote RSK2 activation (cargnello2011:findings:059), while the RSK activation cycle itself depends on ordered phosphorylation in which ERK1/2 docking-dependent input is essential (cargnello2011:findings:023) and RSK isoforms constitutively associate with ERK1/2 through a D-domain-dependent complex whose stability is regulatable (cargnello2011:findings:018). Independently, SRC is characterized as an exceptionally active tyrosine kinase capable of generating thousands of tyrosine phosphosites on heterologous substrate proteomes (bradley2024:findings:002), so RSK is a plausible direct SRC substrate rather than only a downstream consequence of pathway crosstalk. Together these imply a direct SRC→RSK phosphorylation event on tyrosine that feeds into the canonical ERK-dependent activation steps of RSK.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified active SRC will phosphorylate recombinant RSK1/RSK2 on tyrosine in vitro in an ATP- and SRC-activity-dependent manner at mappable Tyr sites; in cells, SRC inhibition or knockdown will reduce RSK tyrosine phosphorylation, weaken ERK1/2–RSK co-immunoprecipitation, and lower RSK activity readouts (RSK Ser380 and rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation) without a comparable loss of ERK1/2 activation-loop phosphorylation, whereas expression of constitutively active SRC will increase RSK pTyr, ERK1/2–RSK association, and RSK activity.
hypotheses.test: Two-part standard bench experiment: (1) in vitro kinase assay combining purified recombinant active SRC with catalytically dead recombinant RSK2 (to exclude autophosphorylation), followed by anti-phosphotyrosine (4G10) immunoblot and LC-MS/MS site mapping, with a kinase-dead SRC and an ATP-free reaction as controls, plus a Tyr→Phe RSK2 mutant at the mapped sites to confirm site assignment; (2) in HeLa cells, compare SRC knockdown/inhibitor treatment versus constitutively active SRC expression, then immunoprecipitate RSK and blot for pTyr, co-precipitating ERK1/2, RSK Ser380, and measure downstream rpS6 Ser235/236 — loss of SRC-dependent RSK pTyr and of the Tyr→Phe mutant's response would rule the direct relationship out.

citations.title: Epidermal growth factor stimulates RSK2 activation through activation of the MEK/ERK pathway and src-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of RSK2 at Tyr-529.
RSK Isoforms in Acute Myeloid Leukemia.

novelty.note: I searched for Src-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation of RSK2, for RSK2 Tyr529/Tyr707 phosphorylation and ERK1/2 docking-complex stabilization, and for the predicted Src-inhibition/constitutively-active-Src readouts. Kang et al. (JBC 2008) report exactly this explanation: purified recombinant Src (and Fyn) directly phosphorylates the RSK2 C-terminal domain at Tyr-529 (plus Tyr-483/488/580/644/707) in vitro, Y529F abolishes it, Src inhibition (PP2) reduces RSK2 pTyr-529 and Ser-386 phosphorylation, and pTyr-529 stabilizes inactive ERK1/2 binding to RSK2 to prime ERK-dependent RSK2 activation — the same directional mechanism, sites, and cellular predictions as the hypothesis. A review of RSK in AML independently restates that Src-family kinases and FGFR3 phosphorylate RSK2 at Tyr529 (ERK recruitment) and Tyr707 (αL-helix autoinhibition relief), so the explanation is mainstream rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: 14-3-3 proteins directly control the intracellular retention and insulin/AKT-stimulated cell-surface delivery of TGFBR2 (TβRII), such that 14-3-3 engagement of phospho-AS160/TBC1D4 is the step that releases TβRII-containing intracellular vesicles.
hypotheses.mechanism: Insulin and high glucose move preformed intracellular pools of TβRII to the plasma membrane through AKT phosphorylation of the RabGAP AS160, which relieves intracellular receptor retention (derynck2019:findings:010). Independently, AKT phosphorylation of AS160/TBC1D4 at multiple sites is reported to act by driving 14-3-3 binding, and it is this 14-3-3 engagement that releases vesicle retention during GLUT4 translocation (manning2017:findings:044). If the same phospho-AS160 switch governs the TβRII pool, then 14-3-3 availability, rather than AKT activity per se, sets the surface abundance of TGFBR2.
hypotheses.prediction: Blocking 14-3-3/phosphopeptide interactions (or depleting 14-3-3 isoforms) should abolish insulin- or glucose-induced increases in surface TβRII and in TGF-β responsiveness without preventing AKT activation or AS160 phosphorylation; conversely, a phospho-mimetic/constitutively 14-3-3-bound AS160 should raise basal surface TβRII, while a 14-3-3-binding-deficient AS160 mutant should trap TβRII intracellularly even under insulin stimulation.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured epithelial or fibroblast line, express the 14-3-3 antagonist difopein (versus inactive mutant) or siRNA-deplete 14-3-3 β/ε/ζ, stimulate with insulin or 25 mM glucose, and quantify surface TβRII by cell-surface biotinylation/streptavidin pulldown and by non-permeabilized anti-TβRII flow cytometry, with parallel immunoblots for phospho-AKT and phospho-AS160 to confirm the upstream kinase arm is intact; repeat in cells reconstituted with wild-type versus 14-3-3-binding-site-mutant AS160 and read out TGF-β-induced SMAD2 phosphorylation as a functional confirmation.

citations.title: The insulin response integrates increased TGF-β signaling through Akt-induced enhancement of cell surface delivery of TGF-β receptors.
A role for 14-3-3 in insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation through its interaction with the RabGAP AS160.
Transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)-induced up-regulation of TGF-β receptors at the cell surface amplifies the TGF-β response.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) the insulin/AKT/AS160 → TGF-β receptor surface-delivery mechanism, (2) 14-3-3 binding to phospho-AS160/TBC1D4 and release of GLUT4 vesicle retention, and (3) the specific prediction (14-3-3 antagonism/difopein or isoform depletion altering surface TβRII, 14-3-3–binding-deficient AS160 trapping TβRII). The two arms are each published separately — Budi/Derynck show AKT phosphorylation of AS160 mobilizes intracellular TβRII/TβRI to the plasma membrane (with no mention of 14-3-3, confirmed also in their 2019 follow-up), while Ramm et al. establish that Akt-dependent 14-3-3 binding at AS160 Thr642 is required for insulin-stimulated GLUT4 translocation. I found no source that makes 14-3-3 the controlling step for TβRII retention/surface delivery or tests the predicted loss of insulin/glucose-induced surface TβRII on 14-3-3 blockade; published 14-3-3–TGF-β links concern 14-3-3ζ stabilizing TβRI and Smad-partner switching, a different mechanism. Hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: 14-3-3 binds TGFBR2 directly in a phosphorylation-dependent manner at its inhibitory autophosphorylation site Ser416, and this binding is what suppresses TβRII kinase activity.
hypotheses.mechanism: TβRII autophosphorylates on cytoplasmic serines with opposite consequences: Ser213/Ser249 (Ser409) autophosphorylation enhances kinase activity while Ser416 autophosphorylation attenuates it (derynck2019:findings:013; hata2016:findings:002), yet no effector is assigned to the inhibitory site. 14-3-3 dimers read exactly this kind of signal — an Arg-containing phosphoserine motif clamped in the conserved amphipathic channel (yaffe1997:findings:002) — and their canonical output is to mask phosphosites and inhibit the activity of the bound enzyme or regulator (bollen2010:findings:022). A phospho-Ser416-dependent 14-3-3 clamp would therefore provide a concrete mechanism for the otherwise unexplained inhibitory autophosphorylation of TGFBR2.
hypotheses.prediction: Endogenous or tagged TβRII should co-precipitate 14-3-3 in a manner that is lost with phosphatase treatment and lost in a S416A mutant but retained or increased in a S416D/E phospho-mimetic; a synthetic TβRII phosphopeptide spanning pSer416, but not its unphosphorylated counterpart, should bind recombinant 14-3-3 in vitro, and adding 14-3-3 to an in vitro TβRII kinase reaction should reduce substrate (TβRI peptide/GST-TβRI-GS) phosphorylation only for the Ser416-phosphorylated receptor.
hypotheses.test: Co-express Flag-TβRII (wild type, S416A, S416D, and kinase-dead) with HA-14-3-3ζ in HEK293 cells, perform reciprocal co-immunoprecipitations ± lambda phosphatase treatment of the immune complex; in parallel run fluorescence-polarization or ITC binding of recombinant 14-3-3ζ to synthetic phospho-Ser416 versus unphosphorylated TβRII peptides, and an in vitro kinase assay with immunopurified TβRII ± recombinant 14-3-3ζ (and ± the R56A/K49E phosphopeptide-binding-dead 14-3-3 as control) measuring autophosphorylation and TβRI-substrate phosphorylation.

citations.title: Positive and negative regulation of type II TGF-beta receptor signal transduction by autophosphorylation on multiple serine residues.
Eukaryotic initiation factor 2 alpha subunit associates with TGF beta receptors and 14-3-3 epsilon and acts as a modulator of the TGF beta response.
14-3-3ζ/TGFβR1 promotes tumor metastasis in lung squamous cell carcinoma.

novelty.note: I searched (a) 14-3-3 plus TGFBR2/Ser416 directly, (b) TβRII Ser416 inhibitory autophosphorylation and its effector, and (c) 14-3-3–TGF-β receptor co-immunoprecipitation/phosphoserine binding. The original Ser416 paper (Luo & Lodish) establishes that Ser416 autophosphorylation inhibits TβRII kinase activity but assigns no binding effector; published 14-3-3–TGF-β receptor links are to TβRI stabilization (14-3-3ζ) or to 14-3-3ε associating with receptors indirectly via eIF2α, with strongest binding to kinase-inactive receptors and enhanced rather than inhibited signaling. No source states or tests a phospho-Ser416-dependent 14-3-3 clamp on TβRII, so the claim is unpublished and unrefuted.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR1 (TβRI) directly recruits and activates STAT1, driving Tyr701 phosphorylation, dimerization and nuclear accumulation of STAT1 in response to TGF-β independently of Smads.
hypotheses.mechanism: TβRI carries a constitutively associated JAK1 that directly activates STAT3 upon TGF-β in fibroblasts without Smad involvement (derynck2019:findings:034), and TβRI is itself tyrosine-phosphorylated and serves as a docking platform for competing SH2/phosphotyrosine-binding effectors such as p52ShcA and Smad3 (derynck2019:findings:028, derynck2019:findings:029). STAT1 is activated by exactly this class of input: it is tyrosine-phosphorylated at a single site, Tyr701, by receptor-associated JAKs, dimerizes through reciprocal SH2–pTyr701 contacts and translocates to the nucleus (darnell1994:findings:009, darnell1994:findings:015), and it is recruited to receptor phosphotyrosine motifs of the restricted pYXPQ type that overlap the STAT3 docking motifs (heinrich2003:findings:006). Because relative STAT1 versus STAT3 abundance dictates which STAT a JAK-coupled receptor activates (ivashkiv2014:findings:007), a JAK1-loaded TβRI should engage STAT1 directly wherever STAT1 is abundant, rather than only STAT3.
hypotheses.prediction: In fibroblasts, TGF-β should induce STAT1 Tyr701 phosphorylation, STAT1 dimerization/GAS-site binding and nuclear STAT1 within minutes and without new protein synthesis; STAT1 should co-immunoprecipitate with TβRI in a TGF-β- and TβRI-phosphorylation-dependent manner; this response should be abolished by TβRI knockdown, TβRI kinase inhibition or JAK1 inhibition but not by Smad4/Smad3 depletion, and raising STAT1 relative to STAT3 should shift the TGF-β-induced STAT output from STAT3 toward STAT1.
hypotheses.test: In cultured fibroblasts, immunoprecipitate epitope-tagged TβRI (or endogenous TβRI) before and after 5–30 min TGF-β and blot for STAT1 and pY701-STAT1, with parallel reciprocal STAT1 IPs; then test dependence by TβRI siRNA, the TβRI kinase inhibitor SB431542, and a JAK1 inhibitor versus Smad3/Smad4 siRNA, reading out pY701-STAT1 by immunoblot, STAT1 dimer/DNA binding by GAS-probe EMSA, and nuclear STAT1 by immunofluorescence; loss of the TβRI–STAT1 co-IP and of TGF-β-induced pY701 in STAT1-reconstituted U3A cells expressing a kinase-dead or docking-site-mutant TβRI would rule the direct relationship out.

citations.title: Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) Directly Activates the JAK1-STAT3 Axis to Induce Hepatic Fibrosis in Coordination with the SMAD Pathway.
Physical interaction of STAT1 isoforms with TGF-β receptors leads to functional crosstalk between two signaling pathways in epithelial ovarian cancer.
Noncanonical JAK1/STAT3 interactions with TGF-β modulate myofibroblast transdifferentiation and fibrosis.

novelty.note: I searched for TGF-β-induced STAT1 Tyr701 phosphorylation, for TβRI/TGFBR1–STAT1 physical association, for Smad-independent JAK1-dependent STAT activation at the TGF-β receptor, and for STAT1:STAT3 ratio effects on TGF-β STAT output. Substantial parts are already published: Tang et al. show JAK1 is constitutively TβRI-bound and required for Smad-independent STAT phosphorylation within minutes, list STAT1 (and STAT2) among TβRI-interacting proteins in their SILAC interactome, and document two-phase TGF-β-induced STAT1 phosphorylation in HepG2/Hep3B/LX-2 cells (though Smad- and JAK1-dependence was tested only for STAT3); Nagaraj/Kumari et al. show STAT1α and STAT1β physically interact with ALK5/TβRII in a TGF-β1-modulated manner and that TGF-β1 alters STAT1 Y701 phosphorylation (increased in normal ovarian epithelial cells, decreased in cancer lines), but there STAT1 suppresses Smad2 rather than acting as a receptor-proximal effector. Nothing found states the specific package for fibroblasts — TβRI-docked, JAK1-driven pY701/dimerization/nuclear STAT1 that survives Smad3/Smad4 loss, plus a STAT1-abundance-dependent switch away from STAT3 — so this is partial, with the lung-fibroblast JAK1–TβRI paper (STAT3 only, no STAT1) as the nearest work in the predicted cell type.

hypotheses.statement: mTOR (via its S6K branch) directly phosphorylates SOS on serine residues in its Grb2-binding proline-rich region, acting as a negative regulator that reduces SOS–Grb2 association and SOS membrane recruitment.
hypotheses.mechanism: In EGF-stimulated cells, mTOR inhibition specifically collapses phosphorylation of mTOR-motif and p70S6K substrate sites (bekkerjensen2020:findings:016), and the mTOR–S6K arm is already documented to place serine marks on receptor-proximal adaptor proteins such as IRS1 (haeusler2018:findings:001). SOS is exactly this class of target: serine/threonine phosphorylation of SOS by an upstream kinase impairs Sos/Grb2 interaction and lowers Sos membrane recruitment (lemmon2010:findings:022), and Grb2 is the dominant determinant of stable SOS membrane residence, with its omission cutting recruitment ~90% and stable dwell times depending on multivalent Grb2 engagement (huang2019:findings:003, huang2019:findings:008). Since SOS dwell time governs how much Ras is activated per molecule (huang2019:findings:007), an mTOR/S6K-deposited phosphate on the SOS proline-rich region would throttle Ras output.
hypotheses.prediction: SOS1 should carry mTOR/S6K-consensus (RXRXXS-type) phosphosites whose occupancy falls upon Torin1/rapamycin treatment; acute mTOR inhibition in EGF-stimulated cells should therefore increase co-immunoprecipitated Grb2–SOS1 complex, increase membrane-fraction SOS1, and elevate/prolong Ras-GTP and downstream pERK, while a phospho-mimetic SOS1 serine mutant should show reduced Grb2 binding and reduced Ras activation and a non-phosphorylatable (S→A) mutant should be insensitive to mTOR inhibition.
hypotheses.test: Two-part: (1) in vitro kinase assay with purified recombinant mTORC1 (or active S6K1) plus recombinant full-length SOS1 and γ-32P/ATP, mapping sites by phosphopeptide LC-MS/MS, followed by a GST-Grb2 pulldown of mock- versus kinase-treated SOS1 to score loss of Grb2 binding; (2) in EGF-stimulated cultured cells (e.g. RPE1 or HEK-293T) ± Torin1, immunoprecipitate endogenous SOS1 and immunoblot bound Grb2 alongside membrane/cytosol fractionation of SOS1 and a Ras-GTP RBD pulldown, then repeat with SOS1-S→A and S→D mutants expressed in SOS1-knockdown cells to confirm that the mTOR-inhibitor effect requires the identified site.

citations.title: RSK phosphorylates SOS1 creating 14-3-3-docking sites and negatively regulating MAPK activation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) the mechanism in words ("S6K1/mTORC1 phosphorylates SOS1 serines, reduces Grb2 binding, negative feedback"), (2) the entities together (mTOR/S6K + SOS1 proline-rich region + Grb2 + Ras recruitment, plus S6K1 substrate phosphoproteomics/RXRXXS screens), and (3) the prediction (rapamycin/Torin1 increasing Grb2–SOS1 association, membrane SOS1, Ras-GTP and pERK). The parts are published separately: serine phosphorylation of the SOS1 C-terminal proline-rich region by ERK reduces Grb2 binding, and the AGC kinase RSK (an S6 kinase family member) phosphorylates SOS1 at RXXS sites S1134/S1161 to dampen ERK output; independently, mTORC1 inhibition is documented to activate Ras-dependent MAPK signalling through an S6K1–PI3K–IRS1 feedback loop, and mTORC1 is known to phosphorylate other receptor-proximal negative regulators (LST2/ZFYVE28). No retrieved source states that mTOR or S6K directly phosphorylates SOS on its Grb2-binding proline-rich region, nor that acute mTOR inhibition increases Grb2–SOS1 complex and SOS membrane recruitment, so the specific kinase-to-substrate connection and its prediction remain unpublished — hence partial.

hypotheses.statement: mTOR activity directly drives the secretory output of senescent cells, such that mTORC1 signalling is a positive regulator of SASP factor secretion (GDF15, SERPINE1, MMP1, IL-6/IL-8, HMGB1).
hypotheses.mechanism: Senescent fibroblasts and epithelial cells release a defined, quantifiable secretome — a core IL-6/IL-8/MCP1 programme plus highly secreted GDF15, SERPINE1 and MMP1 and DAMPs such as HMGB1 — whose magnitude varies with the senescence trigger (di2021:findings:007, basisty2020:findings:015, basisty2020:findings:010). Independently, mTOR inhibition in cells under oxidative-stress-induced senescence enhances autophagic flux, delays senescence onset and restores lysosomal function (di2021:findings:047), i.e. mTOR sets the balance between lysosomal degradation and the senescent state; since the SASP is a proteostatic/secretory output of that same state, lowering mTOR should shunt cargo toward lysosomal catabolism and reduce secretion, while constitutive mTORC1 activation — as occurs in GATOR1-deleted cells where mTOR is permanently lysosomal and amino-acid insensitive (barpeled2013:findings:010) — should raise it.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic mTOR inactivation in senescent human fibroblasts/epithelial cells will lower the concentration of secreted GDF15, SERPINE1, MMP1, IL-6/IL-8 and HMGB1 in conditioned medium per cell, with a smaller or absent drop in the corresponding intracellular mRNA/protein pools; conversely, cells with constitutive lysosomal mTORC1 (DEPDC5/NPRL2 knockdown) will secrete more of these factors, and re-expression of DEPDC5 will reverse the increase.
hypotheses.test: Induce senescence by ionizing radiation or RAS overexpression in human lung fibroblasts and renal epithelial cells; after senescence establishment, treat parallel cultures with rapamycin, Torin-1 or MTOR siRNA versus vehicle/control siRNA for 48 h in serum-free medium, and in a separate gain-of-function arm knock down DEPDC5 or NPRL2 (± DEPDC5 re-expression) to force constitutive mTORC1. Quantify conditioned-medium GDF15, SERPINE1, MMP1, IL-6, IL-8 and HMGB1 by ELISA and western blot normalised to viable cell number, alongside matched lysate mRNA (qPCR) and intracellular protein, with phospho-S6K1/4EBP1 as the mTOR-activity readout; a selective, dose-dependent loss of secreted factors on mTOR inhibition and a mirror-image increase on GATOR1 loss supports the direct regulatory relationship, whereas unchanged secretion despite full S6K1 dephosphorylation rules it out.

novelty.note: I searched for mTOR/rapamycin control of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype in plain mechanistic terms, for the specific factor set (GDF15, SERPINE1, MMP1, IL-6/IL-8, HMGB1) plus rapamycin, and for GATOR1/DEPDC5-NPRL2 loss combined with SASP. Two 2015 Nature Cell Biology papers already establish exactly the core explanation — mTORC1 is a positive regulator of senescent-cell secretory output (via 4EBP1-dependent IL1A and MAPKAPK2/ZFP36L1 translational control), with rapamycin suppressing IL-6/IL-8 and broad SASP secretion in irradiated and RAS-induced senescent human fibroblasts — and Wang et al. 2017 independently confirms rapamycin inhibition of the senescent secretome; Laberge et al. also report that cytokine mRNA falls, so the prediction's 'secretion-selective, mRNA-spared' nuance is not supported, and I found no work testing DEPDC5/NPRL2 loss as a gain-of-function SASP amplifier. Because the hypothesis statement itself is explicitly published for this phenomenon, the status is established rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: SRC directly promotes receptor endocytosis, specifically by tyrosine-phosphorylating TβRII and thereby routing it into c-Cbl-dependent ubiquitylation and lipid raft-mediated internalization.
hypotheses.mechanism: derynck2019:findings:013 states that Src tyrosine-phosphorylates TβRII and alters its activity, placing TβRII directly downstream of Src at the membrane, while hata2016:findings:006 states that the covalent modification state of TβRII (neddylation by c-Cbl versus ubiquitylation) is what determines whether TβRII escapes or enters lipid raft-mediated endocytosis. brozovich2016:findings:084 independently shows that Src activity is required for the endosomal processing of specific cargo proteins (zyxin and VASP but not FAK) upon stimulation, indicating that Src selects which membrane-associated proteins are committed to the endocytic route. Together these imply a direct Src → endocytosis relationship in which Src phosphorylation acts as the switch that shifts TβRII from the c-Cbl-neddylated, stabilized surface pool into the ubiquitylated, raft-internalized pool.
hypotheses.prediction: Expression of constitutively active Src should increase the rate of TβRII internalization from the cell surface and increase its ubiquitylation and turnover, whereas Src inhibition or knockdown should raise steady-state surface TβRII and reduce its ubiquitylation; a Tyr→Phe TβRII mutant lacking the Src sites should internalize slowly and remain at the surface regardless of Src activity, and Src activity should likewise be required for cargo entry into endosomes for other Src substrates but not for Src-independent cargo.
hypotheses.test: In cultured cells, perform a surface-biotinylation internalization assay (biotinylate at 4 °C, warm to 37 °C, strip residual surface biotin, recover internalized pool by streptavidin pulldown and blot for TβRII) comparing vector, constitutively active Src, kinase-dead Src, and Src knockdown or PP2-treated cells, with wild-type versus Tyr→Phe TβRII; in parallel immunoprecipitate TβRII and blot for ubiquitin and NEDD8 in the same conditions, and confirm compartment assignment by confocal colocalization of TβRII with an endosomal marker after stimulation. Src-dependent increases in internalized and ubiquitylated TβRII that are abolished in the Tyr→Phe mutant support the hypothesis; unchanged internalization kinetics across all Src conditions rule it out.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (1) the mechanism in words (Src tyrosine phosphorylation of TβRII driving internalization/turnover), (2) the entities together (c-Cbl neddylation vs ubiquitylation, lipid raft/caveolar endocytosis of TβRII, Y284F mutant trafficking), and (3) the prediction (Src inhibition/PP2 raising surface TβRII, Src requirement for TGF-β receptor endocytosis). The component pieces are published separately — Src phosphorylates TβRII at Tyr284 (but the reported consequence is Grb2/Shc docking and p38 activation, with no data on internalization, ubiquitylation or surface levels), c-Cbl neddylation antagonizes TβRII ubiquitylation and diverts it away from caveolin-positive/lipid-raft compartments (with no Src input), and Src activity is generally linked to caveolae-mediated TGF-β receptor degradation but indirectly, through caveolin-1 Tyr phosphorylation and acting on TβRI, while Src-activated SHP2 destabilizes TβRI via SMAD7/SMURF2 rather than TβRII. No retrieved source states that Src phosphorylation of TβRII is the switch routing it from the c-Cbl-neddylated surface pool into ubiquitylated raft-mediated internalization, so the specific connection and its predictions remain unpublished.

hypotheses.statement: The NCK SH2 domain binds directly to tyrosine-phosphorylated ZAP70, so that activated ZAP70 itself acts as an Nck-docking phosphoprotein (and thus an Nck-recruiting site) independently of the LAT/SLP-76 scaffolds.
hypotheses.mechanism: ZAP70 is itself multiply tyrosine-phosphorylated upon receptor engagement — its autoinhibitory interdomain/kinase-domain tyrosines (the residues analogous to SYK Tyr342, Tyr346, Tyr624, Tyr625) are phosphorylated after stimulation and their phosphorylation accompanies its activation (mcsai2010:findings:011, smithgarvin2009:findings:037), and phospho-ZAP70 is persistently concentrated in receptor/LAT clusters on membranes (case2019a:findings:009, su2016:findings:007). The Nck SH2 domain is a promiscuous pTyr reader that engages short pYDXV-type motifs with 40–370 nM affinity across dozens of phosphoprotein partners (case2019a:findings:011, li2012:findings:015), and Nck is recruited into exactly the same TCR-triggered LAT clusters where phospho-ZAP70 resides (case2019a:findings:008). Co-residence in the same phospho-cluster plus Nck SH2 promiscuity implies phospho-ZAP70 tyrosines are candidate direct Nck SH2 ligands rather than merely upstream of them.
hypotheses.prediction: Purified Nck (or its isolated SH2 domain) should bind ZAP70 only after ZAP70 tyrosine phosphorylation, with measurable affinity in the high-nM to low-µM range to one or more phospho-peptides derived from ZAP70's interdomain/kinase-domain tyrosines; conversely, unphosphorylated ZAP70 and phospho-null (Tyr→Phe) ZAP70 should show no Nck binding, and membrane-anchored phospho-ZAP70 alone should recruit and, with N-WASP, cluster Nck in the absence of any LAT or SLP-76.
hypotheses.test: Phosphorylate purified recombinant ZAP70 in vitro with purified Lck plus ATP (verify with anti-pTyr immunoblot), then perform GST-Nck-SH2 pulldowns and reciprocal immobilized-ZAP70 binding assays against phosphorylated versus unphosphorylated and Tyr→Phe ZAP70; quantify affinity by isothermal titration calorimetry or fluorescence polarization using synthetic phospho- and non-phospho-peptides spanning each ZAP70 tyrosine against the Nck SH2 domain, and confirm functionally by attaching His-tagged phospho-ZAP70 to a Ni-NTA supported lipid bilayer and imaging whether labeled Nck (± N-WASP) is recruited/clustered by TIRF, with unphosphorylated and phospho-null ZAP70 as negative controls.

novelty.note: I searched for direct Nck SH2–phospho-ZAP-70 binding, Nck recruitment independent of LAT/SLP-76, and Nck SH2 phosphopeptide specificity/partner lists. Published work consistently describes Nck recruitment in T cells via SH2 binding to SLP-76 pY113/pY128, TSAd pY280/pY305, and partially phosphorylated CD3ε (plus SH3.1–CD3ε PRS), with ZAP-70 treated as upstream kinase rather than an Nck SH2 ligand; no source states phospho-ZAP-70 as a direct Nck docking site, and none reports a negative test of it. Hence open, with the nearest published Nck-recruitment mechanisms cited.

hypotheses.statement: Ligand-induced, tyrosine-phosphorylated TGFBR2 (TβRII) clusters act directly as membrane nucleation platforms for Arp2/3-dependent actin assembly, driving local actin polymerization at the receptor.
hypotheses.mechanism: The actin evidence shows that a clustered, tyrosine-phosphorylated membrane receptor tail (pNephrin) recruiting Nck/N-WASP raises the specific activity of actin assembly ~6-fold inside clusters, and that this rate tracks the membrane dwell time of the nucleation-promoting assembly rather than its density or affinity, with the same clustering-driven increase in specific actin assembly activity seen for pLAT (case2019:findings:000, case2019:findings:010, case2019a:findings:007). Independently, TβRII is reported to dimerize and cluster on the membrane upon TGF-β binding, with TβRI recruited into a heterotetramer (hata2016:findings:000), and to carry tyrosine phosphorylation, generated by autophosphorylation or by Src, that enhances its activity (derynck2019:findings:013). A long-lived, clustered, tyrosine-phosphorylated TβRII cytoplasmic domain therefore has exactly the two features the actin data identify as sufficient to specify a high-activity actin assembly site, predicting a direct TβRII-to-actin nucleation relationship independent of Smad transcription.
hypotheses.prediction: Phosphotyrosine-bearing TβRII cytoplasmic domains clustered on a membrane should recruit Nck/N-WASP/Arp2/3 and support actin filament assembly at a per-nucleator rate several-fold above unclustered or non-phosphorylated controls, with the rate scaling with the dwell time of the TβRII-associated N-WASP rather than with TβRII surface density; tyrosine-to-phenylalanine substitution in the TβRII tail, or omission of Src-mediated phosphorylation, should abolish the enhancement, whereas kinase-dead TβRII that can still be tyrosine-phosphorylated should retain it.
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute the assay used for pNephrin: purify his-tagged TβRII cytoplasmic domain, phosphorylate it in vitro with recombinant Src (with an unphosphorylated and a Tyr-to-Phe mutant as controls), attach it at defined density to Ni-NTA supported lipid bilayers or Ni-NTA beads, add Nck, N-WASP, Arp2/3 and fluorescent/pyrene actin, and quantify actin assembly rate normalized to local N-WASP or Arp2/3 signal by TIRF (or bulk pyrene-actin fluorescence for beads), together with single-molecule dwell-time measurement of N-WASP; a parallel pulldown of Nck/N-WASP by the phospho- versus Y-to-F TβRII tail tests whether the recruitment step exists at all, and absence of both recruitment and rate enhancement rules the hypothesis out.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in plain words (clustered phosphotyrosine receptor tails nucleating Nck/N-WASP/Arp2/3 actin assembly), the entities together (TGFBR2/TbRII with Nck, N-WASP, Arp2/3, Src, Tyr284), and the prediction (reconstituted TbRII cytoplasmic domain on supported lipid bilayers driving actin assembly). The clustering-to-actin mechanism is published only for pNephrin and pLAT (Case et al. 2019), and TbRII tyrosine phosphorylation at Tyr284 by Src is published as an SH2 docking site for Grb2/Shc feeding p38/MAPK, with no report of Nck/N-WASP recruitment or of receptor-proximal Arp2/3 actin nucleation by TbRII; TGF-beta/actin links in the literature are transcriptional, Rho-GTPase- or formin/vesicle-based instead. Secondary sources hint that Src-phosphorylated TbRII did not bind Nck1/Nck2 SH2 domains, but I could not retrieve a page stating that directly, so I do not call this refuted.

hypotheses.statement: IL-17 directly activates JNK1 as the JNK isoform required downstream of the IL-17RA–ACT1–TRAF6 complex, so that JNK1 (not JNK2) mediates c-Jun phosphorylation and a subset of IL-17-induced target gene expression.
hypotheses.mechanism: IL-17 signaling is stated to run through ACT1-mediated TRAF6 ubiquitination to canonical NF-κB and MAPK activation including JNK, with A20-dependent TRAF6 deubiquitination selectively damping the JNK arm (gaffen2014:findings:022, gaffen2014:findings:027), and IL-17A-induced signaling to JNK1/2 is lost when an upstream Act1/TRAF6-interacting scaffold is absent (li2019:findings:021); independently, JNK1 is the isoform ubiquitously expressed and dominant for cytokine-induced c-Jun phosphorylation and autoinduction, since JNK1-/- cells show reduced p-c-Jun whereas JNK2 loss causes compensatory JNK1 hyperactivation (zeke2016:findings:016), and JNK1 preferentially yields the p46 species that is preferentially phosphorylated in immune cells and fibroblasts (zeke2016:findings:019). Together these imply that the JNK activity IL-17 elicits is carried by JNK1 itself, placing JNK1 as a direct effector kinase of the IL-17 receptor complex rather than a generic MAPK bystander.
hypotheses.prediction: IL-17A stimulation of responsive cells should produce rapid phosphorylation of the p46/JNK1 species and of c-Jun that is abolished or strongly reduced by JNK1 loss but largely preserved (or even increased) by JNK2 loss; IL-17-induced C/EBPδ and target genes such as Il6 and Lcn2 should be partially JNK1-dependent, and the late decline of this JNK signal should track A20 induction while NF-κB-only outputs remain comparatively intact.
hypotheses.test: In an IL-17-responsive line (e.g. keratinocytes or fibroblasts expressing IL-17RA/ACT1), generate isogenic JNK1-knockout, JNK2-knockout and control cells by CRISPR, stimulate with IL-17A alone and with IL-17A+TNFα over 0–120 min, and immunoblot phospho-JNK (resolving p46 vs p54), phospho-c-Jun and A20 while measuring Il6, Lcn2 and Cebpd mRNA by qPCR; confirm directness and kinase dependence by re-expressing wild-type versus kinase-dead JNK1 in the knockout, and by immunoprecipitating IL-17RA or ACT1 after IL-17A treatment to test for recruitment of JNK1 and in vitro phosphorylation of c-Jun by the recovered complex. Loss of the IL-17A-induced p46/c-Jun signal only in JNK1-null cells, rescued by wild-type but not kinase-dead JNK1, supports the hypothesis; equal signalling in JNK1-null cells rules it out.

citations.title: IL-17RC is critically required to maintain baseline A20 production to repress JNK isoform-dependent tumor-specific proliferation.
Cardiopulmonary Bypass-Induced IL-17A Aggravates Caspase-12-Dependent Neuronal Apoptosis Through the Act1-IRE1-JNK1 Pathway.
IL-17 mediates inflammatory reactions via p38/c-Fos and JNK/c-Jun activation in an AP-1-dependent manner in human nucleus pulposus cells.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the plain-language mechanism (IL-17A → Act1/TRAF6 → JNK → c-Jun → Il6/Lcn2/C-EBPδ), the entities together (IL-17 + JNK1 + JNK2 + c-Jun + A20 + TRAF6, via web search and Europe PMC full-text/keyword queries), and the prediction (JNK1-knockout vs JNK2-knockout effects on IL-17-induced p46/c-Jun and target genes). Published work establishes the component parts but not the specific claim: IL-17A is shown to activate JNK and thereby c-Jun/AP-1 to drive target genes using only pan-JNK inhibitors with no isoform resolution (PMID 26988982); one study names JNK1 as the effector downstream of IL-17A–Act1 but routes it through Hsp90/IRE1 in neuronal apoptosis and never compares JNK2 or c-Jun/gene output (PMID 40867579); the nearest isoform-resolved work links the IL-17 receptor and A20 to reciprocal JNK1/JNK2 control of c-Jun activity, but for baseline tumor proliferation after IL-17RC knockdown rather than IL-17-induced signaling, and it explicitly frames its findings as contrary to the expectation that IL-17R signaling activates JNK (PMID 28562353). No retrieved source states that JNK1 specifically, and not JNK2, is required downstream of the IL-17RA–ACT1–TRAF6 complex for c-Jun phosphorylation and a subset of IL-17 target genes.

hypotheses.statement: TRAF6 acts as a direct upstream activator of MAPK14 (p38α), driving activation-loop phosphorylation of p38α specifically among the p38 isoforms through its ubiquitin-dependent TAK1/TAB1 scaffolding function.
hypotheses.mechanism: The TRAF6 claims state that TRAF6 auto-/trans-polyubiquitylation (K63-linked, via Ubc13/Uev1A and RING-finger activity) scaffolds recruitment and activation of TAK1, and that this is what converts TGF-β and IL-17 receptor engagement into p38 MAPK activation, with p38 activation lost when TRAF6 is silenced or deubiquitylated by A20/USP25 (cuadrado2010:findings:052, derynck2019:findings:030, gaffen2014:findings:022, deng2000:findings:009). The p38 claims state that the TAK1-binding partner TAB1 binds p38α and no other p38 family member and induces p38α activation-loop autophosphorylation, and that Thr180/Tyr182 dual phosphorylation is what yields full activity, with p38α being the isoform that carries inflammatory gene expression and MK2 activation (cuadrado2010:findings:008, cuadrado2010:findings:009, cargnello2011:findings:006, cargnello2011:findings:068). Together these imply that the TRAF6 ubiquitin signal is relayed onto MAPK14 itself through a TRAF6-containing TAK1/TAB1 complex, making MAPK14 the isoform-selective direct target of TRAF6 rather than a generic downstream consequence.
hypotheses.prediction: Loss of TRAF6, or replacement with a RING-finger-dead TRAF6 (C70A or C85A/H87A class), should abolish stimulus-induced p38α Thr180/Tyr182 phosphorylation and downstream MK2 Thr334 phosphorylation while leaving p38β/γ/δ phosphorylation comparatively intact; conversely, forced TRAF6 expression or in vitro reconstitution of TRAF6 K63-chain assembly should increase p38α activation-loop phosphorylation and p38α kinase activity, and p38α (not other isoforms) should be recoverable in TRAF6 immunoprecipitates in a TAB1-dependent, ubiquitylation-enhanced manner.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured cell line (e.g. HEK293 or MEFs), compare wild-type, TRAF6-knockout, and TRAF6-knockout cells reconstituted with either wild-type or RING-dead TRAF6, stimulate with IL-1 or TGF-β, and blot for phospho-Thr180/Tyr182 p38α versus other p38 isoforms and phospho-MK2 Thr334; in parallel, perform reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation of TRAF6 and p38α (with and without TAB1 knockdown, and with each p38 isoform expressed individually) and an in vitro assay in which immunopurified TRAF6 plus E1/Ubc13-Uev1A and ubiquitin is added to recombinant TAK1–TAB1 and purified p38α, reading out p38α activation-loop phosphorylation and p38α-dependent MK2 phosphorylation, with the p38α inhibitor SB203580 and a ubiquitylation-incompetent TRAF6 as controls. Loss of the isoform-selective TRAF6 requirement and failure to reconstitute p38α phosphorylation in vitro would rule out the direct relationship.

novelty.note: I searched for TRAF6/TAB1/p38α complex formation and MKK-independent p38α autoactivation, for TRAF6 RING-mutant (C70A) rescue experiments scoring p38 phosphorylation, and for isoform-resolved p38 responses downstream of TRAF6/TAK1. The core relay is already published: Ge et al. detected a TRAF6–TAB1–p38α complex and showed TAB1-dependent activation-loop autophosphorylation of p38α (with TAB1 binding p38α selectively), and Lamothe et al. showed that an intact RING (plus ZF1) of TRAF6 is required for IL-1/LPS/RANKL-induced p38 activation in TRAF6-deficient cells rescued with mutants; the Biochem J study further shows E3-ligase-dead TRAF6 fails to restore IL-1 signalling and that p38α versus p38γ responses differ in their TAB2/3 (K63-chain-binding) requirement. What I did not find is the specific prediction — a TRAF6 requirement that is selective for p38α over p38β/γ/δ, TAB1-dependent recovery of p38α in TRAF6 immunoprecipitates, or in vitro reconstitution of TRAF6 K63-chain assembly driving p38α Thr180/Tyr182 phosphorylation and MK2 Thr334 — and one paper explicitly argues TRAF6 autoubiquitination is dispensable for MAPK activation, so the ubiquitin-dependent, isoform-selective version remains unsupported.

hypotheses.statement: mTOR itself, through its intrinsic kinase-domain catalytic activity rather than only its rapamycin-sensitive output, directly drives de novo lipid biosynthesis (SREBP-1c/FASN-dependent lipogenesis).
hypotheses.mechanism: Claims about lipid biosynthesis show it rises with hyperactive mTORC1 in a rapamycin-sensitive manner and falls when either mTORC1 (raptor) or mTORC2 (rictor) is lost, implicating the shared catalytic subunit rather than one complex-specific function (szwed2021:findings:036, szwed2021:findings:040, manning2017:findings:040). Independently, mTOR's own FRB domain and catalytic domain are separable pharmacologically: FRB mutations confer rapalog resistance while catalytic-domain mutations blunt ATP-competitive inhibitors, and a bivalent inhibitor blocks both (fruman2017:findings:023). If lipogenic control runs through mTOR's catalytic activity, its drug sensitivity should track mTOR's own domain genetics rather than the upstream pathway.
hypotheses.prediction: In TSC2-deficient cells expressing a rapalog-resistant FRB-mutant mTOR, rapamycin should fail to suppress acetate/glucose incorporation into lipids and fail to lower SREBP-1c target expression, while an ATP-competitive mTOR kinase inhibitor or a bivalent inhibitor still suppresses both; conversely, a catalytic-domain mutant should show reduced lipogenic suppression by the kinase inhibitor but retained rapamycin suppression.
hypotheses.test: Express wild-type, FRB-mutant, or catalytic-domain-mutant mTOR in mTOR-knockdown TSC2-deficient fibroblasts, then measure de novo lipid synthesis by 14C-acetate/13C-glucose incorporation into the saponifiable lipid fraction plus SREBP-1 processing and FASN levels by immunoblot, across rapamycin, an ATP-competitive mTOR inhibitor, and the bivalent inhibitor; a domain-specific split in lipogenic rescue establishes direct dependence on mTOR catalytic activity, while uniform responses across mutants rule it out.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: (a) rapamycin vs ATP-competitive/bivalent mTOR inhibitors on SREBP-1c/FASN and de novo lipid synthesis, (b) mTOR FRB (S2035) and kinase-domain mutants combined with lipogenesis readouts, and (c) raptor/rictor loss versus shared mTOR catalytic subunit in lipogenic control. The central mechanistic idea — that lipogenic/SREBP output depends on mTOR's intrinsic kinase activity rather than the rapamycin-sensitive output — is already published: Peterson et al. showed Torin1 suppresses SREBP target genes (FASN, SCD1, ACACA) and lipin-1 S472 phosphorylation while rapamycin is largely ineffective; a PNAS study showed PP242 but not rapamycin represses lipid/cholesterol biosynthetic genes; and an mTORC2/ACL study showed rapamycin fails to block glucose-to-lipid conversion whereas an ATP-competitive dual inhibitor does, implicating mTOR catalytic activity across both complexes. What I could not find is the specific domain-genetics prediction — expression of rapalog-resistant FRB-mutant or TORKi-resistant catalytic-domain mutant mTOR in TSC2-deficient cells with de novo lipogenesis/SREBP-1 processing as the readout, including RapaLink-type bivalent rescue — so the connection is anticipated pharmacologically but not established genetically.

hypotheses.statement: Lysosomal localization of mTOR is the step that gates de novo lipid biosynthesis, so forcing mTOR onto lysosomes is sufficient to raise lipogenesis and displacing it from lysosomes is sufficient to lower it.
hypotheses.mechanism: Lipid biosynthesis rises with hyperactive mTORC1 and falls when mTOR complex components are deleted (szwed2021:findings:036, manning2017:findings:040), but the lipogenic readout has never been tied to where mTOR sits. Separate claims establish direct handles on mTOR's position: GATOR1 (DEPDC5/NPRL2/NPRL3) loss renders mTOR constitutively lysosomal and nutrient-insensitive, reversible by re-expression (barpeled2013:findings:010), and overexpressed SAMTOR displaces mTOR from lysosomes (gu2017:findings:003, gu2017:findings:012). If localization is the gating step, these position-specific manipulations should move lipogenic flux in opposite directions.
hypotheses.prediction: GATOR1-deleted cells should sustain high acetate/glucose-to-lipid flux and SREBP-1 target expression even after amino acid withdrawal, with DEPDC5 or NPRL2 re-expression restoring nutrient-dependent shutdown of lipogenesis; GFP-SAMTOR overexpression should reduce SREBP-1 processing, FASN levels, and lipid labeling in proportion to the loss of mTOR–LAMP2 colocalization.
hypotheses.test: In a GATOR1-deleted cancer line ± DEPDC5/NPRL2 re-expression, and in HEK-293T cells ± GFP-SAMTOR overexpression, run paired measurements in the same wells: mTOR/LAMP2 immunofluorescence colocalization and 14C-acetate or 13C-glucose incorporation into total lipids with SREBP-1/FASN immunoblots, in complete versus amino-acid-free medium; a quantitative correlation between lysosomal mTOR and lipogenic flux that survives these orthogonal, opposite-direction manipulations supports the hypothesis, while flux that is indifferent to localization refutes it.
