RSK regulates activated BRAF signalling to mTORC1 and promotes melanoma growth.
Two widely used RSK inhibitors, BI-D1870 and SL0101, alter mTORC1 signaling in a RSK-independent manner.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: RSK phosphorylation of TSC2 Ser1798 and mTOR/S6K1 output, RSK-mediated Raptor phosphorylation and mTORC1 kinase activity, and negative/specificity tests of RSK inhibitors on S6K1 and 4E-BP1. The exact explanation is already published: Roux et al. (PNAS 2004) show RSK1 binds and phosphorylates tuberin at Ser-1798, that this inhibits TSC1/TSC2 tumour-suppressor function and increases mTOR signalling to S6K1, and that an S1798 mutant suppresses S6K1 better than wild type; Carriere et al. (Curr Biol 2008) show RSK1/2 are required for Ras/MAPK-induced Raptor phosphorylation and that Raptor mutants lacking the RSK sites reduce mTOR phosphotransferase activity, with Roux's later work and the BRAF/melanoma study restating RSK as the ERK-to-mTORC1 link. Status is established rather than open/partial because both arms of the mechanism (TSC2 site and Raptor site, with mTOR immunoprecipitate kinase assays) are stated for this phenomenon; I flag Roffé et al. 2015 as a direct negative on the proposed pharmacological test, since they report that BI-D1870 and SL0101 effects on mTORC1-p70S6K (BI-D1870 actually increasing p70S6K activation) are independent of RSK and ERK1/2, so the inhibitor-based readout would not test the claim.

hypotheses.statement: NF-κB transcriptional activity directly restrains RIPK1-dependent cell death by inducing inhibitory gene products that suppress RIPK1's death-signalling function, forming a negative feedback loop on RIPK1.
hypotheses.mechanism: chen2002:findings:007 states that NF-κB activation drives resynthesis of inhibitory molecules including IκB and the cIAPs, which limit the duration and amplitude of TNF signalling, and chen2002:findings:006 shows that loss of NF-κB activity increases susceptibility to TNF-induced apoptosis while enforced NF-κB activation protects. On the RIPK1 side, van2019:findings:029 shows that when the NF-κB-pathway inhibitor A20 is lost in myeloid cells, RIPK1-dependent necroptosis drives inflammasome activation and pathology, and galluzzi2018:findings:013 shows that removing RIPK1 itself unleashes spontaneous CASP8-driven apoptosis or necroptosis in tissues. The simplest reconciliation is that NF-κB-induced products act on RIPK1 to keep it in its scaffolding/pro-survival mode, so blocking NF-κB output should convert TNF signalling into RIPK1 kinase-dependent death.
hypotheses.prediction: Pharmacological or genetic blockade of NF-κB (IKKβ inhibition, IκBα-super-repressor, or p65 knockdown) followed by TNF should trigger death that is rescued by the RIPK1 kinase inhibitor necrostatin-1 or by RIPK1 deletion, accompanied by loss of NF-κB-induced cIAP/A20 protein and increased RIPK1 autophosphorylation and RIPK1-containing death-complex assembly; enforced NF-κB activity should have the opposite effect.
hypotheses.test: In a standard adherent cell line (e.g. HeLa or L929), pre-treat with an IKKβ inhibitor or express an IκBα super-repressor, then stimulate with TNF and quantify death (viability assay plus LDH release) with and without necrostatin-1 or in RIPK1-knockout cells; in parallel immunoblot for cIAP1/2 and A20 levels and for RIPK1 Ser166 autophosphorylation, and immunoprecipitate RIPK1 to score its shift from the receptor complex into a caspase-8/FADD or RIPK3-containing complex. Necrostatin-1/RIPK1-knockout rescue of death specifically upon NF-κB blockade, with concomitant RIPK1 autophosphorylation, supports the relationship; NF-κB-independent, RIPK1-independent death would rule it out.

citations.title: NF-κB regulated expression of A20 controls IKK dependent repression of RIPK1 induced cell death in activated T cells.
NF-κB inhibition in keratinocytes causes RIPK1-mediated necroptosis and skin inflammation.
NF-κB-Independent Role of IKKα/IKKβ in Preventing RIPK1 Kinase-Dependent Apoptotic and Necroptotic Cell Death during TNF Signaling.
NEMO/IKKgamma regulates an early NF-kappaB-independent cell-death checkpoint during TNF signaling.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (NF-κB-induced inhibitory products restraining RIPK1 death signalling), the entities together (NF-κB + A20/cIAP/cFLIP + RIPK1 + necrostatin-1), and the prediction (IKKβ/p65 blockade + TNF giving RIPK1-kinase-dependent death). The explanation is already published: Blanchett et al. show that NF-κB-driven A20 expression is the transcriptional arm repressing RIPK1-induced death, with the phenotype reversed by RIPK1 kinase inactivation, and Kumari et al. show epidermal NF-κB/IKK2 loss causes TNFR1-driven RIPK1-dependent necroptosis rescued by Ripk1-D138N. One caveat that keeps this from being a clean one-to-one match: Dondelinger et al. directly tested the IKKα/β arm of the prediction and found the protection from RIPK1-kinase-dependent death is exerted by direct IKK phosphorylation of RIPK1 independently of NF-κB transcription, so the IKKβ-inhibitor readout in the proposed test would not isolate transcriptional output; that paper is cited as nearest rather than refuting, since it does not negate the A20/cFLIP transcriptional checkpoint itself.

hypotheses.statement: TGFBR1 (TβRI) activates STAT1 by inducing its Tyr701 phosphorylation through JAK1, which is constitutively associated with TβRI, in fibroblasts responding to TGF-β.
hypotheses.mechanism: In hepatic stellate cells and fibroblasts, JAK1 is constitutively associated with TβRI and directly activates STAT3 in response to TGF-β, independently of Smads (derynck2019:findings:034). JAK1 is also a kinase that tyrosine-phosphorylates STAT1 downstream of IFNAR (ivashkiv2014:findings:000), at Tyr701 (darnell1994:findings:009). STAT1 and STAT3 are co-activated by other non-interferon receptor stimuli such as EGF (darnell1994:findings:022). Together these suggest that TβRI-bound JAK1 could phosphorylate STAT1 as well as STAT3. One limit applies: STAT1 docks at a narrower pYXPQ motif than STAT3 (heinrich2003:findings:006), so STAT1 recruitment to the TβRI–JAK1 complex is uncertain.
hypotheses.prediction: In cultured fibroblasts, TGF-β stimulation should rapidly increase STAT1 Tyr701 phosphorylation. This increase should be abolished by a TβRI kinase inhibitor or TGFBR1 knockdown, and by JAK1 knockdown or inhibition. It should persist when Smad signaling is blocked (e.g. SMAD4 knockdown) and when new protein synthesis is blocked (cycloheximide) in the early phase.
hypotheses.test: Stimulate cultured fibroblasts with TGF-β1 over a 0–60 min time course, with or without a TβRI kinase inhibitor (e.g. SB431542), JAK1 siRNA or a JAK inhibitor, and cycloheximide. Immunoblot for pSTAT1-Tyr701, total STAT1, pSTAT3-Tyr705 and pSmad2/3. In parallel, co-immunoprecipitate TβRI and probe for JAK1 and STAT1 to test whether STAT1 associates with the receptor complex after TGF-β treatment.

citations.title: Transforming Growth Factor-β (TGF-β) Directly Activates the JAK1-STAT3 Axis to Induce Hepatic Fibrosis in Coordination with the SMAD Pathway.
Physical interaction of STAT1 isoforms with TGF-β receptors leads to functional crosstalk between two signaling pathways in epithelial ovarian cancer.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in words (TβRI-associated JAK1 phosphorylating STAT1 Tyr701 in fibroblasts), for the entities together (TGFBR1/ALK5 + JAK1 + STAT1 + SB431542 + Smad-independent), and for the prediction (rapid TGF-β-induced pSTAT1-Y701 blocked by JAK1 knockdown). Tang et al. (JBC 2017) already report that JAK1 is constitutively bound to TβRI and that TGF-β induces a biphasic, SB431542-sensitive, early Smad-independent (MEF) tyrosine phosphorylation of both STAT1 and STAT3, with STAT1 and STAT2 also appearing in the TβRI interactome — but STAT1 phosphorylation was only documented in hepatoma cells (undetectable in AML12), the residue and the JAK1-dependence of the STAT1 arm were not tested, and no TβRI–STAT1 co-IP after TGF-β is shown. A separate study in ovarian epithelial cells found TGF-β1 drives STAT1 Ser727 rather than Tyr701 (Y701 even decreased in cancer lines, increased in non-tumorous cells) via direct STAT1–ALK5/TβRII binding rather than JAK, so the specific fibroblast/JAK1/Y701 claim is neither fully stated nor directly refuted.

hypotheses.statement: ERK2 directly phosphorylates TGFBR1 (TβRI) on its cytoplasmic domain as a negative-feedback modification, in the same way ERK2 phosphorylates other upstream activators of its own pathway.
hypotheses.mechanism: TβRI is an upstream activator of ERK/MAPK: tyrosine-phosphorylated TβRI recruits p52ShcA, which promotes ShcA-Grb2-SOS complex formation and Ras activation (derynck2019:findings:028). Erk MAPK activation in turn down-regulates TβRI and dampens TGF-β signaling (hata2016:findings:007, derynck2019:findings:009). Separately, activated ERK2 directly phosphorylates several upstream activators of its own pathway in vitro and restrains their output, including the receptor FGFR1 on S777, SOS1 (disrupting its Grb2/Shc association), Raf-1 and MEK1 (lake2016:findings:002, lake2016:findings:003, lake2016:findings:007, lake2016:findings:010). Together these suggest ERK2 may also act directly on TβRI as a feedback substrate, not only through TACE-mediated cleavage.
hypotheses.prediction: Recombinant active ERK2 should incorporate phosphate into the purified TβRI cytoplasmic domain in vitro at defined Ser/Thr-Pro sites. In cells, TGF-β- or mitogen-induced phosphorylation at these sites should be ERK1/2-dependent and blocked by MEK1/2 inhibition. Alanine mutation of the sites should prolong TβRI signaling output, either Smad3 activation or ShcA recruitment.
hypotheses.test: Run an in vitro kinase assay with [γ-32P]ATP, active recombinant ERK2 (inactive ERK2 as control) and purified GST-TβRI cytoplasmic domain, then map sites by phosphopeptide mapping or mass spectrometry. In cultured cells, compare phosphorylation of wild-type and site-mutant TβRI with and without U0126 or ERK1/2 knockdown, and measure Smad3 phosphorylation and TβRI–ShcA co-immunoprecipitation. Include a TACE/ADAM17 inhibitor so that direct phosphorylation can be separated from effects of receptor shedding.

citations.title: Phosphorylation of Ser165 in TGF-beta type I receptor modulates TGF-beta1-induced cellular responses.
TACE-mediated ectodomain shedding of the type I TGF-beta receptor downregulates TGF-beta signaling.

ERK-Mediated Phosphorylation of Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1 on Ser
            <sup>777</sup>
            Inhibits Signaling
TGF-beta activates Erk MAP kinase signalling through direct phosphorylation of ShcA.

novelty.note: I searched three ways — the mechanism in words (ERK/MAPK directly phosphorylating the TGF-β type I receptor cytoplasmic domain as feedback), the entities together (TGFBR1/ALK5 + ERK1/2 + Ser/Thr-Pro site + U0126/MEK inhibition + phosphoproteomic ERK substrate screens), and the prediction (site-mutant TβRI prolonging Smad3 activation or ShcA recruitment). No source states that ERK1/2 phosphorylates TβRI directly, and none reports a direct negative test of it; published ERK-driven TβRI down-regulation runs through TACE/ADAM17 ectodomain shedding, while ERK-substrate receptor feedback is documented for FGFR1 (S777) and EGFR (T669) rather than for any TGF-β family receptor. The nearest work is a 1996 report that TGF-β1 induces Ser/Thr phosphorylation in the TβR-I juxtamembrane cytoplasmic region (Ser165) that modulates signalling output, but the responsible kinase is not assigned to ERK, so the specific claim is unaddressed rather than established or refuted.

hypotheses.statement: The paradoxical rise in uORF-mRNA (ATF4) translation is a generic consequence of lowered initiation flux rather than a specific product of eIF2α-Ser51 phosphorylation blocking eIF2B.
hypotheses.mechanism: In C. elegans, raga-1/ragc-1 and rict-1 knockdown each lowered bulk protein synthesis and robustly raised a Patf-4(uORF)::GFP reporter in a genetic background where eIF2α phosphorylation was blocked, and loss of eIF2α phosphorylation did not prevent atf-4-dependent outcomes of translation inhibition. Type I IFN likewise lowers translation at a step other than eIF2 (IFIT1/IFIT2 binding and inhibiting eIF3-mediated preinitiation complex formation), so several distinct lesions converge on reduced preinitiation complex availability. If reduced initiation per se is what favours bypass/reinitiation on uORF-containing transcripts, no eIF2B-specific step is required for the paradox.
hypotheses.prediction: An ATF4 uORF reporter should be induced in cells where eIF2α Ser51 cannot be phosphorylated whenever initiation flux is lowered by a non-eIF2 route (eIF3/eIF4F-level inhibition, mTOR inhibition), with reporter induction scaling with the degree of initiation suppression regardless of which factor is targeted.
hypotheses.test: In an eIF2α S51A (or quadruple-ISR-kinase-inhibited) cell line carrying ATF4-uORF-luciferase and a no-uORF control luciferase, titrate mechanistically distinct initiation inhibitors (hippuristanol/eIF4A inhibition, Torin1, IFIT1 overexpression) against matched reductions in bulk synthesis measured by puromycin/35S incorporation, and plot reporter ratio versus global synthesis rate; a single shared dose-response curve across inhibitors supports the flux hypothesis, whereas induction only in eIF2α-phosphorylation-competent cells supports the eIF2B-specific alternative.

citations.title: mTORC1 Balances Cellular Amino Acid Supply with Demand for Protein Synthesis through Post-transcriptional Control of ATF4.
Regulation of Translation of ATF4 mRNA: A Focus on Translation Initiation Factors and RNA-Binding Proteins

novelty.note: I searched for eIF2α-phosphorylation-independent ATF4 induction, for ATF4 uORF reporters under eIF4A/mTOR-level initiation inhibition, and for whether reduced global initiation per se (vs. ternary-complex availability) drives uORF bypass. The directly relevant test exists and goes the other way: Park et al. showed that in mammalian cells mTOR inhibition acts through the ATF4 5'UTR uORFs and 4E-BPs, independently of eIF2α phosphorylation, to *decrease* rather than increase ATF4 translation, so lowering initiation flux by a non-eIF2 route does not induce the uORF reporter as predicted. The nearest synthesis of the field likewise attributes eIF2α-phosphorylation-independent ATF4 induction specifically to lowered eIF2 ternary-complex availability (eIF2B, eIF5, eIF5B lesions), which can occur with minimal inhibition of global synthesis, decoupling reporter induction from bulk initiation rate.

hypotheses.statement: The eIF2α-phosphorylation-independent arm of uORF derepression runs through mTOR-controlled eIF4F availability, so it should show the rapamycin-resistant, Torin1-sensitive signature of 4E-BP1 regulation rather than the S6K signature.
hypotheses.mechanism: ATF4-uORF reporter induction occurred after knockdown of mTORC1 (raga-1/ragc-1) and mTORC2 (rict-1) components without eIF2α phosphorylation, implicating mTOR complexes in the paradox. Rapamycin invariantly dephosphorylates S6K1 but fails to block 4E-BP1 phosphorylation in many cell contexts whereas Torin1 does, and ablating all five rpS6 phosphoacceptor serines leaves translation efficiency intact, so the S6K/rpS6 branch is unlikely to carry the effect while the 4E-BP1/eIF4E branch remains a candidate.
hypotheses.prediction: In cells unable to phosphorylate eIF2α Ser51, Torin1 but not rapamycin should raise ATF4-uORF reporter output while lowering bulk synthesis, and the Torin1 effect should be blunted in 4E-BP-null cells or by expressing eIF4E-binding-deficient 4E-BP1 mutants.
hypotheses.test: Compare rapamycin versus Torin1 (and an rpS6 phospho-null rescue line) for ATF4-uORF-luciferase induction, 4E-BP1 and S6K1 phosphorylation, and puromycin incorporation in eIF2α S51A cells, then repeat in 4E-BP1/2 knockout versus parental cells; loss of Torin1-driven reporter induction upon 4E-BP deletion assigns the effect to eIF4F availability, while persistence points to a different mTOR substrate.

citations.title: mTORC1 Balances Cellular Amino Acid Supply with Demand for Protein Synthesis through Post-transcriptional Control of ATF4.
Hepatic mTORC1 signaling activates ATF4 as part of its metabolic response to feeding and insulin.
Rapamycin-insensitive mTORC1 activity controls eIF4E:4E-BP1 binding.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the mechanism in words (eIF2α-independent uORF derepression via mTOR/eIF4F), the entities together (ATF4 uORF + 4E-BP + rapamycin/Torin1 + S6K), and the prediction (Torin1 vs rapamycin effect on ATF4 reporter in 4E-BP-null cells). Park et al., Cell Reports 2017 states exactly this explanation: mTOR control of ATF4 translation requires its uORFs, is independent of eIF2α phosphorylation, and is executed by the 4E-BP/eIF4E branch — Torin1's effect on ATF4 is lost in 4E-BP-deficient MEFs — and the rapamycin-vs-Torin1 asymmetry at 4E-BP1 (vs invariant S6K1 dephosphorylation) is itself published; the liver study independently places ATF4 downstream of mTORC1 rather than the ISR. One caveat recorded for completeness: in these mammalian systems mTOR inhibition lowers rather than raises ATF4/uORF reporter output, i.e. the published sign is opposite to the stated prediction, so the pathway assignment is anticipated while the predicted direction is not supported.

hypotheses.statement: The apparent requirement of CARD14/CBM for IL-17A-induced NF-κB, JNK and p38 activation is an indirect consequence of losing constitutive MALT1 protease-mediated destruction of the ubiquitin-editing brakes A20 and CYLD, not of CBM acting as a receptor-proximal transducer.
hypotheses.mechanism: In keratinocytes A20 and CYLD are processed constitutively in a BCL10/MALT1-dependent manner and this processing is not further increased by IL-17A, so removing CARD14 or BCL10 should restore intact A20/CYLD; because TRAF6-dependent NF-κB activation depends on K63-linked polyubiquitin chains that these enzymes edit, restored A20/CYLD would blunt proximal TRAF6-driven signalling even though BCL10 itself is dispensable for IL-17R-, IL-1R- and TNFR-proximal IKK, p38 and JNK activation.
hypotheses.prediction: In CARD14- or BCL10-deficient keratinocytes, A20 and CYLD full-length protein should be elevated and IL-17A-induced TRAF6 K63-ubiquitination reduced; depleting A20 and CYLD in those cells should restore IL-17A-induced IKK/JNK/p38 phosphorylation without restoring the CBM.
hypotheses.test: In CARD14-knockdown and BCL10-knockdown keratinocytes, co-deplete A20 and CYLD by siRNA and compare IL-17A-induced IκBα, JNK and p38 phosphorylation and TRAF6 K63-ubiquitin immunoblots against cells treated with a MALT1 protease inhibitor; the hypothesis predicts rescue by A20/CYLD co-depletion but not by restoring CBM scaffolding alone, whereas the proximal-transducer model predicts no rescue.

citations.title: The paracaspase MALT1 mediates CARD14-induced signaling in keratinocytes.
Keratinocyte-intrinsic BCL10/MALT1 activity initiates and amplifies psoriasiform skin inflammation.
A CARD10-Dependent Tonic Signalosome Activates MALT1 Paracaspase and Regulates IL-17/TNF-α-Driven Keratinocyte Inflammation.

novelty.note: I searched for CARD14/BCL10/MALT1 keratinocyte signaling with A20/CYLD cleavage, for MALT1-protease-dependent relief of ubiquitin-editing brakes upstream of TRAF6 K63 chains, and for rescue experiments depleting A20/CYLD to restore IL-17A-induced IKK/JNK/p38; retrieved the EMBO Reports keratinocyte CARD14-MALT1 paper and Europe PMC records for the Science Immunology and JID keratinocyte MALT1 studies. The component pieces are published — CARD14-driven MALT1 proteolysis of endogenous A20 and CYLD in keratinocytes, with both deubiquitinases shown to negatively regulate CARD14-induced NF-κB, plus the finding that the BCL10/MALT1 signalosome is not part of IL-17R-proximal signaling but amplifies IL-17A/IL-1β/TNF responses — but no retrieved source attributes the apparent CARD14/CBM requirement for IL-17A-induced NF-κB/MAPK specifically to loss of constitutive A20/CYLD processing, and none reports the predicted A20/CYLD co-depletion rescue or reduced TRAF6 K63-ubiquitination. Nothing tested and negated this specific claim, so the status is partial rather than established or refuted.

hypotheses.statement: The CARD14–Bcl10/MALT1 and CARD14–Act1/TRAF6 complexes seen on CARD14 overexpression reflect relief of CARD14 autoinhibition by high expression, so overexpressed wild-type CARD14 phenocopies the gain-of-function mutant rather than reporting the endogenous IL-17R-proximal pathway.
hypotheses.mechanism: Wild-type CARD14 (both full-length and short isoforms) shows little detectable association with MALT1/BCL10, while the E138A psoriasis mutation induces clear association, and these mutations are proposed to act by disrupting inhibitory-domain-mediated autoinhibition analogous to oncogenic CARD11. Mass-action from overexpression can likewise bypass autoinhibition, which would generate CBM and Act1/TRAF6 complexes and a strong NF-κB signal that endogenous CARD14 does not produce proximally.
hypotheses.prediction: Association of CARD14 with BCL10/MALT1 and with Act1/TRAF6 should appear only above a threshold expression level and should be largely absent at endogenous expression even after IL-17A stimulation, while an autoinhibition-deficient mutant forms the complexes at low expression.
hypotheses.test: Perform a graded doxycycline-titration of tagged wild-type versus E138A CARD14 in keratinocytes spanning sub-endogenous to overexpressed levels (quantified against endogenous CARD14 by immunoblot), and at each level measure CARD14 co-immunoprecipitation with BCL10/MALT1 and with Act1/TRAF6 ± IL-17A; a sharp expression-dependent switch for wild type identifies an overexpression artefact, whereas IL-17A-dependent complex formation at endogenous levels supports a genuine receptor-proximal role.

citations.title: CARD14 signalosome formation is associated with its endosomal relocation and mTORC1-induced keratinocyte proliferation.
Psoriasis mutations disrupt CARD14 autoinhibition promoting BCL10-MALT1-dependent NF-κB activation

novelty.note: I searched three ways: CARD14 autoinhibition/inhibitory-domain release and BCL10-MALT1 binding; CARD14-Act1-TRAF6 IL-17R-proximal signalling in keratinocytes; and overexpression-level/threshold dependence of CARD14 signalosome assembly in inducible keratinocyte systems. The autoinhibition framework (psoriasis mutations relieving linker/ID-mediated autoinhibition, analogous to oncogenic CARD11) is published, but the specific premise that high expression alone relieves autoinhibition so that overexpressed wild-type CARD14 phenocopies the gain-of-function mutant was directly tested and failed: in tetracycline-inducible HaCaT keratinocytes expressing tagged CARD14 well above endogenous levels, CARD14-WT did not co-immunoprecipitate BCL10 or MALT1, remained soluble and diffusely cytosolic, and formed no signalosome, whereas E138A did — the same WT/mutant discrimination reported at overexpression in HEK293 cells. The CBM arm of the prediction is therefore contradicted at overexpressed levels (the Act1/TRAF6 arm remains untested), so the status is refuted rather than partial.

hypotheses.statement: The low kcat on soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 reflects that PTEN's catalytically optimal substrate is the D3-phosphate of a membrane-presented phosphoinositide, so a head-group-only substrate lacking the diacylglycerol/membrane context binds the active site but turns over poorly.
hypotheses.mechanism: alonso2004 classifies PTEN within a VH1-like subgroup defined by dephosphorylating the D3-phosphate of inositol phospholipids, and balla2013 shows a single mutation (G129E) can abolish lipid phosphatase activity while leaving generic protein/aryl phosphatase activity intact, implying the lipid-directed catalytic mode is a distinct, separable function. lee2002 measures robust PTEN activity using PI(3,4,5)P3 as substrate. Together these imply that Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 occupies the same D3-phosphate site but, lacking the lipid moiety and membrane interface, fails to achieve productive orientation, giving a tight apparent Km yet very low Vmax.
hypotheses.prediction: Side-by-side under identical conditions, purified PTEN should show a much higher kcat on PI(3,4,5)P3 presented in lipid vesicles than on soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, and the Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 activity should be abolished by the lipid-site mutation G129E even though p-nitrophenylphosphate hydrolysis is retained.
hypotheses.test: Assay one purified PTEN preparation in parallel on (i) soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, (ii) PI(3,4,5)P3 in defined phosphatidylcholine/phosphatidylserine vesicles, and (iii) p-nitrophenylphosphate, fitting Km/kcat for wild type and the G129E mutant; the hypothesis predicts G129E selectively ablates both the vesicle PI(3,4,5)P3 and the Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 activity while sparing pNPP, whereas the alternative (Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 handled by the generic phosphatase mode) predicts G129E spares Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 turnover.

citations.title: Interfacial kinetic analysis of the tumour suppressor phosphatase, PTEN: evidence for activation by anionic phospholipids.
The lipid phosphatase activity of PTEN is critical for its tumor supressor function.
Crystal structure of the PTEN tumor suppressor: implications for its phosphoinositide phosphatase activity and membrane association.
The tumor suppressor, PTEN/MMAC1, dephosphorylates the lipid second messenger, phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate.

novelty.note: I searched for PTEN interfacial/vesicle kinetics versus soluble inositol phosphate substrates, for G129E substrate selectivity, and for the structural basis of membrane presentation. McConnachie et al. (Biochem J 2003) directly reports that PTEN behaves as an interfacial enzyme whose catalytic-centre activity toward vesicle-presented PtdIns(3,4,5)P3 is at least 200-fold (up to ~1000-fold) greater than toward water-soluble Ins(1,3,4,5)P4, with PtdIns(4,5)P2 and salt stimulating lipid turnover while inhibiting soluble-substrate turnover, and a C2-domain mutation reducing interfacial binding — i.e. the stated explanation for the low kcat on the head group is already published. Myers et al. (PNAS 1998) establishes that G129E specifically ablates recognition of inositol phospholipids while sparing protein/aryl phosphatase activity, and Lee et al. (Cell 1999) provides the enlarged active site plus C2-domain membrane-positioning rationale; the only element not crisply settled in what I retrieved is the exact kinetic behaviour of G129E on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 itself.

hypotheses.statement: A substantial fraction of the purified recombinant PTEN used for the kinetic fit was catalytically dead because its active-site cysteine was trapped in a Cys71-Cys124 disulfide, depressing the apparent Vmax without changing the apparent Km.
hypotheses.mechanism: lee2002 shows purified recombinant human PTEN is readily inactivated by low micromolar-to-millimolar oxidant exposure through formation of a defined Cys71-Cys124 disulfide, and that activity is restored only by specific reductants (DTT or thioredoxin, not GSH), so an enzyme preparation handled without an effective reducing system can carry a large inactive population. alonso2004 places PTEN in the cysteine-based VH1-like phosphatase class, whose catalysis depends on that nucleophilic active-site cysteine. Because only the active fraction turns over substrate, Vmax (reported per mg total protein) is scaled down while Km, a property of the active molecules, is unaffected.
hypotheses.prediction: Pre-reducing the same PTEN preparation with DTT or a thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase/NADPH system should raise Vmax and kcat on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 several-fold with little or no change in Km, and the untreated preparation should show a detectable oxidized (faster-migrating) PTEN band on nonreducing SDS-PAGE.
hypotheses.test: Split one purified PTEN preparation into untreated, DTT-reduced, and Trx/TrxR/NADPH-reduced aliquots; quantify the oxidized versus reduced band fraction by nonreducing SDS-PAGE immunoblot and, in parallel, fit Km and Vmax on Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 for each aliquot, repeating with the C124S mutant as a catalytically null control. The hypothesis predicts the Vmax increase upon reduction is proportional to the oxidized fraction measured on the gel with Km unchanged; an intrinsically poor-substrate explanation predicts reduction leaves Vmax essentially unchanged.

citations.title: Redox regulation of PI 3-kinase signalling via inactivation of PTEN.
Reactivation of oxidized PTP1B and PTEN by thioredoxin 1.
Expanding coincident signaling by PTEN through its inositol 1,3,4,5,6-pentakisphosphate 3-phosphatase activity.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the redox mechanism in plain words (PTEN Cys71-Cys124 disulfide, thioredoxin/DTT reactivation), the entities together (purified recombinant PTEN specific activity, oxidized inactive fraction, pre-reduction with DTT), and the prediction (oxidation lowering Vmax while leaving Km unchanged, Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 kinetic parameters). The general mechanism is well published: Leslie et al. (EMBO J 2003) report that PTEN handled in buffers lacking reducing agents loses substantial activity and recovers full activity only after reduction with DTT, and Schwertassek et al. (FEBS J 2014) quantify reactivation of oxidized PTEN by the TRX1/thioredoxin reductase system versus poor reactivation by GSH/Grx — but neither quantifies an oxidized fraction in a preparation used for Michaelis-Menten fitting, nor reports that reduction raises Vmax with Km unaffected. The nearest work on the specific kinetic discrepancy is Caffrey et al. (FEBS Lett 2001), which revisits PTEN activity toward Ins(1,3,4,5)P4 and attributes the earlier low apparent activity to a ~20-fold different Km rather than to a partly oxidized, catalytically dead enzyme population, so the specific Vmax-only explanation is neither stated nor directly tested and refuted.

hypotheses.statement: JNK2's high in vitro activity toward c-Jun reflects its tight docking interaction rather than a productive signalling role, so in cells JNK2 acts as a high-affinity, largely non-activating binder that sequesters c-Jun away from JNK1 and routes it to ubiquitination — which is why removing JNK2 raises, rather than lowers, c-Jun phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Purified-enzyme assays scored JNK2α2 as the better c-Jun kinase, but the same biochemical work attributes to JNK2 a ~25-fold higher binding affinity for c-Jun (sabapathy2004:context:000), and in unstimulated cells most c-Jun is found in complex with JNK2 while after stress it shifts to JNK1 (sabapathy2004:findings:020). Loss of JNK2 also reduces c-Jun ubiquitination (sabapathy2004:findings:021), consistent with the JNK2–c-Jun complex being a degradative/non-productive sink; residual phosphorylation in single knockouts is still JNK-catalysed, since double-null cells have no detectable c-Jun phosphorylation at all (lee2003:findings:003, dong2000:findings:002). Affinity-dominated in vitro assays therefore measure binding, not the in-cell outcome, inverting the apparent isoform ranking.
hypotheses.prediction: A catalytically dead JNK2 should still bind c-Jun, still support its ubiquitination, and still suppress JNK1-dependent c-Jun phosphorylation; conversely, in vitro the apparent superiority of JNK2α2 should vanish or reverse when c-Jun is present in excess over kinase (i.e. under multiple-turnover rather than binding-limited conditions).
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute Jnk1-/-Jnk2-/- fibroblasts with wild-type versus kinase-dead JNK2 (with or without co-expressed JNK1) and measure phospho-S63-c-Jun, total c-Jun, and c-Jun ubiquitination; in parallel run side-by-side recombinant JNK1α1 and JNK2α2 kinase assays across a c-Jun concentration series to extract kcat and Km, and test whether adding kinase-dead JNK2 competitively inhibits JNK1-catalysed c-Jun phosphorylation in vitro.

citations.title: JNK2 is a positive regulator of the cJun transcription factor.
Distinct roles for JNK1 and JNK2 in regulating JNK activity and c-Jun-dependent cell proliferation.

novelty.note: I searched for the sequestration/non-productive-binder model (JNK2 as high-affinity, non-activating c-Jun binder), for the entity combination JNK2 + c-Jun + ubiquitination/degradation, and for the prediction that catalytically inactive JNK2 would still suppress JNK1-dependent c-Jun phosphorylation. The binding/degradative-sink component is indeed published as the interpretation of the Jnk2-/- phenotype (Sabapathy et al., Mol Cell 2004, the corpus source), but Jaeschke et al. (Mol Cell 2006) directly tested the specific claim using an analog-sensitive Jnk2 knock-in in which JNK2 protein remains present at wild-type abundance while only its catalytic activity is acutely inhibited — the opposite of the prediction was observed: blocking JNK2 catalysis lowered rather than raised cJun expression/activation, and both JNK1 and JNK2 were shown to be positive regulators, with the elevated c-Jun of Jnk2-/- cells attributed to compensatory JNK1 rather than to loss of a non-activating sequestering sink. That is a stated negative result against the non-activating-binder claim, hence refuted.

hypotheses.statement: The elevated c-Jun phosphorylation in JNK2-/- cells is largely a substrate-abundance artefact: loss of JNK2 stabilises c-Jun protein post-transcriptionally, enlarging the pool available to JNK1, rather than reflecting genuine JNK1 hyperactivation.
hypotheses.mechanism: In serum-starved Jnk2-/- cells basal c-Jun protein is several-fold higher than wild type while c-jun and c-fos mRNA are unchanged (sabapathy2004:findings:006, sabapathy2004:findings:009), and c-Jun-associated ubiquitin is reduced in Jnk2-/- cells (sabapathy2004:findings:021), pointing to slower degradation as the source of the extra protein. Because all c-Jun phosphorylation requires JNK (none is detectable in JNK1/JNK2 double-null cells; lee2003:findings:003, dong2000:findings:002), a larger substrate pool phosphorylated by unchanged JNK1 would read out as 'constitutive' phospho-c-Jun, and indeed the fold induction of c-Jun kinase activity in Jnk2-/- cells is not significantly different from wild type (sabapathy2004:findings:015).
hypotheses.prediction: Phospho-c-Jun normalised to total c-Jun should be similar in wild-type and Jnk2-/- cells, c-Jun half-life should be longer in Jnk2-/- cells, and raising wild-type c-Jun levels pharmacologically (proteasome inhibition) or by ectopic expression should reproduce the 'constitutive' phospho-c-Jun signal without any change in JNK1 activation.
hypotheses.test: Cycloheximide chase in wild-type, Jnk1-/- and Jnk2-/- fibroblasts to compare c-Jun half-life, combined with quantitative immunoblotting of phospho-S63-c-Jun normalised to total c-Jun and of phospho-JNK1; then titrate exogenous c-Jun (or add a proteasome inhibitor) in wild-type cells to ask whether matching c-Jun levels to the Jnk2-/- level reproduces the elevated phospho-c-Jun signal at constant JNK1 phosphorylation.

citations.title: Distinct roles for JNK1 and JNK2 in regulating JNK activity and c-Jun-dependent cell proliferation.
JNK2 is a positive regulator of the cJun transcription factor.

novelty.note: I searched for JNK2 regulation of c-Jun stability/ubiquitination, for the Jnk2-/- elevated phospho-c-Jun phenotype, and for cycloheximide-chase/substrate-abundance tests of c-Jun phosphorylation; the retrievable literature (Sabapathy et al. 2004 itself) states that JNK2 loss elevates c-Jun stability as well as phosphorylation and that JNK2 bound to unstimulated c-Jun drives its ubiquitination/degradation, so the post-transcriptional stabilisation half of the mechanism is published. What is not published is the specific reinterpretation that the 'constitutive' phospho-c-Jun is merely a substrate-abundance readout at unchanged JNK1 activation: no source reports phospho-c-Jun normalised to total c-Jun, c-Jun half-life comparisons across the three genotypes, or c-Jun titration/proteasome-inhibition reconstitution in wild-type cells. The nearest and partly contrary work is Jaeschke et al. 2006, which used acute chemical-genetic JNK2 inhibition and attributed the Jnk2-/- phenotype to JNK1/JNK2 competition with a compensatory rise in JNK1 activity, i.e. real JNK1 hyperactivation rather than an artefact, but it does not explicitly test and negate the substrate-abundance account, so this is partial rather than refuted.

hypotheses.statement: The high activity of the membrane-tethered TM-ICD construct in COS7 cells may reflect not enforced dimerization but membrane-localized Src-dependent trans-phosphorylation of the EGFR intracellular domain, which the untethered cytosolic ICD cannot access.
hypotheses.mechanism: In COS7 cells specifically, c-Src is reported to act upstream of EGFR, phosphorylating EGFR on Y845 and being required for subsequent EGFR phosphorylation and downstream signalling, with the Src inhibitors PP2 and dasatinib abolishing both Y845 phosphorylation and downstream output (chaturvedi2009:findings:012, chaturvedi2009:findings:013). Src family kinases are also documented to phosphorylate substrates overlapping with EGFR's own specificity (gest2024:findings:208), so anti-phosphotyrosine signal on an immunoprecipitated ICD construct need not be autophosphorylation. Because Src is membrane-associated, appending the transmembrane segment would recruit the ICD to the same compartment, raising its phosphotyrosine content independent of any dimerization-driven change in intrinsic kinase activity.
hypotheses.prediction: Src inhibition should strongly reduce the phosphotyrosine signal on TM-ICD while leaving the GCN4-ICD construct (dimerized but soluble) comparatively unaffected, and the residual TM-ICD signal under Src inhibition should fall toward the low level seen for ICD alone.
hypotheses.test: Transfect COS7 cells with ICD, TM-ICD, and GCN4-ICD at the same low DNA levels, treat with PP2 versus the inactive analogue PP3 (and dasatinib as a second inhibitor), then immunoprecipitate each construct and blot with anti-phosphotyrosine plus a site-specific anti-pY845 antibody; a selective, Src-inhibitor-sensitive loss of signal in TM-ICD but not GCN4-ICD supports Src-mediated membrane trans-phosphorylation, whereas equal insensitivity of both supports the enforced-dimerization interpretation. An in vitro kinase assay on the immunopurified constructs with no added Src provides the complementary intrinsic-activity control.

citations.title: Ligand-Independent EGFR Activation by Anchorage-Stimulated Src Promotes Cancer Cell Proliferation and Cetuximab Resistance via ErbB3 Phosphorylation.
Molecular basis for multimerization in the activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor.
Peptide-based NTA(Ni)-nanodiscs for studying membrane enhanced FGFR1 kinase activities.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the construct comparison (membrane-tethered TM-ICD vs soluble ICD vs GCN4-forced dimer in COS-7), the mechanism in plain words (membrane-localized Src trans-phosphorylating the EGFR intracellular domain at Y845), and the prediction (Src-inhibitor sensitivity of phosphotyrosine on isolated EGFR ICD constructs). The general mechanism is published — Src-driven, ligand-independent EGFR tyrosine phosphorylation reduced by Src inhibition (PMID 31615015) — and the alternative, Src-free explanation is also published, since membrane anchoring alone raises autophosphorylation of an isolated RTK kinase domain in a purified nanodisc system with no Src present (PMID 31372315). Nothing I retrieved states or tests the specific claim that the TM-ICD construct's high activity in COS-7 cells is Src-dependent rather than dimerization-driven; the nearest experimental context (EGFR constructs and membrane-localization tags in COS-7) does not examine Src function at all (PMID 27017828), so this is partial rather than established or refuted.

hypotheses.statement: Residual phosphorylation of TSC2 by kinases redundant with Akt (e.g., RSK, SGK) and by MAP-kinase-pathway kinases maintains 14-3-3 binding when individual Akt sites are mutated, so no single site such as Ser939 appears 'required' in cells even if it can support binding in a purified assay.
hypotheses.mechanism: manning2017:findings:028 states that RSK can phosphorylate the TSC2 sites Ser939 and Thr1462 and that SGK1/SGK3 can substitute for AKT in TSC2 phosphorylation, and ma2005:findings:001 shows TSC2 phosphorylation is driven by both MAP kinase and PI3K/Akt inputs since only combined U0126 plus wortmannin gives a further reduction. Consistent with this, li2002:findings:010 finds single-pathway inhibitors (wortmannin, PD98059) fail to reduce the TSC2–14-3-3 interaction, implying multiple parallel kinase inputs can keep a 14-3-3 site phosphorylated. Under this model a purified Ser939 phosphopeptide competition assay detects a real but substitutable contact.
hypotheses.prediction: Simultaneous blockade of the parallel kinase inputs (PI3K/Akt plus MEK/ERK-RSK, and SGK) should reduce 14-3-3 binding to wild-type TSC2 and to S939A, whereas each inhibitor alone will not, and in vitro rephosphorylation of dephosphorylated S939A TSC2 by RSK or SGK should restore 14-3-3 binding.
hypotheses.test: Co-immunoprecipitate 14-3-3 with HA-TSC2 (wild type and S939A) from HEK293 cells treated with wortmannin, U0126, an RSK inhibitor and an SGK inhibitor alone and in combination; separately dephosphorylate purified GST-TSC2 (wild type and S939A) with lambda phosphatase, rephosphorylate in vitro with recombinant Akt, RSK or SGK1, and assay 14-3-3 pull-down to see which kinases restore binding in the absence of Ser939.

citations.title: PDK1-SGK1 Signaling Sustains AKT-Independent mTORC1 Activation and Confers Resistance to PI3Kα Inhibition.
Tumor-promoting phorbol esters and activated Ras inactivate the tuberous sclerosis tumor suppressor complex via p90 ribosomal S6 kinase.
The p38 and MK2 kinase cascade phosphorylates tuberin, the tuberous sclerosis 2 gene product, and enhances its interaction with 14-3-3.
Identification and characterization of the interaction between tuberin and 14-3-3zeta.

Pharmacological and genetic evaluation of proposed roles of mitogen-activated protein kinase/extracellular signal-regulated kinase kinase (MEK), extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK), and p90(RSK) in the control of mTORC1 protein signaling by phorbol esters.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the redundancy mechanism in words (RSK/SGK substituting for Akt on TSC2 S939/T1462), the entities together (TSC2 + 14-3-3 + Ser939 + Akt-site requirement), and the prediction (combined PI3K/MEK inhibition reducing TSC2-14-3-3 binding). The component kinase redundancy is well published — RSK acting on the TSC1/TSC2 complex downstream of Ras/phorbol esters, and SGK1 sustaining AKT-independent TSC2 phosphorylation and mTORC1 activity — and alternative Akt-independent explanations for the insensitivity of TSC2-14-3-3 binding to single-pathway inhibitors exist (a p38/MK2-phosphorylated site enhancing 14-3-3 binding; multiple 14-3-3 contact sites in tuberin). However, no retrieved source states that parallel kinase inputs maintain 14-3-3 binding when Ser939 is mutated, nor tests combined inhibitor blockade or in vitro RSK/SGK rephosphorylation of S939A TSC2; one study reports MEK inhibition does not reduce Ser939/Thr1462 phosphorylation in cells, which bears on but does not directly test the 14-3-3 prediction, so the status is partial.

hypotheses.statement: The failure of p38 Tyr323/Thr180-Tyr182 phosphorylation in P116 may reflect loss of Zap70-dependent LAT/SLP-76 scaffold assembly feeding the canonical MKK3/6 input to p38, rather than a requirement for Zap70 to phosphorylate p38 directly.
hypotheses.mechanism: Zap70 kinase activity is required to phosphorylate LAT and SLP-76 and assemble downstream signalling complexes, and loss of either scaffold abolishes TCR signal transduction as completely as ZAP-70 loss (good2011:findings:006, smithgarvin2009:findings:007). Since p38 activation-loop Thr-Gly-Tyr phosphorylation is normally catalysed by MKK3/MKK6 (cargnello2011:findings:005, cuadrado2010:findings:000), a kinase-dead Zap70 would abolish the scaffold-dependent MAP2K input and so eliminate both readouts without Zap70 ever acting on p38 itself.
hypotheses.prediction: In P116 the p38 module itself should be intact and inducible by stimuli that engage MKK3/6 independently of the TCR, and supplying an active MAP2K should restore activation-loop phosphorylation while Tyr323 phosphorylation remains absent.
hypotheses.test: In P116 and Zap70-reconstituted cells, compare anti-TCR with osmotic shock/anisomycin stimulation by immunoblot for phospho-Thr180-Tyr182 and phospho-Tyr323; then express constitutively active MKK6 (or knock down MKK3/6 in the wild-type-Zap70 reconstituted line) and ask whether activation-loop phosphorylation is restored (or lost) while Tyr323 phosphorylation behaves independently.

citations.title: Alternative p38 activation pathway mediated by T cell receptor-proximal tyrosine kinases.
Genetic disruption of p38alpha Tyr323 phosphorylation prevents T-cell receptor-mediated p38alpha activation and impairs interferon-gamma production.
Alternative ZAP70-p38 signals prime a classical p38 pathway through LAT and SOS to support regulatory T cell differentiation.

novelty.note: I searched for the ZAP-70/p38 Tyr323 alternative activation pathway, for ZAP-70-deficient P116 cells with MKK3/6-independent p38 activation, and for the prediction that an active MAP2K would restore activation-loop phosphorylation. Salvador et al. (Nat Immunol 2005) directly tested this alternative: TCR-stimulated p38 is phosphorylated on Tyr323 and then autophosphorylates Thr180/Tyr182, this requires Zap70 but explicitly does NOT require the LAT scaffold, and a p38 inhibitor blocks dual phosphorylation in T cells — excluding a scaffold-dependent MAP2K input as the route; Mittelstadt et al. (Blood 2009) confirmed with a p38alpha Y323F knock-in that TCR stimulation fails to phosphorylate the activation motif, concluding the Tyr323 pathway 'and not the classic MAP kinase cascade' is the physiologic means of TCR-induced p38alpha activation. Because the specific proposed mechanism (LAT/SLP-76-dependent MKK3/6 input rather than direct Zap70 action on p38) has been tested and reported not to hold, the status is refuted.

hypotheses.statement: Lck in P116 may be functional basally but rapidly inactivated after TCR ligation because the Zap70-dependent Erk feedback that protects Lck from SHP1 is missing, so the experiment cannot place Lck upstream of Zap70.
hypotheses.mechanism: TCR ligation triggers Lck-mediated SHP1 phosphorylation that dephosphorylates the Lck active site, and this is normally counteracted by Erk-mediated Lck Ser59 phosphorylation during strong agonist signalling (smithgarvin2009:findings:027). Erk activation requires Zap70-dependent LAT/SLP-76 assembly (good2011:findings:006, smithgarvin2009:findings:007), so in Zap70-null P116 cells Lck would be shut off by SHP1 shortly after stimulation, removing the kinase the authors assume is active and able to phosphorylate p38 Tyr323.
hypotheses.prediction: P116 cells should show normal basal but sharply decaying Lck active-site phosphorylation and elevated SHP1 phosphorylation after anti-TCR, with the decay rescued by wild-type but not kinase-inactive Zap70; blocking SHP1 should partially restore p38 Tyr323 phosphorylation in P116.
hypotheses.test: Time-course immunoblots of Lck active-site (Tyr394) and Ser59 phosphorylation plus SHP1 phosphorylation in P116, kinase-dead-Zap70 and wild-type-Zap70 reconstituted lines after anti-TCR, combined with SHP1 knockdown or a tyrosine-phosphatase inhibitor to test whether p38 Tyr323 phosphorylation is recovered in the absence of Zap70.

citations.title: Biophysical basis underlying dynamic Lck activation visualized by ZapLck FRET biosensor.
A THEMIS:SHP1 complex promotes T-cell survival.

novelty.note: I searched three ways: the Erk→Lck-Ser59 / SHP1 feedback mechanism in words, the entities together (P116 Zap70-deficient Jurkat + Lck activity/phosphorylation after TCR stimulation), and the prediction of Zap70-dependent decay of Lck activity. The ZapLck FRET biosensor study directly measured Lck kinase activity in Zap70-deficient P116 cells after CD3/CD28 ligation and reports Lck activation and biosensor responses similar to parental Jurkat and JCam-LckWT cells (PP1-sensitive), i.e. no Zap70 requirement for sustaining Lck activity after stimulation; separately, LCK-Ser59Ala knock-in mice show normal TCR signalling and ligand discrimination, so the Erk-Ser59 arm that the mechanism depends on does not hold in vivo. Both reported negative results contradict the specific claim rather than merely failing to support it, so the status is refuted.

hypotheses.statement: The two readouts may not be independent: a single defect in Tyr323 phosphorylation would also abolish Thr180-Tyr182 signal, so the parallel loss does not require Zap70 to act on both sites.
hypotheses.mechanism: In T cells Tyr323 phosphorylation by Zap70/Lck is reported to drive p38alpha autophosphorylation of the activation loop rather than MAP2K-dependent activation (cuadrado2010:findings:006), and GADD45alpha can block the whole cascade simply by occluding Tyr323. Because activation-loop phosphorylation is also achievable through MKK3/6 (cargnello2011:findings:005), loss of both marks in P116 is consistent with an exclusively Tyr323-initiated, autophosphorylation-dependent route being the only one engaged by anti-TCR in Jurkat cells.
hypotheses.prediction: A p38alpha mutant that cannot be phosphorylated on Tyr323, or one that is catalytically dead, should lose anti-TCR-induced Thr180-Tyr182 phosphorylation in Zap70-replete Jurkat cells, whereas MAP2K-driven stimuli should still phosphorylate the activation loop of the Tyr323 mutant.
hypotheses.test: Express HA-tagged p38alpha wild type, Y323F, and a kinase-dead variant in Jurkat (and wild-type-Zap70-reconstituted P116) cells and immunoblot tagged p38 for phospho-Thr180-Tyr182 after anti-TCR versus osmotic shock; dependence of the activation-loop signal on Tyr323 and on p38's own catalytic activity selectively after anti-TCR discriminates autophosphorylation from MAP2K input.

citations.title: Alternative p38 activation pathway mediated by T cell receptor-proximal tyrosine kinases.
Genetic disruption of p38alpha Tyr323 phosphorylation prevents T-cell receptor-mediated p38alpha activation and impairs interferon-gamma production.
Unique properties of TCR-activated p38 are necessary for NFAT-dependent T-cell activation.

novelty.note: I searched for the alternative T-cell p38 activation route (Tyr323 phosphorylation by Zap70/Lck followed by activation-loop autophosphorylation), for Y323F mutant effects on Thr180/Tyr182 signal after TCR versus stress stimuli, and for MKK3/6-independence of this route. Salvador et al. (Nat Immunol 2005) already report that in TCR-stimulated T cells p38 is phosphorylated on Tyr323 and then autophosphorylates its activation loop in a Zap70-dependent, LAT-independent manner, i.e. the activation-loop mark in TCR signaling is downstream of (not independent of) Tyr323; Mittelstadt et al. (Blood 2009) show genetically that p38alpha-Y323F fails to be activated by TCR stimulation while stress/MKK-driven activation is retained. This is the same explanation and the same prediction, so the hypothesis is established rather than open.

hypotheses.statement: The Syk linker tyrosines act as phosphorylation-dependent docking sites for downstream partners rather than as intrinsic catalytic regulators, so their mutation leaves activity toward a generic exogenous substrate like cdb3 unchanged while disrupting signalling.
hypotheses.mechanism: mcsai2010:findings:012 states that phosphorylated Tyr342 and Tyr346 bind the SH2 domains of VAV1 and PLCγ1 and that mutating them inhibits FcεRI signalling and phenocopies Syk-deficient cytoskeletal defects, and mcsai2010:findings:013 states phospho-Tyr624 recruits SLP65. ishiai1999:findings:010 further shows that losing a Syk-dependent scaffold (BLNK) leaves bulk receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphorylation, i.e. kinase activation, essentially intact. Together these imply the linker tyrosines operate at the level of partner recruitment, a function invisible in a cell-free assay with a non-docking substrate.
hypotheses.prediction: Wild-type and linker-tyrosine mutant Syk should phosphorylate cdb3 equally, but mutants should be markedly impaired at phosphorylating substrates whose phosphorylation depends on SH2-mediated docking to the linker region (e.g. PLCγ or BLNK/SLP65 fragments), and should fail to co-precipitate those partners.
hypotheses.test: Immunoprecipitate equal amounts of wild-type and each linker mutant Syk from the transduced cells and run parallel in vitro [γ-32P]ATP kinase assays on cdb3 versus recombinant PLCγ and BLNK/SLP65 fragments; in parallel, pull down with GST–SH2 domains of VAV1, PLCγ1 and SLP65 from lysates of autophosphorylated wild-type versus mutant Syk. A substrate-selective loss accompanied by loss of SH2 binding, with preserved cdb3 activity, supports docking failure rather than catalytic impairment.

citations.title: Distinct roles for the linker region tyrosines of Syk in FcepsilonRI signaling in primary mast cells.
Regulation of signaling in B cells through the phosphorylation of Syk on linker region tyrosines. A mechanism for negative signaling by the Lyn tyrosine kinase.
Phosphorylation of Tyr342 in the linker region of Syk is critical for Fc epsilon RI signaling in mast cells.

novelty.note: I searched for the Syk interdomain-B/linker tyrosines as phosphotyrosine docking sites, for Y342F/Y346F mutant kinase activity toward exogenous substrates (band 3 cytoplasmic domain), and for Y624–SLP-65 SH2 recruitment, using Europe PMC/PubMed and publisher pages. The docking-site explanation and the substrate-selective consequence are published: Hong/Geahlen-type work shows pTyr342/pTyr346 create an SH2 docking site enhancing PLCγ phosphorylation, and retroviral reconstitution of Syk-deficient primary mast cells with linker mutants shows selective loss of PLCγ1/PLCγ2/Vav1 phosphorylation while degranulation is affected only by the double mutant. However, the premise that these tyrosines are not intrinsic catalytic regulators is not supported in general: Zhang et al. report that Y342F Syk has reduced kinase activity (and reduced ITAM binding), and Tyr317 is an inhibitory regulatory site, so the specific prediction of unchanged activity toward a generic substrate is only partly consistent with the literature.

hypotheses.statement: The Syk linker tyrosines are functionally degenerate for PLCγ1 but not for the adaptor arm, so Y342F selectively breaks the LAT/SLP-76-dependent route that PLCγ2 requires while PLCγ1 is still recruited and phosphorylated via the remaining Y346 site.
hypotheses.mechanism: mcsai2010:findings:012 states that phospho-Y342 binds the VAV1 SH2 domain while BOTH phospho-Y342 and phospho-Y346 bind the PLCγ1 C-terminal SH2 domain, so a single Y342F substitution leaves one intact PLCγ1 docking site but removes the site needed for the rest of the linker-dependent output. Independently, ishiai1999:context:000 and ishiai1999:findings:005 show that coupling Syk to PLCγ2 activation requires a dedicated adaptor (BLNK/SLP-76-type) and that bypassing the adaptor with a membrane-targeted PLCγ2 chimera restores phosphorylation and calcium, i.e. PLCγ2 output is adaptor-scaffold-limited whereas direct linker docking can serve PLCγ1. Combining these, Y342F should read out as reduced LAT/SLP-76 and PLCγ2 phosphorylation and reduced calcium/degranulation with preserved PLCγ1 phosphorylation, exactly the reported pattern.
hypotheses.prediction: In Syk-deficient RBL-2H3 cells, the Y342F/Y346F double mutant (but neither single mutant) should abolish PLCγ1 phosphorylation and PLCγ1 co-precipitation with Syk, while a membrane-targeted PLCγ2 chimera expressed in Y342F cells should restore calcium flux without restoring LAT/SLP-76 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: Reconstitute Syk-deficient RBL-2H3 cells with wild-type, Y342F, Y346F and Y342F/Y346F Syk and compare (i) anti-Syk co-immunoprecipitation of PLCγ1 and Vav1, (ii) PLCγ1, PLCγ2, LAT and SLP-76 phosphoblots, and (iii) Fura-2/Indo-1 calcium flux; in parallel express an FcγRIII/PLCγ2 membrane chimera in the Y342F line and test whether calcium is rescued while adaptor phosphorylation stays low. A degenerate-docking model predicts loss of PLCγ1 binding only in the double mutant and chimera rescue; a model in which Y342F acts through a general upstream defect predicts the single mutant already loses PLCγ1 binding and no chimera rescue.

citations.title: Distinct roles for the linker region tyrosines of Syk in FcepsilonRI signaling in primary mast cells.
Phosphorylation of Tyr342 in the linker region of Syk is critical for Fc epsilon RI signaling in mast cells.
Mast cell signaling: the role of protein tyrosine kinase Syk, its activation and screening methods for new pathway participants.

novelty.note: I searched for the Syk linker tyrosines 342/346 with PLCγ1/Vav docking, for the Y342F/Y346F mutant panel in Syk-deficient mast cells, and for the LAT/SLP-76 vs. PLCγ2 adaptor-requirement angle; the decisive work is Simon et al. (JBC 2005), which reconstituted Syk-deficient primary mast cells with exactly the Y342F, Y346F and double-mutant panel. It reports the opposite of both halves of the prediction: phosphorylation of PLCγ1 (as well as PLCγ2 and Vav1) was strongly decreased by mutation of Tyr342 alone, while mutation of either tyrosine alone had no effect on FcεRI-induced calcium flux or degranulation, which only fell in the double mutant — so Y342/Y346 are not degenerate for PLCγ1, and Y342F does not by itself break calcium/degranulation. Zhang et al. (2002) additionally supports the competing general-upstream-defect reading, since Y342F Syk showed reduced ITAM binding and reduced kinase activity alongside loss of LAT, SLP-76 and PLCγ2 phosphorylation.

hypotheses.statement: Bulk PLCγ1 tyrosine phosphorylation is an unreliable proxy for pathway flux in this system, so 'normal' PLCγ1 phosphorylation in SykY342F cells can coexist with lost calcium and degranulation because the activity-determining phosphosites and the functionally limiting isoform were not assayed.
hypotheses.mechanism: balla2013:findings:056 states that enzyme activity depends on specific residues (PLCγ1 Y783/Y775 relieving autoinhibition; PLCγ2 Y753/Y759 for B-cell activation), so a pan-phosphotyrosine or total-phospho readout need not report activating occupancy. xu2009a:findings:002 directly documents the dissociation: in PLCγ2-deficient cells PLCγ1 remains activated with sustained phosphorylation yet calcium flux is only residual, showing phosphorylated PLCγ1 cannot carry the calcium output. Under this view the Y342F phenotype is internally consistent rather than surprising, and the apparent contrast with mast cell data reflects readout choice, not a different Syk requirement.
hypotheses.prediction: Site-specific blots of SykY342F-reconstituted cells should show reduced phospho-Y783 PLCγ1 and/or reduced PLCγ2 Y753/Y759 despite unchanged total PLCγ1 phosphotyrosine signal, and selective PLCγ2 depletion in wild-type Syk cells should reproduce the calcium/degranulation defect without lowering total PLCγ1 phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In Syk-deficient RBL-2H3 cells reconstituted with wild-type or Y342F Syk, blot in parallel with pan-phosphotyrosine after PLCγ1 immunoprecipitation and with phospho-site-specific antibodies (PLCγ1 pY783, PLCγ2 pY753/pY759) across a 0–10 min stimulation time course, and separately knock down PLCγ1 or PLCγ2 in wild-type-Syk cells and measure calcium flux and degranulation. If the readout-artifact hypothesis holds, site-specific signals and PLCγ2 dependence track the functional defect while total PLCγ1 phosphotyrosine does not; if PLCγ1 activation is genuinely intact and sufficient, pY783 will be unchanged and PLCγ1 knockdown will phenocopy the Y342F defect.

citations.title: Phosphorylation of Tyr342 in the linker region of Syk is critical for Fc epsilon RI signaling in mast cells.
Distinct roles for the linker region tyrosines of Syk in FcepsilonRI signaling in primary mast cells.
Mechanism of phosphorylation-induced activation of phospholipase C-gamma isozymes.
Intramolecular interaction between phosphorylated tyrosine-783 and the C-terminal Src homology 2 domain activates phospholipase C-gamma1.

novelty.note: I searched for the SykY342F mast-cell phenotype (normal PLCγ1 phosphotyrosine with lost calcium/degranulation), for the site-specificity of PLCγ activation (Y783/Y759 relieving cSH2 autoinhibition), and for isoform-selective PLCγ1 vs PLCγ2 requirements in mast cells. The component mechanisms are well published — phosphorylation of PLCγ1 Tyr783 / PLCγ2 Tyr759 and its intramolecular cSH2 engagement are established as the activity-determining event, and the Y342F papers report the dissociation between PLCγ1 and PLCγ2 phosphorylation (with the primary-mast-cell study instead finding PLCγ1 phosphorylation also reduced) — but no retrieved source frames bulk PLCγ1 phosphotyrosine as a misleading proxy in SykY342F cells, nor tests the predicted site-specific blots or PLCγ2-selective depletion phenocopy. Nothing reports a direct negative test of this specific claim, so partial rather than established or refuted.

hypotheses.statement: EGFR activity is a required upstream input for activation of the ERK2 isoform specifically, acting indirectly through the MEK-dependent activation-loop phosphorylation of ERK2 rather than by EGFR phosphorylating ERK2 itself.
hypotheses.mechanism: The EGFR claims show that ERK1/2 activation strictly requires EGFR expression, EGFR kinase activity, and specific EGFR phosphotyrosines (Y845, Y992, and the five major autophosphorylation sites), since kinase-dead K721M, Y5F, Y845F receptors and AG1478 all abolish the response while Y992F prolongs it. The ERK2 claims establish that ERK2's own activating site (Thr183/Thr203) is a near-exclusive MEK substrate selected against by essentially all other human kinases, and that catalytically activated ERK2 phosphorylates defined substrates such as Raptor and hSos1 and homodimerizes upon activation-loop phosphorylation. Together these imply EGFR sits upstream of the MEK-ERK2 module and controls ERK2 catalytic output without contacting ERK2 as a substrate.
hypotheses.prediction: Blocking or mutating EGFR should reduce dual phosphorylation of ERK2's activation loop and the catalytic activity of immunoprecipitated ERK2 toward its substrates (Raptor pS/T-P, hSos1), while recombinant EGFR kinase should fail to phosphorylate purified unphosphorylated ERK2 in vitro; EGFR Y992F should instead give prolonged, not reduced, ERK2 activation-loop phosphorylation and substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293 or B82L cells expressing HA-ERK2 together with wild-type, K721M, Y5F, or Y992F EGFR, stimulate with EGF ± AG1478 ± U0126, then (i) immunoblot HA-ERK2 for pThr183/pTyr185 and (ii) immunoprecipitate HA-ERK2 and assay [γ-32P]ATP incorporation into purified myc-Raptor; in parallel, incubate purified recombinant active EGFR kinase domain with unphosphorylated recombinant ERK2 in vitro and probe for ERK2 activation-loop phosphorylation and acquired Raptor kinase activity, which should be absent if the relationship is upstream and MEK-dependent rather than direct.

citations.title: Targeting Aberrant RAS/RAF/MEK/ERK Signaling for Cancer Therapy.
P2Y2 Receptor and EGFR Cooperate to Promote Prostate Cancer Cell Invasion via ERK1/2 Pathway.
Molecular basis of mitogen-activated protein kinase ERK2 activation by its upstream kinase MEK1.

novelty.note: I searched for the EGF-receptor-to-ERK2 route in plain mechanistic terms (EGFR → Ras/Raf → MEK → ERK activation-loop phosphorylation), for the entities together (EGFR kinase-dead/autophosphorylation-site mutants, AG1478, U0126, Thr183/Tyr185), and for the specificity claim that MEK is the activating kinase of the ERK2 TEY loop. The canonical cascade is explicitly published: reviews state that EGFR initiates signalling that loads RAS with GTP and that it is MEK1/2, not the receptor, that phosphorylates the conserved Thr/Tyr of the ERK1/2 activation loop, and primary work shows EGFR kinase inhibition with AG1478 suppresses ERK1/2 phosphorylation while the same phosphorylation is blocked by the MEK inhibitor U0126, i.e. EGFR is a required indirect upstream input. Structural/biochemical work on MEK1-ERK2 confirms the activation-loop Thr/Tyr of the TxY motif as the MEK1 phosphoacceptor, so the explanation — EGFR upstream, MEK-dependent, not EGFR phosphorylating ERK2 — is already stated rather than novel.

hypotheses.statement: SRC kinase activity acts upstream of ERK2 and is required for growth-factor-induced ERK2 activation, through an indirect route via the MEK pathway rather than by SRC phosphorylating ERK2 itself.
hypotheses.mechanism: Two independent papers show that blocking Src reduces ERK output. Src knockdown in HEK293 cells lowered EGF-stimulated GAB1 phosphorylation and changed phospho-ERK levels without affecting EGFR autophosphorylation. In SW13, B82L and COS7 cells, PP2 and dasatinib abolished rapamycin-induced Erk1/2 phosphorylation. Separately, Gab1–SHP2 association is reported to drive ERK2 activation, and constitutive Gab1-PH–SHP2 signalling activates MEK1 and ERK2. ERK2's activation site is selected against by nearly every kinase except MEK1, so any SRC effect on ERK2 is most plausibly upstream of MEK rather than direct.
hypotheses.prediction: Depleting or inhibiting SRC should markedly reduce EGF-stimulated ERK2 activation-loop phosphorylation and ERK2 kinase activity. Purified active SRC should fail to directly phosphorylate or activate recombinant ERK2 in vitro, whereas MEK1 should.
hypotheses.test: In HEK293 cells, compare EGF-stimulated cells treated with Src siRNA or PP2 against non-targeting siRNA or PP3. Measure ERK2 specifically by anti-ERK2 immunoprecipitation followed by an in vitro kinase assay with a GST-Elk1 substrate, and by immunoblot for ERK2 activation-loop phosphorylation. In parallel, run an in vitro kinase assay using purified active SRC versus active MEK1 with recombinant ERK2 to test for direct phosphorylation.

novelty.note: I searched three ways — the mechanism in words (Src required upstream of MEK for growth-factor-induced ERK activation), the entities together (Src/PP2 + Gab1/SHP2 + EGF + ERK), and the prediction (direct Src phosphorylation of ERK2 in vitro) — using PubMed/Europe PMC and publisher pages. The canonical placement of Src upstream of the Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK cascade, and specifically Src-family-kinase requirement for sustained GAB1–SHP2 signalling and ERK activity downstream of EGFR, is published (Furcht 2015), as is the Gab–SHP2 requirement for EGF-stimulated ERK activation (Gu/Kong 2005) and the loss of ERK1/2 activation upon PP2 treatment with intact receptor-level signalling (Kuwahara 2006); MEK1/2 are also described as the only kinases acting on the ERK activation loop. I found no paper reporting a direct in vitro test of Src phosphorylating ERK2, so only that control remains unaddressed; one study found Src dispensable for GPCR-to-MAPK coupling, which is a context-specific limit rather than a refutation, so I cite it as nearest.

hypotheses.statement: EGFR kinase activity negatively regulates TSC2 by driving its inhibitory phosphorylation at Ser664 (by ERK) and Ser1798 (by RSK). This is a regulatory relationship mediated through ERK/RSK, not a physical interaction.
hypotheses.mechanism: EGFR kinase activity and its autophosphorylation sites (Y992, Y1068, Y1086, Y1148, Y1173) are required for Erk1/2 and RSK activation: kinase-dead K721M, the inhibitor AG1478 and the Y5F mutant each abolish it, and ERK pathway output decays when EGFR is inhibited. Independently, ERK and RSK phosphorylate TSC2 at Ser664 and Ser1798, which suppresses TSC2 GAP activity toward Rheb. Ras/MAPK signaling is also established to inactivate TSC2 through these kinases. Together these imply that EGFR kinase signaling sets the level of TSC2 inhibitory phosphorylation.
hypotheses.prediction: TSC2 Ser664 and Ser1798 phosphorylation should depend on EGFR kinase activity and autophosphorylation sites. Stimulating cells expressing wt-EGFR should increase phosphorylation at both sites. This increase should be lost in cells expressing EGFR K721M or Y5F, or after AG1478 treatment. Rheb-GTP loading should fall in parallel.
hypotheses.test: Use B82L cells expressing wt-EGFR, K721M-EGFR or Y5F-EGFR, with or without AG1478. Stimulate them, then immunoblot for phospho-TSC2 Ser664 and Ser1798, total TSC2, phospho-ERK and phospho-RSK, and measure Rheb-GTP loading. To check that the effect runs through ERK/RSK, test whether constitutively active MEK or a RSK inhibitor uncouples TSC2 phosphorylation from EGFR status.

Polycystin-1 regulates extracellular signal-regulated kinase-dependent phosphorylation of tuberin to control cell size through mTOR and its downstream effectors S6K and 4EBP1.
Lysosomal EGFR acts as a Rheb-GEF independent of its kinase activity to activate mTORC1.

novelty.note: I searched the mechanism in words (EGFR→ERK/RSK→TSC2 inactivation), the entities together (EGFR, TSC2 Ser664, Ser1798, RSK, Rheb), and the prediction (EGF/EGFR-inhibitor dependence of TSC2 S664/S1798 phosphorylation, Rheb-GTP). The ERK→TSC2-Ser664 and RSK→TSC2-Ser1798 inhibitory-phosphorylation mechanism and its suppression of TSC2 GAP activity toward Rheb are well published, and retrieved primary papers show MEK/ERK-dependent Ser664 phosphorylation controlling Rheb/mTORC1, but those used PMA, PDGF or serum rather than EGFR-specific manipulation; I found no work testing dependence of Ser664/Ser1798 phosphorylation on EGFR kinase activity or its autophosphorylation sites (K721M, Y5F, AG1478). The closest EGFR-to-Rheb work reports a kinase-independent EGFR GEF activity acting separately from TSC2 phosphorylation, so the specific EGFR-dependence claim is neither stated nor directly refuted.

hypotheses.statement: Insulin-stimulated PI3K activity positively regulates TGF-β-induced R-Smad (Smad2/3) activation, and it does so by increasing cell-surface TβRI/TβRII available to recruit and phosphorylate R-Smads.
hypotheses.mechanism: In NMuMG cells, the insulin-induced rise in cell-surface TβRI and TβRII is prevented by the PI3K inhibitor GDC0941 and the Akt inhibitor AktVIII, but not by MEK inhibition (budi2015:findings:006). In the same cells, insulin enhances TGF-β/Smad-dependent target gene expression at low TGF-β concentration, and SB431542 prevents this (budi2015:findings:023). Separately, R-Smad activation requires direct engagement of the phosphorylated GS domain of the type I receptor and phosphorylation-dependent receptor modification (derynck2019:findings:016, derynck2019:findings:014). Together these imply that PI3K could raise R-Smad activation by controlling how many activated receptors are available at the surface.
hypotheses.prediction: In NMuMG cells given low-dose TGF-β (0.2 ng/ml), insulin should increase C-terminal phosphorylation of Smad2/3 and Smad-dependent reporter activity, and GDC0941 should abolish this increase. Because GDC0941 alone raises surface receptor levels without insulin (budi2015:findings:006), it should not lower Smad2/3 phosphorylation in the absence of insulin.
hypotheses.test: Pretreat serum-starved NMuMG cells with or without GDC0941 (or PI3K catalytic-subunit siRNA). Stimulate with insulin plus 0.2 ng/ml TGF-β, then immunoblot for C-terminal phospho-Smad2 and phospho-Smad3 over a time course. In parallel, run a Smad-responsive luciferase reporter and surface biotinylation of TβRI. Finally, test whether expressing constitutively active Akt restores the insulin effect when PI3K is inhibited.

novelty.note: I searched for the mechanism in words (insulin/PI3K-Akt raising cell-surface TβRI/TβRII and thereby Smad2/3 activation), for the entity combination (insulin + GDC0941/AktVIII + surface TGF-β receptors + NMuMG), and for the prediction (insulin boosting low-dose TGF-β-induced Smad phosphorylation/reporter activity). The source paper of the corpus claims itself (PMID 26420907, verified via Europe PMC/Crossref) states the full explanation: Akt (downstream of insulin-activated PI3K) phosphorylates AS160 to translocate TGF-β receptors to the plasma membrane of NMuMG cells, which 'enabled insulin to increase TGF-β-induced gene responses' and autocrine Smad signaling; the same mechanism is restated and extended to Smad2/3-dependent transcription in endothelial cells (PMIDs 30684493, 31740700). No source reports a direct negative test; the nearest contrary work (PMID 25998442) finds PI3K/mTORC2 limits Smad2/3 activity duration via linker phosphorylation in human ES cells, a different context and mechanism rather than a refutation of the receptor-availability route.

hypotheses.statement: Mouse SYK acts upstream of MAPK and is required for receptor-induced MAPK activation, and through it for MAPK-dependent downstream substrate phosphorylation.
hypotheses.mechanism: In mouse BMDCs, curdlan induced rapid phosphorylation of p38, Erk and Jnk, and this phosphorylation depended on Syk. In DT40 B cells, Syk deficiency completely abolished BCR-induced ERK2 activation, whereas loss of the Syk substrate BLNK only reduced it. This points to SYK as a required upstream activator of MAPK-family kinases. Ras/MAPK pathway activation drives RSK1/2-specific phosphorylation of rpS6 at Ser235/236, so SYK-dependent MAPK activation should extend to this downstream MAPK output.
hypotheses.prediction: In mouse myeloid cells, loss or inhibition of SYK should abolish or strongly reduce stimulus-induced phosphorylation of ERK and p38. It should also reduce the MAPK/RSK-dependent rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation that follows. Re-expressing kinase-active SYK, but not a kinase-dead mutant, should restore both.
hypotheses.test: In a cultured mouse myeloid cell line responsive to curdlan, knock down SYK by siRNA or CRISPR, or treat with a SYK inhibitor. Then stimulate with curdlan and run immunoblots over a time course for phospho-ERK1/2, phospho-p38 and rpS6 pSer235/236 (with S6K inhibited by rapamycin so the rpS6 signal reflects RSK). Rescue the knockdown with wild-type versus kinase-dead SYK.

novelty.note: I searched for Syk-dependence of Dectin-1/curdlan-induced ERK and p38 phosphorylation in myeloid cells, for Syk inhibitor effects on MAPK, and for any link between Syk and RSK-dependent rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation. The first half of the hypothesis is explicitly published: ERK activation by zymosan/Dectin-1 is completely blocked in Syk-deficient murine DC, and Syk inhibition blunts Dectin-1-driven MAP kinase signalling in DC and macrophages; separately, RSK1/2-specific rpS6 Ser235/236 phosphorylation downstream of RAS/ERK is well established. However, I found no source that tests or states the extension of Syk-dependent MAPK activation to rpS6 Ser235/236 in myeloid cells, nor any kinase-dead-versus-wild-type Syk rescue of that readout, so the specific prediction remains unaddressed rather than refuted.

hypotheses.statement: PKC positively regulates (activates) mTORC1 by driving ERK1/2-mediated phosphorylation of Raptor.
hypotheses.mechanism: In vascular smooth muscle cells, PKC activation leads to C-raf-dependent phosphorylation and activation of ERK (brozovich2016:findings:030). Independently, ERK1/2 directly phosphorylate Raptor, Ras/MAPK signaling activates mTORC1 (carriere2010:context:004), and a phosphorylation-deficient Raptor S3A mutant or MEK1/2 inhibition reduces mTORC1 kinase activity (carriere2010:findings:015). Taken together, PKC activation should raise mTORC1 activity through a PKC→Raf→ERK→Raptor route that requires the ERK sites on Raptor.
hypotheses.prediction: Activating PKC should increase Raptor phosphorylation at the ERK sites and raise mTORC1 output (4E-BP1 Thr37/46 and S6K1 phosphorylation; in vitro mTOR kinase activity toward GST-4E-BP1). Pharmacological PKC inhibition or PKC knockdown should block this increase. MEK inhibition or the Raptor S3A mutant should abolish PKC-induced mTORC1 activation, whereas mTORC1 activation by a non-PKC stimulus should be unaffected by PKC inhibition.
hypotheses.test: In cultured HEK293 cells, express constitutively active PKC or activate endogenous PKC, with or without a selective PKC inhibitor or PKC siRNA, and in cells expressing wild-type versus S3A Raptor, with or without a MEK1/2 inhibitor. Then measure phospho-ERK, Raptor phosphorylation, and phospho-4E-BP1/phospho-S6K1 by immunoblot, and immunoprecipitated mTORC1 kinase activity toward GST-4E-BP1 in vitro.

citations.title: Co-ordinated activation of classical and novel PKC isoforms is required for PMA-induced mTORC1 activation.
